questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is your diagnosis with respect to the findings shown in the peripheral smear given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B12 deficiency

The peripheral smear showing macro-ovalocytes and a hypersegmented neutrophil are suggestive of megaloblastic anaemia. Vitamin B12 deficiency is a cause of megaloblastic anaemia.

Peripheral smear findings in megaloblastic anaemia:

• Macro-ovalocytes
• Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.
• Reticulocyte count is low
• Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anaemia is severe
• Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, having five or more nuclear lobules

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids.

When the tissue sample goes through rapid freezing, it becomes firmer. The ice acts as an embedding media allowing the tissue to be sectioned.

The temperature range in the cryostat machine usually ranges from 0⁰C to -35⁰C. The majority of the tissue can be appropriately sectioned between -15⁰C to -25⁰C. Tissue samples that contain water can be sectioned at a higher temperature. The tissues that contain more fat will need to be cut at a lower temperature.

The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues. It is used in the following conditions:

• Fat emboli in lung tissue
• Renal cell carcinoma
• Sebaceous gland tumors of the skin
• Lipid-rich carcinomas

Fixatives containing alcohols, or routine processing with clearing, will remove lipids. Fixation can be achieved by the following methods:

• Physical methods - heating, microwaving, cryopreservation
• Chemical methods - immersion of specimen in fixative, perfusing vascular system with a fixative

Given below are a few fixatives with their uses:

Technique/Tissue
Fixative

Electron microscopy
Glutaraldehyde

Trephine biopsy-bone marrow
Zenker's fluid (AZF fixative)

GI biopsies
Bouin's fixative

Brain
Formalin ammonium chloride

Adrenal biopsy
Orth's fluid

Pap smear
Ethanol

The most commonly used fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following caspase binds to Cyt c and APAF-1 complex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Caspase 9

Caspase 9 binds to Cyt c and APAF-1 complex.

Apoptotic stimuli cause the release of cytochrome c into the cytosol. Cytochrome-C in turn binds to a protein called APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor-1) to form the apoptosome.

This complex is able to bind caspase-9, the critical initiator caspase of the mitochondrial pathway, and this step is responsible for the activation of other caspases.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following clotting factor deficiency will not affect clotting in vivo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Factor XII

Factor XII deficiency will not affect the clotting in vivo.

Unlike the clotting cascade in the lab (in vitro), the cascade in the body (in vivo) differs slightly - as tissue factor (TF) is the major initiator of the cascade. The TF/VIIa complex is the most important activator of factor IX and factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X. Factor V is involved in both the pathways as shown in the image below.

The coagulation cascade in the laboratory:

• Extrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube):  Tissue factor → Factor VII → Factor X.
• Intrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube): Factor XII →  Factor XI → Factor IX → Factor X

Laboratory methods to initiate clotting include:

• Intrinsic pathway - adding phospholipids, calcium, and either a negatively charged substance such as glass beads
• Extrinsic pathway - a source of tissue factor

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions will have the least chances of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follicular lymphoma

Follicular lymphoma is the least likely cause of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration.

Causes of dry tap are:

• Metastatic carcinoma infiltration
• Chronic myeloid leukemia
• Myelofibrosis
• Hairy cell leukemia
• Acute leukemia
• Hodgkin's lymphoma
• AML- M7

Causes of pancytopenia with cellular marrow are:

Primary disease of marrow-

• Myelodysplastic syndrome
• Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
• Myelofibrosis
• Aleukemic leukemia
• Myelophthisis
• Bone marrow lymphoma
• Hairy cell leukemia

Secondary to systemic disease-

• SLE, sarcoidosis
• B12, folate deficiency
• Copper deficiency
• Hypersplenism
• Alcohol
• HIV infection, TB
• Brucellosis, leishmaniasis

Note: Although marrow is hypercellular in CML, MDS etc., extensive marrow fibrosis (rare) has been proposed to account for a dry tap on bone marrow biopsy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Papanicolaou stain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Eosin B

Eosin B is not a component of Papanicolaou stain.

Papanicolaou stain is the most popular stain used in the practice of histopathology. It is a polychrome stain containing multiple dyes to stain the various components of cells differentially. Papanicolaou stain includes both acidic and basic dyes:

• Hematoxylin is a basic dye and it stains the nucleus.
• Orange G is an acidic counterstain and it stains matured and keratinized cells.
• Eosin A is the second counterstain and it is a polychrome mixture of Eosin Y and Light green SF.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Poor prognosis compared to classical HL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Poor prognosis compared to classical HL

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (NLPHL) has an excellent prognosis.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (NLPHL) is seen in young males <35 years. They present with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. The involved nodes have a nodular infiltrate of mainly small lymphocytes and macrophages, eosinophils, and plasma cells are scanty. It is not associated with EBV.

L&H variant of Reed-Sternberg (RS) cell that has multilobed nucleus resembling a popcorn kernel (popcorn cell) is seen. Immunophenotyping shows CD20 +, BCL6 +, CD15 -, CD30 -. It has an excellent prognosis.

The image shows the L&H variant of RS cell (popcorn cell) which is seen in NLPHL type of Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about stem cells?
options: They can divide without any regulatory stimulus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They can divide without any regulatory stimulus

Stem cells do not divide without any regulatory stimulus.

Stem cells give rise to all the various differentiated tissues. In adults, stem cells replace damaged cells and maintain tissue populations.

The properties of stem cells are:

• Self-renewal
• Asymmetric division - In which one daughter cell enters a differentiation pathway and gives rise to mature cells, while the other remains undifferentiated and retains its self-renewal capacity.

The types of stem cells are:

• Embryonic stem cells which are totipotent
• Adult stem cells present in stem cell niches

The pluripotency of stem cells is due to factors like:

• Oct3/4
• Klf 4
• Sox 2
• cMyc

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about celiac disease?
options: Most common cause of malnutrition in developing countries
Improves with food rich in carbohydrates
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased risk of GI lymphoma

Individuals with celiac disease have an increased risk of GI lymphoma.

Celiac disease is a common cause of diarrhea in developed countries. It is due to permanent sensitivity to gluten in susceptible individuals. It results in partial or total villous atrophy that can be seen on histopathological examination of biopsy samples. CECT is not a modality of diagnosis. The treatment is lifelong gluten free diet.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
options: Cells don't lyse in hypotonic solution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cells are spherical

G6PD deficiency has spherical red cells (Spherocytes).

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme that helps in the synthesis of NADPH. NADPH helps in keeping glutathione in a reduced state (GSH). This reduced glutathione acts as a defense against oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are exposed to oxidants. These cross-linking of the reactive sulphydryl groups in the globin chain of hemoglobin. These are then deposited as inclusions in RBC membranes as Heinz bodies. When these RBCs pass-through spleen, macrophages pluck out these membrane inclusions. The remaining cells are seen as bite cells. Less severely damaged cells lose a part of their membrane, forming spherocytes.

Spectrin is a part of the RBC membrane skeleton. It is commonly defective in hereditary spherocytosis.

Normal biconcave RBCs have a bit of an 'extra space'. They can accommodate a little fluid when exposed to a hypotonic solution. But spherocytes have already lost a part of its membrane, so are relatively full. Hence if they are placed in a hypotonic solution, they absorb more fluid and result in lysis of RBCs. This forms the basis of testing spherocytes in Hereditary spherocytosis or G6PD and is known as osmotic fragility testing.

On the other hand, placing RBCs in a hypertonic solution may cause them to lose water and shrink in size. But hardly any hemolysis takes place.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding liquid-based cytology?
options: Study of fluid in tumour microenvironment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urine specimen is used

Liquid-based cytology can also be done using a urine specimen. It is commonly used in cervical cancer screening in place of a pap smear.

The advantages of liquid-based cytology are:

• The process reduces obscuring inflammatory cells and mucous, blood, and debris
• The cells are deposited on the slide in a monolayer.
• Test sensitivity is improved compared with conventional pap tests.

Liquid-based cytology has found broad acceptance in non-gynecologic cytopreparation such as:

• Thyroid cyst fluid examination.
• Oral pathology: diagnostic for various types of oral lesions.
• This technique is also used to body fluids (e.g. urine, pleural effusions), brushing samples (e.g. gastrointestinal tract, lung), and fine needle aspiration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding Peutz Jeghers syndrome?

1. Arborizing pattern of smooth muscle
2. Loss of heterozygosity in the STK11 gene
3. Multiple GI polyps
4. Autosomal recessive
5. Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium is seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 3

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant, hereditary disorder characterized by multiple intestinal hamartomatous polyps having an arborizing pattern of smooth muscle. Germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 gene are present in approximately half of individuals with familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

It is also characterized by mucocutaneous dark blue to brown melanin pigmentation, which is particularly evident on the face, buccal mucosa, hands, feet, perianal and genital regions. This rare syndrome presents at a median age of 11 years.

The hamartomatous polyps seen in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are characterized by a branching network of smooth muscle fibers continuous with the muscularis mucosa that supports the glandular epithelium of the polyp.

Complications:

• Peutz-Jeghers polyps can cause intussusception, which is occasionally fatal.
• It is associated with a markedly increased risk of many malignant conditions. Lifetime risk is approximately 40% and regular surveillance is recommended from a very young age for sex cord tumors of the testes.
• During later life, there is a risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers.

Histologic image showing the characteristic arborizing network of connective tissue, smooth muscle, lamina propria, and glands lined by the normal-appearing intestinal epithelium.

Note: Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium is seen in Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), not Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy with fever, weight loss, fatigue, and petechia spots came to the hospital. On examination, he was pale and had hepatosplenomegaly as well as sternal tenderness. The clinical scenario described above is most commonly associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

The above described clinical features point towards the diagnosis of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.

ALL is more common in childhood. The child had symptoms related to depression of marrow function including pallor, weight loss due to anemia, and fever secondary to infections. These infections are due to neutropenia and generalized lymphadenopathy, indicating the effect of neoplastic infiltration.

The above image points show lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, scanty agranular cytoplasm which are characteristics of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Pearl PF0574: Morphological Characteristics of Blasts Cells in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia vs. Acute Myeloid Leukemia

Lymphoblasts
Myeloblasts

Blast population tends to be homogeneous
Blast population tends to be heterogeneous, with the exception of the undifferentiated form

Size is variable, mainly small
Size is variable, mainly large

Nucleus is central, mainly round; sometimes indented.

Nucleus tends to be eccentric, round, oval or angulated; sometimes convoluted, particularly in the form with a monocytic component

Chromatin is fine, with dispersed condensation
Very condensed in small lymphoblasts
Chromatin is fine, granular, delicately dispersed

Nucleoli absent in small lymphoblasts
Sometimes indistinct
Nucleoli almost always present, often large and prominent, double or triple

Cytoplasm is scanty, basophilic
Sometimes with a single long projection (‘hand-mirror cell’)
Cytoplasm is variable;
Abundant in monoblasts,
with protrusions in erythroblasts and megakaryoblasts

Granules are rarely present; Negative for peroxidase, esterases and toluidine blue
Granules present in forms with differentiation and positive with cytochemical stains

• Peroxidase in the neutrophil and esoinophil lineages
• Nonspecific esterase in the monocyte lineage

Auer rods are absent
Auer rods can be present;
Typically present in the hypergranular promyelocytic form

Vacuoles can be present
Vacuoles can be present;
Almost always present in forms with a monocytic component

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy was brought to the emergency with contact dermatitis . Which of the following cells is involved in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Helper T cells

Based on the given clinical scenario, the boy had developed Type IV hypersensitivity. T helper cells are involved in type IV hypersensitivity. It is due to the cell-mediated response.

Type IV or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction: These reactions are induced by sensitized T cells which in contact with the specific antigen releases cytokines that produce biological effects on leucocytes, macrophages, and tissue cells.

Condition
Examples/ Synonyms
Description

Exogenous eczemas: external factors predispose to eczema

Allergic contact dermatitis
Nickel dermatitis, Bindi dermatitis
Delayed type of hypersensitivity reaction to a previously sensitized allergen

Irritant contact dermatitis
Wear and tear dermatitis, Housewives eczema
Cutaneous response to the physical/toxic effects of a range of environmental exposures.

Endogenous eczemas: Internal constitutional factors predispose to eczema

Asteatotic dermatitis
Winter eczema/Eczéma craquelé
‘Crazy paving’ pattern on legs due to dry skin, flares in winter

Atopic dermatitis
Eczema infantum, eczema flexurarum, Hay fever eczema, asthmatic eczema
Itchy, chronic relapsing condition that often starts in early childhood (<2 years) with erythema, papules/ papulovesicles, excoriation and lichenification in flexural distribution

Nummular dermatitis
Discoid eczema
Circular or oval plaques of eczema with a clearly demarcated edge

Seborrheic dermatitis

• Dandruff/ Sebo-psoriasis/ Pityriasis capitis/ Pityrosporal dermatitis
• Cradle cap

Erythematous patches with superficial scaling, affecting areas with a high density of sebaceous glands- scalp, face, central chest, and anogenital areas

Pearl PF0794: Examples of Type IV Hypersensitivity

Tuberculin reaction

Lepromin test

Multiple sclerosis

Chronic graft rejection

Contact dermatitis

Sarcoidosis

Primary biliary cirrhosis

Type I lepra reaction

Crohn’s disease

Psoriasis

Image- Mechanisms of T-cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reactions. A, CD4+ TH1 cells respond to tissue antigens by secreting cytokines that stimulate inflammation and activate phagocytes, leading to tissue injury. CD4+ TH17 cells contribute to inflammation by recruiting neutrophils. B, In some diseases, CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) directly kill tissue cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents with the development of seizures for which a CT-guided biopsy was done. The histopathology showed the presence of ‘psammoma bodies’. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meningioma

The clinical vignette and the histopathology showing a tumor with meningothelial whorls, syncytial cells with indistinct cell membranes, and psammoma bodies suggest the diagnosis of meningioma.

Meningioma: They are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid.

* Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

* Prior radiation therapy to the head and neck, typically is a risk factor.

* The most common cytogenetic abnormality is the loss of chromosome 22, especially the long arm (22q).

* Meningiomas are a common lesion in the setting of NF2 (multiple sites, especially in association with acoustic neuromas or glial tumors.

* The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated.

* They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura. This form is commonly associated with hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone.

* The lesions may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies.

Histological subtypes:

* WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic

* WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical

* Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic

* Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth

* Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma

* Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen

* Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

* Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered.

* Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man has been diagnosed with solid cancer of the bowel. He also experienced massive proteinuria a few months after the initial diagnosis of cancer. What do you think is the likely cause of the development of urinary findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Membranous nephropathy

Secondary Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in patients suffering from cancer and other systemic diseases.

Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in older adults, with a peak incidence in 30–50 years and a male: female ratio of 2:1.

It is a form of chronic immune-complex-mediated disease.

It can be primary (75% of cases) or secondary (associated with systemic diseases/identifiable etiologic agents).

Microscopy:

* Light microscopy: diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall without cellular proliferation. Irregular spikes projecting from the basement membrane are best seen with silver stains.

* Immunofluorescence microscopy: granular deposits containing Ig and complement along the glomerular basement membrane

* Electron micrograph: electron-dense subepithelial deposits (epimembranous spikes) and effacement of foot processes of podocytes

Image: The silver stain of the glomerulus highlights the proteinaceous basement membranes in black. There are characteristic "spikes" of the basement membrane between the immune deposits of membranous nephropathy. The black basement membrane material shown here appears as projections in the capillary loops.

The above image is characteristic of membranous nephropathy. The given hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained image shows uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall (intense pink color).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old male underwent bone marrow examination which revealed the presence of the following findings as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Multiple myeloma

The image shows a Mott Cell containing multiple immunoglobulin globules in grapelike cytoplasmic droplets. Mott Cells are seen in Multiple Myeloma.

* Multiple myelomas: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* The disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man was admitted to the emergency ward with severe, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the left arm and profuse sweating. ECG showed ST-segment elevation in precordial leads. The person succumbed after 3 hours. During the autopsy, his heart was taken out and immersed in a solution. The normal area of the heart turned brick red whereas the infarcted portion turned white. Which of the following can be the likely component of the solution?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain imparts a brick red color to the intact non-infarcted myocardium whereas the infarcted portion appears white.

* Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

* This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved.

* Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presented with a midline swelling in the neck and weight loss. The consulting physician decided to go in for a thyroid biopsy. Biopsy revealed the presence of ‘Orphan Annie eye nuclei’. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Papillary thyroid carcinoma

The clinical scenario of midline swelling, weight loss and the presence of empty appearing nuclei, also called Orphan Annie eye nuclei in the biopsy is diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

Microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma:

* The carcinoma shows branching papillae with fibrovascular stalk covered with simple or stratified cuboidal epithelium.

* At high power, the nuclei appear optically clear or empty as the chromatin is dispersed. These empty appearing nuclei are called Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

* Concentric calcified structures called psammoma bodies are usually seen.

* Foci of lymphatic invasion by the tumor are usually present.

Note :

The presence of Orphan Annie-eye nuclei or psammoma bodies is diagnostic of papillary thyroid cancer, regardless of the presence of papillary architecture.

The image below shows papillary thyroid carcinoma with characteristic orphan Annie eye nuclei:

The image below shows psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Among the following, which molecule is required for the presentation of the antigens by the APCs to TH2 cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MHC

Class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules are mainly expressed on cells that present ingested antigens and respond to T-cells (macrophages, B lymphocytes, and dendritic cells). The function of MHC molecules is to display fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells.

In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens (HLA) because they were initially detected on leukocytes by the binding of antibodies. The genes encoding HLA molecules are clustered on a small segment of chromosome 6.

The HLA system is highly polymorphic, meaning that there are many alleles of MHC genes (in the thousands) in humans and each individual’s HLA alleles differ from those inherited by most other individuals in the population. This, as we see subsequently, constitutes a formidable barrier in organ transplantation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Arsenic

Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with arsenic, thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.

Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm. There is equal gender predilection. The tumor may occur at any site, but most often involves skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Macrophages play an important role in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation. Which of the following cells perform the same function in the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages located in the liver that form part of the mononuclear phagocyte system. These are present, lining the walls of the sinusoids, not the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse).

Macrophages can be divided into:

* Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.

* Tissue macrophages survive for months.

2 main functions of macrophages:

* Phagocytosis.

* Antigen presentation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Revised A 70-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain, fatigue, and headaches for the last few weeks. On examination, he has pallor and bony tenderness. Lab investigations revealed an increased ESR and his skull radiograph revealed several punched-out lytic lesions. Which of the following is the best investigation for this patient in the options given below ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum electrophoresis showing IgG

The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma and in the given options,  serum electrophoresis showing M band in the gamma globulin region is preferred for multiple myeloma.

Bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic for multiple myeloma, where the neoplastic plasma cells can be seen.

Plasma cell dyscrasias are B-cell proliferations that contain neoplastic plasma cells that secrete a monoclonal Ig or Ig fragment.

* Multiple myelomas: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* The disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma

• Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.

• Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.

• Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma

• Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.

• Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases

• Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).

• Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

POEMS syndrome- Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal gammopathy, Skin changes.

TEMPI syndrome

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the mode of inheritance in a patient suffering from color blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. XLR

The pattern of inheritance in a patient with color blindness is an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance.

Clues for diagnosis of the pattern of inheritance as X linked recessive:

* Males are affected and females are carriers.

* No male-to-male transmission. Females transmit the disease.

* Females transmit the mutated gene to 50% of the males.

* Affected males have carrier daughters and unaffected sons.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the immortality of the cancer cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Telomerase

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres.

With every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence.

Telomerase is present in some cells, like the germ cells, and absent in most somatic cells.

Reactivation of telomerase is a critical step in the development of about 85% of human cancers, which enables the cells to divide several times than normal.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Barrett’s esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intestinal metaplasia

Barrett's esophagus is characterized by intestinal metaplasia within the esophageal squamous mucosa. It increases the risk of adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.

Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it is estimated to occur in as many as 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD.

Microscopically, it is seen as the replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells.

The greatest concern in Barrett's esophagus is that it confers an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Traditionally, Barrett's esophagus has been treated with esophagectomy, but it was associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an endoscopic treatment for Barrett's esophagus and studies suggest that it is highly effective at removing Barrett's mucosa and associated dysplasia. RFA is performed with the Barrx FLEX system.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy was brought by his parents with concerns about being increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye. As further workup reveals a tumor, the eye is enucleated and the microscopic appearance is as shown in the image. Molecular analysis of the tumor indicates loss of cell cycle control in the tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinoblastoma

The clinical vignette along with the histopathological image showing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes is suggestive of Retinoblastoma.

* Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes and fleurettes reflecting photoreceptor differentiation are seen in retinoblastomas.

* Rosettes consist of a halo or spoke-wheel arrangement of cells surrounding a central core or hub.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-man presents with nosebleeds, bleeding gums and multiple ecchymoses. Lab investigations show Hb: 8.5, Platelet count: 12, 000 and Total leucocyte count: 52,000 with 83% blasts as seen below. The blasts are CD33+. The most likely diagnosis is ______
options: Chronic Lymphocytic leukemia / Small Lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

The morphology of blasts with abundant cytoplasm, fine azurophilic granules and Auer rods, delicate nuclear chromatin with 1-4 prominent nucleoli on peripheral smear and CD33 positivity suggest a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The 2016 WHO classification of acute myeloid leukemia (AML):

* AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities

* AML with myelodysplasia-related changes

* Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms

* AML, not otherwise specified

* Myeloid sarcoma

* Myeloid proliferations of Down syndrome

AML is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. It occurs at all ages, but the incidence rises throughout life, peaking after 60 years of age. Occasionally, blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukemic leukemia). Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukemia in pancytopenic patients

Pearl PF1317: WHO classification of Acute Myeloid Leukemia

The WHO system divides acute myeloid leukemia (AML) into several groups:

AML with certain genetic abnormalities (gene or chromosome changes)

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 8 and 21 [t(8;21)]

* AML with a translocation or inversion in chromosome 16 [t(16;16) or inv(16)]

* APL with the PML-RARA fusion gene

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 11 [t(9;11)]

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 6 and 9 [t(6:9)]

* AML with a translocation or inversion in chromosome 3 [t(3;3) or inv(3)]

* AML (megakaryoblastic) with a translocation between chromosomes 1 and 22 [t(1:22)]

* AML with the BCR-ABL1 (BCR-ABL) fusion gene*

* AML with mutated NPM1 gene

* AML with biallelic mutations of the CEBPA gene (that is, mutations in both copies of the gene)

* AML with mutated RUNX1 gene*

*This is still a "provisional entity," meaning it is not yet clear if there's enough evidence that it is a unique group.

AML with myelodysplasia-related changes

AML related to previous chemotherapy or radiation

AML not otherwise specified (This includes cases of AML that do not fall into one of the above groups and is similar to the FAB classification.)

* AML with minimal differentiation (FAB M0)

* AML without maturation (FAB M1)

* AML with maturation (FAB M2)

* Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (FAB M4)

* Acute monoblastic/monocytic leukemia (FAB M5)

* Pure erythroid leukemia (FAB M6)

* Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (FAB M7)

* Acute basophilic leukemia

* Acute panmyelosis with fibrosis

Myeloid sarcoma (also known as granulocytic sarcoma or chloroma)

Myeloid proliferations related to Down syndrome

Undifferentiated and biphenotypic acute leukemias are not strictly AML, but are leukemias that have both lymphocytic and myeloid features. They are sometimes called mixed phenotype acute leukemias (MPALs).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with weight loss, fever, and a painless swelling in the area of his jaw. CBC reveals anemia and lymphocytosis. Biopsy findings from the swelling are seen in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt lymphoma

The clinical presentation and biopsy findings point to a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma.

The biopsy image shows tumor cells with multiple small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm and high mitotic index closely apposed to each other forming a dark blue background (the "sky"). These cells have a high turnover rate. The macrophages get stuffed in between along with cellular debris which are called tingible body macrophages. Upon fixation, the cytoplasm washes away leaving behind white spaces filled with debris ( the "stars"). This produces a starry sky appearance, which is classical of Burkitt lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma:

* Most common NHL in children <15 years

* Associated with translocation of MYC gene of chromosome 8 (Option A)

* Translocations: t (8;14), t (2;8), t (8,22)

* Three distinct clinical forms:

* Endemic: affects children in Africa, affects jaw, maxilla and is EBV-associated (Option B)

* Sporadic: in adults in western countries

* Immunodeficiency associated: HIV infection

* It is the most rapidly proliferating human tumor, Ki-67 stains for 100% of cells (DLBCL- 40% staining with Ki-67)

Histology: Starry sky pattern

Immunophenotype: These tumours originate from mature B cells. Their phenotype, consistent with germinal center B-cell origin, is marked by expression of CD10, BCL6, CD19, CD20, and surface IgM.

*

* Germinal center-associated markers- BCL-6 and CD10

* HLA-DR and CD43.

* CD21 shows variable expression with the tumour:

* In endemic Burkitt lymphoma, the tumours are EBV-positive with CD21 positivity.

* Non-endemic Burkitt lymphoma occurring in immunocompetent patients is usually EBV-negative, without CD21 positivity.

Note: Although in most cases BCL2 is negative, it can be positive. The expression of BCL2 does not exclude a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma. Hence, this is the most appropriate answer in the MCQ.

Treatment: Begins within 48h of diagnosis in both children and adults with the use of an intensive combination of chemotherapy regimens with high doses of cyclophosphamide and CNS prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient presented with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral smear showed teardrop cells, nucleated RBCs, and giant abnormal platelets and bone marrow biopsy is given below. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary myelofibrosis

The image shows the deposition of numerous collagen fibers in the bone marrow, which indicates marrow fibrosis. The biopsy image along with the clinical and peripheral smear findings are diagnostic of primary myelofibrosis.

In this condition, the neoplastic proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells results in increased and abnormal proliferation of the megakaryocytes. These megakaryocytes release excessive amounts of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and TGF-β. Increased growth factors lead to the deposition of collagen in the bone marrow which eventually leads to fibrosis.

Common clinical features are

* Anemia- occurs as a result of decreased RBC production

* Hepatosplenomegaly- The stem cells may escape from the marrow and get lodged in the liver and spleen. This leads to extramedullary hematopoiesis.

* Peripheral smear findings:

* myeloproliferation will result in thrombocytosis, with large and abnormal platelets, leukocytosis

* marrow fibrosis will result in the teardrop-shaped RBCs and leukoerythroblastosis (premature release of nucleated erythroid and early granulocyte cells into the blood).

* Bone marrow appears hypercellular in the early course with increased cells of all the lineages. As the disease progresses, the marrow becomes hypocellular and fibrotic.

The FDA recently approved FEDRATINIB,  a JAK2-selective inhibitor for the treatment of adult patients with intermediate or high-risk primary or secondary myelofibrosis.

Note:

Dacrocytes, also known as teardrop cells, are tear drop shaped cells observed in the following conditions:

* Myelofibrosis

* Myelodysplastic syndromes

* Hemolytic anemia

* Thalessemias

* Severe iron deficiency

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive pallor and abdominal distention. On investigations, hepatosplenomegaly and malar eminence is seen and his peripheral blood smear is as shown below. He has low Hb, Mentzer index is found to be less than 13. What diagnosis would this signify in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thalassemia

The clinical scenario, peripheral blood smear showing target cells and aniso-poikilocytes, along with the Mentzer index of less than 13 suggests Thalassemia.

Thalassemia syndromes:

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival. Disease severity is inversely correlated with the number of functioning globin chains.

Clinical features in thalassemia:

* Anemia

* Jaundice and pigment gallstones

* Skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, osteopenia/osteoporosis

* Iron overload

* Growth impairment

* Hepatosplenomegaly

* Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus

* Heart failure and arrhythmias

Laboratory studies:

* Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases. These findings are non-specific.

* High RBC count

* Low reticulocyte count

* High LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coomb's test

* High transferrin saturation, normal serum iron levels, elevated ferritin levels

MCV/RBC count also known as Mentzer index can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio.

Mentzer index is:

* More than 13 in iron-deficiency anemia

* Less than 13 in thalassemia

Thalassemia syndromes and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) are the two most common etiologies of microcytic hypochromic anemia in children and adults. The reference standard to diagnose IDA is serum ferritin level. Since it is expensive and not widely available, an inexpensive & simpler way of evaluation is the Mentzer index.

Pearl PF0864: Thalassemia syndromes

Normally each individual carries 4 functional alpha chain genes and 2 functional beta chain genes. Alpha and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively.

* Alpha thalassemia: Gene deletion is the most common cause of reduced α-chain synthesis.

* Beta +- thalassemia: The most common cause is splicing mutation.

* Beta 0- thalassemia: Chain terminator mutations are the most common cause.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A teenager developed swelling of the face, lips, and tongue and also found it difficult to breathe within a few minutes of consumption of prawns. What is the type of hypersensitivity seen here ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 1

Anaphylaxis following consumption of prawns is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or Type 1 hypersensitivity.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.

* These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils.

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Graft from identical twin is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isograft

A graft from an identical twin is called isograft.

Isograft is defined as an organ or tissue that is taken from an individual (donor) and is placed on another individual (recipient) who has the same genetic constitution as of the donor. Example, graft between identical twins.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The body of an 82-year-old man has been seen for post-mortem to know the cause of death. You are examining a histopathological slide containing a section of his cardiac tissue where you notice some pigmentation. Which is the substance that is seen in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lipofuscin

Lipochrome or Lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment in the histopathological image which can be seen in the liver and heart of normal aging patients.

It is also known as a wear-and-tear pigment, which is an insoluble, brownish yellow, granular intracellular material, that accumulates in various tissues like the heart, liver, and brain as a function of age. The brown pigment in large amounts can give a characteristic appearance to the tissue called brown atrophy.

Lipofuscin (brown lipid):

* Derived through lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated lipids of subcellular membranes.

* Not injurious to the cell or its functions.

* Indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation.

* Seen in cells undergoing slow, regressive changes.

* Prominent in the liver and heart of aging patients, patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia.

Other options:

Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived, golden yellow to brown, granular or crystalline pigment. It is one of the major storage forms of iron and can be seen in iron-overload states like hemochromatosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The cell shown below has it's origin from what type of cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B cells

The image shows a Reed Sternberg cell and it is seen classically in Hodgkin's Lymphoma which is of B cell origin.

In classical Hodgkin's lymphoma , activation of the transcription factor NF-κB occurs. NF-κB may be activated by Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) infection. EBV+ tumor cells express latent membrane protein-1 (LMP-1), a protein encoded by the EBV genome that transmits signals that upregulate NF-κB. Activation of NF-κB may occur in EBV tumors as a result of the acquired loss-of-function mutations in TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3). Activation of NF-κB by EBV or other mechanisms rescues “crippled” germinal center B cells that cannot express Igs from apoptosis, eventually leading to the formation of Reed–Sternberg cells.

Reed Sternberg cell: It is a giant cell. It has a classic owl-eyed appearance due to the presence of a symmetric or mirror image bilobed nucleus with prominent nucleoli surrounded by a clear space.

Reed Sternberg cells are not diagnostic for any condition since they are seen in many conditions such as:

* Hodgkin’s lymphoma

* Non Hodgkin’s lymphoma (commonly in immunoblastic type)

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Sarcomas

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman was diagnosed with a large tumor in the right ovary and histopathology shows it has origin from all three germ layers. Which of the following is the most likely tumor she is having?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Teratoma

A cyst with all three germ layers is most likely to be a teratoma, also called a dermoid cyst(mature cystic).

Teratomas arise from pluripotent stem cells that differentiate into any of three germ layers forming tissues of all three germ layers.

A dermoid cyst is the most common germ cell tumor. It is also the most common benign tumor of the ovary in the reproductive age group and in pregnancy. It is bilateral in 10-15% of cases.

A dermoid cyst is derived from all three germ cell layers, but ectodermal derivatives are most common. Rokitansky’s protuberance is the most common site for the development of malignancy. It is seen as a projection covered by skin, sebaceous glands, sweat glands, teeth, and bones. Sometimes thyroid tissue can be seen on histopathological examination, known as struma ovarii.

The image below shows a dermoid cyst with Rokitansky protuberance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year-old female patient presented with malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and multiple joint pain. She has no relevant past history and does not take any medication. On further investigations, thrombocytopenia was seen and the Anti-Sm antibody was positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Systemic Lupus Erythematous

The clinical scenario along with Anti-Sm antibody positivity is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

SLE is an autoimmune disease that mostly affects women of reproductive age. It is characterized by the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes that cause widespread systemic damage.

Diagnosis of SLE requires at least four of the following categories:

Clinical features:

* Skin:

* acute, subacute cutaneous manifestations (photosensitivity, malar or maculopapular rash)

* chronic cutaneous manifestations (discoid lupus, panniculitis, lichen planus like)

* Oral or nasal ulcers

* Nonscarring alopecia

* Synovitis involving 2 or more joints

* Serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis)

* Renal:

* Protein/Creatinine ratio of more than 0.5

* RBC casts

* Biopsy

* Neurologic: seizures, psychosis, myelitis, neuropathy, confusional state

* Hemolytic anemia

* Leukopenia/lymphopenia

* Thrombocytopenia

Immunological manifestations:

* Antinuclear antibodies > reference value

* Anti-dsDNA > reference value

* Anti Smith antibody

* Antiphospholipid antibody (lupus anticoagulant, false-positive rapid plasma reagin)

* Low serum complement

* Positive direct Coombs' test in absence of hemolytic anemia.

Four criteria with one in each category must be positive for it to qualify as a diagnosis of SLE. However, if a renal biopsy is suggestive of lupus nephritis and lupus autoantibodies are positive then four criteria are not required.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year-old male was brought to the emergency department after suffering severe injuries in a motorcycle accident. His blood pressure was 80/60 mm Hg. Ultrasound examination revealed a ruptured spleen. Arterial blood gas analysis was suggestive of metabolic acidosis. The patient most likely suffered from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypovolemic shock

The patient most likely suffered from a hypovolemic shock, due to an internal hemorrhage caused by the ruptured spleen.

The hypovolemic shock caused due to a significant decrease in blood or plasma volume, caused by the loss of fluid from the vascular compartment. Hemorrhage, fluid loss from severe burns, diarrhea, excessive urine formation, perspiration, and trauma are some of the major mechanisms of fluid loss that can lead to hypovolemic shock.

Other options:

Option a: Cardiogenic shock is caused due to the failure of the myocardial pump.

Option b: Septic shock is not likely in this clinical scenario, as there is no evidence of any infection.

Option d: Neurogenic shock occurs in response to traumatic spinal cord injuries, which is not seen in this case.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? * Anemia * Total leucocyte count - 1,50,000/microL * Peripheral blood smear - * 60% neutrophils- 6% * Basophils- 4% * Eosinophils * Myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes * Myeloid to erythroid ratio- 18:1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CML

The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

* Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism

* Fatigability, weakness

* Weight loss and anorexia

* Splenomegaly, or left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction

The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.

* Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

* Hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors.

* Increased eosinophils and basophils.

* Increased megakaryocytes and usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers.

* Sea-blue histiocytes are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm.

The image given below shows the peripheral smear in CML showing a garden party or college girl appearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distention, shortness of breath, and swelling of the ankles over the past 3 months. Physical examination reveals a large pelvic mass, and pitting edema in the lower extremities. CT scan shows a solid right ovarian mass, significant ascites, and right-sided pleural effusion. After surgical removal of the mass, both the ascites and pleural effusion resolve completely, and the ankle swelling subsides. Histopathology confirms a benign ovarian fibroma. What is the mode of inheritance of this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No inheritance pattern (non-hereditary)

The clinical vignette describes Meig's syndrome, it is an acquired disorder without genetic association.

Meigs syndrome triad:

* Ovarian fibroma

* Pleural effusion

* Ascites that disappear after removal of the tumor

Meigs syndrome is mostly caused by ovarian fibroma. CA-125 levels may also be elevated. As it is a diagnosis of exclusion, a workup should be done to rule out malignancy. Exploratory laparotomy with surgical staging is the treatment of choice. Conservative surgery (salpingo-oophorectomy) is done. The clinical features resolve on resection of the fibroma.

Pseudo-Meigs syndrome presents with ascites and pleural effusion in association with benign ovarian tumors such as teratoma, struma ovarii, mucinous cystadenoma, etc.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 48-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling. Investigations for testicular tumours revealed that LDH was raised but AFP was within normal limits. Following orchidectomy, the following histological picture was observed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Seminoma

The clinical scenario, high LDH with normal AFP levels, and the given histology picture showing fried egg appearance are highly suggestive of testicular seminoma.

In yolk sac tumors and embryonal carcinoma, AFP is elevated whereas in teratoma LDH is normal.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumour. It is common in men between 20-40 years of age.

The patients usually present with a painless testicular lump. If a testicular tumour is suspected, blood samples are taken from the patient for the evaluation of the tumour markers (hCG, LDH, and AFP), and a high inguinal orchidectomy is performed for diagnosis.

Further treatment of seminoma depends on the stage of the tumor. Stage I tumors, whose levels of tumor markers decline after orchidectomy may not require further treatment. Stage II-IV tumors require radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The chemotherapeutic agents used are bleomycin, etoposide, and platin-based agents (BEP).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A middle-aged man working in sandblasting developed hemoptysis, and a productive cough. Chest X-ray is suggestive of tuberculosis. Which of the following is associated with the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is associated with tuberculosis.

Silicosis occurs in industries such as sandblasting, pottery and ceramics, mining, and construction. Silicosis patients are prone to developing tuberculosis, in a condition called silico-tuberculosis.

Silica causes pulmonary alveolar macrophage dysfunction and hence, patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing lung infections from organisms like M. Tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, and fungi.

Radiographic imaging of silicotuberculosis shows cavitation.

In silicotuberculosis: it is still unclear whether silico-tuberculotics are really tubercular or purely silicosis, because

* Sputum is rarely AFB+ve

* Children and women of silicotuberculosis patients do not develop tuberculosis

* The post-mortem on silicotuberculosis fail to prove the existence of tuberculosis disease

* Radiological evidence of both the condition is similar

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient who underwent surgery for a lipoma 5 weeks back, now presents with a scar at the incision site that is limited to the original wound boundaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypertrophic scar

The given clinical vignette is of a hypertrophic scar as it stays within the confines of the original wound. Hypertrophic scars rise above the skin level but stay within the confines of the original wound and often regress over time.

Accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair may give rise to hypertrophic scar or keloid. The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen→ raised scars known as a hypertrophic scars. If the scar tissue grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and does not regress → keloid formation. Formation of excessive amounts of granulation tissue, which protrudes above the level of the surrounding skin and blocks re-epithelialization → Exuberant granulation

Inadequate formation of granulation tissue or formation of a scar → wound dehiscence and ulceration. The contraction in the size of a wound is an important part of the normal healing process. An exaggeration of this process gives rise to contractures, which are particularly prone to develop on the palms, the soles, and the anterior aspect of the thorax and are commonly seen after serious burns.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A person was bought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin? IgA- Immunoglobulin A IgE- Immunoglobulin E IgM- Immunoglobulin M IgG- Immunoglobulin G
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE

The given clinical features suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE)

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity is also called allergic reactions or allergies

It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals. Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells by binding to the Fcεg receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines. The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

It occurs in two phases:

* Immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm (in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen and subside in a few hours.

* Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells leading to mucosal epithelial cell damage and tissue destruction. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and may last for several days.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever for the past 2 months. General examination showed pallor and the systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level- 3 gm/dl, TLC- 1500/microL, platelet count- 15000/microL. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte count is 0.5. Bone marrow examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but no immature cells. What is the likely diagnosis? Hb- Hemoglobin TLC- Total leucocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia

The given clinical scenario showing a young male with gum bleeding, fever, pancytopenia, and a low reticulocyte count with bone marrow showing fatty streaks and no immature cells is suggestive of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia.

Aplastic anemia is a syndrome characterized by chronic hematopoietic failure and pancytopenia. The common causes include:

* Acquired

* Idiopathic (most common cause, about 65% of the cases)

* Acquired stem-cell defects

* Immune-mediated

* Chemical agents

* Dose-related (alkylating agents, antimetabolites, benzene, chloramphenicol, inorganic arsenals)

* Idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, organic arsenicals, carbamazepine, penicillamine, gold salts)

* Physical agents

* Whole-body irradiation

* Viral infections (hepatitis, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Varicella-Zoster virus)

* Inherited

* Fanconi anemia

* Telomerase defects

Pathogenesis involves an extrinsic immune-mediated suppression of bone marrow and an intrinsic abnormality of the stem cells.

Clinical features and diagnosis:

There is no age or sex predisposition for aplastic anemia. It presents insidiously with features of pancytopenia such as pallor, petechiae, and ecchymosis. Recurrent infections and fever occur as a result of neutropenia. Reticulocytopenia is seen and splenomegaly is characteristically absent. Bone marrow biopsy is used for diagnosis.

Histology:

Bone marrow aspirate usually results in a dry tap. Examination shows a hypocellular marrow devoid of hematopoietic cells with remnant fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes. Red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. The following image shows a hypocellular bone marrow with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells.

Other options:

Option B - Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. Red cells deficient in these proteins are susceptible to intravascular hemolysis. Patients with PNH usually present with pancytopenia and reticulocytosis with bone marrow biopsy showing a cellular marrow with marked to massive erythroid hyperplasia.

Option C - Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal stem cell disorders. It is a consequence of maturation defects that result in ineffective hematopoiesis with a high predisposition to conversion to AML. They are characterized by a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic cells on bone marrow aspirate. Marrow changes seen in MDS are given in the pearl below.

Option D - Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

Pearl PF0598: Marrow Changes in Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)

The myelodysplastic syndrome can lead to dysplasia of the erythroid series, myeloid series, and megakaryocytes.

Dysplasia of erythroid series appears as

* Ring sideroblasts- Erythroblasts with stainable iron in the cytoplasm

* Megaloblastoid maturation- Abnormally large erythroid cells

* Nuclear budding abnormalities- Nucleus with abnormal shape

Dysplasia of myeloid series

* Neutrophils with a decreased number of secondary granules

* Pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells- neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes

Dysplasia of the megakaryocytes-

* Megakaryocyte with single nuclear lobe

* Pawn ball megakaryocytes- cells with multiple separate nuclei

If only one lineage is affected, then it is called single lineage dysplasia. If multiple lineages are affected, then it is called multilineage dysplasia. If the percentage of ring sideroblasts is more than 15% it is called MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During wound healing, the cells that appear first due to chemotaxis , at the site of the wound is ____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neutrophils

The earliest cells to appear because of chemotaxis are Neutrophils.

Neutrophils appear within 24 hours but the neutrophil peak is seen on day 2 of the inflammatory phase of wound healing.

Wound healing :

Wound healing occurs in two distinct mechanisms -

* Wound healing by first intention / Primary union

* Wound healing by secondary intention / Secondary union

Primary union / Wound healing by the first intention:

This is seen in cases where there is an injury that involves the epithelial layer only. An example of such healing is seen in a clean surgical incision approximated by sutures. The steps involved in primary union are as follows.

* Injury causes the activation of the coagulation cascade and subsequent clot formation. This clot attracts growth factors, cytokines, chemokines, and migrating cells.

* Within the first 24 hours, the neutrophils migrate to the site of injury. Within 24-48 hours, even epithelial cells from both edges of the wound begin to migrate and form a thin layer of epidermis over the wound.

* By day 3 neutrophils are mainly replaced by macrophages and granulation tissue starts forming. This process of neovascularisation reaches its peak on day 5.

* Deposition of collagen and fibroblast proliferation is seen in the second week. By the end of the first month, the scar comprises a cellular connective tissue largely devoid of inflammatory cells and covered by an essentially normal epidermis.

Secondary union / Wound healing by second intention :

Wounds heal by secondary intention when the wound is large involving a more significant loss of cells and tissues. It differs from primary healing in various ways such as:

* Since the wound is large, the blood clot formed is large. This leads to increased inflammation and increased formation of granulation tissue.

* The provisional matrix has fibrin, plasma fibronectin, and type III collagen. In two weeks it is replaced by type I collagen. By the end of 1 month, the scar tissue is mainly made of acellular connective tissue.

* Myofibroblasts present in the connective tissue cause wound contraction.

Note:

However,the cells that appear first at the site of an injury are Platelets, as a part of initially activated coagulation pathways.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the gene mutation seen in hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HFE

Mutation in the HFE gene on the short arm of the 6th chromosome is seen in hemochromatosis.

Hemochromatosis is an inherited genetic disorder. Mutation of the HFE gene leads to excessive absorption of iron which gets deposited in the liver, pancreas, followed by the heart, joints, and endocrine organs. Histopathology shows golden yellow hemosiderin granules in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes which stain positive with Prussian blue stain. Serum iron is raised. Serum ferritin is significantly increased.

Hepatomegaly will be present in the majority of the patients with symptoms. Skin shows bronze pigmentation due to the increased deposition of iron and melanin over the dermis. Glucose levels are deranged or diabetes mellitus is seen due to the direct damage of the pancreatic islet cells by the deposition of iron.

Congestive cardiac failure is the most common cardiac manifestation of hemochromatosis. Features of cardiac failure will develop suddenly, get rapidly progressed, and if left untreated it may cause death. Hypogonadism due to failure of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis by deposition of iron. This may manifest as testicular atrophy or amenorrhea

It is managed by weekly or twice weekly phlebotomy of 500 mL. Chelating agents like subcutaneous deferoxamine, and oral deferasirox are effective. The main cause of death in hemochromatosis is cardiac failure.

Other options:

Option B: PTEN is a tumor suppressor gene. Mutation of this gene is associated with Cowden syndrome that leads to multiple cancers like breast cancer, prostate cancer, endometrial cancer, and colorectal cancer.

Option C: ATP7B gene mutation causes Wilson's disease which is an autosomal recessive disorder.

Option D: MRP2 protein is associated with Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which amongst the following molecules helps in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Selectins

Of the above options, selectins help in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation.

The two major families of molecules involved in leukocyte adhesion and migration are the selectins and integrins. The initial rolling interactions are mediated by a family of proteins called selectins. These are low-affinity interactions with a fast off-rate, and they are easily disrupted by the flowing blood.

There are three types of selectins:

* L-selectin on leukocytes - CD62L

* E-selectin on endothelium - CD62E

* P-selectin in platelets - CD62P

The expression of selectins and their ligands is regulated by cytokines produced in response to infection and injury.

The recruitment of leukocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process, that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases:

* In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs.

* Migration of the leukocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall

* Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus.

The process of leukocyte recruitment is as follows:

* Margination: Because of dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow and hence more leukocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leukocyte redistribution is called margination.

* Rolling: the slowed leukocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall.

* Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: the attachment of leukocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands.

* Adhesions: the weak rolling interactions slow down the leukocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leukocytes and activate them. This is turn converts the ligands for β1 and β2 integrins, VLA-4 and LFA-1 present on the leukocytes to a high-affinity state.

* This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leukocytes leads to firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation.

* Leukocyte migration: this is the movement of leukocytes through intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31.
