questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with hypocalcemia, thymic hypoplasia, cardiac abnormalities, and deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. DiGeorge syndrome

The given symptoms of hypocalcemia, developmental defect of the thymus, cardiac abnormalities, and deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 are suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome.

In this syndrome, the fourth branchial arch and the derivatives of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches (which contribute to the formation of the thymus, parathyroids, and heart) develop abnormally. This syndrome is therefore associated with multiple deficits (memorable through the mnemonic CATCH - 22)

Mnemonic CATCH-22:

* Cardiac abnormality

* Abnormal facies

* Thymic aplasia

* Cleft palate

* Hypocalcemia

* Deletion 22q11.2

Thymic hypoplasia with impaired T cell immunity can manifest as:

* T cells are absent in the lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral blood, and infants with this defect are extremely vulnerable to viral, fungal, and protozoal infections.

* Patients are also susceptible to infection with intracellular bacteria because of defective T cell-mediated immunity.

* B cells and serum immunoglobulins are generally unaffected.

The following image shows a child with DiGeorge syndrome:

Other options:

Option A: Pitt syndrome or Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome or Pitt–Rogers–Danks syndrome (PRDS) occurs due to partial deletion or monosomy of chromosome 4. The main features of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome are typical “Greek helmet” facies secondary to ocular hypertelorism, prominent glabella, frontal bossing and microcephaly.

Option B: Williams syndrome occurs due to a deletion on chromosome 7. Classical facial features include:

* Stellate iris

* Hypertelorism

* Periorbital fullness

* Thick vermilion border of the lips

* Elfin facies

Option D: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by the partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. Affected children have a cat-like cry, microcephaly, mental disability, and congenital heart disease.

Pearl PF0788: Clinical features of DiGeorge syndrome- Mnemonic

DiGeorge syndrome is a cellular immunodeficiency disorder caused by the deletion of a small segment of chromosome 22 (22q11) leading to a developmental defect involving the endodermal derivatives of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. (Thymus and parathyroid glands)

The clinical features can be remembered with the mnemonic – CATCH

* C – Cardiac defects

* A – Abnormal facies

* T – Thymic aplasia

* C – Cleft palate

* H – Hypocalcemia

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents with frequent headaches. Investigation reveals raised intracranial pressure and the presence of a dural-based tumor. Which of the following histological findings correlate with the diagnosis?
options: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells

The clinical vignette of a dural-based tumor presenting with headaches and raised intracranial pressure is most likely a meningioma and they have psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells on histopathological examination.

Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid.

* Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

* Prior radiation therapy to the head and neck, typically is a risk factor.

* The most common cytogenetic abnormality is the loss of chromosome 22, especially the long arm (22q).

* Meningiomas are a common lesion in the setting of NF2 (multiple sites, especially in association with acoustic neuromas or glial tumors.

* The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated.

* They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura. This form is commonly associated with hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone.

* The lesions may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies.

Psammoma bodies are shown below:

Histological subtypes:

* WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic

* WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical

* Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic

* Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth

* Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma

* Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen

* Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

* Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered.

* Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy.

Option A: Fried egg appearance of cells refers to cells with clear cytoplasm and a nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. Fried egg appearance in pathology are:

* Oligodendroglioma on histopathology

* Hairy cell leukemia on bone marrow biopsy

* Seminoma/Dysgerminoma on light microscopy

* Mycoplasma pneumonia fried egg colonies on Eaton agar

Option B: Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes with arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen can be seen in retinoblastoma.

Option D: In medulloblastoma, tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neurophil can be seen.

Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors

Pilocytic Astrocytomas:

* Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas

* Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.

* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions

* Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions

Medulloblastoma:

* Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells

* Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped

* Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil

Ependymoma:

* Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen

* Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel

Oligodendroglioma:

* Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.

* Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries

Retinoblastoma:

* Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei

* Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen

* Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center

* Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man dies due to myocardial infarction. Which of the following stains can be used to see the infarct in the heart while conducting an autopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain can be used to see the infarct in the heart.

Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved. Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

Other options:

Option A: The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues.

Option C: Sudan Black B (SBB) is a lipophilic dye that binds irreversibly to an undefined granule component in granulocytes, eosinophils, and some monocytes. It stains intracellular lipids and phospholipids.

Option D: Collagen fibres are stained blue and muscle fibres are stained red using Masson trichrome stain.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and serum calcium levels are elevated. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42% and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Multiple myeloma

In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. The incidence of multiple myeloma increases with age, and it is more commonly seen in males than in females.

Signs and symptoms

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Pathologic fractures

* Recurrent bacterial infections

* Renal failure

* Normocytic normochromic anemia elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%) and presence of Dutcher bodies, Russel bodies, and Mott cells.

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation)

Option A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen. Peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

Option B: Acute lymphocytic leukemia presents with a hypercellular marrow that is packed with lymphoblasts. These lymphoblasts, when compared to myeloblasts, have more condensed chromatin with less prominent nucleoli.

Option C: In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), patients typically present with a dragging sensation in the abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. The peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described as having a garden party or a college girl appearance.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A family pedigree chart is given below. Identify the mode of inheritance of this condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autosomal dominant

The pedigree chart given is suggestive of an autosomal dominant inheritance. Such an inheritance has a vertical pattern in pedigree charts where individuals of each generation are affected (parents and children). Males and females are equally affected and each affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the deleterious gene to their offspring.

The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart.

According to the above flowchart:

Step 1: All affected individuals have an affected parent. Since multiple generations are affected it is a dominant inheritance pattern.

Step 2: Male-to-male transmission is present. The disorder thus has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

Pedigree charts of different inheritance patterns are given in the pearl below.

Pearl PF0346: Pedigree chart for different inheritance patterns

Autosomal Dominant Disorders:

* With every autosomal dominant disorder, some patients do not have affected parents. Such patients owe their disorder to new mutations involving either the egg or the sperm from which they were derived.

* Clinical features can be modified by variations in penetrance and expressivity.

* In many conditions, the age at onset is delayed, and symptoms and signs may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease).

X-linked Recessive Conditions:

* All sex-linked disorders are X-linked, and almost all are recessive.

* Several genes are located in the “male-specific region of Y;” all these are related to spermatogenesis.

* Males with mutations affecting the Y-linked genes are usually infertile, and hence, there is no Y-linked inheritance.

* An affected male does not transmit the disorder to his sons, but all daughters are carriers.

* Sons of heterozygous women have, of course, a one-in-two chance of receiving the mutant gene.

* Heterozygous females express the disorder partially because of random inactivation of one X chromosome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A lymph node biopsy of a 30-year-old male with cervical lymphadenopathy showed the following picture. The diagnosis is_____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hodgkin disease

In the picture given above, Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells are seen, which is a pathognomonic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL).

Reed–Sternberg cells :

* RS cells are large and either multinucleated or have a bilobed nucleus (thus resembling an "owl's eye" appearance) with prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli.

* The RS cell is clonal in origin and arises from the germinal center B cells but typically has lost most B-cell gene expression and function.

* Reed Sternberg cells are not diagnostic for any condition since they are seen in many conditions such as:

* Hodgkin’s lymphoma

* Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (commonly in immunoblastic type)

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Sarcomas

Hodgkin's lymphoma:

* The patient commonly presents with palpable, firm, rubbery, non-tender lymphadenopathy in the cervical or supraclavicular region. Systemic symptoms that are classified as B symptoms including Hodgkin's lymphoma are persistent fever (>100.4ºF), drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss of >10% body weight over the past 6 months.

* It is characterized by a variable number of RS cells surrounded by an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils in different proportions, depending on the HL histologic subtype.

* The interaction between the RS cell and these background inflammatory cells with their associated cytokine release is important in the development and progression of HL.

Other options:

Option A: A peripheral blood smear showing numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes is characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). There is also the presence of bilobed nuclei and multiple coarse azurophilic granules.

Option C: Histopathology of human papillomavirus lesion shows koilocytes, perinuclear halo, multinucleation, and acanthosis.

Option D: In chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) the peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

Variant Reed–Sternberg cells and the corresponding subtype of Hodgkin's Lymphoma

* Mononuclear variant: Mixed cellularity and Lymphocyte rich

* Pleomorphic/Necrotic/Mummified Variant: Lymphocyte depleted

* L&H/Lymphohistiocytic/Popcorn Variant: Lymphocyte predominant

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young person with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis presents with itchiness and watering in the eyes. What is the most likely cell involved in the immediate phase of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mast cells

The given clinical features of allergic reactions suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity which is mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) binding to mast cells.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity, also called allergic reactions or allergies is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to an IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It has two phases.

Early phase: The mediators produced by the mast cells are responsible for most of the immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Histamine and leukotrienes are released rapidly from the sensitized mast cells and trigger intense immediate reactions characterized by edema, mucus secretion, and smooth muscle spasm.

Other mediators involved in the early phase are,

* Enzymes: neutral proteases (chymase, tryptase) and acid hydrolases

* Proteoglycans: heparin and chondroitin sulfate

* Lipid mediators: Platelet-activating factor (PAF)

Late-phase: The late-phase reaction is characterized by the recruitment of leukocytes, that amplify and sustain the inflammatory response without exposure to the triggering antigen.

Mediators involved in the late phase of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction are:

* Cytokines: TNF, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, and chemokines (eotaxin)

* Leukocytes (eosinophils)

* Major Basic Protein (MBP)

* Eosinophil cationic protein

The sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity

Though eosinophils and neutrophils are involved later in the pathogenesis, mast cells are central to the development of immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and walking difficulties. On examination, pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles was noted. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent dystrophin

History of progressive muscle weakness and walking difficulties with characteristic finding of pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles points to a diagnosis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

Dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), is absent in these patients due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Dystrophin connects actin filaments to the transmembrane protein β-dystroglycan in the sarcolemma by the smaller proteins syntrophins in the cytoplasm. Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability, which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy:

* Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease

* It is an X-linked recessive disorder, and the causative gene is located at Xp21.

* Clinical features

* Progressive weakness with developmental delay occurs.

* Pseudohypertrophy of calves and wasting of thigh muscles are seen.

* Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle is characteristic.

* Gower’s sign: Indicates weakness of proximal muscles: The patient has to use hands and arms to "walk up" their own body from a squatting position.

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Diagnosis

* Elevated serum creatine kinase levels

* Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene

* If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done.

* Treatment: Treatment of cardiac decompensation, nutritional management, physiotherapy, and glucocorticoids.

* Prognosis: Death occurs usually at about 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration.

Other options:

Option A: Abnormal collagen synthesis may be seen in conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes and osteogenesis imperfecta.

Option C: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by expansions of CTG triplet repeats in the 3′-noncoding region of the myotonic dystrophy protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Myotonia, a sustained involuntary contraction of muscles, is a key feature of the disease.

Option D: Marfan syndrome results from an inherited defect in an extracellular glycoprotein fibrillin-1.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Asbestos exposure may be associated with which of the following malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mesothelioma

Asbestosis is most commonly associated with Mesotheliomas.

Asbestos-related diseases include:

* Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis

* Pleural effusion

* Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)

* Lung carcinoma

* Mesotheliomas

* Laryngeal, ovarian, and colon carcinomas

Asbestosis:

* Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis.

* Asbestos is of 2 types i.e Serpentine/Chrysolite variety and Amphibole type

* Amphibole type has the following varieties:

* Crocidolite(blue)

* Amosite(brown)

* Anthophyllite(white)

* Sputum shows asbestos bodies, which are asbestos fibers coated with fibrin.

* They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affect the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

* X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. HRCT shows subpleural fibrotic lines, irregular opacities, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing. Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years).

* The complications that can occur are

* Pulmonary fibrosis

* Carcinoma of the lung

* Malignancy of the Gastrointestinal tract

* Mesothelioma of the pleura

Preventive measures:

* Using a safer type of Asbestos (chrysolite and amosite)

* Substituting other insulants like glass fiber, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams, etc.

* Dust control

* Periodic examination of workers

* Continuing research

Option B: Acute myeloid leukemia may be caused by benzene exposure.

Option C: Hepatic angiosarcoma can be seen in exposure to vinyl chloride.

Option D: Skin carcinoma may be seen with exposure to arsenic and arsenic compounds.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Following urine microscopy and examination, a child is found to have hematuria and RBC casts in the urine. What is the probable cause for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

The clinical findings of nephritic syndrome (hematuria and red cell casts) seen in this child is most likely due to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma.

The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following:

* 1 to 2 weeks after antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or

* 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma

The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens causing the immunologic injury.

In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see the following in most patients:

* Decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalize in 6 to 8 weeks)

* ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks)

Microscopic Findings in PSGN:

* Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration

* Immunofluorescence: Shows granular deposits of IgG and C3 along the GBM and within the mesangium.

* Electron microscopy: Reveals subepithelial electron-dense deposits (“humps”) on the GBM. Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Other options:

Option A: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) represents the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.
Hematuria is not a usual feature of nephrotic syndrome and rather presents with nephrotic range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema.

Option C: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) present in adolescents or young adults with nephrotic syndrome and a nephritic component manifested by hematuria. It is not frequent in children.

Option D: In children, minimal change disease is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein is a major component of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal casts

Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein forms a major component of the organic matrix of renal casts.

Tamm-Horsfall protein, also known as uromodulin, is the most common protein present in urine and is produced in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. They are membrane-bound, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins that are released by proteolytic cleavage at the apical membrane. It is secreted as the most abundant protein in normal human urine (20 to 100 mg/day) and is not expressed by macula densa cells or the downstream distal convoluted tubule (DCT)

They form the major organic matrix of all renal casts and play a role in the modulation of innate immunity in the kidney and inflammation during kidney injury. Uromodulin is coded by the UMOD gene, and mutation of this can lead to medullary cystic kidney disease (MCKD II) and familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy.

Casts are cylindrical structures that are formed in the DCT and collecting ducts. They assume the shape and size of the lumen in which they are formed. Several factors favor cast formation, such as urine stasis, low pH, and high concentration. All casts have an organic matrix composed primarily of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein. Casts are the only elements in urine sediments that are specific to renal origin.

Other options:

Option A: Thrombi occurring in heart chambers or the aortic lumen are designated mural thrombi. Thrombi often have grossly and microscopically apparent laminations called lines of Zahn, which are pale platelet and fibrin deposits alternating with darker red cell–rich layers.

Option B: Curschmann spirals are a characteristic finding in sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage specimens of patients with atopic asthma formed due to the extrusion of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous gland ducts or bronchioles.

Option D: In multiple myeloma, the malignant plasma cells often secrete free, unpaired κ or λ light chains which are referred to as Bence-Jones proteins.

Pearl PF0892: Urinary Casts and Their Significance

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What type of cell is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reed Sternberg cell

In the picture given above, Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells are seen, which is seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL).

Reed–Sternberg cells :

* RS cells are large and either multinucleated or have a bilobed nucleus (thus resembling an "owl's eye" appearance) with prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli.

* The RS cell is clonal in origin and arises from the germinal center B cells but typically has lost most B-cell gene expression and function.

* Reed Sternberg cells are not diagnostic for any condition since they are seen in many conditions such as:

* Hodgkin’s lymphoma

* Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (commonly in immunoblastic type)

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Sarcomas

Option A: Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks. Such cells have been termed as “Faggot cells” and are marked in the image below by the red arrow (faggot in French means bundle of sticks).

Option C: Mott cells are plasma cells with globular cytoplasmic inclusions containing immunoglobulins called Russell bodies. They are characteristically seen in multiple myeloma.

Option D: Sézary-Lutzner cells are cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane). These are neoplastic T cells that are seen in mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome.

* Pleomorphic/Necrotic/Mummified Variant: Lymphocyte depleted

* L&H/Lymphohistiocytic/Popcorn Variant: Lymphocyte predominant

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following cells is responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies in liver sinusoids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages of the liver that are responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies. These cells are present in the walls of the sinusoids and not in the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse). They are responsible for removing cellular and microbial debris from the circulation, and also for secreting cytokines involved in defense.

Macrophages can be divided into:

* Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.

* Tissue macrophages survive for months.

2 main functions of macrophages:

* Phagocytosis.

* Antigen presentation.

All the options given are various types of cells present in an adult liver.

Option A: Hepatocytes are polyhedral cells with a central spherical nucleus, arranged in a single-cell layer. Every hepatocyte has contact with adjacent hepatocytes (with gap junctions for intercellular communication), bile canaliculus, and the space of Disse/perisinusoidal space (hepatocytes project multiple microvilli into this space for active transport of substances.)

Option B: Ito cells or hepatic stellate cells are present in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. They are mesenchymal in origin and take part in the development of hepatic fibrosis.

Option C: Sinusoidal endothelial cells are flat cells with a central nucleus and are joined to each other by junctional complexes. Their cytoplasm contains numerous transcytotic vesicles. These are separated from hepatocytes by the space of Disse (perisinusoidal space).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents the effect of the mutation causing sickle cell anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glutamate by valine at 6th position

Sickle cell anemia is characterized by the replacement of glutamate by valine at the 6th position.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder occurring due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This leads to the formation of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

* Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.

* Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.

* Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.

* Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.

* Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

* Spleen

* In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.

* Adolescence or early adulthood- auto splenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.

* Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

* Other clinical features include priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike.

Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure, and acute chest syndrome

Note: Standard Biochemical Nomenclature counts from the first amino acid of the mature beta-globin protein. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 6. Genomic Convention (as stated in Harrison 21E) includes the initiating methionine (AUG) from the translation start site, even though it is cleaved off in the mature protein. This shifts the numbering by +1, making Glu6 → Val become Glu7 → Val. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 7.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a feature of hemolytic anemia?
options: All of the options given below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased haptoglobin

Serum haptoglobin levels are decreased in hemolytic anemias. In intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells is promptly bound by haptoglobin, producing a complex that is rapidly cleared by mononuclear phagocytes. In cases of extravascular hemolysis, some hemoglobin inevitably escapes from phagocytes and leads to variable decreases in plasma haptoglobin.

Hemolytic anemias are characterized by a shortened red cell life span of less than the normal 120 days. This leads to elevated erythropoietin levels and a compensatory increase in erythropoiesis which is seen as prominent reticulocytosis (OptionC) in the peripheral blood. In addition, there is an accumulation of hemoglobin degradation products produced due to hemolysis.

Types of hemolysis based on location:

* Intravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs mainly within the blood vessels

* Extravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs via macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lymph nodes

Features of intravascular hemolysis are:

* Decreased haptoglobin

* Increased lactate dehydrogenase

* Hemoglobinemia

* Hemoglobinuria

* Hemosiderinuria

* Methemoglobinemia

* Methemoglobinuria

* Indirect hyperbilirubinemia

Features of extravascular hemolysis are:

* Anemia

* Splenomegaly

* Jaundice

* Variable decreases in plasma haptoglobin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a sensitive and specific marker of intestinal inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fecal lactoferrin

Fecal lactoferrin, a glycoprotein present in activated neutrophils is a highly sensitive and specific marker for detecting intestinal inflammation. It is a marker of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and is used to rule out irritable bowel syndrome.

Fecal calprotectin present in neutrophils and monocytes is another marker of IBD and is used to rule out irritable bowel syndrome and bacterial overgrowth. It correlates well with histologic inflammation, predicts relapses, and detects pouchitis.

Option A: Procalcitonin is a commonly used biomarker of severe inflammation. It is an acute-phase reactant produced primarily in the liver, and is more significantly elevated in bacterial than viral infections.

Option C: Tissue transglutaminase IgA test is used in screening for celiac disease.

Option D: C-reactive protein is an acute-phase reactant synthesized primarily by the liver. CRP expression is increased by a number of inflammatory mediators, particularly IL-6.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is implicated in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autoimmunity

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of autoimmune origin that principally attacks the joints, producing nonsuppurative, proliferative, and inflammatory synovitis. The inflammation progresses to the destruction of the articular cartilage and ankylosis of the joints.

In RA, the synovium contains germinal centers with secondary follicles and abundant plasma cells, which produce antibodies, some are autoantibodies. Many of the autoantibodies produced in the lymphoid organs are specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs). 80% of patients have serum IgM or IgA autoantibodies that bind to the Fc portions of their own IgG. These autoantibodies are called rheumatoid factor and may also be deposited in joints as immune complexes.

The characteristic histologic features of RA include:

* Increased vascularity due to angiogenesis

* Dense inflammatory infiltrates

* Synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation

* Fibrinopurulent exudate (synovial and joint surfaces)

* Subcutaneous nodule: Necrotising granulomas with a central area of fibrinoid necrosis.

* Osteoclastic activity (underlying bone)

This all together leads to a mass of edematous synovium called pannus, which grows over the articular cartilage and causes its erosion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old female complained of fatigue for the past 1 year along with incidences of bleeding gums. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly and her hb level was noted to be 8gm/dl. Immature cells were seen in the peripheral smear. Her blood workup showed a Total leucocyte count (TLC) of 1,50,000/microL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CML

The clinical presentation with fatigue, bleeding gums, massive splenomegaly, and peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.

* Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

* Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* There is also an increase in megakaryocytes which usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course.

Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm

Other options:
Acute leukemias have a presence of immature blast cells in the bone marrow and peripheral smear usually (>20%) which is not seen in this patient.

ALL lymphoblast cells have Tdt positive which is due to DNA polymerase. These cells can be B cell or T cell subtype. They are distinguished by cell surface markers. CD 10, 19, 20 are positive on B cells while CD2-8 are positive on T cell ALL.

AML has positive staining for myeloperoxidase and auer rods are seen in the cytoplasm.
CLL is a disease seen in elderly patients(>65) and peripheral smear will show smudge cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with pallor and fatigue. Investigations revealed the following: Hb, 5 gm %; MCH, 24; low MCV; leukocytes, 11,000/uL, and platelets, 5 lakhs. The iron profile showed low ferritin and high TIBC. What is the diagnosis? MCV : Mean corpuscular volume (normal MCV is 82–96 fl) MCH: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (normal MCH is 27–33 pg/cell) TIBC: Total iron binding capacity (normal TIBC is 240 to 450 mcg/dL)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron deficiency anemia

The given clinical scenario of a 30-year-old woman, presenting with fatigue and pallor along with her investigation results are suggestive of iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorption, and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Diagnosis is mainly my laboratory studies. The typical findings in IDA are:

* Low hemoglobin and hematocrit

* Low serum iron and ferritin

* Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)

* Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis)

* IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations of iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia.

Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is defined by a high MCV

Option C: Anemia of chronic disease would present with normal to high ferritin and low TIBC

Option D: Sideroblastic anemia has high ferritin and normal TIBC

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-month-old boy presented with a two-day history of fever and abscess over the neck. The mother reveals that the child had similar recurrent infections in the past. The dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) was found to be positive. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic granulomatous disease

The given clinical history of fever,abscess and recurrent infections in the past and positive dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) most likely suggests chronic granulomatous disease.

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an X-linked recessive disorder due to the deficiency in NADPH oxidase which is important in respiratory or oxidative bursts. In CGD, there is an increased risk of catalase-positive species (Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Aspergillus spp, etc.) leading to granulomas. The condition usually manifests in the first year of life with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms.

Patients have recurrent bacterial and fungal infections. The symptoms begin within the first two years of life, affecting the pulmonary, gastrointestinal, skin, and lymphatic drainage of these organs.

Nitroblue tetrazolium is used as a diagnostic test. The yellow-coloured Nitroblue tetrazolium dye is converted to a purple insoluble substance (positive) in the presence of oxidative burst by the free oxygen radicals so formed. A negative test (yellow color remains) is seen in CGD.

Individuals with CGD will exhibit diminished or absent fluorescence in the DHR test, indicating impaired ROS production by phagocytes. This result confirms the diagnosis of CGD and aids in distinguishing it from other conditions with similar symptoms. It can also assess the effectiveness of treatments like bone marrow transplantation or gene therapy in restoring normal phagocyte function.

Other options:

Option A) Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency due to a disorder of the phagolysosome function of leukocytes, leading to delayed microbial clearance. In addition, there is a disorder of melanin (albinism), nerve defects, and bleeding disorders.

Option C) Severe combined immunodeficiency is a primary immunodeficiency with a disorder of both cellular and humoral immunity. Persons with SCID are susceptible to recurrent severe infections caused by a wide variety of pathogens and usually do not survive beyond the first year of life without a stem cell transplant.

Option D) Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is characterized by the formation of granulomas as an immune response to contain the infection. Tuberculosis presents with cavitary lesions in the upper lobes of the lungs. Histopathology reveals caseous necrosis with multinucleated giant cells. Common manifestations include fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Blood investigations may reveal anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, leukemoid reactions, and polycythemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department complaining of severe pain in her right index finger, back and legs along with fatigue. She states that the pain began suddenly about six hours ago. On examination, the patient appears pale and is grimacing in pain. A peripheral blood smear confirms the presence of sickle-shaped red blood cells. The biochemical analysis revealed high levels of indirect bilirubin. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and there is diffuse tenderness in the joints. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sickle cell crisis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a Sickle cell crisis, which is a complication of Sickle cell anemia.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis.

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated.

Clinical features:

* Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice

* Painful bone crisis - hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.

* Acute chest syndrome - Typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.

* Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.

* The aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

* Spleen In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.
- Adolescence or early adulthood- auto splenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
- Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae septicemia, can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

* Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells on the peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2 and HbF and S spike. The changes in the skull resemble a crewcut in radiographic studies as a result of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During pregnancy, ABO incompatibility does not occur due to which antibody?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgM

IgM antibodies cannot cross the placenta from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Therefore, they do not have a significant role in causing hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) or ABO incompatibility during pregnancy.

ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of hemolytic disease in newborns and affects the firstborn. It is usually mild and subclinical. This incompatibility between the mother and fetus generally results in milder disease than Rh incompatibility does.

It arises when a mother with blood group type O becomes pregnant with a fetus of a different blood type (A/B). The mother's serum contains naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B, which can cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of fetal RBCs.

Although antibodies against A and B factors occur without previous immunisation (natural antibodies), they are usually IgM, which does not cross the placenta. However, IgG antibodies to A antigen may be present, which cross the placenta, resulting in A-O iso-immune hemolytic disease in the firstborn infant (A-O is more common than B-O).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Reiter syndrome is associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HLA-B27

Reiter syndrome is associated with HLA- B27.

Reiter's syndrome has a triad of urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis, with or without iridocyclitis. The exact cause of the syndrome is not fully understood, but it typically affects young males who test positive for the HLA-B27 gene.

It has three forms: postvenereal, postdysenteric, and articular. Ocular symptoms may include acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis and non-granulomatous iridocyclitis in a subset of cases.

Treatrment -Iridocyclitis responds well to usual treatment and in cases suspected of being caused by Chlamydia infection, a course of systemic tetracycline (250 mg QID for 10 days) may be beneficial in postvenereal form.

HLA association and diseases

Vogt–Koyanagi–Haradas disease: HLA-DR1 and HLA-DR4

Possner–Scholssman syndrome: HLA Bw54

Reiters syndrome: HLA- B27

Note: The association between HLA-A29 and birdshot retinochoroidopathy is the most consistent of any medical disorder. Approximately 95% of patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are HLA-A29–positive.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The histological section of a skin lesion is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squamous cell carcinoma

The image shows keratin pearls which are characteristic of Squamous cell carcinoma.

* Squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with 'horn pearls', also called as keratin pearls.

* Macroscopic appearance of SCC may vary from smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous to ulcerating lesions.

* SCC stains positive for cytokeratins 1 and 10.

* SCC can be histologically graded according to Broders' histological grading.

Option A : Basal cell carcinoma histopathology shows basal cells arranged in a palisading pattern.

Option C : Adenocarcinoma shows a lepidic pattern of growth at the periphery of the tumor. The tumor cells appear to crawl along the normal-appearing alveolar septa, as shown in the image below.

Option D: Malignant melanoma histopathology shows dense intracytoplasmic brownish-black melanin pigment. Malignant melanoma primarily arises from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What do apoptotic bodies consist of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All cellular content

An apoptotic body is formed during the late stages of apoptosis when a cell undergoes controlled self-destruction. Apoptotic bodies contain all the cellular components such as organelles and fragmented DNA and are typically smaller than the cell undergoing apoptosis.

Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, plays a vital role in the normal development and renewal of tissues. It can be initiated by external triggers like cytotoxic T cells or inflammatory molecules, as well as internal factors such as DNA damage or cellular stress.

Mitochondria play a key role in processing signals that determine whether a cell will undergo apoptosis or not. If there's a predominance of signals favoring cell death, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) occurs, releasing cytochrome C and other proteins into the cytoplasm. These proteins then activate internal pathways leading to programmed cell death.

Apoptosis has two pathways:

A. Mitochondrial or intrinsic pathway:

* Cell injury results in the release of cytochrome C and other pro-apoptotic proteins from mitochondria.

* These then activate caspase 9 which causes nuclear fragmentation and formation of apoptotic bodies.

B. Death receptor or extrinsic pathway:

* In this pathway, activation of death receptors causes apoptosis by activating caspase-8.

* Prototypic death receptors are the type I TNF receptor and Fas (CD95).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. S

The most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle is the S phase.

The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. The S phase is separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. The cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2.

The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is the G2-M phase. Cells in the G2 or M phase do not have time to repair DNA damage that occurs before they start to divide. This affects mitosis, leading to catastrophe.

Cells become gradually less sensitive to radiation in the G1 phase to the early S phase and are least sensitive in the late S phase.

The most radiosensitive cell in the blood is the lymphocyte.

The least radiosensitive cell in the blood is the platelet.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What should be the target HbA1c level in a diabetic patient whose fasting blood glucose levels are 140mg/dL and post-prandial are 200gm/dL?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. <7.0

It is recommended that HbA1C be maintained below 7% in diabetic patients.

Note that most diabetes associations recommend the target HbA1c must be individualized to the patient. A target of <7% is reasonable in most individuals.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which mutation is linked to the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reciprocal translocation

The mutation associated with the Philadelphia chromosome is a result of reciprocal translocation.

Fusion of BCR-ABL is created by a reciprocal (9;22)translocation (Philadelphia chromosome. This is detected by cytogenetics, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and occurs in Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML). To form the abnormal chromosome, part of the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene of chromosome 22 fuses with part of the ABL gene (encodes a tyrosine kinase) of chromosome 9, directing the synthesis of a chimeric protein that has unregulated tyrosine kinase activity and drives cell proliferation.

The peak incidence of CML is in the fifth to sixth decade.

* Clinical features:

* Anemia weight loss, and anorexia.

* Splenomegaly

* Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis, exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts usually make up less than 5% of circulating cells.

* Bone Marrow:

* Markedly Hypercellular with maturing granulocytic precursors, with an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* Low LAP score

Image – Interphase FISH showing (9;22) translocation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless, rapidly growing lump in her left breast that she noticed over the past few months. On examination, the lump is well-defined, mobile, and firm in consistency. A breast ultrasound reveals a solid mass, and a core needle biopsy is performed. Histopathological examination shows a leaf-like pattern with an overgrowth of the stromal component and ductal structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phyllodes tumor

The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture which is suggestive of phyllodes tumor.

Phyllodes tumor is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes, presents as a large tumor with an unevenly bosselated surface. This tumour does not infiltrate the skin though the overlying skin becomes thin and tense due to swelling. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition.

Phyllodes tumors usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. They are mostly benign even though it is also called as cystosarcoma phyllodes or as serocystic disease of Brodie. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size.

Histologically, there is a wide variation with some of low malignant potential and others having a higher mitotic index.

* They are fibroepithelial tumours that arise from the intralobular stroma.

* It can be benign, borderline or malignant.

* Phyllodes tumor can be differentiated from intracanalicular fibroadenoma by its subepithelial or periepithelial accentuation of stromal cellularity.

* Most phyllodes tumor are of low grade. Recurrence rate is high in intermediate and high grade tumors.

* Increased stromal cellularity, stromal overgrowth (absence of epithelial elements), nuclear atypia, increased mitosis(>10 per 10HPF) suggests the diagnosis of malignant phyllodes tumour.

* Gain in chromosome 1q is the most frequent clonal acquired chromosomal changes seen in Phyllodes tumor. HOXB13 overexpression is associated with more aggressive clinical behaviour.

Microscopy reveals the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture).

Note: "Phyllodes" means "leaf like" in Greek.

Treatment of phyllodes tumor:

* Benign type- Enucleation or wide local excision

* Massive tumors, recurrent tumors and malignant type- Mastectomy

* Axillary dissection is not done if malignant transformation occurs because the lymphatic spread is rare.

Other Options:

Option B: Galactocele: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral.

Option C: Paget's Disease: Presents as a chronic, eczematous eruption of the nipple which may progress to ulceration. In the majority of patients, there is also an underlying breast lump. Histology shows the presence of large, pale, vacuolated cells (Paget cells) with round or oval nuclei in the rete pegs of the epithelium.

Option D: Fibroadenoma is a form of aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI), and it is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15–25 years. It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth or lobular, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). The histopathology shows the proliferation of intralobular stroma, and the epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted (intracanalicular pattern). The histopathology image is given below:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady with a history of long-standing goitre presented with a solitary thyroid nodule. Histopathological examination of the thyroid mass shows nests of polygonal cells and pink eosinophilic extracellular material. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medullary carcinoma

The presence of nests of polygonal cells and pink eosinophilic extracellular material (amyloid stroma) on histopathological examination, makes medullary carcinoma of the thyroid the most likely diagnosis.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells. Most of the MTC are sporadic but they may also be associated with inheritable syndromes like familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.

Most patients present at 50-60 years and have a female preponderance. MTC secretes calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), prostaglandins E2 and F2α, histaminadases, serotonin, and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH).

Features of MTC

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Diarrhea due to increased intestinal motility

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Metastasis is blood-borne

* Diagnosis is by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin, CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles. Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. These lesions secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen.

Total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Papillary carcinoma thyroid shows

* Papillary projections

* Orphan-Annie eyed nuclei (pale empty nuclei)

* Psammoma bodies (microscopic calcified deposits)

Option C: Follicular carcinoma shows uniform cells forming small follicles and they are filled with colloid and normal thyroid tissue. The below image shows follicular thyroid carcinoma.

Option D: Anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid is one of the most aggressive malignancies. They are poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas with varied morphology, including giant cells or spindle-shaped cells or both. There is minimal follicular differentiation with intratumoral necrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 55-year-old female presents with complaints of persistent headaches. A CT scan of the head reveals a brain tumour. On histopathology, psammoma bodies are seen. Based on these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meningioma

The clinical vignette and the histopathology showing a tumour with psammoma bodies is suggestive of meningioma.

Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors in adults, typically attached to the dura and arising from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid. They can develop along any external surface of the brain or within the ventricular system, originating from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

A major risk factor for meningiomas is prior radiation therapy to the head and neck. The most common cytogenetic abnormality associated with these tumors is the loss of chromosome 22, particularly the long arm (22q). Meningiomas are frequently seen in neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), often occurring at multiple sites, especially alongside acoustic neuromas or glial tumors.

The tumor mass is usually encapsulated but may also grow en plaque, where it spreads in a sheetlike manner along the dura, often leading to hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone. Histologically, meningiomas may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies, a characteristic microscopic feature.

Psammoma bodies are concentric, lamellated structures formed as a product of dystrophic calcification. They are associated with papillary histomorphology and are caused by infarction and calcification of papillae tips.

The histological section of meningioma showing psammoma bodies is given below:

Histological subtypes:

* WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic

* WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical

* Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic

* Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth

* Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma

* Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen

* Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

* Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered.

* Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy.

Other Options:

Option A: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes with arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen can be seen in Retinoblastoma.

Option B: Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option D: Oligodendroglioma is composed of tumor cells that resemble oligodendrocytes. The tumor contains sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin, surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm. This gives them a fried egg appearance. They contain a network of anastomosing capillaries, resembling chicken wire and also have calcifications.

Pearl PF2095: Psammoma Bodies

Psammoma bodies are visible in the following:

* Meningioma

* Serous cystadenocarcinoma Ovary

* Papillary carcinoma thyroid.

* Papillary type of renal cell carcinoma

Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors

Pilocytic Astrocytomas:

* Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas

* Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.

* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions

* Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions

Medulloblastoma:

* Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells

* Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped

* Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil

Ependymoma:

* Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen

* Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel

Oligodendroglioma:

* Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.

* Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries

Retinoblastoma:

* Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei

* Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen

* Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center

* Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female presents with a slow-growing, painless mass in her left breast. On physical examination, the mass is soft, well-circumscribed, and mobile. A biopsy is performed, and histopathology reveals the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colloidal carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of colloid/mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intra and extracellular mucin deposition. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the peripherally to form signet ring appearance.

Extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei arranged in clusters floating in pools/lakes of mucin on histopathological examination.

Other options:

Option B: Lobular carcinoma is the most common type of breast carcinoma to present as an occult primary carcinoma. Lobular carcinoma of the breast is seen bilaterally and with multicentricity. Loss of E-cadherin is the hallmark of lobular carcinoma.

The histological hallmark of lobular carcinoma is the presence of discohesive infiltrating tumor cells, often arranged in a single Indian file pattern or in loose clusters or sheets.

Option C: Microscopic image of medullary carcinoma of the breast consisting of sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures (anaplastic cells), lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is shown below.

Option D: Microscopic image of papillary carcinoma of the breast showing true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue lined by the tumor cells is shown below.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 9-month-old child is admitted to the ICU with a history of recurrent sinusitis and otitis media caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Lab results shows low levels of Immunoglobulins (G,A,M,E) and low quantity of plasma B cells. There is a normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bruton's agammaglobulinemia

This child's presentation suggests X-linked or Bruton's agammaglobulinemia.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia) is an immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the failure of B-cell precursors (pro-B and pre-B cells) to develop into mature B-cells. It is caused by a mutation in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase called Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq21.22). The features of the disease are -

* B cells are absent or markedly reduced.

* Decreased levels of all classes of Immunoglobulins.

* Germinal centres are underdeveloped in lymph nodes, peyer's patches, and tonsils.

* T-cell mediated reactions are normal. (normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin.)

* The disease usually becomes apparent after 6 months of age since it is masked by the presence of maternal antibodies until 6 months of age.

The patient has recurrent pharyngitis, otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, and pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, and Hemophilus influenzae. Gastrointestinal infections can occur by viruses or Giardia lamblia due to reduced IgA secretion.
The treatment is replacement therapy with immunoglobulins in the form of prophylactic intravenous IgG therapy.

Other Options:

Option A: Ataxia telangiectasia is caused due to mutation of the ATM gene. This gene is involved in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to impaired Ig isotype switching and the formation of antigen receptors. As a result, the patient is immunodeficient with partial T cell deficiency, and hence live vaccines are avoided.

Option C: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is a rare primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by defects in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex, which is essential for the respiratory burst in phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages). This defect impairs the ability of phagocytes to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to ineffective intracellular killing of certain bacteria and fungi.

Option D: DiGeorge syndrome is caused due to deletion of chromosome 22q11.2. The characteristic features are (Mnemonic CATCH-22) - Cardiac abnormality, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child with a history of recurrent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after minor injuries is diagnosed with von Willebrand disease. He inquires about the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in this condition. Which of the following does vWF primarily bind to facilitate platelet adhesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GpIb/IX

The factor that von Willebrand factor (vWF) binds to is GpIb/IX.

Platelet adhesion is an interplay of interactions between glycoprotein Ib - GpIb/IX and vWF in the subendothelial matrix. Endothelial injury exposes vWF and causes the adhesion of platelets by the GpIb receptor. Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) binding to ADP receptors (Option B) induces conformational changes in platelets. This change in glycoprotein IIb/IIIa that occurs with platelet activation allows it to bind to fibrinogen, which leads to aggregation of platelets to each other and not to the endothelium.

Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder that occurs due to deficiency of or defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is stored in endothelial cells and in platelet Weibel-Palade bodies. It has two important functions:

* Adhesion of the platelets to injured subendothelium

* Carrier protein for factor VIII and preventing its degradation

Clinical features include spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes (epistaxis), excessive bleeding from wounds, or menorrhagia, after dental extractions and surgeries including tonsillectomies. Most individuals are asymptomatic otherwise. Type 3 VWD is the most severe form and presents with symptoms like joint bleeds, similar to those seen in mild haemophilia.

Diagnosis

* Normal platelet count

* Prolonged BT

* Normal PT

* Prolonged aPTT

Factor VIII is found bound to the Von-Willebrand factor(vWF) in the blood. Deficiency of vWF results in Factor VIII deficiency and prolongation of aPTT in this disease. Prolonged BT is due to abnormal platelet-mediated hemostasis.

Classification: 3 types are recognized, with phenotypic variations:

* Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder that is inherited. It manifests as a mild to moderate von Willebrand factor deficiency. It accounts for upto 70% of all cases.

* Type 2 von Willebrand disease is characterized by qualitative defects in vWF. Type 2A is the most common. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.

* Type 3 disease is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting in little to no vWF synthesis. Because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation, factor VIII levels are also reduced in type 3 disease and the associated bleeding disorder is often severe.

Type 1 and type 3 von Willebrand disease are associated with quantitative defects in vWF.

Treatment: Desmopressin for type 1 vWD stimulates the release of vWF and Factor VIII from the endothelial stores. Von Willebrand factor (VWF) concentrates in cases of type 2 and type 3 von Willebrand disease.

Other Options:

Option A: Prothrombin binds to phospholipid membranes as part of its conversion to thrombin during the coagulation process.

Option C: Platelet factor 3 (PF3) is exposed on activated platelet surfaces and provides a negatively charged phospholipid surface that facilitates the assembly of coagulation factor complexes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient is suffering from a rare disease with mitochondrial inheritance. This can be inherited from which of the following members?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mother

Diseases with mitochondrial inheritance are inherited exclusively from the affected mother.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

* Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.

* Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.

* 80% of mitochondrial DNA codes for mitochondrial RNA, and therefore most mitochondrial DNA mutations lead to functional problems, which may be manifested as muscle disorders.

Examples include: Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes (MELAS), Leigh Syndrome

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient suspected of having a myocardial infarction was brought to the emergency department and succumbed after 3 hours. During the autopsy, the heart was stained with triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) to detect myocardial ischemic damage. When is the best time to use TTC staining for optimal visualization of myocardial necrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2-3 hours

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride can best visualize the infarcted tissue within 2 to 3 hours.

Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved. Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

The image below shows cross-section of the heart showing transmural infarction (A. Before staining B. After staining)
