questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumor marker used in the diagnosis and monitoring of various conditions. In which of the following conditions is AFP typically raised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatoma

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is raised in the setting of a hepatoma tumor.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is commonly produced by Hepatomas and is used as a tumor marker. AFP is typically elevated in about 50-70% of HCC cases, with levels above 200 ng/mL being particularly suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The marker is useful for both screening high-risk populations and monitoring treatment response, though it is not entirely specific and can be elevated in other liver conditions and some germ cell tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Dysgerminona is a type of germ cell tumor and it corresponds to the seminoma of the testis. It does not secrete either male or female sex hormones. It secretes placental alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and β-hCG. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is usually used in monitoring individuals or disease recurrence.

Option C: Choriocarcinoma is a type of mixed germ cell tumor. It is highly vascular. Histologically, the tumor shows syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts. It secretes large quantities of beta- human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) hormone, which is used as a tumor marker in the diagnosis and management of the tumor

Option D: Malignant epithelial cell tumors of the ovary secrete CA-125. It is a glycoprotein and surface cell antigen which is secreted by malignant epithelial tumors of the ovary. A level of more than 35 U/mL suggests a malignant and residual tumor and indicates the need for chemotherapy. CA-125 is also raised in abdominal tuberculosis and endometriosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly and rolled margins. Histopathology shows nesting cells with peripheral palisading patterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Basal cell carcinoma

This patient, presenting with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly, rolled margins, and histopathology revealing nesting cells with peripheral palisading, is most likely diagnosed with basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive, malignant tumour of epithelial cells arising from the basal epidermis. It erodes deeply into local tissues, including cartilage and bones, causing extensive local destruction, hence the name rodent ulcer. It does not spread through blood or lymphatics.

The strongest risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is exposure to UV radiation. Therefore it occurs on the sun-exposed areas of the skin, most commonly on the nose and face. Most common site is the inner canthus of eye.

They present as small, slowly growing pearly nodules, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on their surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC). The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

BCC can be divided into generalized and localized. Generalized can be further divided into superficial or infiltrative. The localized can be further divided into

* Nodular and nodulocystic- account for the majority of BCC

* Cystic

* Pigmented

* Naevoid.

The characteristic biopsy finding of BCC is the presence of ovoid cells in nests and palisading of the peripheral cells of the nests.

Treatment of BCC includes excision of the lesion or Moh's micrographic surgery.

Other Options:

Option A: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the malignancy of the keratinizing cells of the epidermis. It is associated with exposure to UV radiation and chronic inflammation (chronic sinus tracts, pre-existing scars, osteomyelitis, and burns). Classically, it appears as a scaly or ulcerated papule or plaque that can bleed with minimal trauma, but the pain is rare. Histologically, SCC is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with the formation of horn pearls or keratin pearls.

Option B: Marjolin's ulcer is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds.

The image below shows a Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar.

Option D: Naevus is a common benign neoplasm caused by mutations in the RAS signalling pathway, characterized by aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or the dermo-epidermal junction. It has various types, such as congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus, halo naevus, and dysplastic naevus. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: cMYC gene mutation is seen in which of the following neoplasms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Burkitt's lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels.

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

* African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.

* Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.

* Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukaemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumour cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: In Hodgkin's lymphoma, the most significant mutation is associated with the BCL6 gene on chromosome 3q27. The BCL6 gene mutation results in aberrant transcriptional regulation and contributes to the characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma, which are large, abnormal lymphoid cells that are diagnostic of this type of lymphoma.

Option B: Pleomorphic adenoma is associated with chromosomal rearrangements that induce overexpression of PLAG1.  It is the most common salivary gland and lacrimal gland neoplasm. Microscopically, it contains a mixture of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells.

Option D: Neuroblastoma is a tumour derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumour in childhood. They are associated with the n-MYC gene translocation. On histopathology, small round blue cells and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes are seen.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purkinje cell

The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell.

Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers.

Pathological significance of Purkinje cells:

* Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.

* In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them.

* Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

Pearl PF2096: Layers of the cerebellar cortex

The cerebellar cortex is divided into 3 layers. They are:

* Molecular layer - It is the outermost layer. It contains stellate cells and basket cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers and form inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. It contains many myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers giving it a pale appearance in H and E staining.

* Purkinje layer - It is the middle layer. It contain flask-shaped cell bodies of Purkinje cells. Their dendrites pass into the molecular layer. The axons of the Purkinje cells passes through the granular layer into the white matter and synapses with the cerebellar nuclei.

* Granular layer - It is the innermost layer. It contains the cell bodies of the granule cells as well as Golgi cells. It receives excitatory input from the mossy fibers. They end on the dendrites of the granule cells and these complexes are called glomeruli. The axon from the granule cells travels to the molecular layer and bifurcates in a T-shape. These branches form the T and are called parallel fibers. These parallel fibers form excitatory synapses with the Purkinje cells. The granule cells form the only excitatory neurons in the cerebellar cortex. Golgi cells receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers. They send inhibitory output to the granule cells.

Neurotransmitters released:

* Stellate, basket, Golgi and Purkinje cells- GABA

* Granule cells - Glutamate

The only output from the cerebellar cortex is inhibitory from the Purkinje cells to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the histological image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymph node

The image is that of a lymph node.

Each lymph node is bean-shaped. The concave part consists of the hilum, through which the blood vessels enter and leave the node. Each lymph node is surrounded by a thin capsule. Below the capsule is the clear space, which is called the subcapsular sinus. The lymph node contains the outer cortex and an inner medulla.

Cortex

* The outermost region of the lymph node, located beneath the capsule.

* Primary follicles: Composed primarily of small, resting B lymphocytes (naive B cells). These follicles are unactivated and appear as small, round clusters.

* Secondary follicles: These form when B cells within the primary follicle are activated by antigenic stimulation. They are characterized by a germinal centre (where B cells proliferate and differentiate) and a mantle zone (where small, resting B cells surround the germinal centre).

* Mantle zone: A ring of small, naive B lymphocytes surrounding the germinal centre.

Paracortex (T-cell Zone)

* Situated between the cortex and the medulla, this area is rich in T lymphocytes, which are involved in T-cell mediated immunity.

* The paracortex also contains dendritic cells that present antigens to T cells and is crucial for T-cell dependent immune responses.

* This zone lacks follicles and is more densely populated with T cells.

Medulla

* The innermost part of the lymph node, containing medullary cords and medullary sinuses.

* Medullary cords: These are dense clusters of plasma cells, B cells, T cells, and macrophages that are responsible for producing antibodies and providing immune surveillance.

* Medullary sinuses: Spaces that allow the passage of lymph and contain macrophages that filter out foreign particles and pathogens.

Option A: The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

Option B: The main features that can be used to identify the spleen are:

* Capsule and trabeculae extending from it.

* Arterioles arising from the network of vessels that have branched from the splenic artery in the trabecular spaces.

* White pulp - composed of aggregation of lymphocytes arranged around an arteriole.

* Red pulp - areas between the white pulp and trabecular spaces regions where blood cells flow into.

* Sinusoids -blood from spaces of the red pulp is collected by wide sinusoids that drain into veins in the trabeculae.

Option C: The tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules, which are surrounded by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oropharyngeal surface. The epithelium dips into the substance of the gland and forms tonsillar crypts.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Patient underwent cholecystectomy and black pigmented gallstones were noticed. Which of the following is the least likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HbD Punjab

Pigmented gallstones are commonly found in chronic hemolytic syndromes such as sickle cell disease, HbH disease, and beta thalassemia minor, but not in HbD Punjab.

Hemoglobin D-Punjab (HbD Punjab), also known as Hemoglobin D-Los Angeles, is one of the most common hemoglobin variants worldwide. It is derived from a point mutation in the beta-globin gene. It is a normal variant and rarely presents as any clinical symptoms. Moreover, this variant can exist in association with other hemoglobinopathies such as thalassemias and sickle cell disease, which can lead to hemolysis. However, just a mere presence of HbD Punjab without associated hemoglobinopathies won't cause hemolysis or pigmented gallstones.

Any type of hemolytic anemia is a risk factor for the development of pigment gallstones.

There are two main types of gallstones:

* Cholesterol stones—which consist of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate

* Pigment stones—made of bilirubin calcium salts

Other Options:

Option A: In sickle cell anemia, HbS is present in which valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta chain. This results in a change in the shape of the RBCs from biconcave to sickle-shaped. This can cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones.

Option B: In HbH disease, excess β-globin chains form β4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with α-thalassemia. This may lead to pigmented gallstones due to hemolysis.

Option C: β-Thalassemia minor arises due to the deficient synthesis of β-chains. Normal adult RBCs have HbA, along with HbA2 and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in small amounts. There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. This can also cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyaline cartilage

The type of cartilage shown in the above image is hyaline cartilage.

On microscopy, hyaline cartilage can be identified by:

* Presence of chondrocytes within lacunae.

* Group of two or more chondrocytes which are known as isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests.

* Basophilic territorial matrix and pale interterritorial matrix

* Presence of perichondrium with outer fibrous and the inner cellular layer

Hyaline cartilage is made up of chondrocytes and matrix. The chondrocytes in the deeper matrix are rounded in shape and may appear in a group of eight that originate from the mitotic divisions of a single chondroblast. These groups of cells are called isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests. The important components of the matrix are type II collagen, aggrecan (proteoglycan) and chondronectin (glycoprotein). The matrix which immediately surrounds the chondrocytes is basophilic and is known as the territorial matrix and the matrix which are more distant from the cells appears pale and is known as the interterritorial matrix.

It is found in:

* Larger respiratory passages (nose, larynx, trachea and bronchi)

* Thyroid cartilage

* Cricoid cartilage

* Base of the arytenoid cartilage

* Ventral end of ribs where they articulate with the sternum

* The epiphyseal plate of long bones

* Articular cartilage of synovial joint

* Temporary skeleton in embryo

Other Options:

Option A: Articular cartilage despite being a type of hyaline cartilage lacks perichondrium.

Option B: The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein and the surface of elastic cartilage is covered by perichondrium.

Option D: The fibrocartilage is an intermediate between dense fibrous connective tissue (tendon and ligaments) and hyaline cartilage. It consists of bundles of collagen fibres (both type I and II) with rows of chondrocytes present between the bundles. They are not covered by perichondrium.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in irreversible cell injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Large amorphous densities in mitochondria

The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix is a feature of irreversible injury.

The presence of vacuoles and phospholipid-containing amorphous densities within mitochondria is typically a sign of irreversible injury, indicating a permanent loss of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.

Severe mitochondrial damage is marked by the influx of calcium ions and the formation of large flocculent densities within the mitochondria. These densities are typically observed in irreversibly injured myocardial cells following reperfusion after injury. Once mitochondrial damage becomes irreversible, cellular recovery is no longer possible.

Small amorphous densities are seen in reversible cell injury.

Reversible cell injury:

* Cellular swelling

* When there is adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion the sodium-potassium pump fails. Sodium and water accumulate within the cell.

* Fatty change

* Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism, e.g., liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells.

* Ultrastructure findings (seen on electron microscopy):

* Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities.

* Plasma membrane blebs (Option B).

* Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).

* Detachment of ribosomes (Option D).

* Nuclear changes: disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments and clumping of chromatin (Option C).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with complaints of hematuria, hypertension, and facial puffiness for 3 days. History reveals he had a throat infection 2 weeks back. Urine examination shows positivity for albumin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Group A beta hemolytic streptococci

The clinical scenario of hematuria, hypertension, and facial puffiness with past history of throat infection is suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma.

Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following:

* 1 to 2 weeks after an antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or

* 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma

The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens cause the immunologic injury.

In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see the following in most patients:

* Decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalize in 6 to 8 weeks)

* ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks)

Microscopic Findings in PSGN:

* Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration

* Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium.

* Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.

Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Group B beta-hemolytic streptococci (Option B) most commonly cause meningitis in neonates. They rarely present with glomerulonephritis

Staph aureus (Option c) causes soft tissue and musculoskeletal infections, infective endocarditis and respiratory infections. Glomerular involvement is rare

Staph epidermidis (Option d) is responsible for most of the prosthetic device associated infections like endocarditis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady presents to the OPD with complaints of fatigue. On examination, there is pallor. Blood investigations showed a hemoglobin of 10g/dl, RBC count of 3 million cells/mm cube, MCV = 70 fL, MCH = 22 pg. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical findings are consistent iron deficiency anemia

This patient has microcytic (N: 82-96 fL) and hypochromic (N: 27-33 pg) anemia. The differential diagnoses of microcytic hypochromic anemia include iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, and anemia of chronic disease. Since there is reduced RBC count (normal 4.5 to 6.5 milllion/cubic mm), the best answer is Iron deficiency anemia.

The single best test to differentiate between various diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anemia is iron profile.  Low Ferritin and high TIBC( total iron binding capacity) is seen in Iron deficiency anaemia, while Thalassemia major has normal/high ferritin and low/normal TIBC.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A girl with intellectual disability presents to the OPD with the following finding (image below). Cardiac evaluation shows a congenital endocardial cushion defect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Down's syndrome

The image shows simian crease. The clinical features of intellectual disability, congenital endocardial cushion defect point towards Down's syndrome

Down’s syndrome is an autosomal disorder. It was described by Langdon Down in 1866. It is also called trisomy 21 or mongolism. The clinical features of Down's syndrome seen in older children are: (Mnemonic: I C A PROBLEM Somewhere)

* Intellectual disability/Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly

* Congenital heart disease

* Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/Alzheimer's disease/Atlantoaxial instability/Atresia of the duodenum

* Protruding tongue

* Round face

* Occiput flat/Open wide fontanelle/Open mouth

* Brachycephalic/Brushfield's spots

* Low (depressed) nasal bridge

* Epicanthal fold/Ears low set and dysplastic

* Mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure)

* Simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes

Image: A child having features of Down’s syndrome

Image: Brushfield's spots

Simian crease is also seen in:

* Fetal alcohol syndrome

* Trisomy 13

* Cri du chat syndrome

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with ascites and edema. On examination, JVP was elevated. Gross examination finding of the tissue biopsy is shown. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-V congestion

The clinical vignette of ascites, and edema with elevated JVP points towards congestive hepatopathy. The image shows a nutmeg liver and chronic passive congestion of the liver. it usually occurs due to congestive heart failure.

Pathogenesis:

* It is seen in patients with chronic cardiac lesions, especially those affecting the right heart (e.g., right-sided heart failure), which causes the blood to be damped back into the inferior vena cava and then into the hepatic veins.

* This leads to increased pressure in the sublobular branches of the hepatic veins, which causes an engorgement of venous blood.

Gross appearance:

* In chronic passive hepatic congestion due to heart failure, the centrilobular regions are grossly red-brown due to congestion and slightly depressed (because of cell death) and are accentuated against the surrounding zones of uncongested tan liver (nutmeg liver).

* The appearance is called the nutmeg liver pattern due to its close resemblance with the cut surface of the nutmeg seed.

The image below liver with gross appearance as described above along with cut section of the nutmeg seed on top left corner.

Microscopic appearance:

Microscopic examination reveals centrilobular hemorrhage, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and variable degrees of hepatocyte dropout and necrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension,palpitations and sweating. His catecholamine and aldosterone levels were found to be elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The clinical vignette of hypertension, sweating and palpitation with elevated catecholamine levels point towards pheochromocytoma.

Pearl PF0334: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A pregnant couple presented to the OPD with concerns about thalassemia in their baby due to a positive family history. Genetic studies revealed that both she and her husband are carriers. What is the probability that the child will have thalassemia major?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 25%

There is 25% probability that their child will have thalassemia major.

β-thalassemia occurs due to mutations causing an impaired synthesis of β-globin chains of hemoglobin (Hb), leading to anemia, hypoxia, and hemolysis. The mutations can be of two types:

* Absent β chain synthesis (β0)

* Reduced β chain synthesis (β+)

Being an autosomal recessive disease, disease occurs only when both alleles are defective. When only one is defective, they are called carriers or trait. Here as both the parents are carriers, their alleles will be β/β0 or β/β+ (1 β-thalassemia allele and 1 normal allele). As the clinical disease doesn't alter much based on it being β+ or β0, its safe to use use β+ to represent a thalassemia allele.

β

β+

β+/β+

Thalassemia major means both alleles are mutated. And from the table, that can occur in one of the four ways possible. Hence the answer is 25%

Clinical syndromes of β-thalassemia depending on the genetic defect:

Major:

* Severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, basophilic stippling, and fragmented red cells (typical Hb: 3 to 6 g/dL), requiring regular blood transfusions

* Crewcut appearance of facial bones and skull (due to cortical bone erosion by expanding marrow and new bone formation)

* Speen, liver, and lymph node enlargement (due to extramedullary hematopoiesis)

Minor:

* More common

* Usually asymptomatic

* Mild microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells and basophilic stippling (important to rule out iron deficiency anemia by serum iron studies)

* Mild erythroid hyperplasia in bone marrow

A third clinical syndrome of moderate severity is called β-thalassemia intermedia. The genotype in this type includes milder variants of β+/β+ or β0/β+ and does not require regular transfusions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following carcinogens is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aflatoxins

Aflatoxin has high association with hepatocellular carcinoma.

Aflatoxins:

* These are a type of mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species of fungi, such as A. flavus (secretes B1) and A. parasiticus (secretes B1, B2, G1 and G2)

* Frequently present in moldy foods, like groundnuts, corn, and peas.

* These toxins are highly toxic to animals, birds, and human beings.

* Known to cause hepatomas in lower animals, and carcinogenic effects in humans have also been seen.

Risk factors for HCC

* HBV, HCV, aflatoxin, alcohol

* Hereditary hemochromatosis, α1AT deficiency, Wilson disease, metabolic syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Other options:

Option A: Arsenic is associated with carcinomas of the lung and skin

Option C: Asbestos is associated with carcinomas in lung, esophageal, gastric, and colon

Option D: Benzene is associated with leukemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is a mediator of chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TGF beta

TGF beta is a chronic inflammatory mediator.

Macrophages are the chief cells of chronic inflammation. The mediators secreted by activated macrophage is primal for the elimination of the trigger of inflammation but also for the deleterious effect on the body. There are 2 major pathways for macrophage activation.

* The classical pathway: triggered by the microbial products and mediated by T cell derived signals like IFN gamma. Activated macrophages will secrete NO and lysosomal enzymes to kill the microbe and promote the initial phase of inflammation

* The alternate pathway: Activated by other t-cell cytokines like IL 4, IL 13. They promote tissue fibrosis and repair via mediators like TGF beta

T cells too play an important role in chronic inflammation. CD4 T cells secrete cytokines and promote the inflammation.

* Th1 secrete cytokine IFN γ to activate macrophages

* Th2 secrete IL 4, IL 5, IL 13 for recruiting eosinophils.

* Th16 along with Th1 involved in response against microbes and in autoimmune diseases

T cells and macrophages act in a bidirectional way, activating each other and continuing the cycle of damage and repair.

The cytokines TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are important mediators of the acute-phase reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is false regarding papillary thyroid cancer?
options: Most common age group is between 30- 50 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcitonin is the tumour marker

The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) . It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50 (option a). Radiation exposure (option c) and a family history of thyroid malignancies are common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion.

Histopathology shows the following features:

* Branching papillae

* Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin

* Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane

* Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae.

Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen.

Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows:

Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as

* Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection

* Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection

For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient.

Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).

The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks.

A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.

A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following inhibits ferroportin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IL-6

IL-6 inhibits ferroportin.

It is an inflammatory mediator  It stimulates the production of hepcidin from the liver and thereby inhibits ferroportin.

Dietary iron is available in two forms - heme and non-heme iron. Initially, the ferric non-heme iron is reduced to ferrous iron by duodenal cytochrome B (ferric reductase) or by vitamin C. The reduced ferrous iron is then transferred into the enterocyte by DMT 1 (divalent metal transporter).

Heme iron moves into the cytoplasm with the help of transporters. Here, it is metabolized to release ferrous iron, which then follows the same pathway as non-heme iron.

Once inside the enterocyte, it can either get stored as ferritin or transferred across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin. In the plasma, iron is transported in the Fe3+ form bound to transferrin, which is a transport protein. Hephaestin is a ferroxidase that oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ before it is transported.

Hepcidin, an acute-phase protein secreted from the liver plays a major role in the regulation of iron absorption. When the body’s iron stores are adequate it downregulates the expression of ferroportin and thereby iron absorption too. Thus, iron is trapped in the intestinal cells which is eventually sloughed off. Hepcidin also inhibits the release of iron from macrophages by binding to ferroportin. High hepcidin levels are seen in systemic inflammation and low hepcidin levels are seen in hemochromatosis

Iron is an important component of

* Hemoglobin

* Myoglobin

* Cytochrome P450 groups of enzymes

* Components of the electron transport chain

* Ribonucleotide reductase

Given below is an image of iron absorption that shows ferroportin being inhibited by hepcidin at intestinal mucosal cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a sign of irreversible injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blebbing plasma membrane

Blebbing of plasma membrane is a feature of reversible injury

Within limits, a cell can repair derangements and, if the injurious stimulus abates, will return to normalcy. This is called reversible cell injury. Persistent or excessive injury, however, causes cells to pass the rather nebulous “point of no return” into irreversible injury and cell death.

The ultrastructural changes of reversible cell injury include:

* Plasma membrane alterations, such as blebbing, blunting, and loss of microvilli

* Mitochondria - swelling and the appearance of small amorphous densities

* Dilation of the ER, with the detachment of polysomes

* Intracytoplasmic myelin figures

* Nuclear alterations- disaggregation of granular and fibrillar elements

Irreversible cell injury

* Increased eosinophilia, glassy homogeneous appearance

* Whorled phospholipid masses called myelin figures derived from damaged cell membranes

* Discontinuities in plasma and organelle membranes

* Marked dilation of mitochondria with the appearance of large amorphous densities

* Intracytoplsmic amorphous debris, and aggregates of fluffy material probably representing denatured protein.

* Nuclear changes- karyolysis, pyknosis and karyorrhexis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following thyroid neoplasia arise from the parafollicular c cells of thyroid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medullary carcinoma of thyroid

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells. Most of MTC are sporadic. Some are associated with inheritable syndromes like familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B, all of which are secondary to RET gene mutations.

Most patients present at 50–60 years and have a female preponderance. It is characterised by the secretion of ACTH, calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).

Features of MTC

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea if there is local invasion

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Blood-borne metastasis

Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma. Raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass, help in diagnosis.

Pearl PF0940: Follicular thyroid malignancy

More common in iodine-deficient areas

Mean age of presentation is 50 years

Commonly present as solitary thyroid nodules

FNAC is unable to distinguish between benign and malignant follicular lesions

Malignancy is defined by capsular and vascular invasion

Associated with P53, PTEN, PAX/PPAR-gamma, RAS

miRNA (miR-197 and miR-346) are associated with follicular carcinoma

Histology:

* Usually solitary lesion

* Encapsulated

* Has uniform micro follicles or sheets of cells devoid of colloid

* Capsular and vascular invasion indicates malignancy

* Tumor thrombus within middle thyroid/ jugular veins may be seen at the time of surgery

Vascular (hematogenous) dissemination is common, with metastases to bone, lungs, liver, and elsewhere.

The prognosis depends largely on the extent of invasion and stage at presentation.

Serum thyroglobulin levels are used for monitoring tumor recurrence because this thyroid protein should be barely detectable in a patient who is free of disease.

Pearl PF0284: Papillary thyroid carcinoma

* Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid carcinoma.

* Most common in iodine sufficient areas, children and in those exposed to ionizing radiation.

* Mean age of presentation is 3rd-4th decade; more common in women than men (2:1)

* Usually cold nodule on the scan

* Branching papillae and follicles with the fibrovascular stalk, Psammoma bodies

* Nuclear changes: Optically clear - Ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei, pseudo-inclusions, nuclear grooves.

* Lymph node metastasis is common

* Lateral aberrant thyroid denotes a cervical lymph node invaded by papillary carcinoma.

* Dysphagia, dysphonia and dyspnea are associated with local invasion

* Most common sites of metastasis : lung > liver > bone > brain

* Excellent prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate in excess of 95%.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presented with cough for 15 days. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the lymph node biopsy showed the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The histopathological findings and clinical history are suggestive of tuberculosis.

Once Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters the macrophage, it inhibits the formation of the phagolysosome. This allows it to replicate unchecked. M. tuberculosis recruits a host protein coronin to block the fusion of phagosome and lysosome. Th1 response to M. tuberculosis is mounted about three weeks following the infection. The antigen-presenting cells (APCs) present mycobacterial antigens to the T-cells in the lymph nodes and release IL-12 and IL-18 to cause the differentiation of T-cells into Th1 cells. Th1 cells produce IFN-γ. IFN-γ is the critical step in the body's defense against M. tuberculosis. It acts by activating macrophages, causing phagolysosome maturation, and inducing nitric oxide synthase enzyme to form more reactive nitrogen species. It also mobilizes anti-bacterial compounds like defensins and stimulates autophagy.

Th1 response leads to the formation of a granuloma and caseous necrosis. Macrophages that are activated by the action of IFN-γ differentiate into epithelioid histiocytes. These are the cells that actually aggregate to form a granuloma. Some epithelioid cells may also fuse to form a giant cell.

The microscopic picture shows the caseating granuloma. Eosinophilic necrotic debris known as caseation, bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhan giant cells and lymphocytes can be seen. Epitheloid cells merge to form Langhan's giant cell where nuclei are arranged in a horseshoe shape (a characteristic feature of tuberculosis).

Clinically, tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, breathing difficulty, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Chest radiograph shows tree-in-bud pattern, infiltrates, and cavity formation predominantly in the upper lobes.

Other options:

Option B: Leprosy presents with skin lesions and nerve involvement with loss of sensation. Histopathology shows noncaseating granulomas.

Option C: Sarcoidosis shows giant cells with cytoplasmic inclusions and noncaseating granuloma with fibroblastic proliferation at the periphery.

Option D: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that shows hyperplasia of the capsule accompanied by fibrosis, perivascular inflammation, and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells with caseating granulomas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with café-au-lait macules and lisch nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis? NF- Neurofibromatosis TSC- Tuberous sclerosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NF-1

The diagnosis of the patient with café-au-lait macules and lisch nodules is Neurofibromatosis- 1.

Neurofibromatosis (NF) is an autosomal dominant disorder. NF type 1 (NF-1) is the most prevalent type and is caused by loss of function mutation of the NF-1 gene. The protein affected is neurofibromin. NF-I is also known as von Recklinghausen's disease.

NF1 is clinically diagnosed when any 2 of the following 7 features are present:

* Six or more café-au-lait macules

* Axillary or inguinal freckling

* Two or more iris lisch nodules

* Two or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma.

* A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia

* Optic gliomas

* A first-degree relative with NF-1

The image below shows axillary freckling and café-au-lait spots seen in NF-1.

Other options:

Option B: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2) is a disorder characterized by the growth of noncancerous tumors in the nervous system. The most common tumors associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 are called vestibular schwannomas or acoustic neuromas. The protein affected is Merlin

Options C and D: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC-1 & TSC-2) is also known as tuberous sclerosis complex or Bourneville disease. It is a neurocutaneous disorder (phakomatosis) characterized by the development of multiple benign tumors of the embryonic ectoderm (e.g. skin, eyes, and nervous system). It is an autosomal dominant condition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with colicky abdominal pain, joint pain and palpable purpura. Urine analysis shows only red blood cells with no other significant findings. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgA vasculitis

The given clinical presentation of palpable purpura, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria point towards a diagnosis of IgA vasculitis also known as Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP).

It is a small vessel vasculitis that occurs due to IgA immune complex deposition within the wall of the blood vessels. It is commonly seen in children and is characterized by:

* Palpable purpura without thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy.

* Arthralgia- commonly affecting the hip, knee, or ankle joints.

* Abdominal pain

* Glomerulonephritis: proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, RBC casts in urine.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP

The skin biopsy will show small vessel vasculitis, with IgA and C3 deposition in the affected organs by immunofluorescence.

Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone are used for the treatment of gastrointestinal manifestations in HSP. Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine.

Other options:

Option B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) is characterized by vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels. It affects the upper respiratory tract (ear, nose, sinuses, and throat), lower respiratory tract (lung), and kidney and is characterized by necrotizing granuloma which is non-caseating.

Option C: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels. It occurs most commonly in elderly males. Patients can present with non-constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and musculoskeletal pain. Renal involvement is very common (79%) in the form of glomerulonephritis, which can rapidly progress, causing renal failure. Lab findings include anemia, raised ESR and or CRP, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and ANCA positive in 75% of patients,

Option D: Behcet's disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Here (Th17) T helper 17 cells play an important contribution in the recruitment of neutrophils, which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents to the haematologist with complaints of weakness and fatigue. Lab investigations reveal a decrease in the haemoglobin and reticulocyte count while WBC and platelet counts are normal. Bone marrow shows a selective decrease in the erythroid precursors. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pure red cell aplasia

The given scenario along with lab investigations showing a decrease in haemoglobin and reticulocyte count, normal WBC, and platelet count with a selective decrease in the erythroid precursors are suggestive of pure red cell aplasia.

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a primary marrow disorder that causes the suppression of erythroid progenitors only. One cause is acute parvovirus B19 infection which may lead to an aplastic crisis in patients who already had underlying hemolytic anemia. The hallmark of PRCA, in an otherwise normal marrow, is the absence of erythroblasts.

Causes of pure red cell aplasia include:

* Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia

* Drug exposure - phenytoin, azathioprine, and isoniazid

* Auto-immune disorders - neutralizing antibodies against erythropoietin

* Parvovirus infection

* Hereditary - Diamond Blackfan syndrome

Patients typically present with symptoms of severe anemia such as fatigue, pallor, and dyspnea. Complete blood count (CBC) shows normocytic or macrocytic anemia with very low reticulocyte count. Bone marrow examination reveals normal cellularity but with a marked reduction or absence of erythroid precursors. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping can be useful in diagnosing associated conditions such as thymoma or lymphoproliferative disorders.

Immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay for idiopathic PRCA, including agents like cyclosporine, corticosteroids, and antithymocyte globulin (ATG). For PRCA associated with parvovirus B19, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is used.

Other options:

Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by folate or vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia). Peripheral smear shows characteristic macro-ovalocytic red cells that appear hyperchromic, hypersegmented nuclei in neutrophils, and reticulocytopenia. Marrow is markedly hypercellular due to an increase in the number of hematopoietic precursors.

Option B: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common nutritional disorder in the world. Peripheral smears show microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. Bone marrow shows an increase in erythroid progenitors. A significant diagnostic finding is an absence of stainable iron in macrophages which is assessed by Prussian blue stain on aspirated marrow smears.

Option C: Aplastic anemia is a chronic primary hematological failure that results in pancytopenia. Clinically, the patients present with features of pancytopenia such as fatigue, recurrent infections, and petechiae and ecchymoses. Characteristically, splenomegaly will be absent.

A peripheral smear will show reticulocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirates often give a 'dry tap' which means that they yield little material. Thus, a marrow biopsy would show a markedly hypocellular marrow that is devoid of hematopoietic cells (some fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes or plasma cells remain).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with a history of fever and weight loss presented with cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy revealed granulomatous necrotizing inflammation. Which of the following statements is true with respect to the patient's condition?
options: Metastatic calcification with normal serum calcium level
Metastatic calcification with increased serum calcium level
Dystrophic calcification with normal serum calcium level
Dystrophic calcification with increased serum calcium level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dystrophic calcification with normal serum calcium level

The given clinical history of fever, weight loss, and cervical lymphadenopathy showing granulomatous necrotizing inflammation suggests the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Dystrophic calcification with normal serum calcium level is seen in tuberculosis.

Dystrophic calcification is encountered in areas of necrosis, whether they are of coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive type and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.

Calcification is almost always present in the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis. It also commonly develops in aging or damaged heart valves, further hampering their function. Calcium salts appear macroscopically as fine, white granules or clumps, often felt as gritty deposits.

Although dystrophic calcification may simply be a telltale sign of previous cell injury, it is often a cause of organ dysfunction. Serum calcium is normal in dystrophic calcification.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient on immunosuppressive therapy presents with a cough, fever and pneumonitis. Urine examination shows the following basophilic inclusion bodies. Which of the following organisms is responsible for the infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cytomegalovirus

The most likely causative agent is cytomegalovirus (CMV) based on the clinical symptoms of immunosuppression and the presence of the owl's eye appearance on urinary examination.

A cytomegalic pneumocyte containing characteristic intranuclear basophilic inclusion surrounded by a clear halo known as an owl’s eye appearance.

CMV is the largest virus in the herpes family of viruses. It causes the following conditions:

* Immunocompetent individuals - asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like infection such as fever and rash

* Neonates - devastating systemic infections

* Immunosuppressed individuals - serious, life-threatening, disseminated CMV infections of the lungs (pneumonitis) and gastrointestinal tract (colitis)

CMV spreads through contact with salivary secretions and sexual contact, blood transfusion, and organ transplantation.

Laboratory diagnosis is by recovery of the virus from urine, saliva, or other bodily fluids into human fibroblast cells. Antibody demonstration using ELISA is used for diagnosis of primary infection.

Other options:

Option B: Epstein Barr virus: Conditions associated with EBV infection are

* Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis): fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy

* Hodgkin lymphoma

* Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

* Burkitt's lymphoma

* Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

* EBV‐associated lymphoproliferative disease

Option C: Herpes simplex virus causes cutaneous infections like herpes labialis caused by viral reactivation in febrile patients. It presents as blisters around the mouth, cheeks, and forehead. Gingivostomatitis and pharyngitis are the most frequent manifestations of primary herpes infections. HSV esophagitis presents as dysphagia, sub-sternal pain, and weight loss.

Option D: Toxoplasma gondii causes Acute congenital toxoplasmosis may manifest as fever, jaundice, petechial rashes, microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, myocarditis, cerebral calcifications, and chorioretinitis.

Most infections in adults who are immunocompetent are usually asymptomatic. Active progression of infection is more likely in immunocompromised individuals.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with cleft lip, cleft palate and mental retardation. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patau syndrome

The given findings of cleft lip, cleft palate with mental retardation in a child are consistent with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).

Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities. Patients can develop holoprosencephaly, which is characterized by fused frontal lobes and a single ventricle. Olfactory bulbs are also absent. The midline facial abnormalities seen with trisomy 13 include cleft lip, cleft palate, mental retardation, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, renal defects, and congenital heart diseases.

The image below shows some facial features of Patau syndrome:

Other options:

Option A: Prader-Willi syndrome occurs due to the deletion of band 15q12 on the paternal chromosome and the silencing of the same set of genes derived from maternal chromosomes. It is characterized by mental retardation, obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism, short stature, small hands and feet.

Option C: Angelman syndrome is characterized by the deletion of the ubiquitin ligase gene (UBE3A) on maternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the paternal chromosomal counterpart. It is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter. Due to inappropriate laughter and ataxia, they are also known as happy puppets.

Option D: Trisomy 18 or Edwards syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart diseases. The most characteristic finding is a clenched fist with overlapping fingers: the index finger overlies the third and fourth fingers, while the fifth finger overlaps the fourth. It is also associated with polyhydramnios and a single umbilical artery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. He had similar episodes in the past along with steatorrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Which of the following types of necrosis is seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat necrosis

The given clinical history of a chronic alcoholic patient presenting with abdominal pain and vomiting and similar complaints in the past with steatorrhea, weight loss, and fatigue is suggestive of chronic pancreatitis. Fat necrosis is seen in such patients.

Fat necrosis refers to the destruction of fat tissue due to various reasons like injury, surgery, etc. Examples of fat necrosis include pancreatitis, breast trauma, and panniculitis.

In pancreatitis, there is a release of activated pancreatic lipases into the substance of the pancreas and the peritoneal cavity. These enzymes act on surrounding tissue to release fatty acids, which then combine with calcium to produce grossly visible chalky-white areas (fat saponification). Histologic examination reveals foci of necrotic fat cells, with basophilic calcium deposits, surrounded by an inflammatory reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Celiac disease

Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with celiac disease.

Dermatitis herpetiformis, also known as Duhring’s disease is an auto-immune disease associated with HLA DQ-2 and HLA DQ-8. The antibodies target epidermal transglutaminase-3, resulting in the collection of neutrophils at the dermal papilla. This condition is closely associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy).

The clinical manifestations include grouped vesicles and papules. These lesions are commonly located over the extensor aspects of knees, elbows, buttocks, back, and scalp with symmetrical distribution and are associated with intense pruritus.

The characteristic histopathology finding is subepidermal blisters with papillary tip microabscesses containing neutrophils, which is shown in the image below:

The image below shows dermatitis herpetiformis on the knee.

Dermatitis herpetiformis targets epidermal transglutaminase 3. Direct immunofluorescence shows focal granular deposits of IgA at papillary tips.

A gluten-free diet is the mainstay of treatment, but it takes months to years to show clinical improvement. Hence, dapsone is used for short-term management in these patients.

Other Options:

Options A & D: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease are chronic inflammatory bowel diseases that are mainly idiopathic with a weak genetic component. The common cutaneous manifestations include erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, psoriasis, aphthous stomatitis, and cutaneous vasculitis.

Options B: Whipple's disease is a chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, classically presents as chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, intermittent fever, weight loss, and arthralgia/arthritis with neurological and cardiological involvement. The morphologic hallmark of Whipple disease is a dense accumulation of distended, foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria. Macrophages contain periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive, diastase-resistant granules that represent lysosomes stuffed with partially digested bacteria.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following blood groups can be given to a patient having Bombay blood group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oh

Among the given options, Oh (Bombay) blood group blood can be transfused to Bombay blood group patients.

The H antigen is present in all four blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). A rare blood group where there is an absence of the H antigen is known as the Bombay blood group. The absence of this H antigen results in the absence of A and B antigens. Their plasma contains anti-A, anti-B, and strong anti-H antibodies. Therefore, they do not react with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-AB antiserums, and get recognized as O blood group on cell typing.

However, the O blood group has an H antigen. Thus if a patient with the Bombay blood group is transfused with the O blood group blood, the anti-H antibodies in the Bombay blood group patient react with the H antigen present in the O blood group. This can lead to fatal transfusion reactions. Therefore, patients with the Bombay blood group require the same blood group during transfusion.

Other less common systems of blood grouping include MNSs, Lutheran, Kell, and Kidd systems of blood grouping.

ABO blood typing is performed by mixing the individual's red blood cells with antisera that contains the various agglutinins on a slide and observing for the presence of clumping or agglutination.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following clinical condition is a hexanucleotide repeat disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a hexanucleotide repeat disorder.

The C9ORF72 gene is associated with a hexanucleotide repeat expansion mutation. It is a common cause of both FTD and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The mutation leads to the production of abnormal RNA and proteins, causing cellular toxicity.

Frontotemporal dementia presents with early personality changes (frontal lobe involvement) and loss of social restraints initially, followed by memory loss. Other features include loss of insight, easy distractibility, reduced concern or empathy for others, emotional lability or withdrawal, impulsiveness, poor self-care, and perseveration.

There is a second type of presentation of FTD, which is characterized by an early and progressive change in language, with problems of expression of language or severe naming difficulty, and problems with word meaning.

The classic imaging findings seen in FTD are preferential atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with occipitoparietal sparing

Histopathology shows Pick cells (swollen neurons) in affected areas of the brain. These neurons appear larger than normal and are typically filled with cytoplasmic inclusions known as Pick bodies (intraneuronal argentophilic inclusions).

Other options:

Option B: Fragile X syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability in males. It occurs due to CGG repeats in the untranslated regions(UTR) of the FMR1 gene.

Option C: Huntington's disease is a degenerative disease of the caudate and putamen caused by an autosomal dominant inheritance of a trinucleotide repeat (CAG) in the Huntington gene (chromosome 4), which results in motor, behavioral, oculomotor, and cognitive dysfunction.

Option D: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by expansions of CTG triplet repeats in the noncoding region of the myotonic dystrophy protein kinase (DMPK) gene.  It is associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary lymphoid organ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymus

Thymus and bone marrow are the primary lymphoid organs (also known as central lymphoid organs). It is the place where immature lymphocytes develop, differentiate, proliferate, and mature into immune competent cells.

A secondary lymphoid organ (also known as a peripheral lymphoid organ) is where the antigen is localized so that it can be effectively exposed to mature lymphocytes. These include the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, appendix, and Peyer’s patches.

Both B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow. B lymphocytes also mature in bone marrow, while T lymphocytes mature in Thymus.

Given below is the histopathological image of the thymus.

The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a tumor marker for carcinoid tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid

The tumor marker for carcinoid tumors is 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid.

The carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine tumors arising from enterochromaffin cells that can occur anywhere in the GIT. The most common site is the appendix followed by the ileum and rectum. A tumor with liver metastasis is likely to produce carcinoid syndrome. The image below shows the histopathologic appearance of carcinoid tumors.

The diagnosis is made by assessing 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) in a 24-hour urine sample. Ultrasonography, CT scan, and MRI may show the primary tumor and metastases. The best method for staging carcinoid tumors is by octreotide scan or somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS).

Somatostatin and its analogs are used in the symptomatic treatment of carcinoid syndrome. Surgery should be undertaken as soon as the diagnosis is made, even in the presence of liver metastases.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is decreased in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Albumin

Albumin, an acute-phase reactant, is decreased in acute inflammation.

Inflammation leads to changes in the levels of certain proteins known as acute phase reactants (APRs), which are regulated by cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6). These changes support the body's defensive and adaptive functions.

APRs are classified as positive and negative based on whether their levels increase or decrease in inflammatory states, respectively.

Positive APRs
Negative APRs

•  C-reactive protein (CRP)
• Hepcidin
• Ferritin
• Serum amyloid A (SAA)
• Fibrinogen
• Haptoglobin

• Transthyretin
• Albumin
• Transferrin

APR levels are nonspecific and do not point to any particular disease. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is an indirect measure of APR levels, particularly influenced by the level of fibrinogen in the blood.

questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication of splenectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow failure

Among the given options, bone marrow failure is not an indication of splenectomy.

Overall, the most common indication for splenectomy is trauma to the spleen, whether external (blunt or penetrating) or iatrogenic (e.g., during operative procedures for other reasons).

The most common indication for:

* Elective splenectomy - Haematological disorders such as hereditary spherocytosis, Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), etc.

* Emergency splenectomy - Trauma

* Splenectomy (overall) - Trauma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following tests can be done for measuring long-term glucose control in patients with diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HbA1c

In patients with diabetes mellitus, HbA1c is the best method to measure long-term glucose control.

Glycated haemoglobin, reported as HbA1c, has been used to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes for many years. HbA1c results from the attachment of glucose to the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain.

The concentration of HbA1c depends on both the glucose concentration in the blood and the lifespan of the erythrocyte.

Since the half-life of an RBC is 120 days, the HbA1c test is primarily used to evaluate the average blood glucose levels over the past 3 months. Normal glucose tolerance is characterised by an HbA1c < 5.7%; any value of HbA1c equal to or exceeding 6.5 % is diagnostic of the patient being diabetic.

Other options:

Fasting blood sugar, random blood sugar, and urine sugar reflect the status of blood glucose level at the instantaneous moment.

questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with a fever and lymphadenopathy. On an H&E stain, a biopsy reveals hallmark cells. An anaplastic large cell lymphoma diagnosis is made. Which translocation is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. t(2:5)

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is frequently associated with the t(2;5) (p23;q35). The biopsy shows characteristic large anaplastic cells, some containing horseshoe-shaped nuclei and voluminous cytoplasm called hallmark cells.

It is a type of T-cell lymphoma that consists of large lymphoid cells. This occurs due to rearrangements in the ALK gene and usually affects children and young adults. It frequently involves soft tissue and carries a good prognosis. T-cell lymphomas with similar morphology without ALK positivity occur in older adults and have a bad prognosis. The genetic defect is found on chromosome 2p23 that results in the production of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) with tyrosine kinase activity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and hypertension. A cerebellar lesion is visible on MRI, and abdominal imaging reveals multiple cysts in the kidneys as well as a solid renal mass, which is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. His father had similar findings and died of a brain tumour in his 40s. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely to cause his condition?

Correct answer: B. Deletion on chromosome 3p

The given clinical scenario of multiple renal cysts, cerebellar lesion, visual disturbances, and hypertension with a family history is most likely to be von Hippel-Lindau disease, which is characterized by deletion on chromosome 3p.

The tumor-suppressor gene VHL, which is linked to von Hippel-Lindau disease, is found on chromosome 3p. It produces a protein called VHL, which is a part of a ubiquitin ligase complex that inhibits hypoxia-induced factor 1 (HIF-1).

It is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by the development of highly vascularized tumors in multiple organs. These include:

* Hemangioblastomas of the retina and central nervous system

* Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

* Pheochromocytoma

* Renal cysts develop into clear renal cell cancer

* Pancreatic cysts

* Ovary cystadenoma

* Epididymal cystadenoma

Those with VHL syndrome inherit an autosomal dominant germline mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. A "second hit" can lead to manifestations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of heartburn and regurgitation of food for the past few years. Endoscopy and biopsy results reveal red, velvety mucosa admixed with white mucosa, along with the presence of goblet cells. Which of the following epithelial transformations will be observed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squamous to intestinal columnar epithelium

This patient's clinical features and biopsy findings are suggestive of Barrett's oesophagus, which is characterised by epithelial transformation from squamous to intestinal columnar epithelium above the gastro-oesophageal junction.

Microscopically, it is seen as the replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells. The greatest concern in Barrett's oesophagus is that it confers an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and it is estimated to occur in about 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD.

Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and sometimes dysphagia. Obese white men over the age of 60 years represent the highest-risk group. On endoscopy, Barrett's is recognised as areas of red, velvety mucosa extending proximally from the gastro-oesophageal junction. Such areas alternate with normal pale squamous esophageal mucosa. Diagnostic confirmation is by endoscopic biopsy. A biopsy reveals intestinal metaplasia characterised by the presence of goblet cells. Goblet cells are seen as cells with pale mucous vacuoles that stain blue.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient presented to the ER with severe bleeding following a road traffic accident. As an intern, you were asked to collect blood for coagulation studies. Which color Vacutainer will you pick?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Light blue

The most commonly used Vacutainer for coagulation studies is a light blue vacutainer containing trisodium citrate.

Other anticoagulants, including oxalate (grey), heparin (green), and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (lavender), are unacceptable for coagulation studies. The labile factors (factors V and VIII) are unstable in oxalate, whereas heparin and EDTA directly inhibit the coagulation process and interfere with end-point determinations.

Additional benefits of trisodium citrate are that the calcium ion is neutralized more rapidly in citrate, and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests are more sensitive to the presence of heparin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with progressive anaemia and cervical lymphadenopathy. The peripheral smear is shown below. Which CD markers will be present in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which is positive for CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+.

Loss of tumour-suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non-specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients.

The chromosomal defects in CLL include

* Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)

* Deletion of 11q

* Trisomy 12q

* Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic features of CLL are CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates, which are referred to as proliferation centres. These proliferation centres are pathognomonic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

Other options:

Option A: CD10, CD22, and CD79 are positive in Burkitt lymphoma.

Option B: CD10, CD19, and CD22 are positive in follicular lymphoma.

Option D: CD10, CD19, and CD79 are positive in pre-B cell acute lymphoid leukaemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A male diabetic patient's radiological examinations reveal a solid organ lesion. On HPE, liquefactive necrosis can be observed. What is the primary mechanism responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enzymatic degradation

Liquefactive necrosis refers to cell death caused by enzymatic degradation.

It involves the digestion of dead cells, transforming the tissue into a viscous liquid. It occurs in focal bacterial or, on occasion, fungal infections because microbes stimulate the accumulation of leukocytes and the release of enzymes from these cells.

Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali. It is associated with liquefactive necrosis. Unlike other mineral acids, hydrofluoric acid (HF) causes liquefactive necrosis due to the formation of fluoride ions. Pseudomonas – produce an irregular sharp ulcer with thick greenish mucopurulent exudate, diffuse liquefactive necrosis, and semiopaque (ground glass) surrounding the cornea.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A newborn presents with upward-slanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, and hypotonia. A 5p deletion is detected through karyotyping. Which of the following genetic syndromes result from the deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cri-du-chat syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Cri-du-chat syndrome.

Cri du Chat syndrome, also known as 5p- syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deletion of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p). The syndrome is named after the characteristic high-pitched cry of affected infants, which resembles a cat's meow due to abnormal laryngeal development. Other key clinical features include microcephaly, low birth weight, micrognathia (small jaw), low-set ears, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and intellectual disabilities. Affected children often experience developmental delays, speech difficulties, and behavioral challenges. The severity varies depending on the size of the chromosomal deletion.

In addition to the physical and cognitive impairments, individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome may have congenital heart defects, scoliosis, and feeding difficulties. While there is no cure, early intervention with speech therapy, physical therapy, and educational support can improve quality of life and functional abilities. The condition is typically diagnosed through genetic testing, such as karyotyping or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), to detect the deletion on chromosome 5. With proper medical care and supportive therapies, many individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome can achieve a degree of independence and lead fulfilling lives.

Option D: Edward's syndrome is caused by trisomy 18.
