questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young boy presents with joint swelling following a fall. Laboratory tests reveal a normal PT and an elevated aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemophilia

This patient with a history of joint swelling on minor trauma and an abnormal coagulation panel points to a probable diagnosis of haemophilia.

This condition is caused by an X-linked recessive mutation leading to a deficiency of Factor VIII of the coagulation factors. This leads to a prolonged partial thromboplastin time. Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and thus the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug.

Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular haematomas, haemarthroses, haematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. Retroperitoneal haemorrhages can accumulate large volumes of blood and may cause hypovolemic shock.

Laboratory findings in haemophilia:

* Factor VIII – reduced

* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) - prolonged

* Platelet count – normal

* Bleeding time – normal

* Prothrombin time – normal

Other options:
Option B: von Willebrand disease often shows an elevated aPTT and normal PT, but the bleeding time is increased.
Option C: IDA would show low haemoglobin and iron, not coagulation abnormalities.
Option D: Platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard–Soulier syndrome, etc.) often have a normal aPTT.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy presents to OPD with a tremor and jerky movements, difficulty in speech, and behavioural changes. The workup revealed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly and a golden brown ring at the limbus of the cornea on slit lamp examination. Which of the following is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatic copper content

The clinical features of hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring, and difficulty with speech, movements and behaviour are suggestive of Wilson's disease. The most sensitive and accurate test in diagnosing Wilson's disease is measuring the hepatic copper content.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is a golden to greenish-brown ring of deposition of copper in the Descemet's membrane of the peripheral cornea. Patients with neurological manifestations manifest with KF rings in >95% of cases.

The diagnosis of Wilson's disease is based on the following:

* Increased 24-hour urinary excretion of copper (the most specific screening test)

* Increase in hepatic copper content (the most sensitive and accurate test)

* A decrease in serum ceruloplasmin

* Kayser–Fleischer rings

* Genetic testing for mutations in the ATP7B gene

Serum copper levels are of no diagnostic use since they may be low, normal, or elevated depending on the stage of the disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An electrician sustains electrical burns while at work. On arrival at the ED, he was hemodynamically stable. ECG monitoring and initial fluid resuscitation are started. His urine is collected for routine lab examination and is positive for myoglobin. On histopathology of the kidneys, which of the following will be observed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metastatic calcification

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is a case of rhabdomyolysis leading to endogenous intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI). In rhabdomyolysis with AKI, calcium-phosphate imbalance leads to metastatic calcification in normal renal tissue, especially interstitium.

* Metastatic calcification can occur in normal tissues whenever there is hypercalcemia.

* The major causes of hypercalcemia are

* Secretion of parathyroid hormone -related protein (PTHRP), due to malignant tumors

* Paget's disease, immobilization, or tumors (increased bone catabolism associated with multiple myeloma, leukemia, or skeletal metastases)

* Vitamin D intoxication and sarcoidosis

* Renal failure

* Metastatic calcification can occur throughout the body but mainly affects the interstitial tissues of the vasculature, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa.

AKI is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features, such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories:

* Renal/intrinsic parenchymal

* Prerenal

* Postrenal

Other options:

Option A: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in conditions like vasculitis(immune mediated), malignant hypertension.

Option B: Caseous necrosis - characteristic of granulomatous infections like tuberculosis.

Option C: Dystrophic calcification:

* It is encountered in areas of necrosis, whether they are of coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive type, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.

* Calcification is almost always present in the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis. It also commonly develops in ageing or damaged heart valves, further hampering their function

* Calcium salts appear macroscopically as fine, white granules or clumps, often felt as gritty deposits

* Tuberculous lymph nodes can be affected by this

* Serum calcium is normal in dystrophic calcification.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Of the following, which gene mutation is most frequently linked to medullary thyroid carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RET

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is most commonly associated with MEN2A and MEN2B, which occur due to mutation in the RET gene.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a tumour of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies. Most of the MTCs occur sporadically. However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.

Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age, whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age. Features of MTC include:

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Metastasis is blood-borne

* Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma

It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib.

Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5 years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1 year of age in MEN2B mutation.

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + level VI LN involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (therapeutic) + Modified radical neck dissection (prophylactic)

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection + Modified radical neck dissection (therapeutic)

questions.text: Which hypersensitivity reaction mediates blood transfusion reactions?

Correct answer: B. Type II

Type II hypersensitivity reactions mediate blood transfusion reactions.

There are 3 mechanisms involved in type 2 hypersensitivity reactions—

* Antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction—antibodies react with antigens present on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix cause disease by destroying these cells, triggering inflammation, or interfering with normal functions

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following fixatives is most appropriate in Pap smear cytology for preserving cellular details immediately after smearing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 95% ethanol

In a Pap smear, 95% ethanol is used to preserve cellular details immediately after smearing.

A Pap, or Papanicolaou, test is a screening test only. A positive test requires further evaluation with colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage. Specific history to be elicited from patients prior to collection of sample:

* The ideal time for the collection of a sample is around ovulation. Cervical squamous cells vary in appearance throughout the menstrual cycle. Thus, asking the patient for their last menstrual period and any use of contraception is a must.

* A prerequisite for a Pap smear is that the patient should avoid intercourse 24 hours prior to the test. Thus, this history should be taken.

* The use of lubricants and douches may prevent the detection of organisms and the cell structure. Thus, asking the patient for this history is a must to prevent missing appropriate findings.

* A history of immunosuppression must be elicited, including a family history of cancer, use of steroids, sexual history for STDs, and HIV/AIDS. In women with such a history, an annual checkup should be advised instead of once every three years.

* The use of intravaginal contraceptive creams should be stopped 24-48 hours before the test. The use of exogenous hormones and intrauterine devices may alter the appearance of cervical squamous cells. Hence, this history should be noted for an accurate interpretation of the test.

Screening guidelines:

* Time for initiation – 21 years, regardless of the age of first sexual intercourse

* Women aged 21-29 years - every 3 years

* Women who are aged 30-65 years – Pap test + HPV testing every 5 years

* Women can stop cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If suspicious PAP, screening till 75 years

* HIV+ women - annual screening

* HPV DNA testing in combination with PAP improves the sensitivity of screening.

Procedure:

The patient is put in a dorsal position, and Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced. The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula. The endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush. Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides. The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol and stained with Papanicolaou stain or short stain.

The most common fixative used in a Pap smear is 95% ethyl alcohol. The instruments used for Pap smears are summarised in the image below.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to cause Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SOD1 gene mutation

A mutation in the SOD1 gene causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

The anterior horn of the spinal cord and the corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord are affected by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The pathologic hallmark of ALS is the death of the affected lower motor neurons (LMN), consisting of the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and their homologs in the brainstem, and upper motor neurons (UMN), consisting of the corticospinal tract and corticobulbar tract originating in the motor cortex. The hereditary forms of ALS have mutations in the genes encoding for superoxide dismutase (SOD 1) present on chromosome 21.

Patients with ALS present with insidious-onset, asymmetric bilateral weakness of the distal part of the lower limbs. There may be a history of cramping, particularly early in the morning. Lower motor neuron death causes muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Upper motor neuron involvement presents as exaggerated tendon reflexes and spasticity.

The involvement of the corticobulbar fibres leads to exaggerated expressions of emotion, such as excessive weeping or laughing. This is called the pseudobulbar effect. Some patients also tend to develop frontotemporal dementia. However, sensory, bowel, and bladder functions and cognition are preserved, even in the late stages of the disease.

Other options:
Option A: FMR1 gene mutation results in Fragile X disease.
Option C: CFTR gene mutation results in cystic fibrosis.
Option D: HTT gene mutation results in Huntington's disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of these triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BAX

BAX triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C.

BAK and BAX are pro-apoptotic factors, whereas BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are anti-apoptotic proteins. Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, occurs due to the activation and release of certain proteases known as caspases. These enzymes are regulated by a balance between the actions of pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins on the permeability of the mitochondrial membrane:

* Pro-apoptotic proteins increase membrane permeability, thereby causing leakage of proteins that initiate apoptosis, like cytochrome c.

* Anti-apoptotic proteins keep the membrane impermeable, preventing the release of cytochrome c.

There are two apoptotic pathways—

* The intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway

* Extrinsic or death-receptor initiated pathway

The intrinsic pathway is triggered by DNA damage, accumulation of misfolded proteins, and loss of survival signals. This leads to leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c binds to APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor-1), forming an apoptosome. This complex activates caspase 9.

The extrinsic pathway is triggered by the engagement of death receptors on the plasma membrane. It activates caspases 8 and 10.

The active forms of these caspases activate executioner caspases (3 and 6), which act on various cell components to cause nuclear fragmentation, DNA degradation, etc. Cytoplasmic blebs and apoptotic bodies are then formed, which are ultimately phagocytosed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction characterizes borderline tuberculoid leprosy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 4

Borderline tuberculoid leprosy is characterized by Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction(Type 1 Leprosy Reaction)

In tuberculoid leprosy, dermal granulomas, consisting of groups of epithelioid cells with giant cells, are seen. The granulomas are elongated and generally run parallel to the surface, following neurovascular bundles. The granulomas extend up to the epidermis, thereby obscuring the Grenz zone. It also shows high positivity of the lepromin skin (dermal) test.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve and the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It has a long incubation period, usually 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

The Grenz zone is most prominent in lepromatous leprosy, as there are scarce granulomas to fill up the space. It is also seen in the borderline spectrum.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

* Characteristic skin lesions—hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.

* Peripheral nerve involvement—thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.

* Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10 year old boy with fever, weight loss came to the hospital. On examination he was pale and had significant lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow histology of the person is as given below. Your diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALL

The above image shows lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, scanty agranular cytoplasm, which are characteristics of ALL.

ALL is more common in childhood. The child had symptoms related to depression of marrow function including pallor, weight loss due to anaemia and fever secondary to infections. These infections are due to neutropenia and generalised lymphadenopathy, indicating the effect of neoplastic infiltration.

ALL:

* Usually seen in adolescent boys with thymic involvement

* Mediastinal thymic masses occur in 50% to 70% of T-ALLs, which are also more likely to be associated with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

* C/F:

* Abrupt stormy onset within days to a few weeks of the first symptoms

* Symptoms related to depression of marrow function including anemia, fever, infections, bleeding

* Mass effects caused by neoplastic infiltration

* Bone pain resulting from marrow expansion and infiltration of the subperiosteum

* Generalized lymphadenopathy Splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly

* Testicular enlargement

* Central nervous system manifestations such as headache, vomiting, and nerve palsies

* B cell ALL: Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement

* T-ALL: Mediastinal mass, lymphadenopathy, compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum

* Ataxia telangiectasia predisposes to ALL

* T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL) is characterized by aberrant activation of NOTCH1 in over 60% of T-ALL cases

Other options:

Option A: AML - Although the presenting symptoms are similar to ALL, bone marrow histology shows the presence of 20% myeloid blasts, delicate nuclear chromatin, 2-4 nucleoli, more voluminous cytoplasm with fine azurophilic granules. Though AML occurs at all ages, it is predominantly seen after 60 years of age.
Option B: Aplastic Anemia - It has a characteristic dry tap on marrow aspiration, bone marrow is markedly hypocellular. It can occur at any age and sex.
Option D: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia - It has characteristics of leukocytosis, monocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, elevated fetal haemoglobin. It is primarily a disease of early childhood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presented with 15 days of cough. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the lymph node biopsy showed the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The clinical history and histopathological findings showing caseating granuloma are suggestive of tuberculosis.

The microscopic picture shows the caseating granuloma. Eosinophilic necrotic debris known as caseation, bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhan giant cells and lymphocytes can be seen. Epitheloid cells merge to form Langhan's giant cell where nuclei arranged in a horseshoe shape (a characteristic feature of tuberculosis).

Clinically, tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, fever, weight loss, swollen lymph nodes.

Other options:

Option B- Leprosy presents with skin lesions and nerve involvement with loss of sensation.

Option C- Sarcoidosis shows giant cells with cytoplasmic inclusions, non-caseating granuloma with fibroblastic proliferation at the periphery.

Option D- Syphilis shows thickened capsule/ hyperplasia of capsule accompanied by fibrosis, perivascular inflammation and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year old male patient presents with anemia. His father and paternal aunt had a similar illness that was treated successfully by splenectomy. His peripheral blood smear is similar to that shown in the illustration below. Which of the following additional abnormalities is expected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Howell-Jolly bodies

The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies is an additional abnormality which can be expected here.

It is an autosomal dominant inheritance disorder. It is due to defective ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2 proteins causing a defect in the red cell membrane. This causes red cells to shed membrane vesicles and transform into spherocytes. The non-deformable spherocytes get trapped in the splenic cords and are phagocytosed by macrophages.

* Most common mode of inheritance of HS: Autosomal dominant

* Most common gene mutation in autosomal dominant HS: Ankyrin > Band 3

Clinical presentation:

The patients usually present with anemia, gall stones, splenomegaly, and jaundice but the age of presentation varies with the severity of the disease. They might also have a family history.

Aplastic crisis might occur where red cell production comes to a halt due to parvovirus infection. This lasts for 1 to 2 weeks which is usually the time required for the immune system to clear the virus. Blood transfusions may be needed during this period.

Morphology :

* The most common finding is spherocytosis, which presents as small, dark-staining (hyperchromic) red cells without the central zone of pallor but this is not specific to HS.

* Features seen in HS are :

* Reticulocytosis- increased reticulocyte count

* Howell-Jolly bodies- dense basophilic nuclear remnants in the RBCs.

* Marrow erythroid hyperplasia

* Hemosiderosis

* Splenomegaly as a result of congested Billroth cords and increased phagocytes.

Diagnosis:

Based on family history, peripheral smear findings, and laboratory investigations an adequate diagnosis is made. Increased osmotic fragility is seen in majority of the cases. They also show an increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) due to cellular dehydration.

Note- Heinz bodies: Undeterred oxidation of hemoglobin in the RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies damage the RBC membrane. When these RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells. They are seen in cases of chemical poisoning, drug toxicity, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, or the presence of unstable hemoglobin (e.g. hemoglobin Köln)

Below image shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presenting with an unsteady gait, forgetfulness, labile moods, and Kayser-Fleischer rings was diagnosed with Wilson's disease. Which of the following options correctly indicate the gene mutated in this condition and its location?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ATP7B gene on chromosome 13

Wilson's disease, an autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13

The ATP7B gene, located on chromosome 13, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane. Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.

Note:

Menkes disease is an X-linked metabolic disturbance of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the copper-transporting ATP7A gene.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of pain in the left knee, which is tender on palpation. X-ray shows a 5 cm mass in the distal femoral epiphysis, with "soap bubble" appearance. Microscopy is as seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteoclastoma

The most likely diagnosis is osteoclastoma/giant-cell tumor (GCT) of bone.

* GCT is a relatively uncommon benign, but locally aggressive, neoplasm that usually arises in individuals in their 20s to 40s.

* The neoplastic cells express high levels of RANKL, which promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts via RANK expressed by these cells.

* GCTs arise in the epiphysis but may extend into the metaphysis.

* The majority arise around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia).

* Most are solitary, multicentric tumors in the distal extremities.

* The tumors destroy the overlying cortex, producing a bulging soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive tissue.

* Sheets of uniform oval mononuclear cells and numerous osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. Necrosis and mitotic activity may be prominent.

* Typically, they are treated with curettage, but 40% to 60% recur locally.

* Up to 4% of tumors metastasize to the lungs, but these sometimes spontaneously regress and they are seldom fatal.

* The RANKL inhibitor, denosumab, has shown promise as adjuvant therapy in GCT.

Remember E mnemonic for GCT-

* Epiphyseal

* Eccentric

* Egg-shell crackling

* Expansile

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Histopathological examination of the mass showed signet ring appearance. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colloidal carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of colloid/mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intra and extracellular mucin deposition. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the peripherally to form signet ring appearance.

Extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei arranged in clusters floating in pools/lakes of mucin on histopathological examination.

Other options:

Option B: Papillary carcinoma consists of true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue, lined by the tumor cells.

Option C: Medullary carcinoma of the breast shows sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and pushing border.

Option D: Phyllodes tumor shows the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with weight loss, fever, and a painless swelling in the area of his jaw. CBC reveals anemia and lymphocytosis. Biopsy findings from the swelling are seen in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt's lymphoma

The clinical presentation and biopsy findings point to a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma.

The biopsy image shows tumor cells with multiple small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and high mitotic index closely apposed to each other forming a dark blue background (the "sky"). These cells have a high turnover rate. The macrophages get stuffed in between along with cellular debris, they are called tingible body macrophages. Upon fixation, the cytoplasm washes away leaving behind white spaces filled with debris ( the "stars"). This produces a starry sky appearance, which is classical to Burkitt lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma:

* Most common NHL in children <15 years

* Associated with translocation of MYC gene of chromosome 8 (Option A)

* Translocations: t (8;14), t (2;8), t (8,22)

* Three distinct clinical forms:

* Endemic: affects children in Africa, affects jaw, maxilla and is EBV-associated (Option B)

* Sporadic: in adults in western countries

* Immunodeficiency associated: HIV infection

* It is the most rapidly proliferating human tumor, Ki-67 stains for 100% of cells (DLBCL- 40% staining with Ki-67)

Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles. The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin

Treatment: Begins within 48h of diagnosis in both children and adults with the use of an intensive combination of chemotherapy regimens with high doses of cyclophosphamide and CNS prophylaxis.

Pearl PF2268: Burkitt's Lymphoma

Burkitt's lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in children < 15 years.

Parameter
Features

Genetic factors

Translocations - t(8;14), t(2;8), t(8,22)

Clinical types

Endemic - affects children in Africa, affects jaw, maxilla and is EBV-associated

Sporadic - in adults in western countries

Immunodeficiency associated - HIV infection

Clinical features

Peripheral lymphadenopathy

• Non-endemic type (EBV-) - lack CD21

Treatment

Intensive chemotherapy regimens with high doses of cyclophosphamide

Prognosis
Good - 70-80% cure rate

A variant of this condition with bone marrow involvement is called Burkitt's leukemia (ALL-L3). It is associated with c-myc dysregulation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 78 year old male presented with complaints of fatigue,breathlessness and palpitations.He has no co-morbidities and does not smoke or drink. On examination there was pedal edema and vitals were: PR-55, BP-100/70, Spo2-94%. An ECG was taken which showed no abnormalities after which he was given oxygen and an ECHO revealed restrictive cardiomyopathy. The physician in doubt of a disease did a cardiac biopsy which showed apple-green birefringence when viewed under polarized light after staining with Congo red stain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac Amyloidosis

The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

Cardiac amyloidosis:

* Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or localized amyloidosis restricted to the heart, particularly in the aged (senile cardiac amyloidosis).

* It is seen in individuals 70 years and older, and it has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis.

* Senile cardiac amyloid deposits are largely composed of transthyretin, a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein.

* Cardiac amyloidosis most frequently produces restrictive cardiomyopathy. But, it can also be asymptomatic, manifest as dilation or arrhythmias, or mimic ischemic or valvular disease.

* Another presentation of cardiac amyloidosis is congestive heart failure due to systolic dysfunction, generally a later finding.

* In approximately 10% of patients with amyloidosis, orthostatic hypotension occurs and is presumed to be a result of amyloid infiltration of the autonomic nervous system.

* Morphology: The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls. Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface, particularly on the left.

* Histologically, hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid may be found in the interstitium, conduction tissue, valves, endocardium, pericardium, and small intramural coronary arteries.

Image: Congo red stain viewed under polarized light, in which amyloid shows characteristic apple-green birefringence in the heart

Other options:

Option C- Hemosiderosis is characterized by deposition of hemosiderin, which is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment. The deposition may occur in any organ or tissue. It is seen in conditions associated with iron overload.

Option D-Dystrophic calcification:When the deposition of calcium occurs in dead or dying tissues, it is called dystrophic calcification. This occurs in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism, i.e the calcium levels are normal. Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type including coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child, upon disturbing a bee hive, had several stings. After a few minutes, the child developed symptoms of shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. Which of the following is the principal mediators of this reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histamine

Anaphylaxis following a bee sting is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or Type 1 hypersensitivity and the mediator involved here is histamine.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presented with midline swelling in the neck. Biopsy revealing orphan Annie's eye nuclei as shown in the image below is suggestive of ________:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Papillary carcinoma

The presence of empty appearing nuclei, also called Orphan Annie eye nuclei as seen in the above image is diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

Microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma:

* The carcinoma shows branching papillae with fibrovascular stalk covered with simple or stratified cuboidal epithelium.

* At high power, the nuclei appear optically clear or empty as the chromatin is dispersed. These empty appearing nuclei are called Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

* Concentric calcified structures called psammoma bodies are usually seen.

* Foci of lymphatic invasion by the tumor are usually present.

Note :

The presence of Orphan Annie-eye nuclei is diagnostic of papillary thyroid cancer, regardless of the presence of papillary architecture.

The image below shows papillary thyroid carcinoma with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei:

The image below shows psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Asbestosis is most commonly associated with which malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mesothelioma

Asbestosis is most commonly associated with Mesotheliomas.

Asbestos-related diseases include:

* Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis

* Pleural effusion

* Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)

* Lung carcinoma

* Mesotheliomas

* Laryngeal, ovarian and colon carcinomas

Asbestosis:

* Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis.

* Asbestos is of 2 types i.e Serpentine/Chrysolite variety and Amphibole type

* Amphibole type has the following varieties:

* Crocidolite(blue)

* Amosite(brown)

* Anthrophyllite(white)

* Sputum shows asbestos body, which are asbestos fibres coated with fibrin.

* They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

* X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. HRCT findings: Honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, irregular opacities, subpleural fibrosis. Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years).

* The complications that can occur are

* Pulmonary fibrosis

* Carcinoma of the lung

* Malignancy of the Gastrointestinal tract

* Mesothelioma of the pleura

Preventive measures:

* Using a safer type of Asbestos (chrysolite and amosite)

* Substituting other insulants like glass fibre, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams etc

* Dust control

* Periodic examination of workers

* Continuing research

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Supravital stains are used in the identification of all except ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Copper in tissue

In the following options all except copper can be visualised by supravital stains like methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue.

Reticulocytes have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA which can be stained by supravital stains.Reticulocytosis indicates effective erythropoiesis, which refers to a good bone marrow response to anemia which is seen hemolytic anemias and acute blood loss.

Heinz bodies are seen in G6PD deficiency where the RBCs are exposed to high levels of oxidants causing the cross-linking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains. The globin chains become denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates known as Heinz bodies which can cause intravascular hemolysis. These can be detected by supravital staining.

Histology of non-hodgkin lymphoma in an elderly male, showing reticulocytosis and spherocytosis:

Note:

To visualize the copper in tissues e.g in Wilson's disease, liver biopsy samples are stained using rubeanic acid/rhodanine stain to visualize the cytoplasmic copper.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is the bone marrow biopsy of a 60-year-old man with easy fatiguability, back pain, and multiple lytic lesions in the skull. Likely diagnosis is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiple myeloma

The clinical history along with the biopsy picture showing Russell bodies is suggestive of multiple myeloma.

Russell bodies are eosinophilic, large, homogeneous immunoglobulin-containing inclusions usually found in a plasma cell undergoing excessive synthesis of immunoglobulins. It is characteristic of the distended endoplasmic reticulum in multiple myeloma.

Clinical features

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Renal failure -Acute oliguric or non-oliguric kidney failure may be present due to hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, light-chain cast injury, or primary amyloidosis

* Pallor and soft tissue masses

* Fever occurs with infection

* Patients may have neurologic signs related to neuropathy or spinal cord compression

* Hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, vertigo, nausea, visual disturbances, alterations in mental status, hypoxia)

Bone marrow biopsy shows round or oval cells with an eccentric nucleus composed of coarsely clumped chromatin, a densely basophilic cytoplasm, and a perinuclear clear zone containing the Golgi apparatus.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for 20 days. He has gingival hyperplasia, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. On investigation, Hb - 11 g/dL, platelet count - 95,000 platelets/mm3, and WBC count - 45000 cells/mm3. Bone marrow biopsy shows 100% cellularity with many blast cells that are peroxidase negative and non-specific esterase positive. The most likely diagnosis is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute myeloid leukemia M5 (AML M5)

The most likely diagnosis from the clinical presentation and cytochemistry is acute myeloid leukemia (AML) M5 or acute monocytic leukemia.

Diagnostic features of AML M5:  20% or more blasts in the bone marrow. Markedly elevated white blood cell count with organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gingival hyperplasia, CNS involvement and other tissue infiltration. Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei, lack Auer rods, and are nonspecific esterase positive. Classified as AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities such as inv(16)(p13;1q22), t(16;16)(p13.1q22) or t(9;11)(p22;q23)

Note:

Myeloperoxidase is present in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils and its precursors. It is positive in AML M1, M2, M3, M4 and negative in AML M0. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive. When positive, the granules are smaller than in neutrophils and diffusely scattered throughout the cytoplasm.

Image: Bone marrow aspirate in AML M5

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A boy was diagnosed with a medical condition, which is believed to have been passed down from his grandmother to his father, and now to him. What is the pattern of inheritance in this particular case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autosomal dominance

The said disease shows an autosomal dominant pattern.

In the autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, both males and females are equally affected, and the affected individual has a 50% chance of passing it on to the offspring.

The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart.

Pearl PF0346: Pedigree chart for different inheritance patterns

Autosomal Dominant Disorders:

* With every autosomal dominant disorder, some patients do not have affected parents. Such patients owe their disorder to new mutations involving either the egg or the sperm from which they were derived.

* Clinical features can be modified by variations in penetrance and expressivity.

* In many conditions, the age at onset is delayed, and symptoms and signs may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease).

X-linked Recessive Conditions:

* All sex-linked disorders are X-linked, and almost all are recessive.

* Several genes are located in the “male-specific region of Y;” all these are related to spermatogenesis.

* Males with mutations affecting the Y-linked genes are usually infertile, and hence, there is no Y-linked inheritance.

* An affected male does not transmit the disorder to his sons, but all daughters are carriers.

* Sons of heterozygous women have, of course, a one-in-two chance of receiving the mutant gene.

* Heterozygous females express the disorder partially because of random inactivation of one X chromosome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child visited the hospital with her mother with complaints of severe fatigue, lethargy, pallor and irritation. She is a known case of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) and is on oral iron supplements. On reviewing the child, the physician in charge plans to start IV iron supplementation. What is the next best test to be done in assessing this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum ferritin

Assessing serum ferritin is the next best step in this diagnosed case of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA).

The reference standard to diagnose and monitor IDA is serum ferritin level. A decrease in the same is the earliest sign of IDA.

Since it is expensive and not widely available, an inexpensive & simpler way of evaluation is the Mentzer index.

The progression to iron deficiency develops in 3 stages:

* Stage of negative iron balance - Decrease in iron stores with normal serum iron and RBC morphology

* Stage of iron-deficient erythropoiesis - Decrease in serum iron levels with normal RBC morphology

* Stage of iron deficiency anaemia - Microcytic hypochromic RBCs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A health care worker has been found to be seropositive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and Anti-HBc: IgM, indicating an acute HBV infection with high infectivity. Liver biopsy in such cases is likely to show all of the following, except________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ground glass hepatocytes

Ground-glass hepatocytes are not seen in acute hepatitis.

“Ground-glass” hepatocytes are a diagnostic hallmark in chronic hepatitis B. They are cells with endoplasmic reticulum swollen by HBsAg.

The below image shows ground glass hepatocytes.

questions.text: A middle-aged woman who presented to the clinic with a lump in her right breast is diagnosed to have breast carcinoma. All of the following are favorable prognostic markers except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Her2 overexpression

The clinical scenario explains breast carcinoma and HER2 overexpression is associated with poor survival.

The main importance of HER2 status is as a predictor of response to agents that target this receptor. Luminal A subtype i.e well-differentiated, ER-positive, HER2-negative, and low proliferation, has the most favorable prognosis.

The proliferative rate can be measured by mitotic counts or by immunohistochemical detection of Ki67 proteins. Carcinomas with high proliferation rates have a poorer prognosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the WHO grading of astrocytomas, which grade does glioblastoma fall under?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IV

Glioblastoma multiforme falls under WHO Grade IV of astrocytomas. It has the worst long-term prognosis with a median survival of roughly 1 year.

Astrocytomas (Graded I to IV) are the most common primary CNS neoplasm. The term often is used to refer to astrocytomas specifically, excluding other glial tumours.

* Grade I - Pilocytic astrocytoma

* Grade II - Diffuse astrocytoma

* Grade III - Anaplastic astrocytoma

* Grade IV - Glioblastoma multiforme

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is macrocytic anaemia seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liver disease

Liver disease features non-megaloblastic macrocytic normochromic anaemia.

MCV >100 fl indicates macrocytic anaemia. The causes for the same, divided by morphology, are:

*

Megaloblastic:

Vitamin B12 deficiency

Folate deficiency

Thiamine deficiency

Drugs - Methotrexate, Zidovudine, Hydroxyurea

Orotic aciduria

*

Non-megaloblastic:

Alcohol use

Liver disease

Hypothyroidism

Hemolysis*

*Note: Hemolysis can be associated with macrocytosis because of compensatory reticulocytosis. However, MCV can be normal depending on the degree of hemolysis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Metastatic calcification occurs in all except _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atheroma

Dystrophic calcification is seen in atheromatous plaque.

* Metastatic calcification can occur in normal tissues whenever there is hypercalcemia.

* The major causes of hypercalcemia are

* Increased secretion of parathyroid hormone, due to malignant tumors

* Paget disease, immobilization, or tumors (increased bone catabolism associated with multiple myeloma, leukemia, or skeletal metastases)

* Vitamin D intoxication and sarcoidosis

* Renal failure

* Metastatic calcification can occur throughout the body, but mainly affects the interstitial tissues of the vasculature, renal system, pulmonary tissue, and stomach mucosa.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: New A 55 yr old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of having a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below. This patient most likely suffers from ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemochromatosis

The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's prussian blue stain.

Hemochromatosis is an inherited or acquired metabolic disorder caused by excessive iron absorption. Iron overload leads to the accumulation of iron in parenchymal organs such as the liver and pancreas followed by heart, joints, and endocrine organs.

The characteristic triad of hemochromatosis includes:

* Micronodular cirrhosis

* Diabetes mellitus in 75% to 80% of patients

* Abnormal skin pigmentation in 75% to 80% of patients

Note: The total body iron pool ranges from 2 to 6 gm in normal adults. In hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm, more than one-third of which accumulates in the liver.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The cells responsible for graft rejection are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T cells

Amongst the given options, T-cells are responsible for graft rejection.

Graft rejection is both humoral and cell-mediated in nature. It is a process in which T-cells and antibodies produced against graft antigens react against tissue grafts and destroy it.

The major antigenic differences that result in the rejection of transplants are differences in HLA alleles. The recipient T-cells are involved in the recognition of the donor MHC molecules and mount an immune response. Depending on the antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that are involved in T-cell activation, there are 2 pathways:

* Direct pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the APCs in the graft

* Indirect pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the recipient’s own APCs (e.g., macrophages)

The early activation of NK cells kill allogeneic target cells directly or via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and release various chemokines and immunomodulatory cytokines.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The X-Ray of a middle aged man showed multiple lytic lesions following which a urine examination was done. The sample revealed Bence Jones proteins. Which is the most common immunoglobulin associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ig G

The given scenario consisting of multiple lytic bony lesions and Bence Jones proteins indicates multiple myeloma.  Most myelomas are associated with more than 3 g/dL of serum Ig and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein. The most common monoclonal Immunoglobulin (M protein) is IgG followed by IgA.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm commonly associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities.

Multiple myeloma usually presents as destructive plasma cell tumors involving the axial skeleton. The bones most commonly affected in descending order of frequency are the vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula.

Morphology:

* Malignant plasma cells have a perinuclear clearing due to a prominent golgi apparatus and an eccentrically placed nucleus.

* Relatively normal-appearing plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate.

* Other cytologic variants include flame cells, Mott cells.

* Flame cells have fiery red cytoplasm, Mott cells contain multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets, a variety of other inclusions, including fibrils, crystalline rods, and globules. The globular inclusions are referred to as Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear).

* Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific. High levels of M protein in the blood causes red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays in smears leading to rouleaux formation.

Image showing peripheral smear of multiple myeloma:

Poor prognostic factors for multiple myeloma:

* Serum β2-microglobulin. It is the single most powerful predictor

* Deletion of 17pITP53 sequences and the translocations t(14;16) and t(14;20)

* Polyclonal serum Immunoglobulins

* Elevated lactate dehydrogenase

* High C-reactive protein

* Increased plasma cell proliferative activity

* High degree of bone marrow replacement

* Presence of plasmablastic morphology

* Elevated serum soluble receptor for IL6

The clinicopathologic diagnosis of multiple myeloma can be done based on the identification of clonal plasma cells in the marrow and the presence of CRAB criteria (hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anemia, and bone lesions).

Other options:

A) Ig A is not the most common immunoglobulin associated with the presence of Bence Jones proteins in the urine. While Ig A can be involved in some cases, Ig G is the most frequently observed immunoglobulin in this context.

B) Ig D is not commonly associated with the presence of Bence Jones proteins in the urine. Bence Jones proteins are typically composed of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, and Ig D is not commonly involved in plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma.

D) Ig M is not the most common immunoglobulin associated with the presence of Bence Jones proteins in the urine. While Ig M can be involved in certain plasma cell disorders, Ig G is the most frequently observed immunoglobulin associated with Bence Jones proteins.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is not routinely screened before conducting a blood transfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatitis A

Blood transfusion does not require routine screening of donor blood for Hepatitis A infection.

Some of the transfusion-transmitted infections routinely tested are:

* Hepatitis C virus

* Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

* Hepatitis B virus

* Syphilis

Transfusion-transmitted diseases currently not routinely tested are:

* Hepatitis A virus

* Hepatitis E virus

* Parvovirus B19

* Dengue fever virus

* Malaria

* Zika virus

Note: In India, malaria is also routinely tested along with HCV, HBV, HIV and syphilis before blood transfusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following stains is used for the detection of hemosiderin deposits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Perl’s prussian blue

Perl's prussian blue stain is used to detect hemosiderin deposits.

Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived granular pigment that is golden-yellow to brown. It accumulates in the tissues when there is a local or systemic excess of iron.

Iron is normally stored within cells in association with the protein apoferritin, forming ferritin micelles. Large aggregates of these micelles are hemosiderin deposits seen both in light and electron microscopy.

Image 1: Hemosiderin deposits in tissue

Image 2: Prussian blue staining of hemosiderin

*Note: Iron dispersed in the cytoplasm is seen in electron microscopy as ferritin micelles.

questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy treated with cytotoxic drugs for leukemia develops numerous shrunken, intensely eosinophilic hepatocytes with pyknotic nuclei on biopsy. These cells are positive for caspase-3. Which protein event is most directly responsible for initiating this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BAX

Why: This is a classic vignette for chemotherapy-induced hepatocyte apoptosis via the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway:

• Shrunken cells with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei = apoptotic bodies (councilman-like bodies), not necrosis (no inflammation, no cell swelling).
• Caspase-3 positivity confirms this is apoptosis, since caspase-3 is the final common executioner caspase for both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.

Mechanism (intrinsic pathway):

1. Cytotoxic drugs cause DNA damage → p53 activation
2. p53 upregulates pro-apoptotic proteins, chiefly BAX (and BAK)
3. BAX oligomerizes and inserts into the mitochondrial outer membrane, increasing its permeability (MOMP)
4. This permeabilization allows cytochrome-c release into the cytosol
5. Cytochrome-c + Apaf-1 → apoptosome → activates caspase-9 → activates caspase-3 → executes apoptosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents for evaluation of multiple painless oral lesions and a long history of “small bumps” on her face. Physical examination shows numerous facial trichilemmomas and papillomatous papules on the oral mucosa. She also has a history of multiple thyroid nodules. Family history reveals that her mother had breast cancer at age 41. Genetic testing shows a germline mutation in a tumor suppressor gene that normally inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Colonic adenomatous polyposis beginning in adolescence
Increased risk of breast and thyroid malignancies
Increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased risk of breast and thyroid malignancies

The clinical features describe Cowden syndrome, caused by a germline mutation in the PTEN gene.

• PTEN normally:

• Inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
• Acts as a tumor suppressor regulating cell growth and survival

• Mutation → loss of inhibition → uncontrolled cell proliferation
• Mucocutaneous lesions:

• Facial trichilemmomas
• Oral papillomas

• Multisystem involvement:

• Thyroid nodules
• Hamartomas in various organs

Increased risk of:

• Breast cancer
• Thyroid cancer (especially follicular)
• Endometrial carcinoma

Why not other options:

A. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas: Seen in Neurofibromatosis type 2

B. Colonic adenomatous polyposis: Seen in Familial adenomatous polyposis

D. Medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma: Seen in Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman with autoimmune hemolytic anemia is treated with high-dose steroids. After therapy, her lymphocyte count falls significantly. Further molecular analysis of these cells shows mitochondrial cytochrome c release and caspase-9 activation. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action responsible for this effect?
options: Inhibition of NF-κB leading to decreased survival signals
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of NF-κB leading to decreased survival signals

Glucocorticoids induce apoptosis of lymphocytes by suppressing transcription of survival-promoting genes, largely through inhibition of NF-κB–mediated signaling. Loss of these survival signals activates the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway, leading to cytochrome c release, caspase-9 activation, and subsequent programmed cell death.

Why not the other options?

• A. Activation of death receptors (Fas–FasL pathway): Fas–FasL pathway activates the extrinsic apoptotic pathway via caspase-8.
• C. Increased intracellular calcium causing necrosis: Increased intracellular calcium causing necrosis leads to uncontrolled cell injury, not apoptosis.
• D. Direct membrane lipid peroxidation: Direct membrane lipid peroxidation is a mechanism of free radical–mediated cell damage.
• E. Activation of complement-mediated cytotoxicity: Complement-mediated cytotoxicity causes cell lysis rather than mitochondrial apoptosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of bilateral cataracts, short stature, premature greying and loss of hair, and skin changes. He also reports joint stiffness and pain, as well as type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, the patient appears older than his stated age, with characteristic "bird-like" facies and a high-pitched voice. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Werner syndrome

Werner syndrome is an autosomal recessive premature aging (progeroid) disorder caused by mutations in the WRN gene, which encodes a DNA helicase involved in DNA repair and replication. Defective DNA repair leads to genomic instability and accelerated aging.

• Premature graying and loss of hair
• Bilateral cataracts
• Short stature
• Bird-like facies
• High-pitched voice
• Skin atrophy/ulceration
• Joint stiffness
• Early-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus
• Increased risk of malignancies (especially sarcomas)

Why not the other options:

A. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome: Presents in early childhood with growth failure and premature atherosclerosis; cataracts and diabetes are uncommon.

C. Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome: Neonatal progeroid syndrome; features are present at birth.

D. Cockayne syndrome: Characterized by photosensitivity, neurologic deficits, microcephaly, and developmental delay, not diabetes or cataracts.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with progressive chorea, behavioral changes, and cognitive decline. Genetic testing reveals an expanded CAG repeat in the coding region of a gene on chromosome 4, resulting in a gain-of-function mutant protein. Which of the following disorders shares this same coding-region, gain-of-function mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1

Huntington disease is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion within the coding region of the HTT gene on chromosome 4, resulting in an abnormal polyglutamine protein with a toxic gain-of-function effect.

Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is also caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the coding region, producing an expanded polyglutamine tract and a toxic gain-of-function mutant protein, similar to Huntington disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic abdominal pain, intermittent fever, and loose stools. Colonoscopy reveals patchy transmural inflammation with a cobblestone appearance of the intestinal mucosa. Which of the following biochemical parameters is most likely to be elevated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibrinogen

The patient’s findings (chronic abdominal pain, intermittent fever, loose stools, patchy transmural inflammation, cobblestone mucosa) are characteristic of Crohn disease, a chronic inflammatory bowel disease. During chronic inflammation, the liver increases production of acute-phase reactants under the influence of cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α.

Positive acute-phase proteins (increase in inflammation):

• Fibrinogen
• C-reactive protein (CRP)
• Serum amyloid A
• Ferritin
• Haptoglobin

Negative acute-phase proteins (decrease in inflammation):

• Albumin
• Prealbumin (transthyretin)
• Retinol-binding protein

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer and found on genetic testing to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation. Her mother, who carries the same BRCA1 mutation (confirmed on cascade testing), is now 74 years old and has never developed breast, ovarian, or any other BRCA-associated cancer. Which genetic principle best explains why the mother, despite carrying the identical disease-causing mutation, never developed the expected phenotype?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incomplete penetrance

Rationale: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals carrying a given genotype who actually go on to express the associated phenotype at all — it is an all-or-none, population-level concept ("does the trait show up or not?"). BRCA1 mutations are classically incompletely penetrant: not every carrier develops cancer, even though the mutation substantially increases lifetime risk (e.g., roughly 55–72% lifetime breast cancer risk, not 100%). The mother in this vignette carries the identical pathogenic mutation as her daughter but has remained unaffected — exactly illustrating incomplete penetrance, since the genotype has not "penetrated" into a phenotype in her case, possibly due to protective modifier genes, hormonal/reproductive factors, or simply chance. Variable expressivity (A) would instead apply if both mother and daughter developed cancer, but with differing severity, age of onset, or tumor characteristics — that describes a spectrum of severity among those who are affected, not whether the disease appears at all. Pleiotropy (C) describes one gene causing multiple different unrelated phenotypic effects (e.g., BRCA1 mutations increasing both breast AND ovarian cancer risk) — not relevant to why the mother is asymptomatic. Anticipation (D) refers to a genetic disease worsening or presenting earlier in successive generations (classically seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease or myotonic dystrophy) — not applicable here.

Quick reference — Penetrance vs Expressivity vs Pleiotropy:

| Concept | Key question it answers | Classic example

| ------- | ----------------------- | ---------------

| Penetrance | Does the phenotype appear at all in carriers? (all-or-none, population-level) | BRCA1/2 mutations; incomplete penetrance

| Expressivity | Among those affected, how severe/variable is the phenotype? | Neurofibromatosis type 1; sickle cell anemia severity

| Pleiotropy | Does one gene cause multiple different types of effects? | Marfan syndrome (eyes, heart, skeleton); sickle cell (crises + malaria resistance)

| Anticipation | Does severity worsen / onset occur earlier in successive generations? | Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman on chemotherapy for choriocarcinoma develops oral mucositis and GI ulceration. Which nucleotide synthesis step is most directly impaired by this drug?
options: Purine ring synthesis via glycinamide ribotide formation
Conversion of dUMP to dTMP via thymidylate synthase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conversion of dUMP to dTMP via thymidylate synthase

Methotrexate, a key chemotherapeutic agent used in choriocarcinoma, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), leading to depletion of tetrahydrofolate required for one-carbon transfer reactions. This impairs thymidylate synthase–mediated conversion of dUMP to dTMP, resulting in defective DNA synthesis and toxicity in rapidly dividing tissues such as the oral and gastrointestinal mucosa.

Why not the other options?

• A. Purine ring synthesis via Glycinamide ribotide formation – an early step in de novo purine synthesis; not the primary target tested here.
• C. Ribonucleotide reduction to deoxyribonucleotides – inhibited by hydroxyurea via ribonucleotide reductase inhibition.
• D. Orotic acid → UMP – Catalyzed by UMP synthase; defective in hereditary orotic aciduria.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with a history of repeated blood transfusions presents with hepatomegaly and skin hyperpigmentation. Liver biopsy shows iron deposition within hepatocytes. During an ischemia–reperfusion episode, there is sudden worsening of hepatic injury due to generation of highly reactive oxygen species. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of cellular injury in this patient?
options: Conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase
Iron-catalyzed conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hydroxyl radicals
Formation of hypochlorous acid by myeloperoxidase
Direct scavenging of free radicals by glutathione peroxidase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron-catalyzed conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hydroxyl radicals

In iron overload states (e.g., transfusional hemosiderosis), excess iron catalyzes the Fenton reaction, converting hydrogen peroxide into highly reactive hydroxyl radicals, leading to severe oxidative cellular injury.

• Iron (Fe²⁺) + H₂O₂ → •OH (hydroxyl radical) via Fenton reaction
• Hydroxyl radicals are the most damaging ROS → cause lipid peroxidation, protein damage, DNA injury
• Ischemia–reperfusion increases ROS generation → worsens injury
• Seen in conditions like hemochromatosis and repeated transfusions

Differentiation:

• A. Superoxide dismutase: converts superoxide → H₂O₂ (protective)
• C. Myeloperoxidase: forms HOCl in neutrophils (not main mechanism here)
• D. Glutathione peroxidase: detoxifies H₂O₂ (protective)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis has inadequate response to methotrexate despite optimal dosing for 3 months. Before starting a TNF-α inhibitor, she is screened and found to have evidence of latent tuberculosis on IGRA testing. Which of the following biologic DMARDs would be most appropriate to avoid in this patient, and why?
options: Rituximab, because it depletes CD20+ B cells and increases infection risk equally regardless of TB status
Infliximab, because TNF-α inhibition impairs granuloma formation and risks reactivation of latent TB
Tocilizumab, because IL-6 blockade has no relevant interaction with TB reactivation risk
Abatacept, because T-cell costimulation blockade carries the highest reactivation risk among all biologics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Infliximab, because TNF-α inhibition impairs granuloma formation and risks reactivation of latent TB

TNF-α plays a critical role in the formation and maintenance of granulomas, which contain latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. In patients with latent TB, treatment with TNF-α inhibitors can disrupt granuloma integrity, allowing dormant bacilli to proliferate and causing reactivation tuberculosis.

Why B?

• Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
• TNF-α blockade impairs macrophage activation and granuloma maintenance.
• This markedly increases the risk of latent TB reactivation, making TB screening mandatory before therapy.

Quick reference — Biologic DMARDs in RA: Target & Key Considerations

| Drug class | Example agents | Target | Key precaution

| ---------- | -------------- | ------ | --------------

| TNF-α inhibitors | Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept, Golimumab, Certolizumab | TNF-α | Screen for latent TB; reactivation risk

| IL-6 receptor antagonists | Tocilizumab, Sarilumab | IL-6R | Monitor lipids, LFTs; GI perforation risk

| B-cell depleting agents | Rituximab | CD20 on B cells | Hepatitis B reactivation; PML risk

| T-cell costimulation blockers | Abatacept | CD80/86–CD28 interaction | Increased infection risk; avoid live vaccines

| IL-1 receptor antagonist | Anakinra | IL-1 | Injection site reactions; less commonly used now

| JAK inhibitors (targeted synthetic, not biologic) | Tofacitinib, Baricitinib | JAK-STAT pathway | VTE and malignancy risk (boxed warning)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. Molecular analysis of the tumor reveals loss of a specific cell-death pathway that normally occurs when epithelial cells lose contact with the extracellular matrix. Loss of which of the following forms of programmed cell death most directly facilitates metastasis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anoikis

Anoikis is a specialized form of apoptosis that occurs when epithelial or anchorage-dependent cells lose attachment to the extracellular matrix (ECM). This mechanism prevents detached cells from surviving and colonizing other tissues.

In malignant tumors, especially carcinomas, cancer cells often develop resistance to anoikis, allowing them to survive after detaching from the primary tumor, circulate in blood or lymph, and establish metastases at distant sites.

Other options:

A. Necroptosis: programmed inflammatory necrosis mediated by RIPK1/RIPK3.

B. Pyroptosis: inflammatory cell death mediated by caspase-1 with IL-1β release.

D. Ferroptosis: iron-dependent cell death due to lipid peroxidation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old male with a history of hypertension and smoking presents with chest pain and shortness of breath. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in inferior leads. He undergoes PCI but, within hours, develops deteriorating cardiac function. What is the most likely primary mechanism of cardiac deterioration in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracellular calcium overload

During myocardial ischemia followed by reperfusion (e.g., after PCI in STEMI), the most critical mechanism of early myocardial cell injury is intracellular calcium overload.

Pathophysiology:

1.      Ischemia → ATP depletion → failure of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

2.      Na⁺ accumulates intracellularly, which activates the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.

3.      This causes excess Ca²⁺ influx into cardiomyocytes.

4.      Calcium overload leads to:

• Activation of proteases, phospholipases, and endonucleases
• Mitochondrial damage
• Hypercontracture of myofibrils
• Cell death

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing bladder tumor. Genetic analysis will reveal:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activation of HRAS

Bladder carcinoma, particularly low-grade papillary urothelial tumors, is commonly associated with activating mutations in the HRAS proto-oncogene.

Mechanism:

• Point mutation in HRAS leads to constitutive activation of the Ras signaling pathway.
• This causes continuous cell proliferation and tumor formation independent of normal growth factor signaling.
