questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive pedal edema, frothy urine, and hepatosplenomegaly. Urinalysis shows nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy reveals amorphous eosinophilic deposits in the mesangium that show apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining. Which of the following findings is most specific for identifying the type of amyloid protein in this patient?
options: Immunohistochemical staining for serum amyloid A protein
Presence of Bence Jones proteins in urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immunohistochemical staining for serum amyloid A protein

• Chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis can lead to secondary (AA) amyloidosis due to prolonged elevation of serum amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant produced by the liver.
• In AA amyloidosis, misfolded SAA protein deposits in tissues (commonly kidneys) causing nephrotic syndrome. On biopsy, amyloid appears as amorphous eosinophilic deposits that show apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light.
• To determine the specific type of amyloid protein, the most specific test is immunohistochemical staining for serum amyloid A protein.

Why not the other options:

A. Elevated serum β₂-microglobulin: Seen in dialysis-related amyloidosis, not in chronic inflammatory disease–related amyloidosis.

C. Presence of Bence Jones proteins in urine: Indicates AL amyloidosis due to light chains from plasma cell disorders (e.g., multiple myeloma).

D. Increased transthyretin levels: Associated with ATTR amyloidosis (familial or senile cardiac amyloidosis).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 59-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging 3.0-cm ulcerated lesion on his left temple. The lesion has been present for 4 months and recently began bleeding spontaneously. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals no palpable cervical or parotid lymphadenopathy. Punch biopsy shows sheets of markedly atypical squamous cells with pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, numerous atypical mitotic figures, and minimal keratinization. The tumor invades into the dermis but does not extend into underlying muscle. MRI shows no perineural spread. CT scan of the chest/abdomen/pelvis shows no evidence of metastasis. These findings are most consistent with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High-grade, low-stage neoplasm

Tumor grade and stage are distinct concepts and must be interpreted independently.

Tumor Grade (Histological Aggressiveness):

• This lesion shows:

• Marked cellular atypia
• Pleomorphism
• Hyperchromatic nuclei
• Numerous atypical mitoses
• Minimal keratinization

These features indicate a high-grade tumor (poorly differentiated, aggressive histology)

Tumor Stage (Extent of Spread):

• Findings:

• Tumor confined to dermis
• No muscle invasion
• No lymph node involvement
• No distant metastasis

Indicates low-stage disease (localized tumor)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive yellowing of the eyes for 3 weeks, associated with dark urine, pale stools, and unintentional weight loss. He denies abdominal pain, fever, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Examination reveals scleral icterus without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation shows: • Total bilirubin: 7.2 mg/dL • Alkaline phosphatase: markedly elevated Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrates a mass in the head of the pancreas causing compression of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct. Which of the following molecular alterations is most commonly associated with the pathogenesis of this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. KRAS activation

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, especially involving the head of the pancreas, commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools, elevated ALP). The most frequent early genetic event in its pathogenesis is activating mutation of the KRAS oncogene, leading to constitutive activation of downstream proliferative signaling pathways (MAPK pathway).

Pancreatic cancer follows a stepwise progression (PanIN lesions) involving:

• Early: KRAS activation
• Intermediate: CDKN2A (p16) loss
• Late: TP53 and SMAD4 mutations

Why not other options?

A. APC mutation → Seen in colorectal carcinoma (adenoma-carcinoma sequence)

B. BCL2 overexpression → Associated with follicular lymphoma (anti-apoptotic protein)

C. BRAF mutation → Seen in melanoma, hairy cell leukemia, some colorectal cancers

c-MYC amplification → Seen in Burkitt lymphoma and various aggressive malignancies

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has difficulty walking. Exam shows pes cavus, scoliosis, and a systolic murmur at left sternal border. Which is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: Expansion of a GAA trinucleotide repeat
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Association with chromosome 19

This child most likely has Friedreich ataxia, the most common inherited ataxia, characterized by progressive gait ataxia, pes cavus, scoliosis, pyramidal tract signs, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It is caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

• Friedreich ataxia is caused by a mutation in the FXN gene on chromosome 9q13, not chromosome 19.
• Therefore, the statement “association with chromosome 19” is false.

Key Clinical Features of Friedreich Ataxia

• Progressive gait and limb ataxia
• Pes cavus
• Scoliosis
• Dysarthria
• Loss of vibration and position sense
• Extensor plantar (Babinski) response
• Absent deep tendon reflexes (especially ankle jerks)
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → systolic murmur
• Diabetes mellitus (in some patients)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with progressive gait instability and slurred speech. Examination shows oculocutaneous telangiectasia. Laboratory studies reveal low IgA levels and marked sensitivity to ionizing radiation. Which of the following malignancies is this child most predisposed to develop?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder due to ATM gene mutation, characterized by cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency (low IgA), and increased sensitivity to radiation, with a high predisposition to lymphoid malignancies.

Key points:

• Defective DNA repair → chromosomal instability
• Immunodeficiency (↓ IgA) → recurrent infections
• Radiation sensitivity → avoid radiotherapy
• Increased risk of malignancy: especially lymphomas and leukemias (ALL)

Differentiation:

C. Medulloblastoma: seen in ataxia syndromes but less common here

A. Hepatocellular carcinoma, D. Osteosarcoma: not typical associations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A child presents with intellectual disability, chronic diarrhea, ichthyosis, peripheral neuropathy, and low serum copper. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MEDNIK syndrome

MEDNIK syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the AP1S1 gene, which affects intracellular trafficking of copper transport proteins.

MEDNIK stands for the major clinical features:

• Mental retardation (intellectual disability)
• Enteropathy (chronic diarrhea)
• Deafness
• Neuropathy (peripheral neuropathy)
• Ichthyosis
• Keratoderma

Patients typically have abnormal copper metabolism with low serum copper and ceruloplasmin, leading to neurologic and dermatologic manifestations.

Why not the other options:

A. Wilson disease: Copper accumulation → liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms, Kayser-Fleischer rings; not ichthyosis or chronic diarrhea.

B. Menkes disease: Infancy onset, kinky hair, severe neurodegeneration.

D. Zellweger syndrome: Peroxisomal disorder with hypotonia, seizures, craniofacial anomalies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A genetic polymorphism leading to deletion of the ATG16L1 gene, which plays a key role in autophagosome formation, predisposes an individual to which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inflammatory bowel disease

ATG16L1 is a key gene involved in autophagy, the cellular process that degrades damaged organelles and intracellular pathogens through autophagosome formation.

Polymorphisms or deletion of ATG16L1 impair autophagy, leading to defective handling of intestinal microbes and abnormal immune responses in the gut. This contributes to chronic intestinal inflammation, particularly Crohn disease, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

questions.text: A patient with acute viral infection shows extensive cell death associated with cell swelling, plasma membrane rupture, and release of intracellular contents, leading to marked inflammation. Caspase-8 activity is found to be inhibited in the affected tissues. Which of the following molecular pathways most likely mediates this form of cell death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL signaling pathway

Necroptosis is a form of programmed necrotic cell death characterized by cell swelling, plasma membrane rupture, and release of intracellular contents, which leads to marked inflammation.

It typically occurs when caspase-8 is inhibited, preventing normal apoptosis. In this situation, signaling shifts to the RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL pathway, which causes membrane disruption and necrotic cell death.

Why not other options:

A. Cytochrome-c–Apaf-1–caspase-9: Intrinsic apoptosis → non-inflammatory.

B. Fas–FADD–caspase-8-dependent apoptosis: Extrinsic apoptosis, requires caspase-8 (here it is inhibited).

D. p53-mediated intrinsic apoptosis: Also intrinsic apoptosis, non-inflammatory.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with restrictive cardiomyopathy is diagnosed with amyloidosis. Genetic testing reveals mutation in transthyretin gene. Which organ is primarily responsible for production of this protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver

Transthyretin (TTR) is a transport protein that carries thyroxine (T4) and retinol-binding protein–vitamin A complexes. It is synthesized predominantly by the liver, and mutations in the TTR gene can lead to misfolding and deposition of amyloid fibrils, causing hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, which may present as restrictive cardiomyopathy and/or peripheral neuropathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bone marrow – produces hematopoietic cells; involved in AL amyloidosis via plasma cells, not TTR production.
• C. Kidney – not a major site of transthyretin synthesis.
• D. Heart – affected by amyloid deposition but does not primarily produce transthyretin.
• E. Spleen – not involved in transthyretin production.

questions.text: A researcher studying immune regulation in the liver observes that viable CD4⁺ T lymphocytes are selectively engulfed by hepatocytes without being immediately destroyed. This specialized cell-in-cell phenomenon is believed to contribute to peripheral immune tolerance. Which of the following terms best describes this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enclysis

Enclysis is a recently described cell-in-cell phenomenon in which hepatocytes selectively internalize live CD4⁺ T cells, particularly regulatory T cells (Tregs), playing a role in hepatic immune homeostasis and immune tolerance.

Unlike classical phagocytosis, the engulfed lymphocytes are viable at the time of uptake, and the process is unique to hepatocytes.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Efferocytosis: Refers to the phagocytic clearance of apoptotic (dead or dying) cells by macrophages and other phagocytes. It does not involve live CD4⁺ T cells.
• B. Entosis: A live cell actively invades another live cell, most commonly seen in epithelial tumors. It is associated with cell competition rather than immune regulation.
• D. Emperipolesis: Describes the passage of intact viable cells through the cytoplasm of another cell without being digested. It is classically seen with megakaryocytes containing neutrophils or lymphocytes (e.g., Rosai–Dorfman disease).

High-yield pearl:

| Cell-in-cell phenomenon | Characteristic feature | Classic example

| ----------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------

| Enclysis | Hepatocyte engulfs live CD4⁺ T cells | Hepatic immune tolerance

| Efferocytosis | Clearance of apoptotic cells | Macrophages removing dying neutrophils

| Entosis | One live epithelial cell enters another | Epithelial cancers

| Emperipolesis | Viable cell passes through another cell without digestion | Megakaryocytes; Rosai–Dorfman disease

Exam tip:

• Enclysis = Hepatocytes + live CD4⁺ T cells (especially Tregs), whereas efferocytosis = apoptotic cells, entosis = tumor cell-in-cell, and emperipolesis = intact cells within another cell without destruction.

questions.text: A researcher studying innate immunity observes neutrophils releasing a web-like extracellular structure rich in chromatin and antimicrobial enzymes at a site of bacterial invasion. The neutrophil undergoes a distinct, lytic form of cell death in this process. This structure is most likely to be implicated as a source of autoantigens in which condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic lupus erythematosus

This describes NETosis — formation of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs), a unique lytic death pathway distinct from apoptosis/necrosis, where decondensed nuclear chromatin studded with antimicrobial peptides is expelled to trap pathogens. NET-derived nuclear chromatin (dsDNA, histones) is a postulated source of nuclear autoantigens specifically driving anti-dsDNA/anti-nuclear antibody formation in SLE. The other options involve different autoantibody targets (RF/CCP, anti-GBM, ANCA respectively) not classically linked to NET chromatin as the antigen source.

questions.text: A scientist is studying the invasion of malignant colon cancer cells into surrounding tissues in an experimental model. Over time, the cancer cells are observed to detach from each other and degrade the extracellular matrix, allowing the tumor cells to invade the basement membrane and access nearby blood vessels. Which of the following substances is most likely upregulated to facilitate basement membrane invasion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metalloproteinases

Tumor invasion and metastasis require cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) and basement membrane to spread into surrounding tissues and blood vessels. A key mechanism is the upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which are enzymes that break down components of the ECM, including:

• Type IV collagen (major component of basement membrane)
• Laminin
• Proteoglycans

This degradation allows tumor cells to penetrate the basement membrane and invade adjacent tissues, facilitating metastasis.

Why not the other options:

A. Acid hydrolases: Lysosomal enzymes involved in intracellular digestion, not the main enzymes degrading the basement membrane during tumor invasion.

B. E-cadherin: A cell adhesion molecule. In cancer invasion it is typically downregulated, allowing tumor cells to detach from each other.

C. Hyaluronic acid: A component of extracellular matrix that helps tissue hydration and cell migration but does not degrade the basement membrane.

questions.text: A tumor biopsy shows a mutation that renders CDK constitutively active regardless of cyclin binding status. Which immediate consequence on the cell cycle restriction point would this produce, independent of p53/p21 status?
options: Rb would remain hypophosphorylated, enforcing permanent G1 arrest
Rb would become hyperphosphorylated, releasing E2F and driving G1-S transition irrespective of growth factor signaling
p53 would compensate by inducing apoptosis directly without involving p21
Cyclin levels would become irrelevant, but CDK would still require growth factor-bound tyrosine kinase receptor signaling to phosphorylate Rb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rb would become hyperphosphorylated, releasing E2F and driving G1-S transition irrespective of growth factor signaling

CDKs are constitutively expressed but normally inactive without cyclin binding — they require phase-specific cyclins for activation. A mutation causing constitutive CDK activity bypasses this regulatory requirement entirely → Rb is hyperphosphorylated regardless of growth factor signaling or p21-mediated inhibition → E2F released → G1-S transition proceeds unchecked. This models oncogenic CDK dysregulation (e.g., cyclin D-CDK4/6 pathway dysregulation in many cancers, therapeutically targeted by CDK4/6 inhibitors like palbociclib).

| Component | Normal regulation | Constitutively active CDK

| --------- | ----------------- | -------------------------

| CDK | Inactive without cyclin | Active regardless of cyclin

| Growth factor dependency | Required for cyclin expression | Bypassed

| Rb phosphorylation | Regulated by cyclin-CDK activity | Hyperphosphorylated unconditionally

| E2F | Released only when appropriate | Constitutively released

| Restriction point | Enforced | Lost

questions.text: All are features of venous thrombus, except:
options: Composed mainly of red cells (red thrombi)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Caused by turbulent blood flow

Venous thrombi (red thrombi) typically form due to blood stasis and hypercoagulability, which are key components of Virchow’s triad.

Features of venous thrombi:

• Commonly occur in deep veins of the legs (DVT).
• Propagate in the direction of blood flow (antegrade) toward the heart.
• Rich in red blood cells and fibrin, giving them a red appearance.

Important distinction:

• Turbulent blood flow is mainly associated with arterial thrombus formation, not venous thrombi.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are examples of physiological apoptosis except:
options: Regression of Müllerian duct structures in the male fetus
Endometrial cell breakdown during the menstrual cycle
Atrophy of the pancreas following duct obstruction
Elimination of neutrophils after an acute inflammatory response
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atrophy of the pancreas following duct obstruction

Pathologic atrophy of parenchymal organs (pancreas, parotid gland, kidney) following duct obstruction is a pathological cause of apoptosis, triggered by injury rather than normal developmental or homeostatic processes. Müllerian duct regression (embryogenesis), endometrial breakdown (hormone-dependent cycling), and neutrophil elimination after inflammation (immune response resolution) are all classic physiological apoptosis triggers — part of normal development, tissue turnover, and immune regulation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following conditions are associated with Neurosecretory bodies except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adrenal cortical tumor

Neurosecretory (dense-core) granules are membrane-bound secretory vesicles present in neuroendocrine cells, storing peptide hormones and amines.

They are typically seen in neuroendocrine tumors, such as:

• Medullary thyroid carcinoma (from parafollicular C cells)
• Pituitary adenoma
• Paraganglioma / pheochromocytoma

Adrenal cortical tumors arise from steroid-producing cortical cells, which synthesize hormones from cholesterol in smooth ER and mitochondria, not from stored secretory granules.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All streptococcal antigen–host antigen–disease associations are true, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyaluronic acid – Skin - Impetigo

Certain streptococcal antigens cross-react with host tissues, causing immune-mediated diseases due to molecular mimicry.

Important associations:

• M protein → Myocardium → Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) due to cross-reactive antibodies.
• Streptococcal cytoplasmic membrane antigens → Glomeruli → Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
• Peptidoglycan → Skin antigens → Guttate psoriasis following streptococcal infection.

Hyaluronic acid capsule of streptococci mainly acts as a virulence factor that prevents phagocytosis and does not cause molecular mimicry leading to impetigo.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All tissues are correctly matched to their stem cell location, except:
options: Intestine – Paneth cells near base of crypt
Skin – Bulge region of hair follicle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cornea – Ciliary body

Adult stem cells reside in specific tissue niches responsible for regeneration and repair.

Correct stem cell locations:

• Intestine: Stem cells located at the base of crypts of Lieberkühn, closely associated with Paneth cells.
• Skin: Stem cells present in the bulge region of hair follicles.
• Liver: Hepatic progenitor cells (oval cells) located in the Canal of Hering.

Incorrect match:

• Cornea – Ciliary body: Corneal stem cells are actually located in the limbus (limbal stem cells) at the junction of cornea and sclera, not the ciliary body.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An 80-year-old man is found to have a malignant tumor whose cells show unlimited replicative potential despite advanced patient age. Molecular studies reveal reactivation of an enzyme normally restricted to germ cells and stem cells. Which best explains why this reactivation promotes tumorigenesis?
options: It accelerates telomere shortening, triggering rapid clonal selection
It maintains telomere length, allowing cells to bypass replicative senescence
It increases p53 expression, inducing apoptosis evasion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It maintains telomere length, allowing cells to bypass replicative senescence

Telomerase reactivation in somatic cells maintains telomere length, allowing cells to escape replicative senescence (the normal "counting" mechanism that limits division via progressive telomere shortening → cell-cycle arrest/apoptosis). This permits unlimited replicative potential, a hallmark of cancer in aging tissue. Option A reverses the actual mechanism; C and D describe unrelated/opposite pathways (senescence induction rather than evasion).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Arrange the steps of the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis in the correct order. i. Binding of Fas ligand of T cells to Fas ii. Trimerization of Fas iii. Activation of caspase 8, 10. iv. Formation of FADD
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. i > ii > iv > iii

The extrinsic pathway of apoptosis (death receptor pathway) is triggered when death ligands bind to death receptors on the cell surface, leading to activation of initiator caspases (caspase-8 and caspase-10).

Correct sequence:

i. Binding of Fas ligand (FasL) on T cells to Fas (CD95) receptor on the target cell.

ii. Trimerization of Fas receptors after ligand binding.

iii. Recruitment of adaptor protein FADD (Fas-associated death domain) forming the death-inducing signaling complex (DISC).

iv. Activation of initiator caspases (caspase-8 and caspase-10) → activation of executioner caspases (3, 6, 7) → apoptosis.

Thus, the correct order: i → ii → iv → iii

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Crizotinib is most appropriately used in the treatment of which of the following lung cancers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer

Crizotinib is a targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used in patients with ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The most common ALK alteration is the EML4-ALK fusion gene, which leads to constitutive activation of ALK signaling and uncontrolled tumor growth. Inhibiting ALK results in significant tumor regression and improved progression-free survival.

Why not the other options?

• A. EGFR-mutated NSCLC – treated with EGFR TKIs such as Osimertinib, Gefitinib, or Erlotinib.
• C. KRAS-mutated NSCLC – specific KRAS-targeted therapies (e.g., KRAS G12C inhibitors) are used, not crizotinib.
• D. Small cell lung cancer – typically managed with chemotherapy and immunotherapy rather than ALK-targeted therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Following the resection of the pituitary adenoma in a patient with Cushing's disease, which intracellular change is most likely in residual adenoma cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crooke hyaline change

Crooke hyaline change refers to the accumulation of cytokeratin filaments in the cytoplasm of pituitary corticotroph cells due to prolonged exposure to high glucocorticoid levels. Excess cortisol suppresses ACTH production, leading to perinuclear hyaline (glassy) cytoplasmic changes in corticotrophs.

In Cushing disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma), surrounding normal corticotroph cells show Crooke hyaline change because of chronic cortisol excess.

Other options:

A. Mallory-Denk bodies: cytokeratin aggregates in alcoholic liver disease / steatohepatitis.

B. Dutcher bodies: intranuclear immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cell disorders.

D. Woronin bodies: structures in fungal cells, not human pathology.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What characteristics define necrosis among the options provided? 1. Disrupted cell membrane 2. Induces inflammation 3. Swelling of the cell 4. Can be seen physiologically 5. Causes nuclear fragmentation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

Necrosis is a form of pathologic cell death caused by severe injury such as ischemia, toxins, or infection. It is characterized by loss of membrane integrity, cell swelling, and leakage of intracellular contents, which triggers inflammation.

Key features of necrosis:

• Disrupted cell membrane
• Cell swelling (oncosis)
• Induction of inflammation

Important distinction:

• Necrosis: pathologic, inflammatory.
• Apoptosis: programmed, physiologic or pathologic, cell shrinkage, no inflammation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What type of collagen is involved in the classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 5

Classic Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS) is caused by mutations in type V collagen genes (COL5A1, COL5A2), leading to defective collagen fibril formation.

Clinical features:

• Hyperextensible skin
• Joint hypermobility
• Easy bruising
• Poor wound healing with atrophic (“cigarette paper”) scars

Other options:

• Type 3 collagen → Vascular EDS

A. Type 1 collagen → Osteogenesis imperfecta

B. Type 2 collagen→ Cartilage disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which color vacutainer will you pick for PT and aPTT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blue

Prothrombin Time (PT) and Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) require blood collection in a light blue-top vacutainer, which contains 3.2% sodium citrate as the anticoagulant. Sodium citrate binds calcium reversibly, preventing clotting while preserving coagulation factors for laboratory testing.

• Blue-top tube = Sodium citrate
• Used for coagulation studies, including:

• PT/INR
• aPTT
• Fibrinogen
• D-dimer
• Coagulation factor assays

| Vacutainer Color | Additive | Common Use

| ---------------- | -------- | ----------

| Blue | Sodium citrate | PT, aPTT, coagulation studies

| Lavender | EDTA | CBC, peripheral smear, HbA1c

| Green | Heparin | Plasma chemistry, ABG

| Red | No anticoagulant/clot activator | Serum biochemistry, serology

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which cyclin-CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase) combination is essential for the G2 to M phase transition of cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cyclin B-CDK1

The G2 → M phase transition of the cell cycle is regulated by the Cyclin B–CDK1 complex, also called the Maturation Promoting Factor (MPF).

Mechanism:

• During late G2 phase, Cyclin B accumulates and binds to CDK1.
• Activation of this complex triggers entry into mitosis by promoting:
• Chromosome condensation
• Nuclear envelope breakdown
• Mitotic spindle formation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following cell types is classified as stable cells in terms of their proliferative capacity and turnover rate?
options: Stratified squamous epithelia of the skin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endothelial cells in blood vessels

Labile Cells

• These cells are continuously being lost and replaced by maturation from tissue stem cells and by the proliferation of mature cells.
• Labile cells include hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow and the majority of surface epithelia.

Stable Cells

• They are quiescent and have minimal proliferative activity from progenitor cells.
• They divide only when required but have limited regeneration compared to labile cells.
• Stable cells constitute the parenchyma of most solid tissues (e.g., liver), endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells.

Permanent Cells

• These cells are considered to be terminally differentiated and non-proliferative in postnatal life.
• Permanent cells include neurons and cardiac and skeletal muscle cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the changes in intracellular sodium (Na⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), and pH during cell injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase, increase, decrease

During reversible cell injury (especially ischemia), ATP depletion leads to failure of membrane ion pumps.

Key intracellular changes:

• Na⁺ increases → due to failure of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → water influx → cell swelling.
• Ca²⁺ increases → due to membrane damage and impaired Ca²⁺ pumps, activating destructive enzymes (proteases, phospholipases).
• pH decreases → due to anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid accumulation.

Therefore: Na⁺ ↑, Ca²⁺ ↑, pH ↓ (Option A).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding necrosis?
options: It is due to denaturation of protein
It is due to enzymatic digestion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is an active process

Necrosis is a form of unregulated cell death that occurs following severe cellular injury. It is characterized by protein denaturation and enzymatic digestion of dead cells, leading to membrane disruption, leakage of cellular contents, and an associated inflammatory response.

Why C is false?

• Necrosis is a passive, uncontrolled process resulting from irreversible cell injury.
• It does not require cellular energy (ATP) and is therefore not an active process.
• In contrast, apoptosis is an active, energy-dependent (programmed) form of cell death.

Why the Other Options Are Correct?

• A. Due to denaturation of proteins → Major mechanism of coagulative necrosis.
• B. Due to enzymatic digestion → Responsible for liquefactive changes and tissue breakdown.
• D. Always pathological → Necrosis occurs only in disease states or injury.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is not a tumor suppressor protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ras

Tumor suppressor genes normally inhibit cell proliferation, promote DNA repair, or trigger apoptosis when cellular damage occurs. Loss-of-function mutations in these genes remove critical growth restraints and contribute to carcinogenesis.

Ras is not a tumor suppressor protein; it is a proto-oncogene that encodes a GTP-binding signaling protein involved in transmitting growth signals from cell surface receptors to the nucleus. Gain-of-function mutations in Ras result in constitutive activation of growth-promoting pathways and uncontrolled cell proliferation.

Why not the other options?

• A. p53 – the “guardian of the genome”; induces cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, or apoptosis in response to DNA damage.
• B. RB protein – regulates the G1→S cell cycle checkpoint by inhibiting E2F transcription factors.
• C. APC – tumor suppressor that negatively regulates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway; mutations are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following proteins functions as a GTP-binding molecular switch in intracellular signaling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ras

Ras is a small GTP-binding protein (small GTPase) that functions as a molecular switch in intracellular signaling pathways controlling cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation.

Mechanism:

• Inactive state: Ras bound to GDP
• Active state: Ras bound to GTP
• Activation occurs after growth factor receptor (RTK) stimulation.
• Active Ras triggers downstream pathways such as the MAPK signaling cascade, leading to gene transcription and cell proliferation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements about apoptosis is false?
options: Characterized by the activation of caspases leading to DNA fragmentation.
Inflammatory response and release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
Chromatin condensation and formation of cytoplasmic blebs.
Eliminates cells that are injured beyond repair without eliciting a host reaction.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inflammatory response and release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).

Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of caspases, DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and membrane blebbing with formation of apoptotic bodies that are rapidly phagocytosed. Because the cell contents remain membrane-bound and are cleared efficiently, apoptosis does not trigger an inflammatory response. In contrast, necrosis leads to cell membrane rupture, release of intracellular components (including DAMPs), and inflammation.

• Apoptosis: caspase activation, cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, no inflammation.
• Necrosis: cell swelling, membrane rupture, DAMP release → inflammation.

So, the false statement is B, because inflammatory response with DAMP release is a feature of necrosis, not apoptosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about proto-oncogenes? 1. KIT has increased expression in GIST. 2. KRAS mutation is more commonly associated with small-cell lung carcinoma. 3. ERBB2 over-expression is associated with breast carcinomas. 4. PDGFR-β has suppressed expression in colorectal cancers.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3

Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes that regulate cell growth, proliferation, and survival. When they undergo mutation, amplification, or overexpression, they become oncogenes, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation.

• KIT overexpression/mutation → Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).
• ERBB2 (HER2/neu) amplification → Breast carcinoma.

Why others are false:

2. KRAS mutations are common in adenocarcinoma of lung, pancreatic, and colorectal cancers—not typically small-cell lung carcinoma.

4. PDGFR-β acts as a growth factor receptor proto-oncogene; cancer usually involves activation/overexpression, not suppression.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are True? 1. The basement membrane remains intact in dysplasia. 2. Dysplasia is an adaptive response to stress or injury. 3. Pleomorphism is observed in metaplasia. 4. Myositis ossificans is an example of dysplasia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 only

Dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation of epithelial cells, characterized by cellular atypia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, and loss of normal tissue architecture. It is considered premalignant, but the basement membrane remains intact. When cells breach the basement membrane, it becomes invasive carcinoma.

1. The basement membrane remains intact in dysplasia. True. Basement membrane is intact in dysplasia.

2. Dysplasia is an adaptive response to stress or injury. False. Dysplasia is not an adaptive response (metaplasia is adaptive).

3. Pleomorphism is observed in metaplasia. False. Pleomorphism occurs in dysplasia, not in metaplasia.

4. Myositis ossificans is an example of dysplasia. False. Myositis ossificans is an example of metaplasia (bone formation in muscle), not dysplasia.

| Feature | Metaplasia | Dysplasia | Anaplasia

| ------- | ---------- | --------- | ---------

| Definition | Differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another cell type | Disordered growth and loss of architectural orientation of cells | Lack of cellular differentiation and organisation

| Nature | Adaptive response to stress or injury | Preneoplastic | Associated with malignant transformation

| Reversibility | Reversible | Reversible in early stages (irreversible if whole epithelium is involved) | Irreversible

| Pleomorphism | Absent | Present in low-grade | Present in high-grade

| Nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio | Normal (1:4 to 1:6) | Increased (↑) | Increased (↑↑↑)

| Mitotic figures | Absent/minimal at normal places | Typical mitotic figures present at abnormal places | Atypical, bizarre mitotic figures present at abnormal places

| Basement membrane integrity | Intact | Intact | Breached

| Example | Barrett’s oesophagus, myositis ossificans | Cervical dysplasia of squamous cells | Carcinoma of the cervix, carcinoma oesophagus

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding phosphorylation of the RB (Retinoblastoma) protein is true?
options: Hypophosphorylated RB allows progression from G1 to S phase
Phosphorylation of RB prevents binding to E2F transcription factors
RB is phosphorylated by cyclin B–CDK1 complex
RB phosphorylation leads to cell cycle arrest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphorylation of RB prevents binding to E2F transcription factors

The retinoblastoma (RB) protein is a tumor suppressor that regulates the G1 → S phase transition of the cell cycle.

• In its hypophosphorylated (active) state, RB binds to E2F transcription factors, preventing transcription of genes required for S-phase entry.
• When RB is phosphorylated by cyclin D–CDK4/6 and cyclin E–CDK2, it becomes inactive and releases E2F.
• Free E2F activates transcription of genes necessary for DNA synthesis and progression into S phase.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of these options is not a mechanism contributing to thalidomide's teratogenic effects?
options: Release of reactive oxygen species and free radicles
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inhibition of IL2, IL4, IL5

Thalidomide teratogenicity occurs through multiple mechanisms that disrupt limb bud development and embryonic vascular formation.

Key mechanisms include:

• Binding to cereblon (CRBN), a protein involved in ubiquitin ligase complexes, altering gene expression important for limb development.
• Anti-angiogenic effects, which impair formation of new blood vessels in the developing limb bud.
• Generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leading to oxidative stress and embryonic cell damage.

Inhibition of IL-2, IL-4, and IL-5 relates mainly to thalidomide’s immunomodulatory effects, not its teratogenic mechanism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Caspases are involved in which of the following types of programmed cell death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis and Apoptosis

Caspases = cysteine proteases

• Exist as inactive precursors
• Get activated during programmed cell death

Caspases are central mediators of apoptosis, with initiator and executioner caspases driving programmed cell death.

Pyroptosis is a caspase-dependent inflammatory cell death mediated mainly by caspase-1.

Necroptosis and ferroptosis are caspase-independent forms of regulated cell death.

Hence, caspases are involved in apoptosis and pyroptosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not helpful for differentiating between necrosis and apoptosis?
options: Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Altered cell shape

Both necrosis and apoptosis show altered cell shape (Necrosis-cell enlarges; apoptosis-cell shrinks), making it non-discriminatory.

| Option | Necrosis | Apoptosis | Discriminates?

| ------ | -------- | --------- | --------------

| A. Intact cell organelle | Organelles disintegrate | Organelles preserved (esp. early) | Yes → points to apoptosis

| B. Altered cell shape | Cell swelling (oncosis) | Cell shrinkage + apoptotic bodies | No — shape changes in both

| C. Caspase-mediated degradation | Lysosomal hydrolases (auto-/heterolysis) | Caspases + endonucleases | Yes → points to apoptosis

| D. Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change | Yes — myelin figures | No | Yes → points to necrosis

Why B is the answer: Both processes distort cell morphology — necrosis via swelling, apoptosis via shrinkage. The mere presence of an altered shape tells you a cell is dying but not by which mechanism, so it has no discriminatory value.

• Mnemonic — Apoptosis = "A SHRINK": ATP-dependent, Shrinkage, Hyperchromatic (chromatin condensation), Regulated (caspases), Intact membrane, No inflammation, Karyorrhexis into apoptotic bodies.
• Nucleus: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis is the necrosis sequence; apoptosis stops at fragmentation into membrane-bound bodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following proteins functions as a pro-apoptotic factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BAX

Cell stress / DNA damage

↓

BAX / BAK activation

↓

Mitochondrial membrane permeabilization

↓

Cytochrome c release

↓

Caspase activation

↓

Apoptosis

BAX is a pro-apoptotic member of the BCL-2 family that promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization. It facilitates release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, activating the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

This leads to caspase activation and programmed cell death.

BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 are anti-apoptotic proteins that inhibit mitochondrial apoptosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about free radicals is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Causes Fibrinoid necrosis

Free radicals = molecules with unpaired electrons → highly reactive

They damage:

• Lipids (membranes)
• Proteins

A. Lipid peroxidation

Correct statement

• MOST IMPORTANT mechanism of free radical injury
• Damages cell membrane → increased permeability → cell death

B. SOD inactivates free radicals- Correct

• Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts:

• Then catalase/glutathione finish detox

C. Produced by neutrophils- Correct

• During respiratory burst
• Used to kill bacteria

NADPH oxidase → ROS generation

D. Fibrinoid necrosis

Incorrect, Why?

• Fibrinoid necrosis = immune-mediated vascular damage
• Seen in:

• Vasculitis
• Malignant hypertension

Mechanism:

• Immune complexes + fibrin deposition in vessel wall
• NOT due to ROS

Fibrinoid Necrosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding neutrophil extracellular trapping (NET)?
options: It is detected in blood during sepsis
It is produced in response to bacterial infection.
It is chromatin with antibacterial enzymes.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mitochondrial DNA is seen.

Bacterial infection

↓

Neutrophil activation

↓

Nuclear chromatin decondensation

↓

DNA + enzymes released

↓

NET formation → traps microbes

Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) consist of decondensed nuclear chromatin decorated with antimicrobial enzymes like elastase and myeloperoxidase.

They are released in response to bacterial infections and are detectable in sepsis.

NETs are composed primarily of nuclear DNA, not mitochondrial DNA.

Hence, the statement regarding mitochondrial DNA is false.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of programmed cell death primarily involves the action of caspase-1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis

Pyroptosis is a form of programmed inflammatory cell death mediated by activation of caspase-1. Occurs in:

• Macrophages
• Infected cells

Caspase-1 is activated via inflammasomes and leads to cleavage of IL-1β and IL-18. This causes pore formation in the cell membrane, cell swelling, and membrane rupture.

Pathogen / Danger signal

↓

Inflammasome activation

↓

Caspase-1 activation

↓

Gasdermin pore formation

↓

Cell swelling + membrane rupture

↓

Release of IL-1β, IL-18 → Inflammation

Apoptosis involves caspase-3, 6, 9. Necroptosis is caspase-independent, and necrosis is unregulated cell death.

| Feature | Apoptosis | Pyroptosis | Necroptosis | Necrosis

| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------

| Type | Programmed | Programmed | Programmed | Uncontrolled

| Inflammation |  No | Yes | Yes | Yes

| Key enzyme | Caspase 3,9 | Caspase-1 | RIPK3 | None

| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells | Swells | Swells

| Membrane | Intact | Ruptures | Ruptures | Ruptures

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man develops fever, chills, back pain, and hemoglobinuria within 1 hour of receiving a blood transfusion. The transfusion is immediately stopped. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum LDH. Which of the following best explains the underlying immunopathogenesis of this reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2 hypersensitivity reaction

Type II Hypersensitivity- Antibodies (IgG/IgM) target cell surface antigens

Leads to:

o    Complement activation

o    Cell destruction

Wrong blood transfusion (ABO mismatch)

↓

Recipient antibodies (IgM)

↓

Bind donor RBC antigens

↓

Complement activation

↓

Intravascular hemolysis

↓

Hemoglobinuria + ↑ LDH

The presentation is consistent with an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

Preformed recipient IgM or IgG antibodies react against donor RBC antigens.

This causes complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria and raised LDH.

Such antibody-mediated cytotoxic reactions are classified as type II hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient is scheduled for coagulation testing, including prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Which one of the following vacutainers is the most appropriate choice for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blue-colored tube

| Vial Color & Additive | Uses

| --------------------- | ----

| Blue (Trisodium citrate) | • Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, D-dimer) • Platelet function studies

| Red (Plain vial / Clot activator) | • Serum samples • Biochemistry, serology

| Yellow (SPS / ACD) | • Blood culture (SPS) • HLA typing (ACD)

| Green (Heparin) | • Light green (Lithium heparin): ABG, electrolytes • Dark green (Sodium heparin): Biochemistry, osmotic fragility

| Lavender / Purple (EDTA) | • CBC (Complete blood count) • Peripheral smear • HbA1c • ESR (Wintrobe method)

| Grey (Sodium fluoride + Potassium oxalate) | • Glucose estimation • Lactate

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A protein is fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin wax. Which of the following methods is the most appropriate means for identification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the preferred technique for detecting and localizing specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. It uses antigen-specific antibodies to identify protein expression while preserving tissue architecture, making it invaluable for tumor diagnosis, classification, and prognostic marker assessment.

• Immunohistochemistry is specifically designed for protein detection in FFPE tissue sections and allows visualization of protein expression within the histological context.

Why not the other options?

• A. Western blot: Detects proteins but requires fresh/frozen tissue lysates and does not preserve tissue architecture.
• C. Flow cytometry: Analyzes proteins on live cells or cell suspensions; not suitable for paraffin-embedded tissue.
• D. In situ hybridization: Detects DNA or RNA (nucleic acids), not proteins.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: For HbA1c sample, the vacutainer used contains which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. EDTA

Need to analyze RBCs

↓

Prevent clotting without damaging cells

↓

Use EDTA

↓

Accurate HbA1c measurement

Vacutainer Vials and Their Uses

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of acquired systemic amyloidosis? 1. Tuberculosis 2. Multiple myeloma 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis 4. Chronic osteomyelitis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Systemic amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. The two major forms of acquired systemic amyloidosis are AL (light-chain) amyloidosis, associated with plasma cell disorders, and AA (secondary) amyloidosis, associated with chronic inflammatory or infectious diseases.

Why is D correct?

• 1. Tuberculosis: Chronic inflammation leads to increased Serum Amyloid A (SAA) protein, resulting in AA amyloidosis.
• 2. Multiple myeloma: Causes AL amyloidosis due to deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains.
• 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis: A classic cause of secondary (AA) amyloidosis due to persistent inflammation.
• 4. Chronic osteomyelitis: Long-standing infection increases SAA production, leading to AA amyloid deposition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are correctly matched with respective stain and its properties? 1. Perl’s – Iron, red 2. Alizarin – Calcium, black 3. Giemsa – Mast cells, purple 4. Von Gieson – Elastin fibres, blue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 only

1. Perl’s – Iron\, red-  Incorrect

Correct fact:

• Perl’s Prussian Blue stain → Iron = BLUE (not red)

• Hemosiderin (iron overload)
• Hemochromatosis
• Old hemorrhage

2. Alizarin – Calcium\, black- Incorrect

Correct fact:

• Alizarin Red S → Calcium = ORANGE-RED (not black)

Alizarin red S staining for mineralization. The calcified nodules appeared bright red in color. Used for:

• Calcification (e.g., dystrophic, metastatic)

3. Giemsa – Mast cells\, purple- Correct

Giemsa stain:

• Mast cells → purple (metachromatic granules)

Bone marrow aspirate showing normal mast cell (arrow). Also stains:

• Blood parasites (e.g., malaria)
• Bone marrow cells

4. Von Gieson – Elastin fibres\, blue-  Incorrect

Correct facts:

• Von Gieson stain:

• Collagen → RED
• Muscle & cytoplasm → YELLOW

Elastin is NOT blue here. Elastin stains:

• Verhoeff-Van Gieson (VVG) → elastin = BLACK

| Stain | Substance | Color

| ----- | --------- | -----

| Perl’s Prussian Blue | Iron (Hemosiderin) | 🔵 Blue

| Alizarin Red S | Calcium | 🔴 Orange-red

| Giemsa | Mast cells | 🟣 Purple

| Von Gieson | Collagen | 🔴 Red

| VVG stain | Elastin | ⚫ Black

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is/are criteria for anaphylaxis? a. Persistent abdominal cramps and vomiting b. Hypertension c. Urticaria and swollen lips d. Respiratory distress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a, c & d

Allergen exposure

↓

IgE on mast cells cross-links

↓

Mast cell degranulation

↓

Histamine, leukotrienes release

↓

Vasodilation + bronchospasm + edema

↓

Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is an acute, systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving skin, mucosa, respiratory, and gastrointestinal systems.

Diagnostic criteria include urticaria with angioedema, respiratory compromise, and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms like cramps and vomiting.

| System | Features

| ------ | --------

| Skin | Urticaria, angioedema

| Respiratory | Dyspnea, wheeze, stridor

| Cardiovascular | Hypotension

| GI | Vomiting, cramps

Hypotension, not hypertension, is the cardiovascular manifestation of anaphylaxis.

Hence, options a, c, and d fulfil criteria for anaphylaxis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following should be prevented when collecting a blood sample for serum calcium?
options: Making a fist with forearm exercise
Tourniquet should be tied and released as soon as possible
Should be collected in sitting position & better to avoid prolonged immobilization
Sample should be analyzed within 15–30 min of collection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Making a fist with forearm exercise

Repeated fist clenching = forearm muscle activity. This causes:

• Local metabolic changes
• Hemoconcentration
• Altered ion balance

Result: Falsely elevated calcium (and other analytes like potassium)

Fist clenching / forearm exercise

↓

Muscle contraction

↓

↑ Local metabolites + hemoconcentration

↓

Altered serum composition

↓

False lab values (↑ Ca, ↑ K)

| Factor | Effect

| ------ | ------

| Fist clenching |  False ↑ calcium

| Prolonged tourniquet | ↑ protein-bound calcium

| Posture change | Alters calcium levels

| Delayed processing | pH changes → affects Ca binding

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following types of amyloid protein is typically seen in a patient who develops amyloidosis secondary to long-standing chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. AA

Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, inflammatory bowel disease). Persistent inflammation increases hepatic production of Serum Amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant, which is cleaved and deposited as AA amyloid in tissues.

• AA amyloid is derived from Serum Amyloid A (SAA) and is the characteristic amyloid protein in secondary amyloidosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. β2-Microglobulin: Associated with long-term hemodialysis-related amyloidosis.
• C. AL: Derived from immunoglobulin light chains; seen in primary amyloidosis and multiple myeloma.
• D. Transthyretin (ATTR): Seen in senile systemic amyloidosis and familial amyloid polyneuropathy/cardiomyopathy.

| Amyloid Protein | Associated Disease

| --------------- | ------------------

| AA | Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis due to chronic inflammation

| AL | Primary amyloidosis, Multiple myeloma

| Aβ | Alzheimer disease

| β2-Microglobulin | Hemodialysis-associated amyloidosis

| ATTR (Transthyretin) | Senile systemic and hereditary amyloidosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which vacutainer is commonly used to collect blood samples for serum electrolyte analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Green

Need electrolyte measurement

↓

Avoid clotting + avoid ion interference

↓

Use heparin (green tube)

↓

Accurate electrolyte values

• Serum electrolyte analysis commonly uses a green-top vacutainer containing heparin as anticoagulant.
• Heparin prevents clotting without chelating ions, thus preserving true electrolyte levels.
• EDTA (purple) chelates calcium and alters potassium, while citrate (blue) dilutes the sample.
• Yellow-top tubes are used for serum separation, but may also be used for routine electrolyte estimation making the answer controversial.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: “Leukemia”, as an occupational cancer, is most commonly related to the exposure to which one of the following industrial chemicals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benzol

Benzene (benzol) is a well-established occupational carcinogen associated particularly with leukemia, especially acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Why not the other options?

• A. Mineral oil: Associated mainly with skin cancers after prolonged occupational exposure.
• B. Auramine: Associated with bladder cancer in occupational exposure.
• C. β-naphthylamine: Classically associated with urinary bladder carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: “Oncogene addiction” seen in tumors refers to:
options: Oncogenes are expressed only during embryonic development
Tumors use immune checkpoints to evade immune destruction
Tumors depend predominantly on a single oncogenic pathway for survival, allowing targeted therapy against that pathway
Dependence of cancer cells on multiple tumor suppressor genes for survival
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tumors depend predominantly on a single oncogenic pathway for survival, allowing targeted therapy against that pathway

Oncogene addiction refers to the phenomenon in which tumor cells become highly dependent on a single activated oncogenic pathway for their growth, survival, and proliferation, despite harboring multiple genetic abnormalities. This dependency forms the basis for targeted cancer therapy, as inhibition of the critical oncogenic driver can produce marked tumor regression.

Examples of oncogene addiction:

• BCR-ABL → Chronic myeloid leukemia (treated with imatinib)
• HER2 (ERBB2) → HER2-positive breast cancer (treated with trastuzumab)
• EGFR mutation → Non-small cell lung cancer (treated with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors)
• BRAF V600E mutation → Melanoma (treated with BRAF inhibitors)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 4-year-old patient presented with a rectal mass 2.5 cm by 3 cm. On biopsy it had the presence of colonic mucosa with multiple dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory cells. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hamartoma

Hamartoma is a benign, disorganized overgrowth of tissue native to the organ.

In the colon, it shows normal colonic mucosa with cystically dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory cells.

These lesions commonly present as rectal polyps in children.

| Feature | Hamartoma | Choristoma | Adenoma | Adenocarcinoma

| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ------- | --------------

| Tissue type | Native | Ectopic | Neoplastic | Malignant

| Organization | Disorganized | Normal | Dysplastic | Atypical

| Age | Children | Any | Adults | Adults

| Malignancy | ❌ No | ❌ No | Premalignant | Yes

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man who has been employed in a shipyard for more than 30 years undergoes a routine medical examination. His occupational exposure places him at increased risk for pulmonary disease. Exposure to which of the following substances is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asbestos

Asbestos exposure is classically associated with shipyard workers, construction workers, insulation workers, and plumbers. Inhaled asbestos fibers cause asbestosis, a diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, and significantly increase the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. The latency period is typically 20–40 years after exposure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cotton dust: Causes byssinosis, seen in textile workers.
• B. Coal dust: Causes coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (black lung disease), seen in coal miners.
• D. Silica: Causes silicosis, commonly seen in sandblasters, quarry workers, and miners.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of working in the dye and chemical industry for more than three decades presents with painless hematuria. Further evaluation reveals urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the urinary bladder. Exposure to which of the following chemicals is most strongly associated with this malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benzidine

Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the urinary bladder is strongly associated with occupational exposure to aromatic amines, particularly benzidine and β-naphthylamine, which are commonly encountered in the dye, rubber, leather, paint, and chemical industries. These carcinogens are excreted in urine, where prolonged exposure to the urothelium promotes malignant transformation.

The patient has:

• Painless hematuria (classic presentation of bladder cancer)
• Long-term employment in the dye and chemical industry

Benzidine, an aromatic amine, is the occupational carcinogen most strongly linked to urothelial carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vinyl chloride: Associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and acro-osteolysis.
• B. Asbestos: Associated with malignant mesothelioma, bronchogenic carcinoma, and asbestosis.
• D. Arsenic: Associated with skin cancers (SCC, BCC), lung cancer, and hepatic angiosarcoma; although it may increase bladder cancer risk, the classic occupational association tested for urothelial carcinoma is benzidine.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presenting with hypercalcemia is found to have multiple pancreatic lesions on evaluation. Further assessment is performed to identify an underlying inherited genetic syndrome. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations
There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells
Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients
Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Menin proto-oncogene mutation is associated with MEN 1

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) on chromosome 11q13. It is classically characterized by tumors of the Parathyroid glands, Pancreatic islet cells, and Pituitary gland (“3 Ps”). In a patient with hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism) and multiple pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, MEN 1 should be strongly suspected.

Why not the other options?

• A. Patients should be screened for RET gene mutations: RET mutations are associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B, not MEN 1.
• B. There is an increased risk of thyroid cancer arising from follicular cells: MEN 2 is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from parafollicular C cells, not follicular cells.
• C. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in such patients: Recommended in RET mutation carriers (MEN 2) to prevent medullary thyroid carcinoma; not indicated in MEN 1.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A researcher is investigating the restriction (R) point, the first major checkpoint of the cell cycle that determines whether a cell will commit to DNA synthesis or exit the cell cycle into a quiescent (G₀) state. This checkpoint is located immediately before which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S phase

The G₁/S checkpoint (Restriction point or R point) is the first and most important checkpoint of the cell cycle. It occurs in late G₁ phase, immediately before the S phase, where the cell decides whether to:

• Proceed to DNA replication (S phase), or
• Exit the cell cycle and enter the quiescent G₀ phase

Once a cell crosses this checkpoint, it is committed to completing the cell cycle, even if external growth factors are withdrawn.

The checkpoint assesses:

• Cell size
• Nutrient and energy availability
• Growth factor stimulation
• DNA damage

It is regulated by:

• Cyclin D–CDK4/6
• Cyclin E–CDK2
• Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein
• p53 (via p21 in response to DNA damage)

Why not the other options?

• A. G₂ phase: Incorrect. The G₂/M checkpoint occurs after DNA replication, ensuring DNA has been completely and accurately replicated before mitosis.
• B. M phase: Incorrect. The spindle assembly checkpoint occurs during metaphase, ensuring proper chromosome attachment before anaphase.
• C. S phase: ✅ Correct. The restriction point is located immediately before the S phase.
• D. G₀ phase: Incorrect. G₀ is not a phase that follows the checkpoint; rather, cells exit from G₁ into G₀ if they do not receive the signals required to pass the checkpoint.

High-yield pearl

| Cell cycle checkpoint | Location | Function

| --------------------- | -------- | --------

| G₁/S (Restriction point) | End of G₁, before S phase | Determines commitment to DNA replication; checks DNA damage, nutrients, growth factors

| G₂/M checkpoint | End of G₂ | Ensures DNA replication is complete and DNA is undamaged before mitosis

| Spindle checkpoint | Metaphase | Ensures all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers before anaphase

Exam tip:

The G₁/S checkpoint is the commitment checkpoint of the cell cycle:

• Pass → Enter S phase and replicate DNA
• Fail → Cell arrests for repair or exits into G₀.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All of the following are growth promoting proto-oncogenes except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TGF beta

TGF-β is growth-inhibitory, not growth-promoting.

Proto-oncogenes encode growth factors that stimulate cell proliferation and survival.

FGF, PDGF, and TGF-α act as mitogenic signals promoting cell cycle progression.

Growth factors (FGF, PDGF, TGF-α)

↓

Receptor activation

↓

RAS/MAPK pathway

↓

Cell proliferation

TGF-β, in contrast, inhibits epithelial cell proliferation by inducing cell cycle arrest via SMAD signalling. Loss of TGF-β signalling contributes to oncogenesis, but the gene itself functions as a tumor suppressor.

| Factor | Function | Role in Cancer

| ------ | -------- | --------------

| FGF | Proliferation, angiogenesis | Oncogenic

| PDGF | Cell growth | Oncogenic

| TGF-α | EGFR activation | Oncogenic

| TGF-β
“Beta” = brake 🛑 | Growth inhibition | Tumor suppressor

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Epithelial mesenchymal transcription is mediated by which transcription factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SNAIL/TWIST

Epithelial cell

↓

SNAIL / TWIST activation

↓

↓ E-cadherin (cell adhesion)

↓

Loss of polarity

↓

Gain of motility

↓

Invasion → Metastasis

Epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) is driven by transcription factors that repress epithelial markers like E-cadherin.

SNAIL and TWIST are key EMT transcription factors that promote loss of cell adhesion and increased motility.

They induce mesenchymal phenotype, facilitating invasion and metastasis.

Cathepsin D and MMP-9 are proteases involved in matrix degradation, while TTF-1 is a lineage-specific transcription factor, not EMT-related.

Tumor cell

↓

EMT (SNAIL/TWIST)

↓

↓ E-cadherin

↓

Basement membrane breakdown (MMPs)

↓

Invasion → Intravasation → Metastasis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mechanism of carcinogenesis of UV radiation is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation of pyrimidine dimers

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, particularly UV-B (280– 320 nm), causes DNA damage by inducing the formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers between adjacent pyrimidine bases. These dimers distort the DNA helix and interfere with DNA replication and transcription. If not repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, they can result in mutations that promote skin carcinogenesis.

• Formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers is the primary mechanism by which UV radiation causes carcinogenesis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Activation of cyclins: Promotes cell cycle progression but is not the direct mechanism of UV-induced DNA damage.
• B. Degradation of TP53: Occurs with oncogenic viruses such as HPV (E6 protein), not UV radiation.
• D. Inhibition of NF-Κb: Not the primary mechanism of UV-induced carcinogenesis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding Li-Fraumeni syndrome? 1. It has autosomal dominant inheritance and is associated with P53 gene. 2. It has autosomal recessive inheritance and is associated with P53 gene. 3. It is associated with an increased risk of sarcomas and leukaemia. 4. It is associated with an increased risk of brain tumours and osteosarcomas. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is a rare autosomal dominant hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome caused by germline mutations in the TP53 (p53) tumor suppressor gene. It is characterized by an increased lifetime risk of developing multiple early-onset malignancies, particularly sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinoma.

Why is B correct?

• 1. It has autosomal dominant inheritance and is associated with P53 gene. ✅

• Li-Fraumeni syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to TP53 mutation.

• 2. It has autosomal recessive inheritance and is associated with P53 gene. ❌

• The syndrome is autosomal dominant, not recessive.

• 3. It is associated with an increased risk of sarcomas and leukaemia. ✅

• Soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcomas, and leukemia are well-recognized malignancies in LFS.

• 4. It is associated with an increased risk of brain tumours and osteosarcomas. ✅

• Brain tumors and osteosarcoma are among the hallmark cancers associated with TP53 mutations.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which mutations in Ras/MAP kinase gene cause oncogenicity?
options: Constitutive activation of GTP-ase domain leading to continuous cell proliferation
Enhanced DNA repair leading to genomic instability
Inactivation of tumor suppressor gene resulting in loss of cell cycle check point
Increased activity of tyrosine kinase receptors through gene amplification
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constitutive activation of GTP-ase domain leading to continuous cell proliferation

RAS protein behaves like a binary switch:

| State | Bound Molecule | Activity

| ----- | -------------- | --------

| OFF | GDP | Inactive

| ON | GTP | Active

Activation pathway:

• Growth factor → receptor tyrosine kinase → RAS activation
• RAS-GTP → activates MAP kinase cascade → cell proliferation

Ras is a proto-oncogene encoding a small GTP-binding protein that cycles between inactive GDP-bound and active GTP-bound states.

Mutations impair intrinsic GTPase activity, locking Ras in the active GTP-bound form.

RAS mutation = GTPase activity is LOST

• RAS cannot hydrolyze GTP → GDP
• It gets stuck in “ON” position

Result:

• Continuous signaling
• Uncontrolled proliferation
• Oncogenesis

This leads to constitutive activation of the MAP kinase signaling pathway independent of growth factor stimulation. Result is continuous transcription of proliferation-related genes and uncontrolled cell division.

Unlike tumor suppressor loss, this is a gain-of-function mutation causing autonomous growth signaling.

| Feature | Oncogene (RAS) | Tumor Suppressor (p53, RB)

| ------- | -------------- | --------------------------

| Mutation type | Gain of function | Loss of function

| Alleles needed | One | Two

| Effect | Increased proliferation | Loss of control

| Example | RAS, MYC | p53, RB

RAS mutation = MOST common oncogene mutation in human cancers

Think of RAS like a car accelerator stuck down. Even if brakes (tumor suppressors) try to act, the engine keeps pushing forward.

Found in:

• Colon carcinoma
• Pancreatic carcinoma (VERY high yield)
• Lung carcinoma

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following cutaneous malignancies does not metastasize through the lymphatics? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Basal cell carcinoma

• Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cutaneous malignancy and is characterized by slow-growing, locally invasive behavior with an extremely low metastatic potential. In contrast to squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and Kaposi sarcoma, BCC rarely spreads through lymphatic channels, making local tissue destruction rather than metastasis its major clinical concern.
• BCC typically presents as a pearly papule with rolled borders and surface telangiectasia on sun-exposed skin. Histology shows basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, reflecting its locally invasive nature.

Key Learning Point:

• Basal cell carcinoma → Locally aggressive, rarely metastasizes
• Squamous cell carcinoma → Frequently spreads via regional lymph nodes
• Melanoma → Early lymphatic and hematogenous dissemination
• Kaposi sarcoma → May involve lymph nodes and visceral organs

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best gene analysis investigation for a female patient with history of breast and ovarian cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BRCA1

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in homologous recombination DNA repair. Think of them as: molecular tailors fixing torn DNA strands

BRCA mutation

↓

Defective DNA repair

↓

Genomic instability

↓

Accumulation of mutations

↓

Cancer (breast, ovary, others)

Germline mutations markedly increase risk of breast and ovarian cancers in women. This combination of cancers is the classic clinical clue for hereditary breast–ovarian cancer syndrome.

| Gene | Function | Associated Cancers

| ---- | -------- | ------------------

| BRCA1/2 | DNA repair | Breast, ovarian, prostate

| PTEN | Cell cycle regulation | Breast, thyroid, endometrium

| p53 | DNA damage checkpoint | Sarcoma, breast, brain

| CDH1 | Cell adhesion | Diffuse gastric, lobular breast

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the incorrect association?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. p53 and mucosal neuroma

p53 mutation is classically associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, predisposing to sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenal carcinoma.

Mucosal neuromas are a hallmark of MEN 2B, caused by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations, not p53.

Typical oral mucosal neuromas or neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.

PTEN is linked to thyroid malignancies (Cowden syndrome), BRCA2 to prostate cancer, and STK11 to breast cancer (Peutz-Jeghers).

| Gene | Syndrome | Associated Tumors

| ---- | -------- | -----------------

| PTEN | Cowden | Thyroid, breast, endometrium

| BRCA2 | Hereditary breast cancer | Breast, ovary, prostate

| STK11 | Peutz-Jeghers | GI polyps, breast, pancreas

| p53 | Li-Fraumeni | Sarcoma, breast, brain

| RET | MEN 2B | MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuroma

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following malignancies has the least or no established association with obesity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastric pyloric cancer

Obesity

↓

↑ Insulin & IGF-1

↑ Estrogen (via adipose)

↑ Inflammatory cytokines

↓

Cell proliferation + ↓ apoptosis

↓

Obesity-Associated Cancers

| Strong Association | Moderate/Other Associations

| ------------------ | ---------------------------

| Breast (postmenopausal) | Meningioma

| Endometrial | Multiple myeloma

| Colon | Thyroid

| Pancreatic | Kidney

| Esophageal adenocarcinoma | Liver

Gastric pyloric cancer is more strongly linked to H. pylori infection, nitrosamines, smoking, and dietary salt.

Gastric Cancer Types

| Type | Location | Risk Factors

| ---- | -------- | ------------

| Intestinal type | Distal (pylorus) | H. pylori, diet

| Diffuse type | Whole stomach | CDH1 mutation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 35-year-old woman comes to the physician complaining of weakness, fatigue, and pallor. Physical examination is unremarkable except for conjunctival pallor. Laboratory results are as follows: Haemoglobin: 7.2 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume: 90 fL Reticulocytes: 0.1% Platelets: 280,000 /uL Leukocyte count: 6,700 cells/uL Iron studies and serum B12 and folic acid levels are within normal limits. Bone marrow biopsy shows absence of erythroid precursors but preserved myeloid and megakaryocytic elements. Further workup would most likely show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thymic tumor

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) presents with severe normocytic anemia, very low reticulocyte count, and absence of erythroid precursors in bone marrow with normal leukocytes and platelets. Key association:

• Thymoma (thymic tumor) is strongly associated with acquired PRCA due to autoimmune destruction of erythroid precursors.

Other causes of PRCA include:

• Parvovirus B19 infection
• Autoimmune disorders
• Lymphoproliferative malignancies
• Drugs

Thus, patients with isolated erythroid aplasia should be evaluated for thymoma (CT chest).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 6 month-old girl has developed seborrheic skin eruptions over the past 3 months. She has had recurrent upper respiratory and middle ear infections with streptococcus pneumoniae for the past year. Physical examination indicates that she also has hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy. Her hearing is reduced in the right ear. A skull radiograph shows an expansile, 2 cm lytic lesion involving the right temporal bone. Laboratory studies show no anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukopenia. The mass is curetted. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination of this mass?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histocytes with Birbeck granules

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is characterized by clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that form lytic bone lesions, especially in the skull and temporal bone, often causing recurrent ear infections and hearing loss.

• Seborrheic dermatitis–like rash
• Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
• Usually normal blood counts early

Langerhans cells containing Birbeck granules (tennis-racket shaped organelles) on electron microscopy. Immunopositive for CD1a and S-100

Why not others:

• CD3 lymphoblasts → T-cell ALL
• Plasma cells with Russell bodies → multiple myeloma
• Reed–Sternberg cells → Hodgkin lymphoma

questions.subject: Pathology
