questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to prolonged epistaxis. The girl says that she picked her nose immediately before the bleeding started. Her parents decided to take her to the emergency department after the epistaxis persisted for 20 minutes despite constant compression. The patient has had frequent nosebleeds that often last >10 minutes. Laboratory tests are ordered, and results are as follows: Hematocrit: 43% Bleeding time: prolonged Partial thromboplastin time (PTT): prolonged Prothrombin time (PT): normal Thrombin time (TT): normal D-dimer: normal Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. von Willebrand disease

Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and presents with mucocutaneous bleeding such as recurrent epistaxis. Lab pattern in vWD:

• Bleeding time ↑ → platelet adhesion defect
• PTT ↑ → decreased factor VIII stabilization
• PT normal
• Platelet count normal
• Thrombin time normal

Why not others (short):

A. Factor XIII deficiency: PT, PTT, bleeding time all normal; delayed bleeding after trauma.

B. Hemophilia A: ↑PTT only; bleeding time normal (deep tissue/joint bleeds, not epistaxis).

C. Vitamin K deficiency: ↑PT first (±↑PTT); bleeding time normal.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 1-year-old boy presents with acute onset painful swelling of both hands and feet. The child cries when the affected areas are touched. There is no history of trauma or recent infection. Family history reveals that an older sibling died of severe pneumococcal infection in childhood. On examination, there is bilateral tender swelling of the hands and feet (dactylitis). Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased serum haptoglobin

Dactylitis in an infant is often the first manifestation of sickle cell disease, caused by vaso-occlusion and hemolysis. Chronic intravascular hemolysis leads to decreased serum haptoglobin due to binding and clearance of free hemoglobin.

• African origin / family history of infections
• Painful hand-foot swelling (dactylitis)
• Age: infancy (first presentation of SCD)
• Sickled RBCs → hemolysis + vaso-occlusion
• Free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin → ↓ serum haptoglobin

Why Other Options are Incorrect?

A. Decreased left ventricular systolic function → cardiac causes (not fitting acute dactylitis)

B. Decreased serum albumin → nephrotic/liver disease

C. Decreased serum C4 complement levels → complement disorders (angioedema, autoimmune)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy was brought to OPD with complaint of fatigue. Serum investigations revealed findings as given below. What is the likely diagnosis? Hemoglobin – 9 g/dl Mean cell volume (MCV) – 60 fL Mean cell Hb (MCH) – 20 pg Serum Ferritin – 185 mcg/L Total leukocyte count – Elevated lymphocyte and Neutrophils [Normal values: Serum Ferritin: 50-200 mcg/L; Mean cell volume (MCV) - 80-100 fL; Mean cell Hb (MCH) - 27-31 pg]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thalassemia

Thalassemia should be suspected in a patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia (low MCV, low MCH) but normal or increased serum ferritin, indicating adequate iron stores.

• Low MCV and MCH (microcytic hypochromic anemia)
• Normal/high ferritin → rules out iron deficiency anemia
• Often normal or elevated RBC count relative to Hb
• Peripheral smear may show target cells
• Confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis

Differentiation:

A. Anemia of chronic disease: usually normocytic or mild microcytic with low iron/TIBC

C. Iron deficiency anemia: low ferritin

D. Sickle cell anemia: normocytic with sickled RBCs

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with progressive pallor, fatigue, and mild jaundice. Peripheral smear suggests hemolytic anemia, and an autoimmune etiology is suspected. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is performed. A positive direct Coombs test indicates which of the following?
options: Free circulating antibodies against red blood cells are present in the patient's serum
Red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins and/or complement components
Donor red blood cells carrying foreign antigens are present in the circulation
Red blood cells have increased osmotic fragility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins and/or complement components

The Direct Coombs (Direct Antiglobulin Test, DAT) detects IgG antibodies and/or complement (C3) that are already bound to the patient's red blood cells in vivo.

A positive test is characteristic of:

• Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)
• Hemolytic disease of the newborn
• Hemolytic transfusion reactions
• Drug-induced immune hemolysis

The patient's RBCs are washed and then mixed with Coombs (antihuman globulin) reagent. Agglutination indicates that immunoglobulin and/or complement is attached to the RBC surface.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Free circulating antibodies against red blood cells are present in the patient's serum – This is detected by the Indirect Coombs test, which identifies free circulating anti-RBC antibodies.
• C. Donor red blood cells carrying foreign antigens are present in the circulation – The Direct Coombs test does not detect foreign RBCs; it detects antibodies or complement bound to the patient's own RBCs.
• D. Red blood cells have increased osmotic fragility – This is assessed by tests such as the osmotic fragility test, used in hereditary spherocytosis, and is unrelated to the Coombs test.

High-yield pearl

| Test | Detects | Common use

| ---- | ------- | ----------

| Direct Coombs (DAT) | IgG and/or C3 bound to patient RBCs | Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn, transfusion reactions

| Indirect Coombs (IAT) | Free anti-RBC antibodies in serum | Antenatal antibody screening and pre-transfusion compatibility testing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 2-week-old girl is brought to her primary care provider for a routine visit. Newborn screening results from hemoglobin electrophoresis are as follows: Hemoglobin F: 70% Hemoglobin A: 20% Hemoglobin S: 10% Examination shows a well-appearing infant with no pallor or splenomegaly. Which of the following is most likely true about this patient?
options: Life expectancy will be shorter than average
Mean corpuscular volume will be decreased
She has relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. She has relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum

A 2-week-old infant with Hemoglobin F = 70% is completely normal.

At birth, HbF makes up about 60–80% of total hemoglobin. It gradually declines over the first 6 months as HbA increases.

So this electrophoresis result is physiologic, not pathologic.

Now let’s evaluate the options:

• Life expectancy shorter than average → ❌ No disease indicated.
• Mean corpuscular volume decreased → ❌ Not suggested here.
• Reticulocyte count elevated → ❌ No hemolysis present.
• Relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum → ✅ Correct.

Because:

HbF interferes with the growth of P. falciparum inside red blood cells.

That’s why newborns (and people with persistent HbF like in sickle cell disease treated with hydroxyurea) have some protection against severe malaria.

Why does HbF not let P. Falciparum survive inside rbcs?

Ans: Parasite-infected RBCs normally stick to vascular endothelium (via PfEMP1).

HbF-containing RBCs show reduced expression of these adhesive proteins, meaning:

Less sequestration → milder disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to bloody stools. For the past month, she has also had decreased energy. Skin examination shows pallor and scattered bruises in various stages of healing throughout the trunk. The abdomen is soft without organomegaly. Complete blood count results are as follows: Hemoglobin: 7.2 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 90 um³ Platelets: 10,000/mm² Leukocytes: 1050/mm³ Neutrophils 5% Lymphocytes 95% Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
options: Autoimmune-induced loss of self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells
Bone marrow replacement by constitutively active tyrosine kinase-stimulated cells
Splenic hyperactivity with cell trapping by the reticuloendothelial system
Ineffective hematopoiesis secondary to micronutrient deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autoimmune-induced loss of self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells

Aplastic anemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, leading to pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow and absence of organomegaly.

• Pancytopenia: anemia + thrombocytopenia + leukopenia
• Normocytic anemia with low reticulocyte count
• No splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy
• Bone marrow: markedly hypocellular with fatty replacement
• Pathogenesis: autoreactive T-cell–mediated stem cell destruction

Common triggers include drugs, radiation, viral infections, and idiopathic autoimmune mechanisms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and recent onset of hematochezia. Over the past month, she has noted progressive weakness and decreased energy. On examination, she is pale with multiple ecchymoses over the trunk. There is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings: • Hemoglobin: 7.2 g/dL • MCV: 90 fL • Platelets: 10,000/mm³ • Leukocytes: 1,050/mm³ (Neutrophils 5%, Lymphocytes 95%) Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient’s condition?
options: Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells
Bone marrow infiltration by malignant proliferating cells
Splenic sequestration due to reticuloendothelial hyperactivity
Immune-mediated platelet destruction via anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells

A plastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow due to immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, most commonly by cytotoxic T cells. It presents with anemia, infections (neutropenia), and bleeding (thrombocytopenia) in the absence of organomegaly.

• Pancytopenia (↓ RBC, ↓ WBC, ↓ platelets)
• Normocytic anemia (MCV normal)
• No hepatosplenomegaly
• Bleeding + infections

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

B. Leukemia → usually organomegaly + blasts

C. Hypersplenism → splenomegaly present

D. ITP → isolated thrombocytopenia

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of yellowing of his eyes. He has also noticed a decrease in his exercise capacity and gets quickly exhausted after minor physical activity. Examination shows scleral icterus and pale mucous membranes. He has splenomegaly. His hemoglobin concentration is 7.9 mg/dL, leukocyte count 8500/mm³ and platelet count is 1.8 lakhs/mm3. Direct antiglobulin and heterophile antibody tests are positive. Which of the following additional laboratory findings are most likely present in this patient?
options: Increased direct to total bilirubin ratio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased haptoglobin levels

21-year-old

Jaundice

Pallor

Splenomegaly

Hb 7.9 (low)

Direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) positive , Heterophile antibody positive

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) ,likely triggered by infectious mononucleosis.

Pathophysiology in hemolysis :

RBCs are destroyed → body tries to compensate. So:

• ↑ Reticulocyte count (NOT decreased ❌)
• ↑ LDH
• ↑ Indirect bilirubin
• ↓ Haptoglobin (binds free hemoglobin)

❌ A: Decreased reticulocyte count

In hemolysis, retics go UP because marrow compensates.

✅ B: Decreased haptoglobin levels

Correct.

Free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin → gets used up → levels drop.

❌ C: Decreased MCV

Hemolytic anemia is usually normocytic or slightly increased MCV (due to reticulocytosis).

❌ D: Increased direct/total bilirubin ratio

Hemolysis increases indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, not direct.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 22-year-old patient with β-thalassemia major is on regular packed RBC transfusions every 3–4 weeks. Despite adequate chelation therapy, the patient remains transfusion dependent. A newer drug is started that reduces transfusion requirement by enhancing late-stage erythroid maturation via TGF-β superfamily inhibition. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Luspatercept

Luspatercept is a novel erythroid maturation agent used in transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia to reduce transfusion requirements. It works by enhancing late-stage erythroid maturation.

Clinical use:

• Transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia
• Some cases of myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts
• Reduces need for repeated RBC transfusions

Why not others:

• A. Deferasirox → iron chelator
• B. Erythropoietin → stimulates early erythropoiesis (less effective in thalassemia major)
• C. Hydroxyurea → increases HbF in sickle cell disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old man met with a road traffic accident and was brought to the casualty after 6 hours. His B.P. was 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate was 110/min, and SpO2 was 92%. After a few hours of receiving damage control resuscitation, the patient is febrile, tachypneic, and starts bleeding from the IV and NG tube sites. His SpO2 levels started falling. What could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemolytic Transfusion reaction

A patient who develops fever, hypotension, tachycardia, respiratory distress, and bleeding from IV/NG sites soon after receiving blood during resuscitation most likely has an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR), usually due to ABO incompatibility.

• Recipient antibodies (usually IgM anti-ABO) attack donor RBCs
• Complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis
• Release of free hemoglobin and inflammatory mediators
• Can trigger DIC (consumption coagulopathy) and shock

Immediate management:

• Stop transfusion immediately
• Maintain IV access with normal saline
• Send blood for crossmatch and hemolysis workup
• Supportive care (fluids, diuretics, treat DIC)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, recurrent infections, and spontaneous gum bleeding for the past 3 months. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count shows pancytopenia with normal red cell indices. Reticulocyte count is markedly reduced. Which of the following bone marrow findings is most consistent with the underlying condition in this patient?
options: Markedly hypocellular marrow with extensive fatty replacement and reduced hematopoietic cells
Increased neutrophils with distorted architecture giving a “crumpled tissue paper” appearance
Hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and reduced myeloid lineage
Hypercellular marrow with dysplastic changes in all three cell lineages
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Markedly hypocellular marrow with extensive fatty replacement and reduced hematopoietic cells

The patient’s pancytopenia with low reticulocyte count, absence of organomegaly, and bleeding/infections is characteristic of aplastic anemia, a bone marrow failure disorder causing immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells. It can be idiopathic or due to drugs, toxins, radiation, viral infections.

Bone marrow findings in aplastic anemia:

• Markedly hypocellular marrow
• Extensive fatty replacement
• Severe reduction of hematopoietic stem cells
• No malignant infiltration or fibrosis

Distinguishing from other options:

• Myelofibrosis → “dry tap,” fibrotic marrow
• Pure red cell aplasia → only erythroid suppression
• Myelodysplastic syndrome → hypercellular marrow with dysplasia

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the medicine OPD with easy fatigability, exertional breathlessness, and palpitations for the past few months. Examination reveals pallor. As part of her initial evaluation, haemoglobin concentration is estimated using the technique demonstrated in the accompanying video. Which of the following best describes the principle of the method demonstrated?
options: Haemoglobin is converted to cyanmethemoglobin and measured spectrophotometrically
Haemoglobin is converted to acid hematin and its colour is visually matched against a standard
Oxyhaemoglobin formation is measured by light absorption at a specific wavelength
Haemoglobin is precipitated and quantified after centrifugation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Haemoglobin is converted to acid hematin and its colour is visually matched against a standard

The video demonstrates Sahli’s haemoglobinometer, which estimates haemoglobin by the acid hematin method.

A measured quantity of blood is added to N/10 (0.1 N) hydrochloric acid. Haemoglobin is converted into brown-coloured acid hematin. Distilled water is then added gradually until the colour of the solution visually matches the permanent colour standards in the comparator. The haemoglobin concentration is then read from the graduated Sahli tube.

The major limitation is that colour matching is subjective, so observer variation, lighting conditions and deterioration of the comparator standards can affect accuracy. Also, not all haemoglobin derivatives are converted equally to acid hematin, making it less accurate than standard laboratory photometric methods.

High-yield:

• Sahli method → 0.1 N HCl → acid hematin → visual colour matching → Hb estimation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent epistaxis, gum bleeding, and easy bruising for the past 2 days. One week earlier, she had a self-limiting upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, there is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals isolated thrombocytopenia, while the peripheral smear demonstrates large platelets with increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, consistent with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Which of the following is not an appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Imatinib

This patient has immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), an autoimmune disorder characterized by antibody-mediated destruction of platelets and impaired platelet production.

Typical features include:

• Recent viral illness
• Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, petechiae, gum bleeding)
• Isolated thrombocytopenia
• Normal spleen
• Increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow due to compensatory platelet production

Treatment options for ITP

• First-line: Corticosteroids or IVIG (anti-D immunoglobulin in selected Rh-positive, nonsplenectomized patients)
• Second-line/Refractory disease:

• Splenectomy
• Rituximab
• Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim)
• Fostamatinib (SYK inhibitor)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 25 yr old women G2P1L1 is brought to the emergency at 30 weeks gestation in active labor. The patient had severe anemia during pregnancy and received multiple blood transfusions during past months. An uncomplicated Vaginal delivery is performed and 2.5kg infant is delivered. Post operatively she continues to bleed and receives a transfusion of 1 unit of packed RBC. One hour later, the patient appears to have flank pain and in acute distress. Temperature is 101° F, pulse 115/min and BP is 92/66 mmHg. Foley catheter shows dark brown urine. Further evaluation is most likely to show:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Positive Direct Coomb’s

• Within 1 hour of RBC transfusion → flank pain, fever (101°F), hypotension
• Dark brown urine in Foley = hemoglobinuria :(intravascular hemolysis)

This pattern = ABO incompatibility (Type II hypersensitivity) → complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

✅ So further evaluation most likely shows: Positive Direct Coombs test (Option B)

❌ Option A: Serum antibodies against Class I HLA

That’s Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (cytokines/anti-HLA antibodies from prior transfusions/pregnancy).

Presents with fever + chills

❌ Option C: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on CXR

That’s TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury). clinically ,Acute hypoxemia, respiratory distress within 6 hours.

❌ Option D: Low serum IgA

That’s anaphylactic transfusion reaction in IgA deficiency.

• Sudden wheezing, angioedema, urticaria, hypotension

Flank pain + dark urine after transfusion = ABO hemolytic reaction → Direct Coombs positive ✅

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle accident. She is found to have a pneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and long bone fractures, for which she undergoes surgical fixation. On postoperative day 1, she develops respiratory distress, oliguria, and diffuse bleeding from IV sites and chest tube drains. Laboratory evaluation is most likely to show which of the following patterns?
options: Normal fibrinogen, ↑ Protein C, ↑ Factor VII
Normal fibrinogen, ↑ Protein C, ↓ Factor VII
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ↓ Fibrinogen, ↓ Protein C, ↓ Factor VII

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characterized by widespread activation of coagulation leading to consumption of clotting factors and anticoagulant proteins (including protein C), resulting in decreased fibrinogen and clotting factors (e.g., factor VII) with a paradoxical bleeding tendency.

• Trauma → tissue factor release → coagulation cascade activation
• Leads to:

• Consumption of clotting factors → ↓ fibrinogen
• Consumption of natural anticoagulants → ↓ protein C
• ↓ Factor VII (short half-life → early fall)

• Simultaneously:

• Microthrombi → organ dysfunction (kidney, lung)
• Bleeding due to factor depletion

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 32 weeks' gestation is evaluated for vaginal bleeding. Five days ago, she was admitted to the hospital and started on treatment for a deep vein thrombosis in the right leg. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure is 95/67 mm Hg. Physical examination shows large hematomas on the upper limbs and swelling in the right calf. There is a large amount of bright red blood in the vaginal vault. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8.9 mg/dL, platelet count of 185,000/mm3, and activated partial thromboplastin time of 160 seconds (N-30s). Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to rapidly reverse this patient's coagulopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Protamine sulfate

Protamine sulfate is the antidote for heparin overdose and is used to rapidly reverse anticoagulation when severe bleeding occurs.

• Pregnant patient treated for DVT → most likely on unfractionated heparin (safe in pregnancy).
• Findings: severe bleeding + markedly prolonged aPTT (160 sec) with normal platelets → indicates heparin toxicity.
• Protamine sulfate binds and neutralizes heparin → rapid reversal of anticoagulant effect.

Why not others:

B. PCC: used for warfarin reversal

C. Vitamin K: reverses warfarin, not heparin

D. Alteplase: thrombolytic, would worsen bleeding

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with easy fatigability and exertional dyspnea for the past 6 months. She has been treated with iron and vitamin supplements without significant improvement. There is no history of bleeding. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous spherocytes. Reticulocyte count is increased. Which of the following investigations would be most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coombs test

The presence of spherocytes with increased reticulocyte count suggests hemolytic anemia, most commonly autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) or hereditary spherocytosis. The most useful confirmatory test for AIHA is the Direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test, which detects antibodies or complement bound to RBC surfaces.

• Findings: anemia, reticulocytosis, spherocytes, elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin
• Caused by IgG or complement-mediated RBC destruction

Distinguishing from other options:

A. Osmotic fragility test: confirms hereditary spherocytosis

B. Flow cytometry: used for PNH (CD55/CD59 deficiency)

C. Hemoglobin HPLC: evaluates hemoglobinopathies

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, G3P0L0, is being evaluated prior to an elective surgical procedure. She has no history of excessive bleeding during previous dental procedures or childbirth. General physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory investigations show: Bleeding time: 5 minutes PT: 15 seconds APTT: 60 seconds Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

A prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with normal bleeding history and normal or near-normal PT suggests the presence of a circulating anticoagulant rather than a true bleeding disorder. One important cause is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS).

• Autoantibodies (eg, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin)
• Paradoxically increased risk of thrombosis, not bleeding
• Recurrent pregnancy loss may occur
• Bleeding time normal

Distinguishing from other options:

A. Hemophilia/acquired factor inhibitors → bleeding history present

B. Factor XII deficiency → prolonged aPTT but usually incidental finding without thrombosis history

C. Vitamin K deficiency → prolonged PT and aPTT with bleeding tendency

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman develops progressive swelling and pain of her thigh after a trivial bump against a table. Examination reveals a large expanding hematoma and multiple ecchymoses over the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies show: • Hemoglobin: 12.5 g/dL • Platelet count: 240,000/mm³ • PT: Normal • aPTT: Prolonged She has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. Which of the following best explains this patient's bleeding tendency?
options: Development of an acquired coagulation factor inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Development of an acquired coagulation factor inhibitor

This patient has acquired hemophilia A, caused by autoantibodies against factor VIII.

Typical findings include:

• Large spontaneous hematomas
• Normal platelet count
• Normal PT with isolated prolonged aPTT
• No family history of bleeding
• Adult onset

These antibodies neutralize factor VIII, producing an intrinsic pathway defect.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Reduced clotting factor synthesis: Liver disease or vitamin K deficiency usually prolongs PT.
• C. Endothelial dysfunction: Causes thrombosis rather than isolated prolonged aPTT.
• D. DIC: Causes thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT and aPTT.

High-yield pearl:

• Adult-onset bleeding with isolated prolonged aPTT and no family history strongly suggests an acquired factor VIII inhibitor.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. He has a history of chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. Examination reveals small testes. Laboratory evaluation shows low early-morning testosterone levels with elevated luteinizing hormone (LH). He is started on transdermal testosterone replacement therapy. Which of the following parameters should be periodically monitored during treatment to prevent a major complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hematocrit

Testosterone therapy stimulates erythropoiesis by increasing erythropoietin production and bone marrow activity. This can lead to:

• Polycythemia (↑ hematocrit)
• Increased blood viscosity
• Risk of thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT)

Therefore, hematocrit must be regularly monitored, and therapy should be adjusted or stopped if levels become elevated.

Why not other options?

A. ECG → Not routinely required unless cardiac disease

C. Serum cortisol → Not affected by testosterone therapy

D. Serum creatinine → No direct nephrotoxicity

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 41-year-old woman with a long history of menorrhagia comes to the physician due to a low hemoglobin level identified on routine laboratory evaluation. She is diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia and started on oral ferrous sulfate. Which of the following cells secrete a substance that controls iron storage and release by other cells involved in iron homeostasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hepatic parenchymal cells

Hepcidin, the master regulator of iron homeostasis, is produced by hepatic parenchymal cells (hepatocytes) and controls iron storage and release. Key actions of hepcidin:

• Inhibits ferroportin → decreases iron export
• ↓ Iron release from macrophages
• ↓ Iron absorption from enterocytes
• ↓ Iron release from liver stores

Clinical relevance:

• ↑ Hepcidin → anemia of chronic disease (iron trapped in stores)
• ↓ Hepcidin → iron overload (e.g., hemochromatosis)
• In iron deficiency → hepcidin levels fall to increase absorption

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever, abdominal pain, and persistent fatigue for 2 days. On examination, her blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg, and she is pale with scattered petechiae on the extremities. Laboratory evaluation reveals low hemoglobin, elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase, thrombocytopenia, and normal prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time. Peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thromboic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

Hints Provided:

• Adult woman, fever +
• No diarrheal illness mentioned
• Hemolytic anemia → ↓Hb, ↑LDH, schistocytes
• Thrombocytopenia → petechiae
• Renal involvement → hematuria, proteinuria
• Fever and fatigue
• Normal PT and aPTT (distinguishes from DIC)

❌ Option A: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

FSGS is a glomerular disease — not a microangiopathic hemolytic process.

So it cannot explain fragmented RBCs.

❌ Option B: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

PSGN is immune-complex mediated nephritis — not a thrombotic microangiopathy.

✅Option C: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

• TTP: is a life-threatening microangiopathic hemolytic anemia caused by severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, leading to widespread platelet-rich microthrombi.
• Adults, neurologic ± renal features, normal PT/PTT

❌Option D: HUS: haemolytic uremic syndrome

• HUS: Usually children, post-diarrheal (E. coli O157:H7), More severe renal failure predominates,fever/neurologic features-Less prominent

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man presents with severe fatigue, bone pain, recurrent infections, and bleeding manifestations for 2 months. Examination reveals pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations show: Hemoglobin: 6.8 g/dL Serum calcium: 12.2 mg/dL Serum creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL Peripheral blood smear reveals >25% circulating plasma cells. There is no prior history of multiple myeloma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary plasma cell leukemia

Primary plasma cell leukemia (PCL) is a rare, aggressive plasma cell dyscrasia defined by >20% circulating plasma cells (or absolute count >2,000/µL) in peripheral blood without prior history of multiple myeloma.

• Severe anemia
• Hypercalcemia
• Renal dysfunction
• Bone pain
• Hepatosplenomegaly
• Recurrent infections and bleeding

Types:

• Primary PCL: arises de novo without prior multiple myeloma
• Secondary PCL: occurs as leukemic transformation of known multiple myeloma

Distinguishing from other disorders:

A. Multiple myeloma → plasma cells mainly in bone marrow, not high circulating levels

D. Waldenström macroglobulinemia → lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM excess

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old male with small cell carcinoma of the lung presents with cyanosis of the neck and face, epistaxis, headache, dizziness, and swelling over the face, neck, and upper chest. He is currently undergoing chemotherapy sessions. A chest X-ray reveals widening of the superior mediastinum. What is the investigation of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT scan

The patient’s symptoms (facial swelling, cyanosis of face/neck, epistaxis, headache, dilated chest veins) with mediastinal widening suggest superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, most commonly caused by lung malignancy (especially small cell carcinoma).

Investigation of choice: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest

• Confirms SVC obstruction
• Identifies cause (tumor, lymph nodes, thrombosis)
• Determines extent of compression
• Helps plan treatment (stenting, radiotherapy, chemotherapy)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the OPD by her mother d due to leg pain. One week ago mother saw the patient fall onto the living room floor after climbing on a couch. Since the incident, she has had persistent leg pain that appears to be worse at night, and for the last 2 days she has been refusing to walk asking her mother to carry her. The patient has no chronic medical conditions but has had a mild, non-productive cough for the past month. Temperature is 38.3⁰C (100.9⁰F); all other vital signs are normal. Examination shows a pale child. The abdomen is nontender and moderate hepatosplenomegaly is noted. Palpation of the bilateral anterior proximal tibias elicits pain. There are a few scattered bruises across the chest and back. Complete blood count results are as follows: Hemoglobin-8g/dL Platelets-30,000/mm³ Leukocytes-3,000/mm³ Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in children commonly presents with bone pain, pallor, fever, bruising, and hepatosplenomegaly due to bone marrow infiltration by malignant lymphoblasts.

• Marrow infiltration → pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia)
• Bone expansion and periosteal irritation → bone pain, refusal to walk
• Extramedullary infiltration → hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
• Often mistaken for trauma or infection initially

Diagnosis:

• Peripheral smear/bone marrow: lymphoblasts
• Immunophenotype: TdT+, CD10+, CD19+ (B-ALL)

Thus, leukemia should be suspected in any child with bone pain + pancytopenia + organomegaly.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with complaints of intense, generalized itching that occurs specifically after taking hot showers, ongoing for the past several months. He also describes a burning sensation affecting his fingers and reports frequent headaches. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin level of 18 g/dL along with a low serum erythropoietin level. Which of the following is not part of the appropriate management for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Heparin

• The clinical picture — aquagenic pruritus (itching after hot showers), erythromelalgia (burning sensation in fingers/toes), headaches, elevated hemoglobin, and low erythropoietin — is classic for polycythemia vera (PV), a myeloproliferative neoplasm typically driven by a JAK2 mutation.
• Phlebotomy (B) is a first-line management strategy to reduce red cell mass and hematocrit, directly lowering blood viscosity and thrombotic risk.
• Low-dose aspirin (C) is routinely used in PV to reduce the risk of thrombotic events (arterial and venous), given the increased thrombosis risk from hyperviscosity.
• Doxepin (A), a tricyclic antidepressant with antihistaminic properties, is commonly used to manage the refractory aquagenic pruritus seen in PV, which often doesn't respond well to conventional antihistamines.
• Heparin (D) is not a standard part of PV management — PV is not treated with routine anticoagulation; managing the underlying erythrocytosis (via phlebotomy ± cytoreductive therapy like hydroxyurea) and antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) are the mainstays, not anticoagulants.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening fatigue and recurrent bleeding from his gums for 2 weeks. Physical examination shows marked pallor. There are scattered red, nonblanching pinpoints spots on his trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8.0 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 80,000/mm3, and a platelet count of 104,000/mm3. Genetic analysis of a bone marrow aspirate shows leukemic cells with a balanced translocation between the long arms of chromosome 15 and 17. These cells are most likely to stain positive for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myeloperoxidase

A balanced translocation t(15;17) is characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a subtype of AML.

• Fusion gene: PML-RARα
• Blocks myeloid differentiation at promyelocyte stage
• Promyelocytes accumulate with Auer rods
• High risk of DIC and bleeding
• Myeloid lineage cells → myeloperoxidase (MPO) positive

Why not others:

B. TRAP → hairy cell leukemia

C. PAS → lymphoblasts (ALL)

D. CD1a → Langerhans cells/T-cell lineage

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with fatigue, acrocyanosis, and dark-colored urine that worsens on exposure to cold. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia with elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and reduced haptoglobin. A direct Coombs test is positive. Red blood cells show agglutination when the blood sample is cooled to 0–4°C, which reverses on warming. The hemolysis in this condition is primarily due to binding of which of the following antibodies?
options: IgG active at 37°C causing splenic macrophage–mediated hemolysis
IgM binding to RBCs at 0–4°C with complement fixation
IgG with maximal activity at alkaline pH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgM binding to RBCs at 0–4°C with complement fixation

Cold agglutinin disease is a type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia caused by IgM antibodies that bind to red blood cells at low temperatures (0–4 °C) and activate the complement system, leading to extravascular hemolysis in liver (and sometimes intravascular). On warming, IgM dissociates but complement remains.

• Dark urine
• Elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin
• Reduced haptoglobin
• Direct Coombs positive (C3 complement)

Distinguishing from warm AIHA:

• Warm AIHA → IgG antibodies active at 37 °C
• Cold agglutinin disease → IgM complement-mediated hemolysis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, paresthesia of both feet, and gait instability for 6 months. Examination reveals pallor, loss of vibration sense, and a positive Romberg sign. Laboratory investigations show: • Hemoglobin: 6.8 g/dL • MCV: 122 fL • Peripheral smear: macro-ovalocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils • Serum LDH: markedly elevated • Serum vitamin B12: very low He is diagnosed with severe megaloblastic anemia due to pernicious anemia and started on intramuscular hydroxocobalamin therapy. Within 48 hours of initiating treatment, the treating physician closely monitors a specific electrolyte because rapid hematopoietic recovery may precipitate a life-threatening complication. Which of the following best explains this precaution?
options: Rapid intracellular shift of potassium causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias
Sudden intracellular shift of phosphate leading to respiratory muscle paralysis
Increased renal magnesium loss precipitating refractory tetany
Acute calcium influx into regenerating erythrocytes causing prolonged QT interval
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rapid intracellular shift of potassium causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias

Treatment of severe vitamin B12 deficiency can cause rapid bone marrow recovery with brisk erythropoiesis, leading to increased cellular uptake of potassium. This may precipitate:

• Acute hypokalemia
• Cardiac arrhythmias
• Sudden death in severe cases

Therefore, serum potassium should be monitored after initiating therapy for severe megaloblastic anemia. Features of vitamin B12 deficiency:

• Macrocytic megaloblastic anemia
• Hypersegmented neutrophils
• Elevated LDH (ineffective erythropoiesis)
• Neurologic deficits:

• Loss of vibration/proprioception
• Sensory ataxia
• Positive Romberg sign

Pernicious anemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leading to intrinsic factor deficiency and impaired B12 absorption.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma presents with confusion, nausea, constipation, and bone pain. Investigations reveal: • Serum calcium: 14.8 mg/dL • Serum creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL • Hemoglobin: 8.2 g/dL Skeletal survey shows multiple lytic lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous normal saline infusion

Severe hypercalcemia is a medical emergency commonly seen in multiple myeloma due to osteolytic bone resorption. Initial management focuses on rapid reduction of serum calcium and stabilization.

First-line initial treatment: Aggressive intravenous normal saline infusion.

Subsequent treatments (after hydration):

• IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid, pamidronate)
• Calcitonin for rapid temporary reduction
• Treat underlying malignancy (chemotherapy)

Why other options are incorrect initially:

• A. Lenalidomide + Bortezomib + Dexamethasone + Daratumumab: Myeloma chemotherapy → started after stabilization
• B. Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Vincristine: Rituximab regimens → not used in myeloma
• D. Autologous stem cell transplant → long-term managemen

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with progressive fatigue and exertional palpitations over the past 6 months. She has no history of overt bleeding, including hematemesis, melena, or vaginal bleeding. She consumes a balanced diet and has no known chronic illnesses. On examination, she appears pale. Laboratory studies reveal: • Hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL • Peripheral smear: microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Occult blood loss

In postmenopausal women, microcytic hypochromic anemia is most commonly due to chronic occult gastrointestinal blood loss, often from colorectal malignancy or peptic pathology, even in the absence of overt bleeding symptoms.

• Microcytic anemia → iron deficiency
• In postmenopausal women → always assume GI blood loss until proven otherwise
• Absence of visible bleeding does NOT exclude chronic occult loss

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

A. Drug abuse → no link to microcytic anemia

B. Malignancy → may cause anemia, but typically normocytic unless via blood loss

C. Hemolysis → normocytic + ↑ retics, jaundice

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 59-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to right leg swelling and pain for 2 days. The patient was started on hemodialysis 2 months ago for end-stage renal disease from diabetes mellitus. Duplex ultrasound shows a right popliteal vein thrombosis. The patient is started intravenous heparin infusion. On the third day of hospitalization, the right leg is more swollen and painful. Repeat ultrasound shows an extension of thrombus to the right femoral vein. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin-14.0 g/dL Platelets-50,000/mm³ Leukocytes-7,500/mm³ Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's worsening condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antibody-mediated platelet activation

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is caused by IgG antibodies against heparin–platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexes, leading to platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, and paradoxical thrombosis.

• Occurs 5–10 days after starting heparin (earlier if prior exposure)
• Platelet count falls >50% from baseline
• New or worsening thrombosis despite heparin therapy
• Mechanism: Antibody-mediated platelet activation → prothrombotic state

Management:

• Stop all heparin immediately
• Start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux)
• Avoid platelet transfusion unless severe bleeding

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent infections, easy bruising, and failure to thrive. Examination reveals short stature, café-au-lait spots, absent thumbs, and microcephaly. Laboratory investigations show pancytopenia with macrocytosis. Bone marrow examination reveals a hypocellular marrow. The disorder described above most commonly follows which pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal recessive

The clinical picture describes Fanconi anemia, an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by congenital anomalies, pancytopenia, and hypocellular marrow. It is a defect in

DNA repair.

• Pancytopenia with macrocytosis
• Short stature and failure to thrive
• Skeletal anomalies (eg, absent or hypoplastic thumbs)
• Café-au-lait spots and skin pigmentation
• Microcephaly
• Increased risk of AML and solid tumors

Inheritance pattern:

• Most commonly autosomal recessive
• Rare X-linked forms exist but are uncommon

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old male patient with heart failure is scheduled for a heart transplant. His renal function test is deranged, and hemoglobin is 6 g/dL. The physician ordered 2 units of whole blood. Four hours after transfusion, he developed severe respiratory distress. On examination, he is hypoxemic, has tachycardia, and his mean arterial pressure is elevated. Which of the following are the best investigations for the above scenario? 1. Chest X-ray 2. Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level 3. Absolute neutrophil count 4. Leukocyte 5. Platelets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

Acute respiratory distress occurring within hours of blood transfusion in a patient with heart failure suggests transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) rather than TRALI.

• Occurs within 6 hours of transfusion
• Dyspnea, hypoxemia
• Hypertension, tachycardia
• Pulmonary edema due to volume overload
• Elevated BNP
• Common in elderly or cardiac/renal failure patients
• Chest X-ray: shows pulmonary edema/cardiomegaly

Distinguishing from TRALI:

• TRALI → hypotension, normal BNP, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
• TACO → hypertension, elevated BNP, cardiogenic pulmonary edema

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with bone pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. Investigations show anemia and elevated serum calcium. Urinalysis reveals proteins that precipitate at 50–60°C and redissolve on further heating. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Presence of intact immunoglobulin molecules in urine
Free monoclonal light chains filtered through glomerulus
Increased albumin due to glomerular damage
Excess β2-microglobulin due to tubular dysfunction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Free monoclonal light chains filtered through glomerulus

Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal light chains produced in multiple myeloma that are filtered by the glomerulus and show characteristic heat precipitation at 50–60°C with redissolution on further heating.

• Derived from excess light chains (κ or λ) produced by malignant plasma cells
• Small size → freely filtered in urine
• Unique property:

• Precipitate at 50–60°C
• Dissolve on boiling → reappear on cooling
• Can cause renal damage (myeloma kidney)

Differentiation:

• Intact immunoglobulins → too large to be filtered
• Albuminuria → seen in glomerular disease, no heat property
• β2-microglobulin → marker of tubular dysfunction
• Amyloid → tissue deposition, not urine precipitation pattern

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy for the past 4 months. There is no history of fever or weight loss. Examination reveals mild splenomegaly. Complete blood count shows Hb 11 g/dL, total leukocyte count 58,000/µL with absolute lymphocytosis. Peripheral blood smear reveals numerous small mature-appearing lymphocytes with smudge cells. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is characterized by persistent absolute lymphocytosis with small mature-appearing lymphocytes and smudge cells on peripheral smear. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis is flow cytometry of peripheral blood.

• Monoclonal B cells expressing CD19, CD20, CD23
• Aberrant CD5 expression on B cells (key feature)
• Light chain restriction (kappa or lambda)

Other tests:

• A. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy → staging/prognosis, not initial confirmation
• C. FISH → detects prognostic cytogenetic abnormalities (eg, del17p)
• D. Lymph node excisional biopsy → used if transformation suspected (Richter syndrome)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the OPD due to persistent back pain, constipation, and easy fatigability for the last several months. Blood pressure is 115/75 mm Hg and pulse is 88/ min. The patient has dry mucous membranes. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin: 8.6 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume: 92 fL Blood urea nitrogen: 68 mg/dL Creatinine: 1.9mg/dl Renal biopsy is performed, and light microscopy shows atrophic tubules, many of which contain large, obstructing, waxy casts that stain intensely with eosin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multiple myeloma

Multiple myeloma commonly causes renal failure due to light-chain cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney). Key clinical features (CRAB criteria):

• Calcium elevation → constipation, dehydration
• Renal failure → ↑ BUN, creatinine
• Anemia → normocytic anemia
• Bone pain → lytic lesions/back pain

Renal pathology:

• Filtered monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones proteins)
• Form waxy eosinophilic casts in renal tubules
• Cause tubular obstruction and atrophy
• Leads to chronic kidney injury

This patient has:

• Back pain
• Constipation + dehydration (hypercalcemia)
• Fatigue (likely anemia)

This fits Multiple Myeloma perfectly.

Other options:

A. Acute pyelonephritis → Fever, flank pain, urinary symptoms.

B. Aminoglycoside toxicity → Acute kidney injury after drug exposure.

C. Allergic interstitial nephritis → Rash, fever, eosinophilia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 64-year-old man with chronic kidney disease secondary to long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for follow-up. Six months ago, he developed fatigue and was found to have normocytic normochromic anemia with normal iron studies. He was started on recombinant erythropoietin therapy. His symptoms have improved, and current hemoglobin is 12 g/dL. Continued therapy is planned. Which of the following complications is this patient at greatest risk of developing with ongoing treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Venous thromboembolism

In CKD, anemia occurs due to decreased erythropoietin production. Treatment with recombinant EPO increases RBC mass and hemoglobin.

However, excessive correction of hemoglobin:

• ↑ Blood viscosity
• ↑ Platelet activation

• Leads to increased risk of thromboembolic events

Why not other options?

A. Bone marrow fibrosis → Seen in myeloproliferative disorders, not EPO use

B. Gallstones → Associated with chronic hemolysis, not increased RBC production

C. Iron overload → Occurs with repeated transfusions, not EPO alone

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient comes to the clinic with unbearable itching while taking a shower which has been present for many months. Physical examination shows the presence of facial plethora. Laboratory examination shows a hemoglobin of 20 g/dL. What would be the best match for this patient?
options: RBC mass increased, O2 saturation increased, EPO decreased
RBC mass increased, O2 saturation normal, EPO decreased
RBC mass increased, O2 saturation increased, EPO normal
RBC mass normal, O2 saturation normal, EPO increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RBC mass increased, O2 saturation normal, EPO decreased

The patient’s aquagenic pruritus, facial plethora, and markedly elevated hemoglobin suggest polycythemia vera (PV), a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm. It has a risk of thrombosis, splenomegaly and shows hyperviscosity symptoms. Characteristic laboratory findings in polycythemia vera:

• Increased RBC mass (true polycythemia)
• Normal oxygen saturation (not due to hypoxia)
• Decreased erythropoietin (EPO) due to negative feedback from autonomous RBC production
• JAK2 mutation positive in most cases

Distinguishing from secondary polycythemia:

• Secondary → increased RBC mass with high EPO and often low O₂ saturation
• PV → low EPO with normal O₂ saturation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 66-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue. CBC shows Hb 7.6 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, TLC 4,800/µL, and platelet count 4.9 × 10⁵/µL. Bone marrow examination reveals hypolobated megakaryocytes. Cytogenetic analysis shows an isolated deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lenalidomide

An isolated deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5 (del(5q)) in a patient with macrocytic anemia and dysplastic megakaryocytes indicates myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated del(5q), a distinct subtype with relatively good prognosis.

Treatment of choice: Lenalidomide

• Improves anemia
• Reduces transfusion dependence
• Can induce cytogenetic remission

Other options:

A. Azacitidine → for higher-risk MDS

C. Allogeneic Stem cell transplant → for younger/high-risk patients

D. Erythropoietin → less effective in del(5q) subtype

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with chronic lower back pain, fatigue, and progressive weakness. Laboratory evaluation reveals normocytic anemia, elevated serum creatinine, and hyperproteinemia. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates a sharp monoclonal (M) spike in the gamma region. Bone marrow examination shows clonal proliferation of plasma cells. The patient is started on a drug that inhibits the 26S proteasome, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins within malignant cells. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this therapy on the neoplastic cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased apoptosis

Proteasome inhibitors (e.g., bortezomib) used in multiple myeloma block degradation of misfolded and ubiquitinated proteins, leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress and activation of intrinsic apoptosis in malignant plasma cells.

• Multiple myeloma clues:

• Back pain + anemia + renal dysfunction
• M spike on SPEP

• Drug mechanism: Proteasome inhibition → protein accumulation → ER stress → apoptosis

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

A. Augmented cytotoxic T-cell response → Immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors), not proteasome inhibitors

B. Decreased DNA methylation → DNA hypomethylating agents (azacitidine, decitabine)

C. Impaired RNA splicing → Seen with spliceosome defects (MDS)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, weight loss, and early satiety over several months. On examination, he has pallor, hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly. Laboratory and molecular evaluation reveal a gain-of-function mutation in a non-receptor tyrosine kinase (JAK2) leading to constitutive activation of the JAK–STAT signaling pathway in hematopoietic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Primary myelofibrosis

Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 mutation, leading to constitutive JAK–STAT activation, abnormal megakaryocyte proliferation, and release of fibrogenic cytokines (e.g., TGF-β), resulting in bone marrow fibrosis.

• Extramedullary hematopoiesis → massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly
• Bone marrow failure → anemia, fatigue
• Peripheral smear → teardrop (dacrocyte) RBCs

Conceptual Highlights:

• JAK2 mutation → hallmark of myeloproliferative disorders
• Fibrosis → “dry tap” on marrow aspiration
• Spleen enlarges due to compensatory hematopoiesis

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

A. APL → t(15;17), DIC

B. CLL → lymphocytosis, smudge cells

C. NHL / Mantle cell → lymphoid malignancies, not JAK2-driven

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of persistent fever, fatigue, and pallor. His parents note that he bruises easily and has had episodes of gum bleeding. On examination, he appears pale, with petechiae over both legs, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory workup reveals severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, and an elevated white blood cell count with circulating blast cells. What is the most appropriate initial treatment regimen for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prednisolone + Vincristine

• This presentation — fever, pallor, easy bruising/bleeding, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and circulating blasts — is classic for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the most common childhood malignancy.
• Induction chemotherapy for ALL classically uses a combination of vincristine, a corticosteroid (prednisolone/dexamethasone), and asparaginase (± an anthracycline in some protocols), aiming to achieve remission by eliminating leukemic blasts.
• Doxorubicin + Idarubicin (B) are anthracyclines more typically used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) induction regimens, not as the primary initial combination for ALL.
• IVIG (A) is used for immune-related conditions (e.g., ITP, Kawasaki disease) — not appropriate as leukemia treatment.
• Radiotherapy to lymph nodes (D) is not part of standard initial leukemia management; radiotherapy has a role in specific scenarios (e.g., CNS prophylaxis in high-risk ALL or in lymphoma), not as first-line systemic treatment here.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with left knee swelling following a trivial injury. His platelet count and bleeding time are normal. His aPTT is prolonged and factor VIII levels are decreased. Which of the following can be used in the management of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Emicizumab

A child with hemarthrosis, normal platelet count/bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, and low factor VIII has Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency). Emicizumab is a newer therapy used in hemophilia A:

• Bispecific monoclonal antibody
• Bridges factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIII function
• Used for prophylaxis in patients with or without inhibitors
• Reduces frequency of bleeding episodes

Why not others:

B. Voxelotor → sickle cell disease

C. Eculizumab & D. Ravulizumab → complement inhibitors for PNH/aHUS

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant presents with severe pallor, failure to thrive, and hepatosplenomegaly. He has been receiving repeated blood transfusions since early infancy. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells. Which of the following hemoglobin patterns best supports the diagnosis in this child?
options: Predominant HbA with mildly increased HbA₂
Markedly increased HbF with absent HbA
Normal HbA with mildly reduced HbF
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Markedly increased HbF with absent HbA

A transfusion-dependent infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and target cells is most consistent with β-thalassemia major. It is caused due to defective β-globin chain synthesis causing ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis.

• Markedly increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin)
• Absent or very low HbA
• Variable increase in HbA₂

Clinical features:

• Severe anemia beginning in infancy (after 6 months when HbF declines)
• Transfusion dependence
• Hepatosplenomegaly
• Growth failure
• Bone marrow expansion → skeletal changes

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A first-year medical student performs a manual RBC count using a Neubauer chamber. After proper dilution and charging of the chamber, 210 red blood cells are counted in the appropriate counting area. What is the RBC count of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2.1 million / mm³

The manual RBC count using a Neubauer hemocytometer is calculated based on the number of cells counted, dilution factor, and chamber volume.

RBC count (cells/mm³) = Cells counted × dilution factor × 10⁴ ÷ number of squares counted

For RBC counting:

• Dilution = 1:200
• Area counted = 5 small RBC squares
• Depth = 0.1 mm
• Conversion factor gives simplified formula:

RBC count = Cells counted × 10,000

210 × 10,000 = 2,100,000/mm³ = 2.1 million/mm³

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient is started on unfractionated heparin (UFH) for acute venous thromboembolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate method for monitoring the anticoagulant effect of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti–factor Xa assay

Unfractionated heparin (UFH) exerts its anticoagulant effect by enhancing antithrombin activity, which inhibits factor Xa and thrombin (factor IIa). Monitoring is required due to variable pharmacokinetics and risk of bleeding.

Best monitoring test:

• Anti–factor Xa assay → directly measures heparin activity and is the most accurate method
• Therapeutic range typically: 0.3–0.7 IU/mL (varies by protocol)

Other monitoring methods:

• aPTT traditionally used but less reliable due to variability
• PT → used for warfarin monitoring, not UFH
• LMWH → usually no routine monitoring except in special populations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent mucosal bleeding and menorrhagia. Lab findings: • Platelets: Normal • PT: Normal • aPTT: Mildly prolonged • Bleeding time: Prolonged Which defect explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Defective platelet adhesion

This patient has the classic laboratory profile of von Willebrand disease (vWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder. von Willebrand factor (vWF) mediates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen and also serves as a carrier protein for factor VIII.

• Deficiency or dysfunction of vWF leads to:

• Impaired platelet adhesion → prolonged bleeding time and mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding).
• Reduced stabilization of factor VIII → mild prolongation of aPTT.

• Platelet count and PT remain normal.

Why not the others?

• B. Defective platelet aggregation → Seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa deficiency), which causes impaired platelet-platelet binding.
• C. Defective fibrin stabilization → Seen in Factor XIII deficiency, characterized by delayed bleeding and poor wound healing.
• D. Defective coagulation factor synthesis → Produces coagulation factor deficiencies with abnormal PT and/or aPTT rather than isolated mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with cervical lymphadenopathy has (11;14) positive. Which of the following markers would be positive? 1. CD10 2. CD 200 3. CD5 4. Cyclin D1 5. CD23
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

A t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). This translocation causes overexpression of cyclin D1, leading to uncontrolled cell cycle progression. Immunophenotype of mantle cell lymphoma:

• CD5 positive (T-cell marker aberrantly expressed on B cells)
• Cyclin D1 positive (hallmark finding)
• CD20 positive
• CD23 negative (helps differentiate from CLL)
• CD10 negative (distinguishes from follicular lymphoma)

Genetic basis:

• t(11; 14) → cyclin D1 gene (CCND1) overexpression
• Promotes G1→S phase cell cycle transition

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with chronic liver disease has thrombocytopenia before an elective dental extraction. Which thrombopoietin receptor agonist is specifically approved in this setting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Avatrombopag

Avatrombopag is approved for thrombocytopenia associated with chronic liver disease in patients scheduled for invasive procedures. It stimulates thrombopoietin receptors, increasing platelet production and reducing the need for platelet transfusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A young boy from high altitude came with fever and weakness and had the following lab reports: • Hemoglobin 17 gm% • TLC is 21,000 with neutrophils 25, lymphocytes 30, eosinophils 5, myelocytes and metamyelocytes 40 percent Next step in the investigation should be:
options: Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Erythropoietin levels

An elevated hemoglobin level in a patient from high altitude is most likely due to secondary polycythemia caused by chronic hypoxia.

Why EPO level is the next investigation:

• Helps differentiate secondary polycythemia from polycythemia vera
• Polycythemia vera → low EPO, JAK2 mutation
• Secondary polycythemia → high EPO

Other findings:

• Leukocytosis with left shift may be reactive due to infection or stress
• Not necessarily suggestive of myeloproliferative neoplasm initially

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are causes of anemia due to diminished erythropoiesis except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

Anemia can result from decreased red blood cell production (diminished erythropoiesis), increased destruction (hemolysis), or blood loss. Disorders that impair bone marrow function, DNA synthesis, or erythropoietin-mediated RBC production cause anemia due to reduced erythropoiesis.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia, not a disorder of decreased RBC production. A defect in RBC membrane proteins (e.g., spectrin, ankyrin, band 3) leads to formation of spherocytes that are prematurely destroyed in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis).

Why the Other Options Are Correct?

• A. Aplastic anemia → Direct failure of hematopoietic stem cells.
• B. Megaloblastic anemia → Ineffective erythropoiesis due to defective DNA synthesis.
• D. Anemia of chronic disease → Cytokine-mediated suppression of erythropoiesis and iron sequestration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are the correct statements about Blood transfusion except:
options: Blood received from blood bank should be completely transfused within 4 hours of receiving
Calcium can be added to the blood product to prevent hypocalcemia
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction may present in first 24hrs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium can be added to the blood product to prevent hypocalcemia

Correct transfusion principles:

• Blood should be completely transfused within 4 hours of issue from blood bank to reduce risk of bacterial proliferation
• Pre-warmed blood may be required in massive transfusion or in patients at risk of hypothermia
• Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions usually occur during transfusion or within the first 24 hours

Important precaution: Calcium must NOT be added directly to blood products

• Stored blood contains citrate (anticoagulant)
• Calcium added to the blood bag can overcome anticoagulation → clot formation
• If hypocalcemia occurs (eg, massive transfusion), calcium should be given separately via IV line, not mixed with blood

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are true regarding the management of Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) except:
options: Splenectomy is considered after glucocorticoid therapy failure
IVIG is a treatment option in life-threatening bleeding
Romiplostim and eltrombopag are avoided post-splenectomy
Rh(D) immune globulin is used in Rh-positive patients
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Romiplostim and eltrombopag are avoided post-splenectomy

Management of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) aims to reduce bleeding risk by increasing platelet count. Standard treatment approach:

• First line: corticosteroids
• Severe/life-threatening bleeding: IVIG or platelet transfusion
• Rh(D) immune globulin: option in Rh-positive, nonsplenectomized patients
• Second line: splenectomy if steroid failure
• Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) stimulate platelet production and are used in refractory ITP, including post-splenectomy patients

Thus, the false statement is that romiplostim and eltrombopag are avoided after splenectomy; they are actually effective second-line therapies

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following cause intravascular hemolysis, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

Intravascular hemolysis occurs when red blood cells are destroyed within the circulation, leading to hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and decreased haptoglobin levels. Common causes include mechanical trauma (e.g., prosthetic heart valves, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia), Clostridial sepsis (due to hemolytic toxins), and ABO-incompatible transfusion reactions, which cause complement-mediated RBC destruction.

• Hereditary spherocytosis is a classic cause of extravascular hemolysis, where spherocytes are trapped and destroyed by splenic macrophages due to membrane defects.

Why not the others?

• A. Mechanical trauma → intravascular RBC fragmentation (schistocytes).
• B. Clostridial sepsis → toxin-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
• D. ABO incompatibility → complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following parameters are true for anemia of chronic disease except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased ferroportin

Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation) is mediated by increased hepcidin production from the liver in response to inflammatory cytokines (especially IL-6). Hepcidin inhibits ferroportin, reducing iron release from macrophages and intestinal absorption, leading to decreased serum iron despite normal or increased iron stores.

Typical findings include:

• ↑ Hepcidin
• ↓ Ferroportin activity
• ↓ TIBC
• Normal or ↑ ferritin (iron stores)

Thus, increased ferroportin is incorrect, as ferroportin is suppressed in anemia of chronic disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An investigator is studying the changes that occur in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve of different types of hemoglobin under various conditions. The blood obtained from a male infant shows decreased affinity for 2,3-bisphosphoglyceric acid. Which of the following is the most likely composition of the hemoglobin molecule in this sample?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a2y2

Fetal hemoglobin (HbF: α₂γ₂) has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA: α₂β₂) because its γ chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly.

Mechanism:

• 2,3-BPG normally binds β chains of adult HbA → stabilizes deoxygenated state → promotes O₂ release
• In HbF, γ chains replace β chains → reduced 2,3-BPG binding
• Result → hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly → left shift of O₂ dissociation curve

Hemoglobin variants:

• HbA (adult): α₂β₂
• HbF (fetal): α₂γ₂ → ↓2,3-BPG binding
• HbA₂: α₂δ₂ (minor adult Hb)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Assertion (A): The pH of stored whole blood gradually decreases with increasing duration of storage. Reason (R): Even during storage, red blood cells continue anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid, which accumulates and lowers the pH of the blood.
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion

Stored blood undergoes storage lesions, a series of biochemical and structural changes that occur over time.

One important change is the progressive fall in pH, primarily because:

• Red blood cells remain metabolically active during storage.
• They continue anaerobic glycolysis, even at refrigerated temperatures.
• This leads to lactic acid accumulation, causing gradual acidification of the stored blood.

Other important storage lesions

• ↓ ATP
• ↓ 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)
• ↑ Potassium (K⁺) in plasma
• ↓ pH
• Reduced RBC deformability
• Progressive depletion of coagulation factors (especially Factors V and VIII)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Four days after admission to the hospital for acute pancreatitis, a 41-year-old man develops hypotension and fever. His temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F), pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows warm extremities, asymmetric calf size, and blood oozing around his Iv sites. There are numerous small, red, non blanching macules and patches covering the extremities, as well as several large ecchymoses. His hemoglobin concentration is 9.0 g/dl. A PBS shows schistocytes and decreased platelets. Which of the following sets of serum findings are most likely in this patient?
options: PT increased, aPTT increased, Fibrinogen decreased, D-dimer normal
PT normal, aPTT increased, Fibrinogen decreased, D-dimer increased
PT increased, aPTT normal, Fibrinogen normal, D-dimer normal
PT increased, aPTT increased, Fibrinogen decreased, D-dimer increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PT increased, aPTT increased, Fibrinogen decreased, D-dimer increased

This patient has disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a consumptive coagulopathy triggered by severe illness such as acute pancreatitis, sepsis, trauma, or malignancy.

Key clinical clues:

• Hypotension, fever (sepsis/pancreatitis trigger)
• Bleeding from IV sites
• Petechiae, ecchymoses
• Schistocytes on smear (microangiopathic hemolysis)
• Thrombocytopenia

Characteristic lab findings in DIC:

• PT ↑ (extrinsic pathway consumption)
• aPTT ↑ (intrinsic pathway consumption)
• Fibrinogen ↓ (consumed)
• D-dimer ↑ (fibrin degradation products)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Gaisböck syndrome includes all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypotension

Gaisböck syndrome (stress polycythemia or relative polycythemia) is characterized by relative erythrocytosis due to reduced plasma volume rather than true increase in RBC mass.

• Middle-aged obese men
• Hypertension (not hypotension)
• Smoking and stress association
• Increased hematocrit with normal RBC mass
• Normal leukocyte and platelet counts
• No splenomegaly

Distinguishing from polycythemia vera:

• Polycythemia vera → increased RBC mass, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly
• Gaisböck syndrome → relative polycythemia with normal cell counts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Identify the causes of dry tap on bone marrow aspiration 1. Hairy cell leukemia 2. Follicular lymphoma 3. AML M7 4. Myelodysplastic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4
