A dry tap on bone marrow aspiration occurs when marrow cannot be aspirated due to marrow fibrosis, hypercellularity, or infiltration, and is often followed by a trephine biopsy for diagnosis. Common causes of dry tap:

• Hairy cell leukemia: marrow fibrosis due to leukemic infiltration
• AML M7 (acute megakaryoblastic leukemia): associated with marked marrow fibrosis
• Myelodysplastic syndrome (especially fibrotic variant): may produce fibrosis and ineffective hematopoiesis
• Primary myelofibrosis (classic cause, though not listed)

Follicular lymphoma is less common cause it Usually causes marrow infiltration but not significant fibrosis leading to dry tap.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The Philadelphia chromosome seen in chronic myeloid leukemia is best described as which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?
options: Balanced translocation between the short arms of chromosomes 9 and 22
Balanced translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22
Unbalanced translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22
Unbalanced translocation between the short arms of chromosomes 9 and 22
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Balanced translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22

The Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) results from a balanced reciprocal translocation between the long arms (q arms) of chromosomes 9 and 22, designated t(9;22)(q34;q11).

• Translocation forms the BCR-ABL fusion gene
• Produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase
• Leads to uncontrolled myeloid cell proliferation

Clinical relevance:

• Diagnostic hallmark of CML
• Also seen in some cases of ALL
• Targeted therapy: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (eg, imatinib, dasatinib)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following are reduced in Iron Deficiency Anemia? 1. Ferritin 2. TIBC 3. Transferrin saturation 4. RDW 5. Hepcidin 6. Soluble transferrin receptor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3, 5

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) results from depleted iron stores and adaptive changes to increase iron absorption.

Reduced in IDA:

• Ferritin ↓ → reflects depleted iron stores (most specific)
• Transferrin saturation ↓ → less iron bound to transferrin
• Hepcidin ↓ → body increases iron absorption and release

Increased in IDA (not reduced):

• TIBC ↑ (more transferrin produced)
• RDW ↑ (anisocytosis)
• Soluble transferrin receptor ↑ (increased iron demand)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following conditions has the same underlying pathophysiology as the mechanism of action of Eptifibatide?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia

Eptifibatide is a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor that prevents platelet aggregation by blocking fibrinogen binding to the GPIIb/IIIa receptor on platelets. Glanzmann thrombasthenia has the same underlying pathophysiology:

• Inherited deficiency or dysfunction of GPIIb/IIIa receptor
• Platelets cannot bind fibrinogen
• Impaired platelet aggregation despite normal platelet count
• Presents with mucocutaneous bleeding

Comparison with other disorders:

A. Bernard–Soulier syndrome: defect in GPIb → impaired platelet adhesion

B. Von Willebrand disease: vWF deficiency → impaired adhesion

D. Gray platelet syndrome: deficiency of alpha granules

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is approved for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in patients who have failed two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omacetaxine

Omacetaxine mepesuccinate is a protein synthesis inhibitor approved for treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) by blocking ribosomal elongation in patients who have failed or are resistant to two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Reduces levels of BCR-ABL oncoprotein.

Other drugs:

• Imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib → TKIs (first/second-line)
• Ponatinib → used for T315I mutation or resistant disease but still a TKI

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following factors increases sickling of red blood cells in patients with sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presence of HbC

Sickling of red blood cells in sickle cell disease (SCD) occurs due to polymerization of deoxygenated HbS, which distorts RBCs into a sickle shape.

Factors that increase sickling:

• Presence of HbC → promotes RBC dehydration and HbS polymerization
• Low oxygen tension (hypoxia)
• Acidosis (low pH)
• Dehydration
• Infection or stress

Factors that decrease sickling:

• Increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin inhibits HbS polymerization)
• Adequate hydration
• Alkaline pH
• Oxygenation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is a histone deacetylase inhibitor that can be used in the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vorinostat

Vorinostat is a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor used in the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), including mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome.

Mechanism of action:

• Inhibits histone deacetylase → increases histone acetylation
• Leads to altered gene expression
• Promotes tumor cell differentiation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis

Why not others:

A. Lonafarnib → farnesyl transferase inhibitor

B. Alemtuzumab → anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody

C. Vemurafenib → BRAF inhibitor (melanoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is false about hemolytic uremic syndrome?
options: Symptoms and signs of HUS develops as diarrhea begins to improve.
Only supportive management of acute Renal Failure is done in typical HUS
Eculizumab improves microangiopathic hemolytic anemia in atypical HUS
Coomb’s positive Hemolytic anemia is seen in HUS.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coomb’s positive Hemolytic anemia is seen in HUS.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by the triad of:

• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) with schistocytes on peripheral smear finding
• Thrombocytopenia
• Acute kidney injury

Key points:

• Typical HUS (Shiga toxin–associated) usually follows diarrheal illness; symptoms often begin as diarrhea improves
• Management is mainly supportive (fluids, dialysis, transfusions if needed)
• Atypical HUS involves complement dysregulation and is treated with eculizumab, a C5 inhibitor
• Hemolysis in HUS is Coombs negative because it is mechanical (microangiopathic), not immune-mediated

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is used in the treatment of hemophilia B? a) Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) b) Cryoprecipitate c) PCC d) Cryo poor Plasma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a & d

Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is caused by factor IX deficiency. Treatment focuses on replacing factor IX or providing factor IX–containing products. Treatment options for hemophilia B:

• Fresh frozen plasma (FFP): contains factor IX and can be used when specific concentrates are unavailable
• Cryo-poor plasma (cryosupernatant): contains factor IX and can be used as replacement therapy
• Recombinant or plasma-derived factor IX concentrates: preferred treatment (if available)

Not useful:

b. Cryoprecipitate: rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF → used in hemophilia A, not B

c. PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate): contains factor IX but mainly used for warfarin reversal; not routine first-line for hemophilia B in many settings

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following peripheral blood smear findings is not typically seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymphoblasts

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a malignancy of mature B lymphocytes and typically shows characteristic findings on peripheral blood smear. Typical smear findings in CLL:

• Small mature lymphocytes with clumped chromatin
• Smudge cells (fragile lymphocytes disrupted during slide preparation)
• Occasional prolymphocytes may be present in small numbers

Not seen in CLL:

• Lymphoblasts → seen in acute leukemias (eg, ALL), not in CLL
• Presence of numerous blasts suggests transformation or acute leukemia rather than CLL

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presented with complaints of recurrent bleeding. He has a retroperitoneal hematoma and develops joint pain with swelling on slight exercise. There is no mucosal bleeding in the patient. Which of the following coagulation factor can be responsible for the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor 8/9 deficiency

Correct answer is B because recurrent deep tissue bleeding, hemarthrosis, and retroperitoneal hematoma without mucosal bleeding is typical of hemophilia due to factor VIII (Hemophilia A) or factor IX (Hemophilia B) deficiency.

| Test | Finding

| ---- | -------

| Bleeding time | Normal

| PT | Normal

| aPTT | ↑

| Platelets | Normal

Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding. Lupus anticoagulant causes thrombosis rather than bleeding. Factor XII deficiency prolongs aPTT but does not cause clinical bleeding.

| Feature | Hemophilia | vWD

| ------- | ---------- | ---

| Bleeding type | Deep | Mucosal

| Platelets | Normal | Normal

| Bleeding time | Normal | ↑

| aPTT | ↑ | Mild ↑

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with fever and rashes over the lower limbs. Laboratory investigations reveal normal PT and aPTT with a reduced platelet count. Peripheral blood smear shows increased megakaryocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ITP

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia due to IgG-mediated destruction of platelets. The bone marrow responds with compensatory megakaryocytic hyperplasia, resulting in increased megakaryocytes. Since the coagulation cascade is unaffected, PT and aPTT remain normal.

Key differentiating features:

• ITP:

• Isolated thrombocytopenia
• Normal PT and aPTT
• Increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow
• Petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding

• Dengue:

• Thrombocytopenia with fever, often accompanied by leukopenia, hemoconcentration, and positive NS1/IgM tests.

• Hemophilia:

• Normal platelet count
• Prolonged aPTT
• Deep tissue and joint bleeding (hemarthrosis)

• Thalassemia:

• Microcytic hemolytic anemia, not isolated thrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with recurrent bleeding into the joints since childhood. There is no history of mucocutaneous bleeding. Family history reveals similar symptoms in a maternal male relative. Laboratory investigations show normal platelet count, normal bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, and a 50% reduction in Factor VIII levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemophilia A

Hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII, which presents with deep tissue bleeding, especially recurrent hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints) and intramuscular hematomas. The diagnosis is suggested by a positive family history in maternal male relatives, isolated prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelet function, and reduced Factor VIII levels.

•        Laboratory findings: ↑ aPTT, normal PT, normal bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal ristocetin test.

•        Diagnosis: Low Factor VIII activity; mixing study corrects the prolonged aPTT (unless inhibitors are present).

•        Treatment: Recombinant Factor VIII replacement, desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild disease, and emicizumab for prophylaxis in selected patients.

Why not the other options?

• B. Von Willebrand disease: Causes mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising), prolonged bleeding time, abnormal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, and may have mildly reduced Factor VIII.
• C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: Defect of GpIIb/IIIa causing impaired platelet aggregation; presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, and normal coagulation tests.
• D. Bernard–Soulier syndrome: Defect of GpIb causing impaired platelet adhesion; presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, thrombocytopenia with giant platelets, prolonged bleeding time, and abnormal ristocetin test.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents to the ER with menorrhagia. She mentions that her father and sister also suffer from bleeding disorders. Which of the following is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Von Willebrand Disease

vWF deficiency/dysfunction

↓

↓ Platelet adhesion (GpIb interaction)

↓

Primary hemostasis defect

↓

Mucocutaneous bleeding

↓

Also ↓ Factor VIII stability

Correct answer is D because von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and commonly presents with mucocutaneous bleeding such as menorrhagia, with possible family history affecting both sexes due to autosomal inheritance.

It causes defective platelet adhesion and reduced factor VIII stability.

Treatment:

• Desmopressin (DDAVP) → releases vWF from endothelium
• vWF concentrates (severe cases)

Factor VIII and IX deficiencies are X-linked and typically present with deep tissue and joint bleeding, mainly affecting males. Factor X deficiency is rare.

| Feature | vWD | Hemophilia

| ------- | --- | ----------

| Inheritance | AD | X-linked

| Gender | Both | Males

| Bleeding type | Mucocutaneous | Deep

| Bleeding time | ↑ | Normal

| aPTT | Mild ↑ | ↑

| Platelets | Normal | Normal

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with widespread purpura and easy bruising. Laboratory tests reveal a significantly low platelet count with normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count, indicating a diagnosis of isolated thrombocytopenia. The patient has no prior history of autoimmune disorders or recent viral infections. Considering these symptoms and diagnosis, which tyrosine kinase inhibitor would be appropriate for this patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fostamatinib

Fostamatinib (SYK inhibitor) is used in chronic/refractory ITP to reduce immune-mediated platelet destruction.

Correct answer is B because fostamatinib is a spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK) inhibitor used in chronic immune thrombocytopenia by reducing antibody-mediated platelet destruction.

Autoantibody-coated platelets

↓

Bind Fc receptors on macrophages

↓

SYK activation

↓

Platelet destruction

↓

Fostamatinib blocks SYK

↓

↓ Platelet destruction

Fostamatinib impairs Syk-mediated phagocytosis of platelets.

| Drug | Mechanism | Use

| ---- | --------- | ---

| Fostamatinib | SYK inhibitor | ITP

| Eltrombopag | TPO agonist | ITP

| Rituximab | Anti-CD20 | ITP

| Bosutinib | BCR-ABL inhibitor | CML

Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that increases platelet production, not a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Oprelvekin is an IL-11 analog that stimulates platelet production. Bosutinib is a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in CML, not thrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A male patient sustained a fall after which he developed swelling of the knee. Laboratory investigations show increased APTT, with normal bleeding time and normal PT. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemophilia A

Solution- Key clues:

• Male patient → think X-linked disorder
• Knee swelling after trauma → hemarthrosis (deep bleeding) ⭐
• Labs:

• ↑ aPTT
• Normal PT
• Normal bleeding time

Diagnosis: Hemophilia A

Correct answer is B because isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT and normal bleeding time indicates intrinsic pathway factor deficiency, most commonly factor VIII deficiency (Hemophilia A).

Clinical presentation with hemarthrosis after minor trauma is typical of hemophilia.

| Test | Result | Meaning

| ---- | ------ | -------

| Bleeding time | Normal | Platelets OK

| PT | Normal | Extrinsic pathway OK

| aPTT | ↑ | Intrinsic pathway defect

Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding with prolonged bleeding time. ITP causes thrombocytopenia. DIC prolongs PT, aPTT, and reduces platelets.

| Feature | Hemophilia | vWD | ITP

| ------- | ---------- | --- | ---

| Bleeding type | Deep | Mucosal | Mucosal

| Platelets | Normal | Normal | ↓

| Bleeding time | Normal | ↑ | ↑

| PT | Normal | Normal | Normal

| aPTT | ↑ | Mild ↑ | Normal

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A newborn presents with umbilical cord stump bleeding and a history of recurrent bleeding episodes. Laboratory results reveal normal PT, APTT, and platelet count, but a positive urea clot solubility test. What coagulation factor deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Factor XIII

• Stabilizes fibrin clot by cross-linking fibrin strands

Correct answer is D because Factor XIII deficiency causes defective cross-linking of fibrin, leading to unstable clot formation despite normal initial coagulation, so PT, APTT, and platelet count remain normal.

It classically presents with delayed bleeding such as umbilical stump bleeding and recurrent poor wound healing, and shows a positive clot solubility test.

Normal coagulation cascade

↓

Fibrin clot forms (unstable)

↓

Factor XIII deficiency

↓

No cross-linking

↓

Clot dissolves easily

↓

Delayed bleeding

Factor VIII and XI deficiencies prolong APTT, while Factor XII deficiency prolongs APTT but does not cause clinical bleeding.

| Factor Deficiency | PT | aPTT | Bleeding | Special Feature

| ----------------- | --- | ---- | -------- | ---------------

| Factor VIII | Normal | ↑ | Deep bleeding | Hemophilia A

| Factor XI | Normal | ↑ | Mild bleeding | Rare

| Factor XII | Normal | ↑ | No bleeding | Lab finding only

| Factor XIII | Normal | Normal | Delayed bleeding | Clot dissolves

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of petechiae, ecchymosis, thrombocytopenia, and large platelets on peripheral smear. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

Correct answer is A because the findings suggest immune thrombocytopenic purpura, characterized by immune-mediated platelet destruction with compensatory release of large, young platelets from bone marrow.

Autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet GpIIb/IIIa

↓

Splenic destruction of platelets

↓

Thrombocytopenia

↓

Bone marrow compensation → ↑ megakaryocytes

↓

Large (giant) platelets in blood

PBS showing giant platelet

Lab Findings in ITP-

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Platelet count | ↓↓↓

| Bleeding time | ↑

| PT / aPTT | Normal

| Bone marrow | ↑ Megakaryocytes

IVIG rapidly increases platelet count by blocking Fc receptor–mediated platelet destruction in the spleen and is used when rapid platelet rise is needed.

First-line:

• Steroids (Prednisolone)

Urgent / Severe bleeding:

• IVIG
• Platelet transfusion (only if life-threatening)

Chronic/refractory:

• Splenectomy
• Rituximab

| Feature | ITP | TTP | DIC

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Platelets | ↓↓↓ | ↓ | ↓

| PT/aPTT | Normal | Normal | ↑

| Smear | Large platelets | Schistocytes | Schistocytes

| Cause | Autoimmune | ADAMTS13 deficiency | Consumption

| Treatment | Steroids, IVIG | Plasma exchange | Treat cause

Aspirin worsens bleeding by impairing platelet function. Methotrexate is not standard therapy for ITP. Bone marrow transplant is not indicated as marrow production is usually normal or increased.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding due to factor IX deficiency. In which of the following conditions will you find an improvement after administering Vitamin K parenterally?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bile duct obstruction

Vitamin K–dependent factors

Without Vitamin K → these factors are produced but non-functional

Correct answer is B because vitamin K is required for hepatic synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), and in bile duct obstruction fat-soluble vitamin absorption is impaired, leading to deficiency that improves with parenteral vitamin K.

Pernicious anemia is due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Hepatitis A causes hepatocellular injury where vitamin K response may be limited. Classical hemophilia (factor VIII deficiency) does not respond to vitamin K.

| Condition | Problem | Vitamin K effect

| --------- | ------- | ----------------

| Bile duct obstruction | ↓ absorption | ✅ Improves

| Vitamin K deficiency | ↓ activation | ✅ Improves

| Hemophilia | Factor absent | ❌ No effect

| Liver disease | ↓ synthesis | ❌ Limited

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A woman at 30 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate for this patient for prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH)

Mechanism:

Advantages:

• Does NOT cross placenta
• Predictable action
• Less bleeding risk
• No monitoring needed (usually)
•

Correct answer is B because low molecular weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy as it does not cross the placenta and has predictable anticoagulant effect with good safety profile.

Warfarin is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. Direct oral anticoagulants like apixaban and fondaparinux are generally avoided due to limited safety data in pregnancy.

| Drug | Placental Transfer | Use

| ---- | ------------------ | ---

| LMWH | No | Drug of choice

| Unfractionated heparin | No | Alternative

| Warfarin |  Yes | Contraindicated

| DOACs | ? | ❌ Avoid

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young patient began taking a weight loss medication that works by preventing fat absorption from food. She developed easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding after a few weeks. Which of the following vitamins deficiency is likely to be responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin K

Correct answer is B because fat absorption inhibitors reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and vitamin K deficiency leads to impaired synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, causing bleeding tendency.

Fat absorption blocked

↓

↓ Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

↓

↓ Vitamin K

↓

↓ Clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X)

↓

Bleeding

This explains easy bruising and menorrhagia.

Vitamin E deficiency causes neuropathy. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone disease. Vitamin B6 is water soluble and not affected by fat malabsorption.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Regarding ticagrelor, which statements are correct? 1. It blocks P2Y12 receptors of ADP 2. It is a reversible antagonist 3. It has a higher risk of intracranial bleeding than clopidogrel 4. It requires hepatic activation for action
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

• Ticagrelor blocks: Platelet ADP P2Y12 receptor
• Unlike clopidogrel: Ticagrelor is reversible
• Ticagrelor is active directly. It is not a prodrug.
• Ticagrelor causes more total major and minor bleeding events.

Comparison:

| Drug | Reversible? | Prodrug?

| ---- | ----------- | --------

| Clopidogrel | No | Yes

| Prasugrel | No | Yes

| Ticagrelor | Yes | No

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following anticoagulants requires coagulation profile monitoring?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lepirudin

Lepirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor) requires monitoring with aPTT.

Correct answer is B because lepirudin is a direct thrombin inhibitor with variable anticoagulant effect and requires monitoring using aPTT to maintain therapeutic range and avoid bleeding.

| Drug | Class | Monitoring

| ---- | ----- | ----------

| Heparin | Indirect thrombin inhibitor | aPTT

| Warfarin | Vitamin K antagonist | PT/INR

| Lepirudin | Direct thrombin inhibitor | aPTT

| DOACs (dabigatran, etc.) | Direct inhibitors |  Not routine

| Drug | Target | Route | Monitoring

| ---- | ------ | ----- | ----------

| Heparin | Thrombin + Xa | IV | aPTT

| Enoxaparin | Xa > Thrombin | SC | ❌

| Fondaparinux | Xa | SC | ❌

| Lepirudin | Thrombin | IV | ✅ aPTT

| Dabigatran | Thrombin | Oral | ❌

Enoxaparin and fondaparinux have predictable pharmacokinetics and usually do not require routine coagulation monitoring. Dabigatran also has predictable effect and routine coagulation monitoring is not required.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following infections is transmitted by all components of the blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malaria

Malaria

• The parasite (Plasmodium) lives inside RBCs
• During component preparation, no component is 100% RBC-free:

• Platelets → contain residual RBCs
• Plasma → may have minimal RBC contamination

• Even very small numbers of infected RBCs can transmit malaria

Therefore, malaria can be transmitted via:

• Packed RBCs
• Platelets
• Plasma

Hence, effectively transmitted by all components

Why other options are wrong

A) Hepatitis B / Hepatitis C

• Virus is mainly plasma-borne
• Conceptually linked to plasma transmission, not the “all components via contamination” principle tested here

B) Filariasis

• Not a routine transfusion-transmitted infection
• Not relevant to component-based transmission

D) Syphilis

• Organism is fragile
• Killed by storage at 4°C
• Transmission mainly via fresh blood only

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is an oral anticoagulant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dabigatran

Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor (Direct Oral Anticoagulant; DOAC) used for the prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Unlike heparin and other parenteral anticoagulants, it is administered orally and does not require routine INR monitoring.

• A. Dabigatran: Oral direct thrombin (Factor IIa) inhibitor.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Heparin: Parenteral anticoagulant (IV/SC); potentiates antithrombin III.
• C. Fondaparinux: Subcutaneous indirect Factor Xa inhibitor.
• D. Bivalirudin: Intravenous direct thrombin inhibitor, commonly used during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is false about von Willebrand disease?
options: Type I vWD presents with severe bleeding since birth
Type II vWD has reduced activity of von Willebrand factor
Type III vWD has very low levels of von Willebrand factor
Type III vWD presents clinically as a severe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type I vWD presents with severe bleeding since birth

Correct answer is A because Type I von Willebrand disease is a partial quantitative deficiency and usually causes mild bleeding, often presenting later in life rather than severe bleeding since birth.

Type II vWD is a qualitative defect with reduced functional activity of vWF. Type III vWD has near absence of vWF and presents with severe bleeding resembling hemophilia.

| Type | Defect | Severity | Key Feature

| ---- | ------ | -------- | -----------

| Type I | Partial quantitative ↓ | ⭐ Mild | Most common

| Type II | Qualitative defect | Moderate | Dysfunctional vWF

| Type III | Severe deficiency | ⭐ Severe | Almost absent vWF

| Feature | vWD | Hemophilia

| ------- | --- | ----------

| Bleeding type | Mucosal | Deep (joints)

| Platelet function | Abnormal | Normal

| Bleeding time | ↑ | Normal

| aPTT | Mild ↑ | ↑

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an inherited cause of thrombosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PNH (Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria)

PNH causes thrombosis but is an acquired disorder, not inherited. Pathophysiology of PNH

PIGA mutation (acquired)

↓

↓ GPI anchors

↓

Loss of CD55 & CD59

↓

Complement-mediated RBC destruction

↓

Hemolysis + thrombosis

Correct answer is C because Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal stem cell disorder caused by PIGA gene mutation leading to deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59), resulting in complement-mediated hemolysis and thrombosis. Inherited thrombophilia = genetic defects → ↑↑ tendency to clot

Major inherited causes:

• Antithrombin III deficiency
• Protein C deficiency
• Protein S deficiency
• Factor V Leiden mutation
• Prothrombin gene mutation

Protein S deficiency and antithrombin III deficiency are inherited thrombophilias causing increased risk of venous thrombosis. Homocystinuria is a genetic disorder associated with endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Thus, PNH is not inherited, unlike the other options.

Inherited Thrombophilia-

| Disorder | Defect | Mechanism | Clinical Clue

| -------- | ------ | --------- | -------------

| Protein S deficiency | Cofactor loss | ↓ Protein C activity | DVT

| Antithrombin III deficiency | ↓ thrombin inhibition | ↑ clotting | Heparin resistance

| Protein C deficiency | ↓ factor Va/VIIIa inhibition | Hypercoagulable | Warfarin skin necrosis

| Factor V Leiden | APC resistance | Persistent clotting | Most common inherited

Inherited vs Acquired Thrombosis-

| Feature | Inherited | Acquired

| ------- | --------- | --------

| Onset | Young age | Any age

| Family history | Present | Absent

| Examples | Protein C/S, AT-III | PNH, DIC, APS

| Mechanism | Genetic | Secondary

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Von Willebrand Disease

vWF: Platelet adhesion + Factor VIII stabilization

Dual function:

1. Platelet adhesion

• Bridges platelets to exposed subendothelium (via GpIb)

2. Carrier of Factor VIII

• Protects it from degradation

Correct answer is A because Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder due to quantitative or qualitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor, leading to defective platelet adhesion and secondary reduction in factor VIII stability.

It typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis, menorrhagia, and gum bleeding with prolonged bleeding time and often normal platelet count.

| Parameter | vWD

| --------- | ---

| Bleeding time | ↑

| Platelet count | Normal

| PT | Normal

| aPTT | ↑ (due to ↓ Factor VIII)

| vWF antigen | ↓

| Ristocetin test | Abnormal

Ristocetin Test

Ristocetin causes platelet aggregation via vWF

In vWD → NO aggregation

Hemophilia is also inherited but is less common and presents with deep tissue and joint bleeding rather than mucosal bleeding. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is an acquired consumptive coagulopathy, not inherited.

| Feature | vWD | Hemophilia

| ------- | --- | ----------

| Type of defect | Platelet + Coagulation | Coagulation only

| Bleeding | Mucocutaneous | Deep (joints, muscles)

| Bleeding time | ↑ | Normal

| aPTT | ↑ | ↑

| Platelets | Normal | Normal

| Inheritance | AD | X-linked recessive

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is used in the treatment of hemophilia A? a) Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) b) Cryoprecipitate c) Factor VIII concentrates d) Cryo-poor Plasma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a, b, c

Correct answer is C because hemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency, and treatment requires replacement of factor VIII–containing products. Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate contain factor VIII and can be used when specific factor VIII concentrates are unavailable.

| Product | Contains

| ------- | --------

| FFP | All clotting factors

| Cryoprecipitate | Fibrinogen, Factor VIII, vWF, XIII

| Cryo-poor plasma | Factor IX, XI, albumin

| Factor VIII concentrate | Only Factor VIII

Cryoprecipitate and factor VIII concentrates are used in hemophilia A, not hemophilia B.

| Feature | Hemophilia A | Hemophilia B

| ------- | ------------ | ------------

| Deficiency | Factor VIII | Factor IX

| Treatment | Cryo, FVIII concentrate | FFP, FIX sources

| Common? | More common | Less common

| Name | Classic hemophilia | Christmas disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following represent the primary defect in patients with Bernard–Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Defect in GpIb

Solution- Normal:

Vessel injury

↓

vWF binds exposed collagen

↓

Platelet GpIb binds vWF

↓

Platelet adhesion

Correct answer is D because Bernard–Soulier syndrome is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of platelet GpIb receptor, leading to defective platelet adhesion to subendothelial vWF.

GpIb defect

↓

No binding to vWF

↓

No platelet adhesion

↓

Bleeding

It presents with thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and prolonged bleeding time.

GpIIb/IIIa defect is seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. vWF defect is seen in von Willebrand disease. Fibrinogen defects cause coagulation abnormalities, not platelet adhesion defects.

| Disorder | Defect | Problem | Key Feature

| -------- | ------ | ------- | -----------

| Bernard–Soulier | GpIb | Adhesion | Giant platelets

| Glanzmann | GpIIb/IIIa | Aggregation | Normal size platelets

| vWD | vWF | Adhesion + Factor VIII | ↑ aPTT

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an antidote for Rivaroxaban and Apixaban, when reversal of anticoagulation is needed due to uncontrolled bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Andexanet Alfa

Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent (antidote) for Factor Xa inhibitors, including Rivaroxaban and Apixaban. It is indicated in patients with life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding requiring rapid reversal of anticoagulation.

It acts as a recombinant modified factor Xa decoy protein, which binds Factor Xa inhibitors with high affinity, thereby restoring normal coagulation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Idarucizumab: Specific antidote for Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor).
• C. Hydroxocobalamin: Antidote for cyanide poisoning.
• D. Glucarpidase: Used to treat methotrexate toxicity by rapidly degrading methotrexate.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is used to reverse the anticoagulant effects of Dabigatran?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Idarucizumab

Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent (antidote) for Dabigatran, a direct thrombin (Factor IIa) inhibitor. It is indicated in patients with life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding or when urgent surgery or invasive procedures require rapid reversal of anticoagulation.

Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) that binds dabigatran with very high affinity, neutralizing its anticoagulant effect within minutes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucarpidase: Used to treat methotrexate toxicity by rapidly metabolizing methotrexate.
• B. Desferrioxamine (Deferoxamine): Chelating agent used for acute iron poisoning and chronic iron overload.
• D. Protamine: Reverses unfractionated heparin (and partially reverses low-molecular-weight heparin), but has no effect on dabigatran.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: With regard to management of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, consider the following statements: I. All patients with ITP with platelet count less than 100 × 10⁹/L should receive high dose glucocorticoids. II. For patient with spontaneous bleeding, 40 mg of dexamethasone daily is indicated for 4 days. III. Intravenous immunoglobulin can raise the platelet count. IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L) due to autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired platelet production. Treatment is based on the severity of thrombocytopenia and the presence of bleeding, not the platelet count alone.

• I. All patients with ITP with platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L should receive high-dose glucocorticoids:

• Incorrect. Not all patients require treatment. Patients with mild thrombocytopenia and no bleeding may be observed. Treatment is indicated for clinically significant bleeding or platelet count <20–30 × 10⁹/L.

• II. For patients with spontaneous bleeding, 40 mg of dexamethasone daily is indicated for 4 days:

• High-dose dexamethasone (40 mg/day for 4 days) is a standard first-line corticosteroid regimen in adults with symptomatic ITP.

• III. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) can raise the platelet count:

• IVIG rapidly increases platelet counts by blocking Fc receptor-mediated platelet destruction and is used when a rapid platelet rise is required.

• IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion:

• Platelet transfusion is indicated only in life-threatening bleeding and should be combined with IV corticosteroids and IVIG, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 15-year-old adolescent with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is started on intensive induction chemotherapy. Two days later, he develops reduced urine output, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory evaluation shows marked hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and worsening renal function, indicating tumor lysis syndrome. Which of the following agents is most effective for rapidly lowering the serum uric acid concentration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rasburicase

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency caused by rapid destruction of tumor cells after chemotherapy, leading to the release of intracellular contents. It is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and acute kidney injury. Agents that convert uric acid to the highly soluble metabolite allantoin rapidly reduce serum uric acid levels and are preferred in established severe hyperuricemia.

Rasburicase is a recombinant uricase enzyme that converts:

• Uric acid → Allantoin
• Allantoin is highly water-soluble and is rapidly excreted by the kidneys.

Why not the other options?

• A. Allopurinol: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor that prevents new uric acid formation but does not reduce pre-existing uric acid, so it is less effective for rapid treatment.
• C. Febuxostat: Also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; decreases uric acid production but does not rapidly lower existing serum uric acid.
• D. Probenecid: A uricosuric drug that increases renal uric acid excretion; ineffective and potentially harmful in TLS because it may increase uric acid precipitation in renal tubules.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 26-year-old female complains of severe fatigue and myalgia. Examination reveals pallor and mild splenomegaly. Haematological investigations are shown below: Haemoglobin – 10 g/dL Peripheral smear – Microcytic hypochromic picture with anisocytosis Reticulocyte count – 5% Serum ferritin – 300 microgram/L What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. β-Thalassemia

The key clues are microcytic hypochromic anemia + elevated reticulocyte count + splenomegaly + normal/high ferritin. This favors a hemoglobinopathy with ongoing hemolysis, particularly β-thalassemia, rather than iron deficiency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Iron deficiency: Causes microcytosis, but typically has low serum ferritin and usually does not cause splenomegaly or reticulocytosis.
• B. Folic acid deficiency: Causes macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia, not microcytic anemia.
• C. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency: Also causes macrocytic anemia, often with neurological manifestations.
• D. β-Thalassemia: Causes microcytic hypochromic anemia, increased RBC destruction → reticulocytosis and splenomegaly, with ferritin generally normal or increased.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presents with multiple cervical lymphadenopathies. IHC markers were positive for CD10 and BCL-2. Peripheral smear shows a large number of small cells (centrocytes) and occasional large cells (centroblasts). What is the most common genetic defect in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. t (14;18) BCL2-IGH

Lymphadenopathy

↓

IHC: CD10+

↓

BCL2+

↓

Centrocytes + centroblasts

↓

Follicular lymphoma

↓

t(14;18)

Correct answer is A because CD10 and BCL-2 positivity with centrocytes and centroblasts is characteristic of follicular lymphoma, most commonly associated with t (14;18) translocation causing BCL2 overexpression and inhibition of apoptosis.

Features:

• Centrocytes → small cleaved cells
• Centroblasts → large cells
• Follicular architecture

| Marker | Meaning

| ------ | -------

| CD10 | Germinal center B-cell

| BCL2 | Anti-apoptotic protein

| CD20 | B-cell marker

t (2;5) ALK is seen in anaplastic large cell lymphoma. t (11;18) is seen in MALT lymphoma. t (11;14) Cyclin D1 is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma.

| Lymphoma | Translocation | Gene

| -------- | ------------- | ----

| Follicular lymphoma |  t(14;18) | BCL2

| Mantle cell lymphoma | t(11;14) | Cyclin D1

| Burkitt lymphoma | t(8;14) | MYC

| MALT lymphoma | t(11;18) | MALT1

| ALCL | t(2;5) | ALK

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with fatigue, dark-colored urine on waking, recurrent abdominal pain, and episodes of venous thrombosis. Laboratory evaluation shows anemia with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin, and flow cytometry demonstrates deficiency of CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells, confirming paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eculizumab

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a PIGA gene mutation, resulting in deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins, particularly CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL). Loss of these complement regulatory proteins makes red blood cells susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, causing episodic hemoglobinuria (classically in the morning), anemia, and a high risk of venous thrombosis. Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody against complement protein C5, is the treatment of choice as it prevents terminal complement activation and intravascular hemolysis.

Why not the other options?

• Rituximab: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used for B-cell lymphomas and autoimmune diseases; no role in PNH.
• Imatinib: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for CML (BCR-ABL) and GIST; ineffective in PNH.
• Prednisolone: May provide temporary symptomatic benefit in some hemolytic disorders but does not target the underlying complement-mediated pathogenesis of PNH.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is found to have anemia during routine antenatal evaluation. Despite adequate iron and folic acid supplementation, her hemoglobin remains at 9 g/dL, and she continues to be symptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thalassemia trait

Thalassemia trait (thalassemia minor) should be suspected in a pregnant woman with persistent microcytic hypochromic anemia that does not improve despite adequate iron and folic acid therapy. Diagnosis is confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC (e.g., **elevated HbA₂ in β-thalassemia trait).

Why not the other options?

• A. Sickle cell anemia: Causes hemolytic anemia with vaso-occlusive crises, not isolated iron-refractory microcytic anemia.
• B. Thalassemia major: Presents in early childhood with severe transfusion-dependent anemia; patients rarely present for the first time during pregnancy.
• D. Hereditary spherocytosis: A hemolytic anemia characterized by spherocytes, jaundice, splenomegaly, and increased MCHC, not microcytic anemia unresponsive to iron.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female presents with easy fatigability. Investigations show that Hb is 6 g%; red cell morphology is normocytic normochromic; and reticulocyte production index is 5.5. Which one of the following conditions favours this abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravascular hemolysis

The Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) is used to determine whether the bone marrow response to anemia is appropriate.

• RPI >3 → Indicates an appropriate marrow response, suggesting hemolysis or acute blood loss. ⭐
• RPI <2 → Indicates inadequate marrow response, suggesting decreased RBC production (e.g., nutritional deficiency, bone marrow failure).

This patient has:

• Hb = 6 g/dL (severe anemia)
• Normocytic normochromic RBCs
• RPI = 5.5 (markedly elevated)

These findings strongly suggest hemolytic anemia, particularly intravascular hemolysis. In intravascular hemolysis:

• RBCs are destroyed within the circulation.
• Bone marrow compensates by increasing erythropoiesis, resulting in a high reticulocyte count/RPI (>3). ⭐
• The anemia is typically normocytic normochromic.

Why not the other options?

• A. Iron deficiency anemia: Produces microcytic hypochromic anemia with low RPI because iron deficiency limits erythropoiesis.
• B. Sideroblastic anemia: Usually microcytic or dimorphic anemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte response.
• C. Folate deficiency: Causes macrocytic megaloblastic anemia with low RPI due to ineffective erythropoiesis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 39-year-old female presents with severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which of the following should be the initial step in its management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prednisolone

Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA) is the most common type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia and is caused by IgG autoantibodies directed against red blood cells, leading to extravascular hemolysis, primarily in the spleen. Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) are the first-line treatment, as they suppress autoantibody production and reduce red cell destruction.

• A. Prednisolone:

• First-line therapy for warm AIHA.
• Produces remission in the majority of patients.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Rituximab: Used in steroid-refractory or relapsed AIHA or when steroids are contraindicated.
• C. Emergency splenectomy: Considered second-line therapy for patients not responding to steroids.
• D. Plasmapheresis: Has a limited role and is reserved for life-threatening, refractory hemolysis, particularly in cold antibody-mediated disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presented with sudden onset of fatigue due to severe anemia, multiple bruises on his limbs, and WBC count of 40,000/cm³. What is the likely karyotype of the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 47XX (+21)

Correct answer is C because Down syndrome (Trisomy 21; 47XX +21 / 47XY +21) is strongly associated with increased risk of acute leukemia in children, especially acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia.

Child with anemia + bruising + leukocytosis

↓

Bone marrow infiltration

↓

Acute leukemia (ALL)

↓

Check genetic associations

↓

Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)

The clinical picture of severe anemia, bruising, and high WBC suggests acute leukemia, which is more common in children with trisomy 21.

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Hb | ↓

| Platelets | ↓

| WBC | ↑ or ↓

| Blasts | ↑

t(9;22) is associated with CML or some adult ALL cases. 45X0 is Turner syndrome. Normal 46XY has no increased leukemia risk.

| Condition | Associated Malignancy

| --------- | ---------------------

| Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) | ⭐ ALL, AML (M7)

| t(9;22) | CML, some ALL

| t(8;14) | Burkitt lymphoma

| t(15;17) | APL

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 42-year-old female has Hb 9.2 g/dL and MCV 72 fL. Which of the following conditions can be the cause of this presentation? 1. Iron deficiency 2. Thalassemia 3. Lead poisoning 4. Vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Correct answer is A because Hb 9.2 g/dL with MCV 72 fL indicates microcytic anemia.

Microcytic Anemia = ↓ Hemoglobin synthesis

Major mechanisms:

• ↓ Iron → Iron deficiency
• ↓ Globin → Thalassemia
• ↓ Heme synthesis → Lead poisoning / Sideroblastic anemia

The major causes include iron deficiency (most common), thalassemia (reduced globin chain synthesis), and lead poisoning (impaired heme synthesis due to enzyme inhibition).

| Cause | Serum Iron | Ferritin | TIBC | RDW | Key Feature

| ----- | ---------- | -------- | ---- | --- | -----------

| Iron deficiency | ↓ | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ | Most common

| Thalassemia | Normal/↑ | Normal/↑ | Normal | Normal | Target cells

| Lead poisoning | Normal/↑ | Normal/↑ | Normal | ↑ | Basophilic stippling

| Sideroblastic anemia | ↑ | ↑ | Normal | ↑ | Ring sideroblasts

Iron deficiency anemia. Hypochromic red blood cells

Hereditary hemolytic anemia. Smear show hypochromia and anisopoikilocytosis, target cells.

Blood smear showing red blood cells with coarse basophilic stippling in lead poisoning

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic megaloblastic anemia due to defective DNA synthesis, so it does not fit this presentation.

| Feature | Microcytic | Macrocytic

| ------- | ---------- | ----------

| MCV | <80 fL | >100 fL

| Causes | Iron deficiency, Thalassemia, Lead | B12, Folate

| Problem | Hb synthesis | DNA synthesis

| Smear | Small pale RBCs | Large RBCs + hypersegmented neutrophils

Thus, conditions 1, 2, and 3 are consistent with microcytic anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man who follows a strict vegetarian diet presents with gradually worsening fatigue, numbness and tingling in both feet, and difficulty walking for the past six months. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Megaloblastic anemia

A strict vegetarian presenting with anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesias and gait difficulty) most likely has vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, resulting in megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, and also leads to demyelination of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration), producing neurological manifestations.

The patient has:

• Strict vegetarian diet (risk factor for vitamin B₁₂ deficiency)
• Fatigue due to anemia
• Numbness and tingling
• Difficulty walking (posterior column involvement)

These findings are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B₁₂ deficiency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Aplastic anemia: Presents with pancytopenia due to bone marrow failure, without neurological symptoms.
• B. Sideroblastic anemia: Characterized by microcytic anemia with ring sideroblasts and iron overload; neurological symptoms are not typical.
• D. Iron deficiency anemia: Causes microcytic hypochromic anemia, fatigue, koilonychia, and pica, but does not cause neurological deficits.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 46-year-old lady on a vegan diet for a decade presents with chief complaints of tingling and numbness in lower limbs for two months and a history of swaying while walking through narrow corridors. Which one of the following blood tests is advisable for diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B12 levels

This patient has features suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency, including:

• Long-term vegan diet (lack of dietary vitamin B12) ⭐
• Paresthesias (tingling and numbness) in the lower limbs
• Sensory ataxia (swaying while walking), indicating posterior column involvement

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord, affecting the:

• Posterior (dorsal) columns → Loss of vibration and joint position sense, sensory ataxia
• Lateral corticospinal tracts → Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response

Therefore, the most appropriate initial blood test is serum vitamin B12 level.

Why not the other options?

• A. Serum protein electrophoresis: Used to evaluate multiple myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy, not nutritional neuropathy.
• B. Anti-gliadin antibodies: Used in the evaluation of celiac disease (anti-tTG IgA is preferred), not the first investigation here.
• C. Vitamin 25(OH) D level: Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia and proximal muscle weakness, not posterior column dysfunction or paresthesias.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy who was started on treatment for Burkitt lymphoma develops acute onset respiratory distress and decreased urine output. Investigations reveal: Hb 8 g/dL TLC 15000/mm³ Platelet count 1 lakh/mm³ Serum potassium 6.5 mEq/L Corrected serum calcium 6.7 mg/dL Serum creatinine 2 mg/dL The most important drug for emergency management is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rasburicase

This child has tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) following treatment of Burkitt lymphoma, a highly proliferative tumor with a high tumor burden.

The findings strongly support TLS:

• Hyperkalemia: K⁺ 6.5 mEq/L
• Hypocalcemia: corrected Ca²⁺ 6.7 mg/dL
• Acute kidney injury: creatinine 2 mg/dL
• Respiratory distress may result from severe metabolic disturbances/fluid overload.

Rasburicase rapidly converts uric acid → allantoin, which is much more soluble, thereby rapidly reducing uric acid and preventing/worsening uric acid nephropathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dexamethasone: Used in ALL/lymphoma treatment but does not provide the rapid metabolic correction required in established TLS.
• B. Broad-spectrum antibiotics: No evidence of bacterial sepsis is provided.
• D. Folinic acid rescue: Used to reduce methotrexate toxicity, not TLS.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 56-year-old man presents with dragging pain in the abdomen. On examination, there is massive splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes and basophils. Which of the following translocation is seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. t (9:22)

Correct answer is A because massive splenomegaly with marked leukocytosis and left shift (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, basophilia) is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia -peripheral blood film

CML is associated with t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome causing BCR-ABL fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.

t(15;17) is seen in APL. t(8;14) is seen in Burkitt lymphoma. t(8;22) is also linked to Burkitt variant translocations.

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| WBC | ↑↑↑

| Basophils | ↑

| LAP score | ↓

| Platelets | Variable

| Splenomegaly | Massive

| Disease | Translocation | Key Feature

| ------- | ------------- | -----------

| CML | ⭐ t(9;22) | BCR-ABL

| APL | t(15;17) | DIC

| Burkitt | t(8;14) | MYC

| Follicular | t(14;18) | BCL2

Treatment: Imatinib (BCR-ABL inhibitor)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with chronic kidney disease presents to the OPD with paleness, progressive dyspnea and signs of congestive cardiac failure. His lab results show a normocytic normochromic anemia. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Darbepoetin alfa

CKD → ↓ Erythropoietin → normocytic anemia → treat with EPO analog (Darbepoetin alfa)

Correct answer is A because anemia in chronic kidney disease is classically normocytic normochromic due to decreased erythropoietin production by diseased kidneys, and darbepoetin alfa (long-acting EPO analog) corrects this deficiency.

Chronic kidney disease

↓

↓ Erythropoietin production

↓

↓ Bone marrow stimulation

↓

↓ RBC production

↓

Normocytic anemia

Iron therapy is useful only if iron deficiency is present. Blood transfusion is reserved for severe or symptomatic anemia not controlled with EPO therapy.

| Anemia Type | MCV | Cause | Treatment

| ----------- | --- | ----- | ---------

| Iron deficiency | ↓ | Iron lacks | Iron

| Megaloblastic | ↑ | B12/Folate | Vitamins

| CKD anemia | Normal | ↓ EPO | ⭐ EPO analog

Thus, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are first-line management in CKD-related anemia. Do keep in mind that iron stores must be adequate before starting EPO, hence the patient is always screened for IDA before therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old vegetarian patient presented with weakness and reduced work capacity. He had a Hb of 10gm/dl and MCV-110. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Megaloblastic anaemia

Vitamin B12/Folate deficiency→Impaired DNA synthesis→Nuclear maturation defect

Correct answer is C because Hb 10 g/dL with MCV 110 fL indicates macrocytic anemia, and in a vegetarian patient the most likely cause is vitamin B12 deficiency leading to megaloblastic anemia due to defective DNA synthesis.

↓ Vitamin B12 / Folate

↓

↓ DNA synthesis

↓

Nuclear maturation delayed

↓

Cytoplasm grows normally

↓

Large RBCs (macrocytes)

Hallmarks:

• Macro-ovalocytes
• Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes)

Hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes in the setting of B12 deficiency

Iron deficiency anemia and thalassemia cause microcytic anemia. Aplastic anemia is usually normocytic with pancytopenia rather than isolated macrocytosis.

| Feature | Microcytic | Macrocytic

| ------- | ---------- | ----------

| MCV | <80 | >100

| Causes | Iron deficiency, Thalassemia | B12, Folate

| RBC size | Small | Large

| Mechanism | ↓ Hb synthesis | ↓ DNA synthesis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with symptoms of bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, and renal impairment. A bone marrow biopsy confirms the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. The patient is started on a treatment regimen. Which of the following treatments is most likely associated with the reactivation of herpes zoster?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bortezomib

Latent viruses reactivate when:

• Cell-mediated immunity ↓

Bortezomib impairs:

• T-cell function

Correct answer is A because bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor) is associated with increased risk of herpes zoster reactivation due to impaired cellular immunity, so antiviral prophylaxis is often given.

Mechanism:

Lenalidomide is an immunomodulatory drug mainly associated with cytopenias and thrombosis risk. Daratumumab is an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody. Melphalan is an alkylating agent and not classically linked with zoster reactivation.

Clinical Correlation-

| Drug | Key Side Effect

| ---- | ---------------

| Bortezomib | ⭐ Herpes zoster reactivation

| Lenalidomide | Thrombosis

| Daratumumab | Infusion reactions

| Melphalan | Myelosuppression

| Drug | Class | Side Effect

| ---- | ----- | -----------

| Bortezomib | Proteasome inhibitor | ⭐ Herpes zoster

| Lenalidomide | IMiD | Thrombosis

| Daratumumab | Anti-CD38 | Infusion reactions

| Melphalan | Alkylator | Myelosuppression

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with persistent back pain, fatigue, recurrent infections, and anemia. Investigations reveal hypercalcemia, multiple osteolytic lesions on X-ray, and an M-protein spike on serum protein electrophoresis. Bone marrow examination confirms multiple myeloma. Which of the following drugs is a proteasome inhibitor used in the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bortezomib

Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that is a cornerstone in the treatment of multiple myeloma. It inhibits the 26S proteasome, preventing degradation of ubiquitinated proteins, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins, induction of apoptosis, and inhibition of NF-κB signaling in malignant plasma cells. Plasma cells are particularly sensitive to proteasome inhibition because they produce large amounts of immunoglobulins.

The patient has classic features of multiple myeloma:

• Persistent back pain
• Anemia
• Recurrent infections
• Hypercalcemia
• Osteolytic lesions
• M-protein spike on serum protein electrophoresis

Bortezomib is a first-line proteasome inhibitor used in the treatment of newly diagnosed and relapsed multiple myeloma.

Why not the other options?

• B. Busulfan: An alkylating agent primarily used for chronic myeloid leukemia (historically) and as part of bone marrow transplant conditioning, not a proteasome inhibitor.
• C. Melphalan: An alkylating agent used in multiple myeloma but not a proteasome inhibitor.
• D. Cyclophosphamide: An alkylating agent used in many hematologic malignancies and autoimmune disorders, but not a proteasome inhibitor.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presented with fatigue. On examination, there were scattered purpuric rashes, and abdominal examination was notable for cervical lymphadenopathy and hepato-splenomegaly. Lab parameters are shown – Hb 7 g/dL, WBC 50,000, platelets 60,000. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prednisolone + Vincristine

Correct answer is D because the presentation suggests acute lymphoblastic leukemia with anemia, thrombocytopenia (purpura), leukocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Prednisolone

↓

Lymphoblast apoptosis

Vincristine

↓

Inhibits mitosis (microtubules)

↓

Kills leukemic cells

Initial induction therapy for ALL commonly includes combination chemotherapy with steroids (prednisolone) and vincristine to induce remission.

IVIG is used in immune thrombocytopenia. Doxorubicin/epirubicin are used in other malignancies. Radiotherapy is not first-line for systemic leukemia.

| Phase | Treatment

| ----- | ---------

| Induction | ⭐ Steroid + Vincristine

| Consolidation | Chemo

| Maintenance | Methotrexate, etc.

ALL markers:

• TdT positive
• CD10 (CALLA)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presented with fatigue, jaundice, and splenomegaly. His father also has had a similar history. On peripheral smear, MCHC was found to be elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

↑ MCHC + splenomegaly + family history = Hereditary spherocytosis (HS)

Correct answer is C because hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by increased MCHC due to membrane loss and RBC dehydration, along with hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly with positive family history.

Membrane protein defect

↓

Loss of RBC membrane surface area

↓

Spherical RBC (spherocyte)

↓

↓ Deformability

↓

Trapped in spleen

↓

Extravascular hemolysis

Hallmarks:

• Spherocytes (round RBCs)
• No central pallor
• Dense appearance

It is caused by RBC membrane protein defects (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3). Thalassemia and sickle cell disease do not show increased MCHC. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is acquired and not typically familial.

| Feature | HS | AIHA

| ------- | --- | ----

| Cause | Genetic | Autoimmune

| Family history | ✅ | ❌

| MCHC | ↑ | Normal/slightly ↑

| Coombs test | Negative | Positive

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with anemia, frontal bossing, and jaundice. Which of the following statements are true for the given condition? 1. Ineffective erythropoiesis 2. Systemic iron overload 3. Intravascular hemolysis 4. Increased hepcidin degradation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2

This child most likely has β-thalassemia major, characterized by severe anemia, frontal bossing (marrow expansion), jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly. The disease is caused by defective β-globin synthesis, leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and extravascular hemolysis.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Ineffective erythropoiesis ✓: Defective hemoglobin synthesis causes destruction of erythroid precursors within the bone marrow.
• 2. Systemic iron overload ✓: Results from repeated blood transfusions and increased intestinal iron absorption due to suppressed hepcidin.

Why not the other statements?

• 3. Intravascular hemolysis ✗: Hemolysis in thalassemia is predominantly extravascular, occurring in the spleen.
• 4. Increased hepcidin degradation ✗: Hepcidin levels are decreased/suppressed because of increased erythroferrone production from expanded erythropoiesis, leading to increased iron absorption. The term “increased hepcidin degradation” is not the accepted mechanism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A female patient presents with iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and glossitis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plummer Vinson syndrome

Correct answer is C because Plummer–Vinson syndrome is characterized by the triad of iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia due to esophageal webs, and glossitis.

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Iron deficiency anemia | ↓ Hb

| Dysphagia | Esophageal web

| Glossitis | Mucosal atrophy

• Premalignant condition

Risk of: Squamous cell carcinoma

It is classically seen in middle-aged females and is associated with increased risk of upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Achalasia causes dysphagia without iron deficiency anemia. Dysphagia lusoria is due to vascular compression. Esophageal carcinoma presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss.

| Feature | PVS | Carcinoma

| ------- | --- | ---------

| Dysphagia | Intermittent | Progressive

| Iron deficiency | ✅ | ❌

| Glossitis | ✅ | ❌

| Cancer risk | Increased | —

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident was admitted to the emergency department. During the first 2–4 hours, he received 4 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypocalcemia

Stored blood contains citrate

↓

Citrate binds calcium

↓

↓ Ionized calcium

↓

Hypocalcemia

Answer is B because stored blood contains citrate as an anticoagulant, which binds ionized calcium during rapid or massive transfusion, leading to hypocalcemia.

Mechanism:

This can cause tetany, hypotension, and arrhythmias during transfusion.

Sodium abnormalities and hypocitratemia are not typical complications of blood transfusion.

Massive Transfusion Complications-

| Complication | Mechanism

| ------------ | ---------

| Hypocalcemia | Citrate binding

| Hyperkalemia | RBC lysis

| Hypothermia | Cold blood

| Acidosis | Poor perfusion

Prevention:

• Monitor calcium
• Give IV calcium gluconate if needed

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with pancytopenia, and bone marrow examination reveals a markedly hypocellular (hypoplastic) marrow. Which of the following conditions is most characteristically associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fanconi anemia

Fanconi anemia is an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by progressive pancytopenia with a hypocellular/hypoplastic bone marrow.

It results from mutations affecting the Fanconi DNA-repair pathway, leading to defective repair of DNA interstrand cross-links and increased chromosomal breakage.

Important features include:

• Progressive pancytopenia
• Hypocellular bone marrow
• Short stature
• Café-au-lait pigmentation
• Skeletal abnormalities, particularly thumb and radial-ray defects
• Increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors

Why not the other options?

• B. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): An acquired clonal hematopoietic stem-cell disorder due to a PIGA mutation, resulting in deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins such as CD55 and CD59. PNH can coexist with aplastic anemia and marrow failure, so marrow cellularity can vary; however, Fanconi anemia is the classic inherited hypoplastic marrow disorder among these options.
• C. Hypersplenism: Causes cytopenias primarily through splenic sequestration and destruction of blood cells. Bone marrow is usually normal or hypercellular rather than hypoplastic.
• D. Myelofibrosis: Characterized by progressive bone marrow fibrosis with extramedullary hematopoiesis, massive splenomegaly, and a leukoerythroblastic blood picture rather than a primarily hypoplastic marrow.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with an unknown blood group experiences trauma and is unstable, requiring an urgent blood transfusion. Which types of blood should be transfused? a. A+ b. AB+ c. O+ d. O-
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. c & d

Unknown blood group + unstable patient

↓

Need immediate transfusion

↓

Use O group blood

↓

If female / childbearing → O negative

If adult male → O positive acceptable

Correct answer is B because in emergency transfusion with unknown blood group, group O blood is safest as it lacks A and B antigens, minimizing risk of acute hemolytic reaction.

O negative is universal donor and preferred, especially in females of reproductive age to prevent Rh sensitization. O positive can be used in life-threatening emergencies, especially in males or when O negative is unavailable.

| Term | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Universal donor (RBC) | O−

| Universal recipient (RBC) | AB+

| Plasma donor (universal) | AB

| Plasma recipient (universal) | O

A+ and AB+ contain A and/or B antigens and can cause severe hemolytic transfusion reactions in incompatible recipients.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with anemia and a regular history of blood transfusions since an early age was carrying his daily activities normally. He experiences a mild respiratory infection following which he developed fatigue, severe pallor, and shortness of breath. Which of the following is the likely organism involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parvovirus

Solution- Key clues:

• Chronic transfusions since childhood → chronic hemolytic anemia (e.g., thalassemia, sickle cell)
• Sudden worsening after mild infection
• Severe pallor + fatigue

Diagnosis: Aplastic crisis due to Parvovirus B19

Correct answer is B because parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursor cells in bone marrow causing transient aplastic crisis, especially in patients with chronic hemolytic anemia who depend on high erythropoiesis.

Parvovirus B19

↓

Infects erythroblasts

↓

Stops erythropoiesis

↓

Reticulocytopenia

↓

Sudden severe anemia

It presents with sudden severe anemia, pallor, and fatigue following mild viral illness.

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Hb | ↓↓↓

| Reticulocyte count | ↓↓↓ (very important)

| WBC/Platelets | Normal or mildly ↓

| Bone marrow | ↓ erythroid precursors

CMV, EBV, and HSV do not typically cause pure red cell aplasia or aplastic crisis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with reduced hemoglobin and gum bleeding presented to you. He has thrombocytopenia (platelet count 25,000/ul) elevated PT, and aPTT. Which of the following can the probable cause of his finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. AML t (15;17)

Cytogenetic abnormality:

Correct answer is B because AML t(15;17) corresponds to acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is strongly associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation leading to thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT and aPTT and bleeding manifestations.

Abnormal promyelocytes

↓

Release procoagulant granules

↓

Coagulation activation

↓

DIC

↓

Severe bleeding

This occurs due to release of procoagulant granules from abnormal promyelocytes.

Promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods (“faggot cells”)**

t(8;21) and inv(16) are other AML subtypes not classically associated with severe DIC. NPM mutation AML is not specifically linked to coagulopathy.

| AML Type | Mutation | Key Feature

| -------- | -------- | -----------

| APL (M3) | ⭐ t(15;17) | DIC

| AML M2 | t(8;21) | Good prognosis

| AML M4 | inv(16) | Monocytes

| AML (NPM1) | NPM1 mutation | Common

Immediate treatment:

• ATRA (All-trans retinoic acid)

Prevents fatal bleeding

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All blood products are separated by Centrifugation except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum albumin

Whole blood donation

↓

Centrifugation

↓

Packed RBCs \| Platelets \| Plasma

↓

Further processing

↓

Cryoprecipitate

But-

Plasma

↓

Industrial fractionation (Cohn method)

↓

Albumin, Immunoglobulins, Factor concentrates

| Product | Method | Source

| ------- | ------ | ------

| RBCs | Centrifugation | Whole blood

| Platelets | Centrifugation | Whole blood

| Cryoprecipitate | Centrifugation + freezing | Plasma

| Serum Albumin | Fractionation | Plasma proteins

Correct answer is C because serum albumin is obtained by plasma fractionation using biochemical processing methods, not by simple centrifugation.

RBCs, platelets, and plasma (from which cryoprecipitate is prepared) are separated from whole blood using centrifugation based on density differences.

Cryoprecipitate is prepared by controlled thawing of fresh frozen plasma after centrifugation separation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy is brought with a rapidly enlarging mass involving the jaw. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. t(8;14)

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly presents in children. The endemic (African) variant classically presents as a rapidly enlarging jaw or facial bone mass and is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. The hallmark genetic abnormality is the t(8;14)(q24;q32) translocation, which places the c-MYC oncogene under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IgH) promoter, resulting in uncontrolled B-cell proliferation.

Why not the other options?

• A. t(15;17): Seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), producing the PML-RARA fusion gene.
• B. t(11;22): Characteristic of Ewing sarcoma, a malignant bone tumor with onion-skin periosteal reaction.
• D. t(9;22): The Philadelphia chromosome, seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and some cases of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), producing the BCR-ABL fusion gene.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with back pain and recurrent infections. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M spike. Which of the following factors are used to determine the prognosis in this patient?
options: Serum IgG level and LDH levels
Serum beta 2 microglobulin and hemoglobin levels
Serum albumin levels and hemoglobin levels
Serum beta 2 microglobulin levels and albumin levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum beta 2 microglobulin levels and albumin levels

Correct answer is D because prognosis in multiple myeloma is classically determined by International Staging System, which uses serum beta-2 microglobulin (tumor burden and renal function marker) and serum albumin (overall disease severity marker).

ISS (International Staging System)

Higher beta-2 microglobulin and lower albumin indicate worse prognosis.

IgG, LDH, and hemoglobin may reflect disease status but are not the primary staging parameters.

| Stage | β2-microglobulin | Albumin | Prognosis

| ----- | ---------------- | ------- | ---------

| I | Low | High | Good

| II | Intermediate | – | Moderate

| III | High | Low | Poor

| Marker | Role

| ------ | ----

| β2-microglobulin | ⭐ Tumor burden

| Albumin | Disease severity

| M protein | Diagnosis

| Calcium | CRAB feature

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with low-grade fever and long-standing lymphadenopathy. Flow cytometry reveals CD19+, CD5+, and CD23+ cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small lymphocytic lymphoma

• Elderly patient
• Long-standing lymphadenopathy
• Low-grade fever (indolent course)
• Flow cytometry:

• CD19+ → B cell
• CD5+ → aberrant expression
• CD23+ → key marker

Diagnosis: Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL)

(Tissue counterpart of CLL)

Correct answer is B because CD19+, CD5+, and CD23+ immunophenotype is characteristic of CLL/SLL, representing mature B-cell neoplasm.

SLL is the tissue counterpart of CLL and presents with lymphadenopathy and indolent course.

| Feature | CLL | SLL

| ------- | --- | ---

| Main site | Blood | Lymph nodes

| Cells | Same | Same

| Markers | CD5+, CD23+ | CD5+, CD23+

Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5 positive but usually CD23 negative. Follicular lymphoma is CD10 positive. Burkitt lymphoma is CD10 positive with very high proliferation index.

| Disease | CD5 | CD23 | Key Feature

| ------- | --- | ---- | -----------

| CLL/SLL | ✅ | ✅ | Indolent

| Mantle cell | ✅ | ❌ | Cyclin D1

| Follicular | ❌ | ❌ | BCL2

| Burkitt | ❌ | ❌ | MYC

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: As per the WHO expert group, the cutoff point of haemoglobin in venous blood for the diagnosis of anaemia in adult males is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 13 g/dL

According to the WHO criteria, anemia in an adult male is diagnosed when the hemoglobin concentration is <13 g/dL in venous blood.

• Adult male: Hb <13 g/dL → Anemia
• Adult non-pregnant female: Hb <12 g/dL → Anemia
• Pregnancy: Hb <11 g/dL → Anemia

Therefore, the correct cutoff is 13 g/dL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement I: Signs of thalassemia major usually develop after 6 months of age. Statement II: This is the time when haemoglobin synthesis switches from haemoglobin F to haemoglobin A. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I

β-Thalassemia major is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by absent or markedly reduced β-globin chain synthesis. Clinical manifestations usually appear after 6 months of age, when fetal hemoglobin (HbF) declines and adult hemoglobin (HbA) becomes the predominant hemoglobin.

• Statement I. Signs of thalassemia major usually develop after 6 months of age: ✓

• Infants with β-thalassemia major are usually normal at birth and develop severe anemia after 6 months of age.

• Statement II. This is the time when haemoglobin synthesis switches from haemoglobin F to haemoglobin A: ✓

• Around 6 months of age, hemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF (α₂γ₂) to HbA (α₂β₂).
