• Since β-globin chains are deficient in thalassemia major, HbA cannot be produced adequately, leading to severe anemia.

• Statement II correctly explains Statement I.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Decreased transferrin saturation is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron deficiency anemia

Correct answer is B because iron deficiency anemia causes low serum iron with increased transferrin (TIBC), leading to decreased transferrin saturation.

↓ Body iron stores

↓

↓ Serum iron

↓

↑ TIBC (more empty transferrin)

↓

↓↓ Transferrin saturation

Hemochromatosis and hemosiderosis are iron overload states with increased transferrin saturation. Macrocytic anemia is usually due to B12 or folate deficiency and does not typically cause low transferrin saturation.

| Parameter | Iron Deficiency | Hemochromatosis

| --------- | --------------- | ---------------

| Serum iron | ↓ | ↑

| TIBC | ↑ | ↓

| Transferrin saturation | ↓↓↓ | ↑↑

| Ferritin | ↓ | ↑

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythropoietin is primarily used in the treatment of which type of anemia? 1. Nutritional anemia 2. Chronic kidney disease (CKD)-related anemia 3. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)-related anemia 4. Aplastic anemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 & 3

Erythropoietin (EPO) is used when the problem is ↓ RBC production due to inadequate or ineffective marrow stimulation.

Correct answer is B because erythropoietin is primarily used in anemia due to decreased endogenous EPO production, classically seen in chronic kidney disease, where peritubular interstitial cells fail to produce adequate EPO.

Hypoxia / ↓ O2 delivery

↓

Kidney senses hypoxia

↓

↑ EPO secretion

↓

Bone marrow stimulation

↓

↑ RBC production

It is also used in selected myelodysplastic syndrome cases to stimulate erythroid precursors and reduce transfusion requirement.

| Condition | Problem | EPO Level | EPO Useful?

| --------- | ------- | --------- | -----------

| CKD | ↓ production of EPO | ↓ | ✅ Yes

| MDS | Ineffective erythropoiesis | Variable | ✅ Yes

| Iron deficiency | ↓ substrate | ↑ | ❌ No

| B12 deficiency | DNA synthesis defect | ↑ | ❌ No

| Aplastic anemia | Marrow failure | ↑ | ❌ No

Nutritional anemia requires replacement therapy (iron, B12, folate), and aplastic anemia is due to stem cell failure where EPO is usually ineffective.

| Type of Anemia | MCV | Reticulocyte Count | EPO Role

| -------------- | --- | ------------------ | --------

| CKD | Normal | ↓ | Replace EPO

| MDS | Usually macrocytic | ↓ | Stimulate marrow

| Iron deficiency | Microcytic | ↓ | No role

| Aplastic anemia | Normocytic | ↓↓↓ | No role

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythropoietin is secreted by which of the following? a. Liver b. Kidney c. Spleen d. Heart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a, b

Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced mainly by the kidney in adults, and by both liver and kidney (especially liver in fetus).

Source of EPO

Correct answer is A because erythropoietin is mainly produced by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in adults, while the liver is a significant source during fetal life and contributes minimally in adults.

Hypoxia (↓ O2)

↓

Kidney (peritubular cells)

↓

EPO secretion

↓

Bone marrow stimulation

↓

↑ RBC production

Spleen and heart do not produce erythropoietin.

Thus, kidney is the primary source and liver is a secondary source.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: First line therapy in chronic phase of chronic myeloid leukemia is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imatinib

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)], which creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene. This fusion gene encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells.

Imatinib, a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is the first-line treatment for chronic-phase CML and has dramatically improved survival.

Why not the other options?

• A. Rituximab: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used for B-cell lymphomas and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), not CML.
• B. Thalidomidel Used in multiple myeloma, not CML.
• D. Chlorambucil: Alkylating agent historically used for CLL, not first-line therapy for CML.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with the development of which one of the following lymphoid malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma

Helicobacter pylori infection is strongly associated with the development of gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, an extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma.

• Chronic H. pylori infection induces persistent inflammation, leading to the formation of acquired MALT.
• Continuous antigenic stimulation causes B-cell proliferation, which can eventually progress to MALT lymphoma.

Evaluation of the options:

• A. Burkitt’s lymphoma: False. Strongly associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and c-MYC translocation [t(8;14)].
• B. Hodgkin’s lymphoma: False. Some cases are associated with EBV, but not with H. pylori.
• D. Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma: False. Caused by Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the type of anemia. • Hb = 8 g/dL • MCV = 68 fL • Ferritin = Low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA)

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia and is characterized by depleted iron stores, reflected by low serum ferritin. A low hemoglobin, low MCV (<80 fL), and low ferritin are highly suggestive of IDA.

• Hb = 8 g/dL → Anemia
• MCV = 68 fL → Microcytic anemia
• Low ferritin → Depleted iron stores, the most specific laboratory marker of iron deficiency

Why not the other options?

• A. Aplastic anemia: Typically presents with normocytic anemia and pancytopenia, with normal or increased ferritin.
• B. Hemolytic anemia: Usually normocytic with reticulocytosis, elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin, and low haptoglobin.
• C. Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia: Causes macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia with an elevated MCV.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Imatinib, Dasatinib, Nilotinib and Ponatinib are examples of which class of drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors

Imatinib, Dasatinib, Nilotinib, and Ponatinib are tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) that inhibit the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)]. This inhibits:

• Uncontrolled cell proliferation
• Cell survival
• Leukemic cell growth

Evaluation of the options:

• A. Interferons: False. Interferon-α was previously used in CML but has largely been replaced by TKIs.
• B. Monovalent antibodies: False. These drugs are small-molecule inhibitors, not monoclonal antibodies.
• C. Bivalent antibodies: False. They are not antibody-based therapies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In a patient, ileal resection led to fatigue with Hb = 8 g/dL, MCV = 110 fL. Peripheral smear showed macrocytic anemia. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B12 deficiency

Ileal resection → loss of B12 absorption → macrocytic anemia (MCV 110)

| Vitamin | Site

| ------- | ----

| Vitamin B12 | ⭐ Terminal ileum

| Folate | Jejunum

Correct answer is B because ileum is the site of vitamin B12 absorption (via intrinsic factor–B12 complex), so ileal resection leads to B12 deficiency causing megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

The high MCV (110 fL) supports macrocytic anemia. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia. Folate is absorbed in proximal jejunum, not ileum. Vitamin B1 deficiency causes neurological and cardiac manifestations, not macrocytic anemia.

| Feature | B12 deficiency | Folate deficiency

| ------- | -------------- | -----------------

| Absorption | Ileum | Jejunum

| Cause | Ileal disease, vegetarian | Poor diet

| Neurological signs |  Present | Absent

| MCV | ↑ | ↑

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Normal Direct bilirubin, Increased Indirect Bilirubin, Increased Urine urobilinogen
Increased Direct bilirubin, Normal Indirect Bilirubin, Absent Urine urobilinogen
Normal Direct bilirubin, Normal Indirect Bilirubin, Normal Urine urobilinogen
Decreased Direct bilirubin, Decreased Indirect Bilirubin, Increased Urine urobilinogen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Normal Direct bilirubin, Increased Indirect Bilirubin, Increased Urine urobilinogen

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes episodic hemolytic anemia due to increased oxidative damage to RBCs.

• G6PD is a key enzyme of the Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt that generates NADPH.
• NADPH maintains glutathione in the reduced form, which protects RBCs from oxidative stress.
• In G6PD deficiency, oxidant drugs, infections, or fava beans lead to RBC hemolysis.

Biochemical consequences of hemolysis:

1.      Increased indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin

o    Hemoglobin breakdown → heme → bilirubin → overload of liver conjugation.

2.      Normal direct (conjugated) bilirubin

o    Liver function is normal; the problem is excessive hemolysis.

3.      Increased urine urobilinogen

o    More bilirubin reaches the intestine → more urobilinogen formation → increased reabsorption and urinary excretion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In haemolytic anaemia, which of the following is correct? 1. Urobilinogen is high 2. Serum conjugated bilirubin is elevated 3. Serum transaminases are increased 4. Indirect van den Bergh reaction is positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 4

Hemolysis → ↑ unconjugated bilirubin + ↑ urobilinogen → indirect Van den Bergh positive. Correct answer is B because hemolytic anemia causes increased breakdown of RBCs leading to increased heme metabolism, resulting in raised urobilinogen levels and increased unconjugated bilirubin, giving a positive indirect Van den Bergh reaction.

RBC destruction

↓

↑ Hemoglobin breakdown

↓

↑ Unconjugated bilirubin (indirect)

↓

Liver conjugation (overwhelmed)

↓

More bilirubin reaches intestine

↓

↑ Urobilinogen and stercobilinogen

| Feature | Hemolytic (Prehepatic) | Hepatic | Obstructive (Posthepatic)

| ------- | ---------------------- | ------- | -------------------------

| Bilirubin | ↑ unconjugated | Mixed | ↑ conjugated

| Urobilinogen | ↑ | Variable | ↓

| Stool color | Dark | Variable | Pale

| Urine bilirubin | Absent | Present | Present

Conjugated bilirubin is usually normal or mildly elevated as liver conjugation capacity is not primarily impaired. Serum transaminases are typically normal as there is no primary hepatocellular injury.

Van den Bergh Reaction-

| Type | Detects | Seen in

| ---- | ------- | -------

| Indirect | Unconjugated bilirubin | Hemolysis

| Direct | Conjugated bilirubin | Obstruction

| Biphasic | Both | Hepatic disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In India, the most widely prevalent stage of iron deficiency is:
options: Decreased iron stores without any other detectable abnormalities
Fall in percentage saturation of transferrin
Overt iron deficiency with impaired haemoglobin synthesis
Decrease in the concentration of circulating haemoglobin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased iron stores without any other detectable abnormalities

Iron deficiency develops in stages, progressing from depletion of iron stores to iron deficiency anemia. In India, the most common stage is depletion of iron stores without anemia, also called prelatent iron deficiency. Serum ferritin decreases first, while hemoglobin and serum iron remain normal. Individuals are usually asymptomatic.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Fall in percentage saturation of transferrin: Occurs in the second stage (latent iron deficiency) after iron stores are depleted.
• C. Overt iron deficiency with impaired haemoglobin synthesis: Represents iron deficiency erythropoiesis, a later stage before frank anemia.
• D. Decrease in the concentration of circulating haemoglobin: This is the final stage, i.e., iron deficiency anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Regarding ABO blood grouping, which statement is false?
options: IgM is the most common antibody in ABO
ABO antibodies are natural and present since birth
Antibodies are present only if antigens are absent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ABO antibodies are natural and present since birth

Birth → No ABO antibodies

↓

Exposure to gut bacteria / food antigens

↓

Immune system recognizes similar antigens

↓

Formation of IgM antibodies

Correct answer is B because ABO antibodies are naturally occurring but are not present at birth; they develop within the first few months of life due to exposure to environmental antigens (e.g., gut bacteria).

| Blood Group | Antigen | Antibody

| ----------- | ------- | --------

| A | A | Anti-B

| B | B | Anti-A

| AB | A & B | None

| O | None | Anti-A & Anti-B

ABO antibodies are predominantly IgM. ABO antigens are carbohydrate structures on RBC membrane. Antibodies develop against ABO antigens that are absent on an individual’s RBCs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The 190 kDa BCR-ABL protein is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ALL

The 190 kDa BCR-ABL protein is most commonly associated with B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (B-ALL). This specific form of the BCR-ABL fusion protein results from the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22). While BCR-ABL is also found in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), the size of the protein is different. In B-ALL, the BCR-ABL protein is usually 190 kDa in size, whereas in CML, a BCR-ABL protein of 210 kDa is typically present. The 190 kDa variant has stronger tyrosine kinase activity than the 210 kDa form and is strongly associated with a subset of B-ALL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The BCR-ABL1 oncoprotein exhibits constitutive activity of which one of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tyrosine kinase

The BCR-ABL1 fusion gene is formed by the t(9;22)(q34;q11) reciprocal translocation, known as the Philadelphia chromosome. This fusion gene encodes the BCR-ABL1 oncoprotein, which has constitutively active tyrosine kinase activity. This leads to:

• Uncontrolled cell proliferation
• Decreased apoptosis
• Increased survival of myeloid cells
• Genomic instability

Evaluation of the options:

• A. Alanine kinase: False. No such clinically relevant kinase is associated with BCR-ABL1.
• C. Leucine kinase: False. Not involved in BCR-ABL1 pathology.
• D. Cysteine kinase: False. Not the enzyme activity of the BCR-ABL1 oncoprotein.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The Rai staging system and Binet staging system are the two widely used staging systems used for staging which of the following hematological malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is the most common leukemia in adults and is characterized by the clonal proliferation of mature but functionally incompetent B lymphocytes. The disease is staged using the Rai and Binet staging systems, which are based on the extent of lymphoid tissue involvement and the presence of anemia or thrombocytopenia, and help determine prognosis and the need for treatment.

• D. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL): Rai and Binet staging systems are used exclusively for CLL.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): Classified using WHO/ELN risk stratification based on cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities, not Rai or Binet staging.
• B. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML): Staged into chronic, accelerated, and blast phases, not Rai or Binet.
• C. Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL): Risk stratified using age, WBC count, cytogenetics, and minimal residual disease (MRD), not Rai or Binet.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which mutation is seen in sickle cell anemia?
options: Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at position 6 of the α -globin chain
Substitution of glutamic acid by leucine at position 6 of the β-globin chain
Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain
Substitution of glutamic acid by leucine at position 6 of the α-globin chain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain

🔹 Gene level:

• HBB gene (β-globin)S
• Missense mutation
• DNA: GAG → GTG

Correct answer is C because sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene leading to substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position, producing HbS. This causes polymerization of deoxygenated HbS, leading to RBC sickling, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion.

β-globin mutation (Glu → Val)

↓

Hydrophobic HbS formation

↓

Polymerization in deoxygenated state

↓

RBC sickling

↓

Hemolysis + vaso-occlusion

• Glutamic acid = hydrophilic
• Valine = hydrophobic

This creates a “sticky patch” → Hb molecules aggregate → polymer formation. Key features:

• Sickled RBCs
• Target cells
• Howell-Jolly bodies (autosplenectomy)

A Howell–Jolly body (marked by arrow) within an erythrocyte

| Feature | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Pain crises | Vaso-occlusion

| Hemolytic anemia | RBC destruction

| Dactylitis (children) | Bone infarcts

| Autosplenectomy | Repeated infarction

| Infection risk | Encapsulated organisms

| Disorder | Mutation | Chain affected | Key feature

| -------- | -------- | -------------- | -----------

| Sickle cell anemia | Glu → Val | β-chain | Sickling

| HbC disease | Glu → Lys | β-chain | Mild hemolysis

| Thalassemia | ↓ synthesis | α or β | Imbalance of chains

Mutations involving α-globin chain are seen in thalassemia variants, and leucine substitution is not the mutation seen in sickle cell disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are recommended for the management of tumour lysis syndrome? 1. Urinary alkalinization 2. Intravenous fluids 3. Rasburicase 4. Febuxostat Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency caused by rapid destruction of tumour cells, leading to the release of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids. This results in:

• Hyperkalemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Secondary hypocalcemia
• Hyperuricemia, which can cause acute kidney injury.

Evaluation of the statements:

• 1. Urinary alkalinization: False.

• Previously recommended but no longer advised routinely.
• Alkalinization decreases uric acid precipitation but increases the risk of calcium phosphate crystal deposition in the kidneys, potentially worsening renal injury.

• 2. Intravenous fluids: True.

• Aggressive IV hydration is the cornerstone of TLS prevention and treatment.
• It enhances renal perfusion and promotes excretion of uric acid, potassium, and phosphate.

• 3. Rasburicase: True.

• Rasburicase is the preferred agent for high-risk patients or established TLS.
• It rapidly converts uric acid to allantoin, which is highly soluble and easily excreted.

• 4. Febuxostat: True.

• Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production.
• It is an alternative to allopurinol, particularly in patients who cannot tolerate allopurinol or have renal impairment. It is used mainly for TLS prophylaxis, not for rapid reduction of existing uric acid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are secondary iron overload conditions? I. Transfusion related iron load II. Thalassemia III. Hepatitis C associated liver disease Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Secondary iron overload is an acquired condition resulting from excessive iron accumulation due to repeated blood transfusions, increased intestinal iron absorption, or chronic liver disease. Unlike hereditary hemochromatosis, it is not caused by a primary genetic defect in iron metabolism.

Iron overload is broadly split into:

• Primary (hereditary) iron overload — genetic defects directly in iron-regulatory genes (HFE, hemojuvelin, hepcidin, TfR2, ferroportin) → classic hereditary hemochromatosis
•

Secondary (acquired) iron overload — iron accumulation as a consequence of another underlying disease process, not a primary defect in iron-handling genes

•

I. Transfusion-related iron overload ✔

• Repeated blood transfusions (e.g., in thalassemia major, myelodysplastic syndrome, aplastic anemia) lead to progressive iron accumulation because the body has no physiological mechanism for iron excretion.

• II. Thalassemia ✔

• Patients with thalassemia major develop iron overload due to:

• Repeated blood transfusions
• Increased intestinal iron absorption caused by ineffective erythropoiesis and low hepcidin levels.

• III. Hepatitis C-associated liver disease ✔

• Chronic hepatitis C can cause secondary hepatic iron overload, which may accelerate liver fibrosis and worsen disease progression.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following chromosomal translocations is characteristic of Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. t(2;5)

ALCL = t(2;5) → NPM–ALK fusion → ALK-positive lymphoma

Correct answer is C because anaplastic large cell lymphoma is classically associated with t(2;5) translocation causing NPM-ALK fusion protein leading to constitutive ALK tyrosine kinase activation.

t(2;5)

↓

NPM–ALK fusion

↓

Tyrosine kinase activation

↓

Uncontrolled growth

↓

ALCL

anaplastic large-cell lymphoma

• Hallmark cells with horseshoe/kidney-shaped nucleus
• CD30 positive
• Often ALK positive

t(8;14), t(2;8), and t(8;22) are associated with Burkitt lymphoma involving MYC gene translocations.

| Disease | Translocation | Gene

| ------- | ------------- | ----

| ALCL | ⭐ t(2;5) | ALK

| Burkitt | t(8;14) | MYC

| Follicular | t(14;18) | BCL2

| CML | t(9;22) | BCR-ABL

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs are effective in preventing uric acid nephropathy in patients receiving chemotherapy? 1. Probenecid 2. Forced saline diuresis 3. Rasburicase 4. Acetazolamide Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Tumor lysis syndrome can cause uric acid nephropathy. Prevention includes IV hydration (forced saline diuresis) and rasburicase.

Why?

• 1. Probenecid ❌: Increases urinary uric acid → may worsen crystal deposition.
• 2. Forced saline diuresis ✔️: Prevents uric acid precipitation.
• 3. Rasburicase ✔️: Converts uric acid to soluble allantoin.
• 4. Acetazolamide ✔️: Historically used for urine alkalinization (accepted in this question).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used to prevent painful vaso-occlusive crises and decrease long-term complications in sickle cell anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A. Hydroxyurea

Hydroxyurea increases HbF → prevents sickling → reduces vaso-occlusive crises.

Correct answer is A because hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production, which inhibits HbS polymerization and reduces frequency of vaso-occlusive crises and long-term complications.

Hydroxyurea

↓

↑ Fetal hemoglobin (HbF)

↓

Dilution of HbS

↓

↓ Polymer formation

↓

↓ Sickling

↓

↓ Vaso-occlusive crises

Clinical Benefits of Hydroxyurea-

| Benefit | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| ↓ Pain crises | ↓ sickling

| ↓ Acute chest syndrome | ↓ vaso-occlusion

| ↑ Hb levels | Improved erythropoiesis

| ↓ transfusion need | Less hemolysis

Methotrexate plus leucovorin is used in malignancies and autoimmune disorders. Methionine has no role in sickle cell disease, is an amino acid. Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist used in thrombocytopenia, not sickle cell disease.

| Drug | Role

| ---- | ----

| Hydroxyurea | ↑ HbF

| L-glutamine | ↓ oxidative stress

| Crizanlizumab | Anti-P-selectin (↓ adhesion)

| Voxelotor | ↑ Hb oxygen affinity

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following infectious agents are associated with the development of lymphoid malignancies? 1. HIV 2. Hepatitis B 3. Hepatitis C Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

• 1. HIV: Correct

• Associated with HIV-related non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly aggressive B-cell lymphomas such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma.

• 2. Hepatitis B: Correct

• Chronic HBV infection is associated with an increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, although the association is less characteristic than with HCV.

• 3. Hepatitis C: Correct

• Chronic HCV infection is strongly associated with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly marginal zone lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
• HCV-associated lymphoproliferation may occur through chronic antigenic stimulation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a feature of delayed blood transfusion reaction? 1. Increased unconjugated bilirubin 2. Cola colored urine after 2 hours 3. Increased LDH 4. Failure of rise of hemoglobin after transfusion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Delayed transfusion reaction = extravascular hemolysis → ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, poor Hb rise

Correct answer is C because delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction occurs days after transfusion due to anamnestic IgG-mediated extravascular hemolysis, leading to increased unconjugated bilirubin and increased LDH.

| Type | Reaction

| ---- | --------

| IgM | Acute (complement-mediated)

| IgG | Delayed (extravascular)

Previous sensitization (pregnancy/transfusion)

↓

Re-exposure to same antigen

↓

IgG antibodies produced

↓

Extravascular hemolysis (spleen)

↓

Gradual RBC destruction

There is poor post-transfusion hemoglobin rise due to destruction of transfused RBCs.

Cola-colored urine within hours suggests acute intravascular hemolytic transfusion reaction, not delayed reaction.

| Feature | Acute | Delayed

| ------- | ----- | -------

| Onset | Minutes–hours | Days–weeks

| Mechanism | Intravascular (IgM) | Extravascular (IgG)

| Urine | Hemoglobinuria (cola) | No

| Bilirubin | Mild ↑ | ↑ indirect

| Hb | Rapid fall | Poor rise

| LDH | ↑ | ↑

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a true/correct statement about paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
options: It is an inherited red blood cell disorder causing intravascular hemolysis
The diagnosis of the disorder is confirmed by sucrose lysis test
Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing this condition
The commonest cause of mortality is cardiac failure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing this condition

Correct answer is C because paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is diagnosed by flow cytometry demonstrating deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55 and CD59) on blood cells, which is the gold standard test.

PIGA gene mutation

↓

Defective GPI anchor

↓

Loss of CD55 & CD59

↓

No protection from complement

↓

Intravascular hemolysis

| Feature | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Hemoglobinuria (morning) | Night-time acidosis → complement activation

| Pancytopenia | Stem cell disorder

| Thrombosis | Platelet activation

| Dark urine | Hemolysis

Treatment:

• Eculizumab (C5 inhibitor)

Prevents complement-mediated destruction

PNH is an acquired clonal stem cell disorder, not inherited. Sucrose lysis test is an older screening test, not confirmatory. Major causes of mortality are thrombosis and complications of hemolysis, not cardiac failure.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of G6PD deficiency?
options: Males and females are equally affected
Characterized by presence of Heinz bodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Males and females are equally affected

Correct answer is A because G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder, so it predominantly affects males, while females are usually carriers and less commonly symptomatic.

The disease causes reduced NADPH generation, making RBCs vulnerable to oxidative stress, leading to hemolysis.

G6PD deficiency

↓

↓ NADPH

↓

↓ Reduced glutathione

↓

Oxidative damage to RBCs

↓

Hemoglobin denaturation

↓

Heinz bodies formation

↓

Hemolysis

Key features:

Heinz bodies (denatured Hb) on supravital stain

Blister cell

Bite cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in an elderly patient with ileal resection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Microcytic hypochromic anemia

Terminal ileum → absorbs B12 (with intrinsic factor)

Correct answer is C because ileal resection causes vitamin B12 deficiency leading to megaloblastic macrocytic anemia with nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony and neurological features such as posterior column involvement causing positive Romberg sign and possible reversible cognitive impairment.

Microcytic hypochromic anemia is seen in iron deficiency, not B12 deficiency.

| Feature | B12 Deficiency | Iron Deficiency

| ------- | -------------- | ---------------

| MCV | ↑ (macrocytic) | ↓ (microcytic)

| Neurological signs |  Present |  Absent

| Smear | Macrocytes | Hypochromic

| Cause | Ileal issue | Iron lack

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in a patient having a ↓ MCV, ↓ MCH, ↓ transferrin saturation, ↓ serum ferritin, and ↑ Total iron binding capacity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iron deficiency anemia

Correct answer is C because iron deficiency anemia shows microcytosis (↓MCV), hypochromia (↓MCH), low ferritin (depleted iron stores), low transferrin saturation, and increased TIBC due to compensatory increase in transferrin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about red blood cells in Sickle cell anemia:
options: Low mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility
High mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility
Low mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility
High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility

Sickle RBCs are rigid → break easily (↑ mechanical fragility) but resist swelling (↓ osmotic fragility).

Correct answer is D because sickled RBCs are rigid and easily damaged while passing through microcirculation, leading to increased mechanical fragility and hemolysis.

Due to dehydration and increased intracellular Hb concentration, sickled RBCs show decreased osmotic fragility compared to normal RBCs.

Thus, sickle cells are mechanically fragile but relatively resistant to osmotic lysis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are incorrect about Hodgkin's lymphoma?
options: Nodular sclerosis is the most common and involves the mediastinum
CD15 & CD30 positivity in Reed Sternberg cells
Reed Sternberg cells are derived from B cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Waldeyer's ring is commonly involved

Hodgkin lymphoma typically involves nodal regions (especially mediastinum), NOT extranodal sites like Waldeyer’s ring.

Correct answer is B because Hodgkin lymphoma commonly involves cervical, mediastinal, and supraclavicular lymph nodes, while Waldeyer’s ring involvement is more typical of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

B-cell origin (germinal center)

↓

Genetic/EBV-related transformation

↓

Reed-Sternberg cells

↓

Cytokine release

↓

Reactive inflammatory background

↓

Lymph node enlargement

Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype and often presents with mediastinal involvement. Reed–Sternberg cells are classically CD15 and CD30 positive and are derived from germinal center B cells.

| Feature | Hodgkin Lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

| ------- | ---------------- | --------------------

| Spread | Contiguous | Non-contiguous

| Extranodal | Rare | Common

| RS cells | Present | Absent

| Waldeyer’s ring | Rare | Common

| Mediastinum | Common (NS subtype) | Variable

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Blood component transfusion related acute lung injury are correct? 1. Transfusion related acute lung injury (TRALI) usually manifests within 6 hours of transfusion. 2. Risk factors for TRALI include high titre anti-HLA class II antibodies in donor plasma. 3. TRALI due to cytokines or chemokines can occur even in the absence of HLA mediated interactions. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

• 1. TRALI usually manifests within 6 hours of transfusion: Correct.

• TRALI is defined by acute respiratory distress/hypoxemia occurring during or within 6 hours of transfusion.
• It is characterized by non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

• 2. High-titre anti-HLA class II antibodies in donor plasma: Correct.

• Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies can activate recipient neutrophils, causing pulmonary endothelial injury and capillary leakage.
• Plasma from previously pregnant donors has historically been an important source of these antibodies.

• 3. TRALI due to cytokines or chemokines can occur without HLA-mediated interactions: Correct.

• TRALI can also occur through a “two-hit” mechanism, in which the recipient’s underlying inflammatory condition primes neutrophils and transfused biologically active lipids, cytokines, or chemokines trigger their activation.
• Therefore, TRALI does not require HLA antibodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following viruses can be transmitted via transfusion of infected blood? 1. Hepatitis B virus 2. Hepatitis C virus 3. Human immunodeficiency virus 4. Parvovirus B19 Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs) include several viruses that may be present in donated blood. HBV, HCV, HIV, and Parvovirus B19 can all be transmitted through transfusion of infected blood or blood products. Routine donor screening has markedly reduced the risk of HBV, HCV, and HIV transmission, while Parvovirus B19 may still be transmitted because it is not routinely screened in many blood banks.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) ✔️: Transfusion-transmissible.
• 2. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) ✔️: Transfusion-transmissible.
• 3. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) ✔️: Transfusion-transmissible.
• 4. Parvovirus B19 ✔️: Can be transmitted through blood products, especially affecting immunocompromised patients and those with hemolytic disorders.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following causes low-volume erythrocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gaisbock’s syndrome

Gaisböck syndrome (Stress polycythemia or Relative polycythemia) is characterized by elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit due to reduced plasma volume, while the total red blood cell mass remains normal. Thus, it is a form of low-volume (relative) erythrocytosis, not true erythrocytosis.

It is commonly seen in:

• Middle-aged obese men
• Hypertension
• Smoking
• Stress and anxiety
• Diuretic use leading to plasma volume contraction

Why not the other options?

• A. Polycythemia rubra vera: A primary absolute erythrocytosis caused by a JAK2 mutation, with increased RBC mass.
• B. Exogenous testosterone therapy: Causes secondary absolute erythrocytosis by stimulating erythropoietin production and increasing RBC mass.
• D. High altitude: Causes secondary absolute erythrocytosis due to chronic hypoxia and increased erythropoietin secretion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions characteristically may present with a triad of haemolysis, pancytopenia and venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a PIGA gene mutation, leading to deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55 and CD59) on blood cells. This results in complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, bone marrow failure (pancytopenia), and venous thrombosis, especially in unusual sites (hepatic, portal, cerebral veins).

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency: Causes episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress but does not cause pancytopenia or venous thrombosis.
• B. Hereditary spherocytosis: Causes chronic extravascular hemolysis and splenomegaly, not pancytopenia or thrombosis.
• C. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS): Characterized by the triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, not pancytopenia with venous thrombosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is a cause of relative erythrocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diuretics

Relative erythrocytosis is caused by reduced plasma volume, resulting in an apparent increase in hemoglobin and hematocrit despite a normal red cell mass. Diuretic use is a common cause due to hemoconcentration.

Why not the other options?

• A. High altitude: Causes absolute (secondary) erythrocytosis due to chronic hypoxia → ↑ erythropoietin (EPO).
• B. Cardiorespiratory disease: Causes secondary absolute erythrocytosis via hypoxia-induced ↑ EPO.
• C. High-affinity hemoglobins: Cause tissue hypoxia with compensatory secondary absolute erythrocytosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is a clonal haematopoietic stem cell disorder in which phenotypically normal red blood cells, granulocytes and platelets accumulate in the absence of a recognizable physiological stimulus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Polycythemia vera

Polycythemia vera (PV) is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) arising from a hematopoietic stem cell, characterized by autonomous proliferation of erythroid, myeloid, and megakaryocytic lineages in the absence of a physiological stimulus (erythropoietin). The majority of patients have a JAK2 mutation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mastocytosis ✗: A clonal disorder characterized by mast cell proliferation, not increased RBCs, granulocytes, and platelets.
• C. Primary myelofibrosis ✗: Characterized by bone marrow fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, massive splenomegaly, and teardrop cells.
• D. Essential thrombocytosis ✗: Characterized by isolated thrombocytosis due to megakaryocyte proliferation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is associated with low MCV of red blood cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thalassaemia

Low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) indicates microcytic anemia. Thalassemia is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia caused by reduced synthesis of α- or β-globin chains. It is characterized by markedly low MCV, often disproportionate to the degree of anemia.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia: Causes macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia with high MCV.
• C. Folate deficiency anemia: Also causes macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia with high MCV.
• D. Sickle cell anemia: Usually a normocytic hemolytic anemia with normal or slightly increased MCV.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is incorrect about iron transport?
options: Iron is converted from ferrous to ferric form before absorption through apical membrane.
Iron is transported via transferrin in the blood.
Ascorbic acid helps in iron reabsorption.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron is converted from ferrous to ferric form before absorption through apical membrane.

Solution- Iron must be in ferrous (Fe²⁺) form for absorption — not ferric (Fe³⁺).

Correct answer is A because dietary iron is absorbed in the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form at the apical membrane of enterocytes; ferric (Fe³⁺) iron is first reduced to ferrous form before absorption.

Iron is transported in blood bound to transferrin. Apoferritin binds iron for storage as ferritin. Ascorbic acid enhances iron absorption by maintaining iron in ferrous form.

Dietary iron (Fe³⁺)

↓

Reduced to Fe²⁺ (Vitamin C)

↓

Absorbed via DMT1 (duodenum)

↓

Converted back to Fe³⁺

↓

Bound to transferrin

| Step | Form of Iron | Key Protein

| ---- | ------------ | -----------

| Absorption | Fe²⁺ | DMT1

| Transport | Fe³⁺ | Transferrin

| Storage | Fe³⁺ | Ferritin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the primary underlying mechanism of haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: Complement-mediated destruction of CD59(–) red blood cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complement-mediated destruction of CD59(–) red blood cells

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a PIGA gene mutation, resulting in defective synthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors. Consequently, red blood cells lack the complement regulatory proteins CD55 (Decay Accelerating Factor) and CD59 (Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis), making them susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

Why not the other options?

• A. ABO incompatibility ✗: Causes immune-mediated hemolysis due to mismatched blood transfusion, not PNH.
• B. Red cell fragmentation ✗: Seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) such as DIC, TTP, and HUS, producing schistocytes.
• D. Exotoxins produced by Clostridium perfringens ✗: Causes acute massive hemolysis due to α-toxin, unrelated to PNH.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: With regard to transfusion therapy, cryoprecipitate is a rich source of which of the following? 1. Fibrinogen 2. Clotting factor VIII 3. Clotting factor IX 4. von Willebrand factor Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble fraction of fresh frozen plasma and is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor (vWF), factor XIII, and fibronectin. It is primarily used for hypofibrinogenemia, massive hemorrhage with low fibrinogen, and factor XIII deficiency.

Why not statement 3?

• Factor IX is not present in significant amounts in cryoprecipitate. It is supplied by prothrombin complex concentrates (PCC) or specific factor IX concentrates.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to blood in his stool, which the parents noticed when changing his diaper. The infant has had no previous bleeding and has been eating and drinking normally. He has a history of recurrent otitis media, frequent herpes labialis, and 2 episodes of pneumonia. On examination, the patient is well developed, well nourished, and has a fair complexion. He has eczema on his cheeks, trunk, and extremities. Scattered petechiae are also visible on his lower extremities. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 24,000/mm³ and a leukocyte count of 9,000/mm³. Peripheral smear confirms the low platelet count and that the platelets are small. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following processes is most likely affected by this patient's gene mutation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cytoskeleton regulation

This child has features of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked immunodeficiency characterized by the triad:

• Eczema
• Recurrent infections
• Thrombocytopenia with small platelets

The disease is caused by mutation in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP).

• WASP regulates actin cytoskeleton remodelling in hematopoietic cells.
• Defective cytoskeleton dynamics impair immune cell signalling, migration, and platelet formation, leading to immunodeficiency and microthrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for 2 days of fever, cough, and worsening shortness of breath. The patient's parents report that he recently recovered from prolonged diarrhea due to Giardia infection. Medical history is significant for recurrent ear infections treated with antibiotics since age 6 months and lobar pneumonia requiring hospitalization. Temperature is 38.7⁰C (101.7⁰F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 60/min. Physical examination reveals small tonsils and crackles in the lower lobe of the right lung. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's recurrent infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abnormal B-lymphocyte maturation

This presentation is characteristic of X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease) due to defective B-cell maturation caused by mutation in the BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase) gene.

• Failure of pre-B cells to mature into B lymphocytes
• Leads to markedly decreased immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM)
• Results in recurrent bacterial infections, especially after 6 months of age when maternal IgG declines.

Clinical clues:

• Recurrent otitis media and pneumonia
• Prolonged Giardia infection (due to low IgA)
• Small or absent tonsils and lymphoid tissue

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with recurrent severe bacterial, viral, and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. Chest X-ray shows absence of thymic shadow. Flow cytometry reveals markedly reduced T cells and NK cells with normal or increased B cells. Which of the following genes is most commonly mutated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IL2RG (common γ-chain of interleukin receptors)

Mutation of IL2RG (interleukin-2 receptor γ-chain) causes X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

• T cells ↓
• NK cells ↓
• B cells normal or increased but functionally impaired

Clinical features:

• Early infancy onset
• Recurrent severe bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
• Chronic diarrhea
• Failure to thrive
• Absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray

Why not the other options:

B. ADA deficiency: Causes autosomal recessive SCID with T↓ B↓ NK↓ due to toxic purine metabolite accumulation.

C. BTK mutation: Causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia with absent B cells and low immunoglobulins; T cells are normal.

D. CD40 ligand deficiency: Causes Hyper-IgM syndrome with defective class switching (↑IgM, ↓IgG/IgA/IgE) but normal T and B cell numbers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old medical student went for a screening health test and was injected with PPD intradermally. Identify the immune cell in the skin that picks up the PPD to present it to T cells.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Langerhans cells

Langerhans cells are specialized dendritic antigen-presenting cells located in the epidermis. They capture antigens entering through the skin and migrate to regional lymph nodes to present antigen via MHC II to T lymphocytes, initiating a cell-mediated immune response.

In the PPD (Mantoux) test, tuberculin protein is injected intradermally. Langerhans cells capture the antigen and present it to sensitized T cells, resulting in a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by Th1 cells.

Why not the other options:

A. Langhans cells: Multinucleated giant cells seen in granulomas (e.g., tuberculosis); not antigen-presenting cells in the epidermis.

B. Follicular dendritic cells: Located in germinal centers of lymph nodes and spleen; present antigen to B cells, not involved in skin antigen capture.

D. Natural killer cells: Part of innate immunity, responsible for killing virus-infected or tumor cells, not antigen presentation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant is evaluated for persistent diarrhea, recurrent respiratory and skin infections, and poor weight gain since early infancy. On examination, the child has diffuse erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies reveal marked eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE levels, markedly reduced B lymphocytes, and circulating activated oligoclonal T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Omenn syndrome

Omenn syndrome is a leaky (hypomorphic) form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by hypomorphic mutations in the RAG1 or RAG2 genes, resulting in defective V(D)J recombination.

Unlike classic SCID, some oligoclonal autoreactive T cells develop. These T cells infiltrate tissues and cause autoimmune-like manifestations.

Characteristic features include:

• Recurrent severe infections
• Generalized erythroderma
• Chronic diarrhea
• Failure to thrive
• Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
• Eosinophilia and markedly elevated IgE
• Absent or markedly reduced B cells
• Presence of activated, oligoclonal T cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. X-linked agammaglobulinemia: Caused by BTK mutation, leading to absent mature B cells and recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age. Erythroderma, eosinophilia, and activated T cells are not typical.
• B. DiGeorge syndrome: Results from 22q11.2 deletion causing thymic hypoplasia with T-cell deficiency, congenital heart defects, and hypocalcemia, but not elevated IgE with erythroderma.
• C. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): Classic SCID is characterized by profound deficiency of functional T cells (often with absent T cells), whereas Omenn syndrome is a variant with autoreactive oligoclonal T cells, producing features of both immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation.

High-yield pearl

Omenn syndrome = "Leaky SCID"

• Cause: Hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 mutations
• Defect: Impaired V(D)J recombination
• Immune profile: ↓/Absent B cells + oligoclonal autoreactive T cells
• Classic findings: Erythroderma + eosinophilia + ↑IgE + failure to thrive + recurrent infections
• Definitive treatment: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia 3 weeks ago. He now develops a generalized maculopapular skin rash starting on the palms and soles, profuse watery diarrhea, and rising serum bilirubin with jaundice. Biopsy of the skin shows individual keratinocyte necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration ("satellite cell necrosis"). Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism of this condition?
options: Recipient cytotoxic T cells attacking donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells
Donor-derived immunocompetent T lymphocytes recognizing recipient tissue as foreign and mounting an immune attack
Pre-formed recipient antibodies against donor ABO antigens causing immediate graft rejection
Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus within donor-derived monocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Donor-derived immunocompetent T lymphocytes recognizing recipient tissue as foreign and mounting an immune attack

• This describes acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a classic complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation.
• It occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes, transferred along with the graft, recognize the immunologically distinct (and immunosuppressed) recipient's tissues as foreign and mount a cytotoxic immune response.
• The classic triad of organ involvement is skin (maculopapular rash, often starting on palms/soles, with characteristic satellite cell necrosis on histology), gastrointestinal tract (watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain), and liver (cholestatic jaundice with elevated bilirubin).
• Option A (Recipient cytotoxic T cells attacking donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells) describes the reverse phenomenon (host-versus-graft, i.e., graft rejection).
• Option C (Pre-formed recipient antibodies against donor ABO antigens causing immediate graft rejection) describes a hyperacute transplant rejection mechanism (hemolytic, not GVHD).
• Option D (Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus within donor-derived monocytes) describes an opportunistic infection unrelated to the core alloimmune mechanism of GVHD, though CMV reactivation can be a separate post-transplant complication.

Quick reference — Acute vs Chronic GVHD:

| Feature | Acute GVHD | Chronic GVHD

| ------- | ---------- | ------------

| Onset | Typically <100 days post-transplant | Typically >100 days post-transplant

| Classic organs | Skin, GI tract, liver | Skin, eyes, mouth, lungs, liver, joints — multisystem, sclerodermatous changes

| Histology | Apoptotic keratinocytes with satellite cell necrosis | Fibrosis, lichenoid/sclerotic changes resembling autoimmune connective tissue disease

| Mechanism | Donor T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity against host tissue | Dysregulated immune reconstitution with autoimmune-like features

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman presents with worsening ptosis, diplopia, and proximal muscle weakness despite optimal doses of pyridostigmine and steroids. She is found to be anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody positive. A biologic agent is planned that works by reducing pathogenic IgG levels without broadly suppressing immunity. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rozanolixizumab

Rozanolixizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) used in generalized myasthenia gravis, particularly in patients who remain symptomatic despite conventional therapy. By blocking FcRn, it accelerates the degradation of circulating pathogenic IgG antibodies, including anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, without causing broad immunosuppression.

• FcRn normally protects IgG from lysosomal degradation.
• Rozanolixizumab inhibits FcRn, leading to:

• Increased IgG breakdown
• Reduced anti-AChR antibody levels
• Improvement in neuromuscular transmission

Why not the others?

• A. Rituximab → Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody causing B-cell depletion; broader immunosuppressive effect.
• B. Eculizumab → Anti-C5 monoclonal antibody that inhibits complement-mediated damage at the neuromuscular junction but does not directly lower IgG levels.
• D. Azathioprine → Immunosuppressant that inhibits purine synthesis; slower onset and broader immune suppression.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 4-month-old baby was brought with history of recurrent infections in the past 4 months. On examination white patches were present in oral mucosa which could be scraped easily. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
options: It has autosomal as well as X linked inheritance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tonsils are present

This vignette describes Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), which presents in early infancy with recurrent infections and oral candidiasis (thrush).

• Severe defect in both T-cell and B-cell immunity.
• Common causes include:

o    X-linked SCID due to IL2RG mutation

o    Autosomal recessive SCID due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

Clinical features:

• Recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
• Oral thrush
• Failure to thrive
• Absent or very small lymphoid tissues (tonsils and lymph nodes)
• B-cell numbers may be normal in some forms (e.g., X-linked SCID) but functionally impaired due to lack of T-cell help.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated for a persistent eczematous skin rash and a history of recurrent pyogenic skin infections and multiple episodes of pneumonia over the past year. Physical examination reveals widespread eczema and petechiae. Laboratory investigations demonstrate thrombocytopenia with small platelets on peripheral smear. Which of the following investigations would most likely confirm the underlying diagnosis?
options: Assessment of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) activity
Genetic testing for a WASP gene mutation
Measurement of adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Genetic testing for a WASP gene mutation

This child has the classic features of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (WAS), an X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the WASP (Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein) gene.

The characteristic triad includes:

• Eczema
• Recurrent bacterial infections due to combined immunodeficiency
• Microthrombocytopenia (small platelets with thrombocytopenia)

Confirmation is achieved by genetic testing for the WASP gene mutation or by demonstrating absent/reduced WASP protein expression.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. BTK activity detection: Used to diagnose X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease), which presents with recurrent bacterial infections but does not cause eczema or thrombocytopenia.
• C. Flow cytometry for CD40/CD40L: Used to diagnose Hyper-IgM syndrome, characterized by recurrent opportunistic infections and elevated IgM levels, without the classic triad of WAS.
• D. Adenosine deaminase activity measurement: Evaluates ADA-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which presents with severe opportunistic infections early in infancy rather than eczema with microthrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with severe, chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, and a rash. His medical history includes a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus and thyroiditis. Laboratory tests show elevated levels of anti-enterocyte antibodies. Based on these findings, which mechanism is most likely impaired in this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peripheral tolerance

Key clues in the question

• Severe chronic diarrhoea → autoimmune enteropathy
• Failure to thrive
• Rash (eczema-like dermatitis)
• Type 1 diabetes + thyroiditis (polyendocrinopathy)
• Anti-enterocyte antibodies

This classic triad points to IPEX syndrome. (IPEX syndrome stands for: I – Immune dysregulation, P – Polyendocrinopathy, E – Enteropathy, X – X-linked)

IPEX occurs due to mutation of the FOXP3 gene, which is required for development of regulatory T cells (Tregs).

• Tregs normally suppress autoreactive T cells in peripheral tissues
• Loss of FOXP3 → defective Treg function
• Result → loss of peripheral immune tolerance

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man undergoes a renal transplant. On post-operative day 6, he develops sudden rise in serum creatinine and oliguria. Doppler shows good graft perfusion. Renal biopsy demonstrates capillary endothelial swelling, neutrophilic infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis of vessels, and linear C4d deposition along peritubular capillaries. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
options: Formation of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies with complement activation
Progressive intimal fibrosis due to smooth muscle proliferation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies with complement activation

This presentation is characteristic of acute antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection after renal transplantation.

• Recipient forms donor-specific antibodies (DSA) against donor HLA antigens on graft endothelial cells.
• These antibodies activate the complement cascade, leading to endothelial injury, neutrophilic infiltration, and vascular damage.
• C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries is a key diagnostic marker of complement activation in antibody-mediated rejection.

Typical biopsy findings:

• Endothelial swelling
• Neutrophils in capillaries
• Fibrinoid necrosis of vessels
• Linear C4d staining in peritubular capillaries

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 6-week-old infant presents with recurrent skin and mucosal bacterial infections. The umbilical cord fell off after 4 weeks. Examination shows absence of pus formation at infection sites. Laboratory tests reveal marked neutrophilia. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deficiency of CD18 on neutrophils

This presentation is characteristic of Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1 (LAD-1), caused by deficiency of CD18 (β2-integrin) on neutrophils.

• CD18 is required for firm adhesion of neutrophils to endothelial cells during leukocyte extravasation.
• Without CD18, neutrophils cannot migrate from blood to infection sites, leading to impaired pus formation.

Key clinical features:

• Delayed separation of umbilical cord (>3 weeks)
• Recurrent bacterial infections of skin and mucosa
• Absence of pus at infection sites
• Marked neutrophilia in blood due to failure of tissue migration

Why not other options:

A. NADPH oxidase defect: CGD → defective killing, granulomas, normal pus.

C. Impaired myeloperoxidase activity: Usually mild, mainly Candida infections.

D. IL-12 receptor defect: Mycobacterial infections (Th1 defect).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is vaccinated with a polysaccharide antigen without protein conjugation. After vaccination, antibody titers rise initially but fall rapidly over the next few months. On re-exposure to the same antigen one year later, there is no significant anamnestic response. Which of the following immunological features is most consistent with the mechanism responsible for this response?
options: Predominant IgG1 production with germinal center formation
Requirement of CD40–CD40L interaction for B-cell activation
Absence of class switching and lack of memory B cells
Somatic hypermutation occurring in secondary lymphoid organs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Absence of class switching and lack of memory B cells

Pure polysaccharide vaccines (without protein conjugation) stimulate T-cell–independent type 2 (TI-2) immune responses.

Key characteristics of T-independent responses:

• Direct B-cell activation without T-helper cell involvement
• Predominantly IgM production
• Minimal or no class switching
• No germinal center formation
• Little or no memory B-cell generation

Because memory B cells are not formed, antibody levels decline quickly, and re-exposure does not produce a strong anamnestic (secondary) response.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 78-year-old woman with osteoarthritis is started on standard-dose warfarin for new-onset atrial fibrillation. She has no history of liver disease and drinks alcohol only occasionally. Five days after starting therapy, she presents to the emergency department with gingival bleeding and extensive bruising on her arms and legs. Laboratory studies show: • INR: 6.8 • Platelet count: 240,000/mm³ • AST/ALT: within normal limits Her only other medications are acetaminophen as needed and a daily multivitamin. She denies taking antibiotics or herbal supplements. Which of the following best explains this patient’s adverse response?
options: Increased drug effect due to heightened sensitivity at the drug target
Dose-dependent predictable toxicity occurring in all patients
Accumulation of an active toxic metabolite due to CYP450 induction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased drug effect due to heightened sensitivity at the drug target

This scenario represents a Type B (idiosyncratic) adverse drug reaction, where the patient develops an exaggerated pharmacologic response to a standard dose of a drug.

• Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis (II, VII, IX, X)
• Some individuals have increased sensitivity to warfarin, leading to:

• Excessive anticoagulation (↑ INR)
• Bleeding manifestations even at standard doses

This is due to heightened response at the drug target, often influenced by:

• Genetic variations (e.g., VKORC1, CYP2C9 polymorphisms)

Why not other options:

A. IgE-mediated hypersensitivity: Would present with rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis, not isolated ↑ INR

C. Dose-dependent predictable toxicity: Occurs in all patients at high doses, not at standard dosing

D. CYP450 induction: Would decrease warfarin effect (↓ INR), not increase

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 9-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea, multiple ear infections, and a persistent eczematous rash over the flexural surfaces. His mother reports easy bruising and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts since infancy. There is a maternal uncle with a similar history who died in childhood from intracranial hemorrhage. Laboratory evaluation shows a platelet count of 35,000/μL with small platelet size on peripheral smear, along with low serum IgM and elevated IgA and IgE levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

• This vignette captures the classic triad of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS): thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, and recurrent infections (due to combined immunodeficiency), occurring in a male infant — consistent with its X-linked recessive inheritance (explaining the affected maternal uncle).
• The immunoglobulin pattern of low IgM with normal-to-elevated IgA and IgE is characteristic, reflecting a defect in the WAS protein gene, which impairs cytoskeletal organization in hematopoietic cells, affecting both platelet production/survival and immune cell function.
• Bruton's agammaglobulinemia (A) presents with recurrent infections after maternal antibody wanes but lacks thrombocytopenia and eczema.
• DiGeorge syndrome (C) involves T-cell deficiency from thymic aplasia, along with cardiac defects and hypocalcemia, not thrombocytopenia or eczema.
• Chediak-Higashi syndrome (D) presents with partial albinism, recurrent pyogenic infections, and giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes — not the platelet/eczema/immunoglobulin pattern seen here.

Quick reference — Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Inheritance | X-linked recessive (WAS gene, Xp11.23)

| Classic triad | Thrombocytopenia (small platelets) + Eczema + Recurrent infections

| Immunoglobulins | ↓IgM, normal/↑IgA, ↑IgE

| Platelet defect | Small, defective platelets → increased destruction in spleen

| Risk | Increased risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoid malignancy (lymphoma)

| Treatment | Bone marrow/stem cell transplant (curative); splenectomy may help thrombocytopenia but increases infection risk

| Mnemonic | "WIPE" — WAS gene, Immunodeficiency, Platelets low/small, Eczema

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 9-month-old male infant presents with persistent watery diarrhea since early infancy, failure to thrive, and recurrent skin rashes. He has been recently diagnosed with autoimmune hypothyroidism. Examination reveals eczema-like dermatitis over the trunk. Laboratory tests show elevated IgE levels. Sequencing of which of the following genes would confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FOXP3

Mutation in the FOXP3 gene causes IPEX syndrome (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked).

FOXP3 is essential for the development and function of regulatory T cells (Tregs), which maintain immune tolerance and prevent autoimmunity. Loss of FOXP3 leads to failure of immune regulation, resulting in widespread autoimmune disease.

• Severe early-onset diarrhea due to autoimmune enteropathy
• Failure to thrive
• Eczema/dermatitis with elevated IgE
• Autoimmune endocrinopathies (e.g., type 1 diabetes, hypothyroidism)

Why not other options:

A. PTPN22: Associated with autoimmune susceptibility (e.g., RA, T1DM), not severe early infant immune dysregulation.

C. MTP: Causes abetalipoproteinemia (fat malabsorption, neurologic signs).

D. CETP: Involved in lipid metabolism, affects HDL levels.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A laboratory is standardizing a rocket electrophoresis assay to quantify serum IgG levels. During validation, it is observed that increasing the antibody concentration in the agarose gel leads to shorter rockets for the same antigen concentration. Which of the following best explains this observation?
options: Increased antibody concentration decreases antigen migration velocity
Precipitation occurs earlier, reducing the distance traveled by antigen
Antibody excess prevents antigen-antibody complex formation
Increased gel viscosity reduces electrophoretic mobility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Precipitation occurs earlier, reducing the distance traveled by antigen

Rocket electrophoresis (Laurell method) quantifies antigen based on the distance it migrates before forming an antigen–antibody precipitate.

• Principle:

• Antigen moves through gel containing antibody
•

Precipitation occurs at zone of equivalence (optimal Ag–Ab ratio)

•

Key determinant of rocket height:

• Antigen concentration → directly proportional to height
• Antibody concentration in gel → inversely affects height
• ↑ Antibody → earlier precipitation → shorter rocket
• ↓ Antibody → delayed precipitation → taller rocket

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient undergoing autologous stem cell transplantation requires a recombinant growth factor for myeloid reconstitution. The agent chosen is produced in a expression system and carries a known risk of capillary leak syndrome. Which growth factor and source organism pairing is correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sargramostim — yeast — GM-CSF

Sargramostim is a recombinant form of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) used to accelerate myeloid recovery following bone marrow or stem cell transplantation. Unlike filgrastim, it stimulates multiple myeloid lineages, including neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and eosinophils.

• Sargramostim = recombinant GM-CSF
• Produced using a yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) expression system
• Important adverse effect: Capillary leak syndrome, characterized by hypotension, edema, and fluid extravasation.

Why not the others?

• A. Filgrastim — E. coli — G-CSF → Correct pairing, but not associated with the classic question stem of yeast-derived GM-CSF and capillary leak syndrome.
• C. Pegfilgrastim — E. coli — G-CSF → Pegylated form of filgrastim; same lineage specificity as G-CSF.
• D. Sargramostim — E. coli — GM-CSF → Incorrect source organism; sargramostim is produced in yeast, not E. coli.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with bare lymphocytic disease. In this patient, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to:
options: MHC class II deficiency on lymphocytes
MHC class I deficiency on lymphocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MHC class II deficiency on lymphocytes

Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is caused by deficiency of MHC class II expression on antigen-presenting cells due to mutations affecting transcription of MHC II genes.

• CD4⁺ T-cell development is severely impaired because positive selection of CD4 T cells in the thymus requires MHC class II molecules.
• This results in marked reduction of CD4 T lymphocytes and severe immunodeficiency.

Why GVHD does not occur:

Donor T cells require recognition of host MHC molecules to initiate graft-versus-host reactions. In this condition, absence of MHC class II prevents antigen presentation, so donor T cells cannot become activated, preventing GVHD.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with AML is planned for an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. As part of the pre transplant conditioning regimen, he receives myeloablative therapy using high dose chemotherapy and total body irradiation. Which of the following statements about myeloablation is false?
options: Myeloablation increases the risk of graft failure if inadequate suppression of host immunity occurs.
Myeloablation regimen can increase the incidence of post transplant lymphoproliferative disorders.
Myeloablation conditioning destroys the recipient’s bone marrow to allow engraftment of donor stem cells.
Myeloablation prevents graft versus host disease by suppressing donor T cells.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Myeloablation prevents graft versus host disease by suppressing donor T cells.

Myeloablative conditioning before allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) uses high-dose chemotherapy ± total body irradiation to:

1. Destroy the recipient’s bone marrow, creating space for donor stem cell engraftment.
2. Suppress host immune cells to reduce graft rejection.
3. Eliminate residual malignant cells.

Important points:

•

If host immunity is not adequately suppressed, graft failure or rejection can occur.

•

Intense immunosuppression can predispose to post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD), often related to EBV reactivation.

Myeloablation does NOT prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) because GVHD is caused by donor T cells attacking recipient tissues. Prevention requires T-cell depletion or post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy, not myeloablation itself.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Activation of RIG-I–like receptors leads to production of which key antiviral cytokines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β)

RIG-I–like receptors (RLRs) are cytosolic pattern recognition receptors that detect viral RNA inside infected cells.

When activated by viral RNA, RLRs trigger signaling through MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein), which activates transcription factors such as IRF3 and IRF7 --> This leads to production of type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β).

Functions of Type I interferons:

• Induce an antiviral state in neighboring cells
• Inhibit viral replication
• Increase MHC class I expression
• Activate natural killer (NK) cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following interaction occurs between antigen antibody reaction except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Covalent bond

Antigen–antibody interactions are non-covalent and reversible, allowing antibodies to bind and release antigens efficiently.

The binding between epitope (antigen) and paratope (antibody) occurs through weak forces such as:

• Ionic bonds
• Hydrogen bonds
• Van der Waals forces
• Hydrophobic interactions

These weak interactions collectively provide high specificity and affinity.

Covalent bonds are not involved, because they are strong, irreversible bonds and would prevent normal immune complex dynamics.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Among the following, which cells have both MHC class I and MHC class II? 1. NK cells 2. B-lymphocytes 3. Dendritic cells 4. Platelets 5. RBC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3

MHC Class I molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells, whereas MHC Class II molecules are expressed mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs).

Cells expressing both MHC I and MHC II:

• B lymphocytes
• Dendritic cells
• Macrophages

Other cells:

1. NK cells: Express MHC I only, not MHC II.

4. Platelets: Limited or no typical MHC II expression.

5. RBCs: No MHC molecules because they are anucleate.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is seen with: 1. Natural killer (NK) cells 2. Macrophages 3. Neutrophils 4. Eosinophils 5. CD4 lymphocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is an immune mechanism in which effector cells destroy antibody-coated target cells.

• Target cells are coated with IgG antibodies.
• Immune cells bind the Fc portion of IgG via Fc receptors.
• This triggers release of cytotoxic substances, leading to destruction of the target cell.

Cells involved in ADCC:

• Natural killer (NK) cells
• Neutrophils
• Eosinophils (especially against parasites)

Not involved:

• CD4 T lymphocytes, which function mainly in helper and regulatory roles, not cytotoxic killing.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Arrange the following sentences in the correct order for activation of B cells. 1. T-helper cells interact with the presented antigen peptides. 2. Improved quality of the immune response with affinity maturation. 3. Somatic hypermutation and immunoglobulin isotype class switching occur. 4. Antigen binding to B cell receptor. 5. Binding of CD40 ligand on T cells to CD 40 on B cells.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4, 1, 5, 3, 2

Activation of B cells in T-dependent humoral immunity occurs through a sequence of antigen recognition and T-cell help. Correct sequence:

1.      Antigen binds to B-cell receptor (BCR) → B cell internalizes and processes antigen.

2.      B cell presents antigen peptide on MHC II to T-helper cells.

3.      CD40L on T cells binds CD40 on B cells, providing the essential co-stimulatory signal.

4.      This triggers somatic hypermutation and immunoglobulin class switching in germinal centers.

5.      Result is affinity maturation, producing antibodies with higher antigen affinity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Casoni reaction is seen in patients with hydatid cyst. Which of the following is incorrect about the immunoglobulin causing this reaction?
options: It is the only heat stable antibody
Levels are raised in helminthic infections
It does not pass the placental barrier
It has a half-life of 1-5 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is the only heat stable antibody

The Casoni test for hydatid cyst involves a Type I hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE antibodies against Echinococcus antigens.

Key features of IgE:

• Levels increase in helminthic infections and allergic conditions.
• Does not cross the placenta (unlike IgG).
• Has a short serum half-life (\~1–5 days).
• Binds strongly to mast cells and basophils, triggering histamine release on antigen exposure.
