questions.text: Given below is an image of activation of the coagulation cascade, following closed endothelial injury. Identify the factor ‘L’ which combines with tissue factor to activate factor IX.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor VII

The factor marked as ‘L’ is factor VII, which combines with tissue factor that is produced following a close endothelial injury to activate factor IX.

As the image represents the in vivo coagulation cascade, the tissue factor is the major initiator of coagulation. It is believed that in vivo, factor VIIa/tissue factor complex is the most important activator of factor IX and that factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X.

Tissue factor is expressed on the surfaces of the subendothelial cellular components of the vessel wall, such as smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. This tissue factor is exposed to blood when there is a vascular damage. This activates the in vivo extrinsic pathway of coagulation cascade, which is as follows:

• Tissue factor binds with serine protease factor VIIa
• This complex then activates factor IX to factor IXa
• Factor IXa then activates factor X to factor Xa
• Factor Xa can be formed through the actions of either the tissue factor-factor VIIa complex or factor IXa (with factor VIIIa as cofactor)
• Factor Xa then converts prothrombin to thrombin, which is the pivotal protease of the coagulation cascade.
• The cofactor essential for this conversion is factor Va.
• The thrombin then formed converts the soluble plasma fibrinogen to an insoluble fibrin matrix.
• Thrombin also activates factor XIII, which is the fibrin stabilizing factor, to factor XIIIa. This factor XIIIa forms covalent cross-links and thereby stabilizes the fibrin clot.

The below image shows the in vivo coagulation cascade.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Human Papilloma Virus inactivates RB gene by which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. E7

E7 protein of Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) binds to the hypophosphorylated RB protein and displaces the E2F transcription factors, thereby promoting G1/S transition.

RB gene is a key negative regulator of the cell cycle at the G1/S transition. RB gene exists in an active hypophosphorylated state in resting cells and in an inactive hyperphosphorylated state in cells undergoing G1/S transition.

E7 protein from the high-risk types of HPV (such as HPV 16) binds to the hypophosphorylated RB through the same pocket that RB uses to bind and sequester the E2F transcription factors, thereby displacing the E2F which leads to the progression of the cell cycle and thus the proliferation of tumor cells. E7 proteins also inactivate the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. E7 proteins from high-risk HPVs (types 16,18 and 31) also bind and presumably activates cyclins  A and E.

Oncogenic activities of protein E6:

The E6 protein binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase, thereby helping in the longevity of the cells. E6 from high-risk HPV types has a higher affinity for p53 than E6 from low-risk types.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies.

Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa. The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

Other options:

B) Leprosy: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous lesions, without much bacilli. Hence called paucibacillary leprosy. Lepromatous lesions contain large aggregates of lipid-laden macrophages (lepra cells), often filled with masses (globi) of acid-fast bacilli. Because of the presence of abundant bacteria, it is also called as multibacillary.

Given below are the images that depict lepromatous lesion showing foamy macrophages with globi of pink/red acid-fast bacilli and tuberculoid leprosy showing granulomatous lesions, respectively.

C) Mycosis fungoides: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characterized by polymorphic patches and plaques with fine scaling usually present on the limbs, breast, and buttocks. The lesions may be pruritic or even asymptomatic.  Histological hallmarks include: 1. Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/ hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane), 2. Pautrier's microabscesses - tumor cells invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters, forming a collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis and 3. Epidermotropism - pronounced invasion of the tumor cells into the epidermis.

Given below is the image of Sezary-Lutzner cells.

Given below is the arrow pointing at Paurtier's microabcess.

D) Visceral leishmaniasis: In visceral leishmaniasis, parasites invade and activate the macrophages throughout the mononuclear phagocyte system. Hence, these phagocytic cells are enlarged and filled with leishmania species; many plasma cells are also present.

The given slide shows macrophages infested with intracellular Leishmania donovani bodies (arrows) characterized by a kinetoplast and characteristic double dot appearance (Leishman stain).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In cystic fibrosis, which of the following structure is affected in pancreas?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The part labeled ‘B’ in the image is the exocrine pancreas which is affected in cystic fibrosis.

Features of cystic fibrosis in the pancreas:

• Accumulation of mucus in the ducts leads to dilation of exocrine glands.
• Complete blockage of ducts with mucus leads to atrophy of the exocrine pancreas and progressive fibrosis
• Due to atrophy, there will be loss of exocrine secretions, which in turn leads to impaired absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins
• Associated loss of vitamin A leads to squamous metaplasia of the pancreatic duct lining epithelium

Other options:

A- Endocrine pancreas

C- Pancreatic ducts

D- Blood vessels

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Mediators involved in the early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity are?

1. Mast cell
2. Histamine
3. Neutrophils
4. Prostaglandins
5. Leukotrienes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 5

The mediators involved in the early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity are,

• Mast cells,
• Histamine,
• Prostaglandins (D2) and
• Leukotrienes (C4 and D4).

Early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity:

The mediators produced by the mast cells are responsible for most of the immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Histamine and leukotrienes are released rapidly from the sensitized mast cells and trigger intense immediate reactions characterized by edema, mucus secretion and smooth muscle spasm.

Other mediators involved in the early phase are,

• Enzymes: neutral proteases (chymase, tryptase) and acid hydrolases
• Proteoglycans: heparin and chondroitin sulfate
• Lipid mediators: Platelet-activating factor (PAF)

Late-phase of type 1 hypersensitivity:

The late phase reaction is characterized by the recruitment of leukocytes, that amplify and sustain the inflammatory response without exposure to the triggering antigen.

Mediators involved in the late phase of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction are:

• Cytokines: TNF, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, and chemokines (eotaxin)
• Leukocytes (eosinophils)
• Major Basic Protein (MBP)
• Eosinophil cationic protein

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Oil red O stain is used in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

Oil red O (ORO) stain is used in frozen section.

Oil red O stains lipid/ fats and gives a characteristic orange/red appearance. It is used in the unfixed frozen sections as the fixation of fats with other routine processes may lose the lipid content. 10% Neutral buffer formaldehyde (NBF) is the preferred fixative in histopathological sections staining with Oil red O. Zenker's fixative and Helly's fixative are best avoided during staining with ORO.

Oil red O stains the lipid in the vacuoles in the pulmonary vasculature. It can be useful in identifying fat emboli in lung tissue, diagnosing renal cell carcinoma, and sebaceous gland tumors of the skin.

Other stains used for lipids or fats:

• Nile blue sulfate. The preferred fixative is formal calcium.
• Osmic acid is used in the frozen section. 10% NBF is the preferred fixative
• Sudan black B is used in the frozen section. The preferred fixative is 10% NBF.

Other Options:

Option A: Formalin fixation- Formalin as 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) is the most common fixative used in diagnostic pathology.

Option C: Ethyl alcohol- Ideal fixative for cytological smears because they act quickly and give good nuclear detail.

Option D: Glutaraldehyde- Preferred fixative in electron microscopy. The standard solution is a 2.5% buffered glutaraldehyde.

Image below shows microscopy of a oil red O stained bronchoalveolar lavage sample from a patient with acute lung injury.

The image shows the lipid vesicles in the adipocytes stained using oil-red-O staining.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Naive B cells

The cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)/ Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) is either naive B cells or post-germinal centre memory B cell.

The CLL and SLL differ only in the degree of peripheral blood lymphocytes. CLL is the most common leukemia of adults in the western world. The median age of diagnosis is 60 years. The most common genetic anomalies seen are deletions of 13q14.3, 11q, and 17p and trisomy 12q. Loss of tumor suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2.

The growth of CLL/SLL cells is confined to the proliferation centers (pathognomonic for CLL/SLL), where the tumor cells receive critical factors from the surrounding environments, such as NF-κB for cell survival, MYC for cell growth, Bruton Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) signaling pathway, etc.,

The tumor cells express CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5. Smudge cells are also characteristic of CLL. Clinical features include easy fatiguability, weight loss, anorexia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, hemolytic anemia, etc. CLL/SLL has a tendency to transform to a more aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)  - this is called Richter syndrome.

Factors with a bad prognosis include:

1. Presence of deletions of 11q and  17p.
2. Lack of somatic hypermutation.
3. Expression of ZAP-70, a protein that augments signals produced by the Ig receptor.
4. Presence of NOTCH1 mutations

BTK inhibitors and BCL2 inhibitors produce sustained therapeutic responses in a higher fractions of people with CLL/SLL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endo-myocardial biopsy

An endo-myocardial biopsy is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis.

Myocarditis can be due to

• Infections: Coxsackie A and B, HIV, C.diphtheriae, Ricketssiae, Candida, Protozoa and helminths.
• Immune-mediated reactions: Post-viral, post-streptococcal, drug hypersensitivity (e.g: methyl dopa, sulfinamides), transplant rejection, etc.,
• Unknown: Sarcoidosis, Giant cell myocarditis

Active myocarditis is characterized by an interstitial inflammatory infiltrate associated with degenerating or apoptotic myocytes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Graft versus host disease

Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD) associated with the transfusion.

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too.

GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes.

Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibodies production.

Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not likely to be seen in a patient with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leukemia

Leukemia is least likely to be seen in patients with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH).

Clinical manifestations of PNH include:

• Hemolytic anemia
• Pancytopenia
• Intermittent hemoglobinuria- acute hemolytic episodes occur at night owing to a slight fall in pH during sleep
• Haemosiderinuria
• Venous thrombosis (a leading cause of death in PNH)
• Patients diagnosed with PNH can later develop aplastic anemia and vice versa

PNH is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. PNH blood cells are abnormally susceptible to lysis or injury by complement since they are deficient in three GPI- linked proteins that regulate complement activity:

• Decay-accelerating factor or CD55
• Membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis or CD59 (Inhibitor of C3 convertase) and
• C8-binding protein

Diagnosis:

• Ham’s test: The abnormal sensitivity of red blood cells, leukocytes, and platelets to complement can be demonstrated in vitro using red cell lysis at acidic pH.
• Flow cytometry detects the red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.

Treatment:

Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody, that prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a has been proven effective in PNH. The definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following is true?

1. BRCA1 is an oncogene.
2. HER2neu is amplified only in a fraction of breast cancer.
3. EGFR(+) is seen in non-small cell lung cancer.
4. N-MYC is a tumour suppressor gene.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3

Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is a proto-oncogene.

BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17q21 and its function is to repair the double-stranded breaks in DNA. It is associated with familial breast and ovarian carcinoma. BRCA1-associated breast cancers are commonly poorly differentiated.

All breast cancers are separated into 3 major groups based on the expression of two proteins, ER and HER2 (also known as ERBB2). HER2 cancers are defined as cancers overexpressing HER2 and can be either ER-positive or ER-negative. Thus HER2neu is expressed only in a fraction of people with breast cancer.

EGF-receptor family has two proto-oncogenes: ERBB1 that codes for EGFR and ERBB2 that codes for HER. Mutation in EGFR results in adenocarcinoma of the lung, which is one of the main subtypes of non-small cell lung carcinoma.

MYC is a proto-oncogene, that is expressed in all eukaryotic cells and belongs to the immediate-early response genes, which are rapidly induced by RAS/MAPK signaling following growth factor stimulation of quiescent cells. Normally, MYC protein concentration are tightly controlled at the level of transcription, translation and protein stability. The mechanisms by which MYC promotes neoplastic cell growth may be follows:

• MYC activates the expression of many genes like D cyclins, that are involved in cell cycle progression
• MYC regulates the expression of telomerase
• MYC is one of the transcriptional factors that can act together to reprogram somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells

MYC gene is deregulated in a number of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, breast, colon, lung and other cancers. The functionally identical NMYC and LMYC genes are also amplified in neuroblastomas and small cell cancers of the lung, respectively.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B6

Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anaemia.

Pyridoxine 200mg per day for 2-3 months is administered routinely to all cases of sideroblastic anaemia. This cofactor is essential for ALA-synthase activity, and mutations in the pyridoxine binding site of the enzyme have been found in several responsive patients. Blood transfusion and other supportive therapy are also indicated. In cases of secondary sideroblastic anaemia, the primary focus is the removal of the offending agent. But no definitive treatment is available for hereditary and idiopathic types of sideroblastic anaemia.

Sideroblasts are nucleated red cells (normoblasts) containing siderotic granules which stain positively with Prussian blue stain. Based on aetiology, sideroblastic anaemia are classified into hereditary and acquired types.

Hereditary sideroblastic anaemia is an X-linked disorder caused due to a defect in the activity of aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase required for heme synthesis. Affected females act as carriers while males have moderate to marked anaemia and manifest in childhood or during early adulthood

Acquired sideroblastic anaemia:

I) Primary acquired:

• Also called idiopathic or refractory acquired sideroblastic anaemia
• Occurs in middle-aged and older individuals of both sexes
• Due to the reduced activity of the enzyme ALA synthetase, there is disturbed growth and maturation of the erythroid precursors at the level of hematopoietic stem cell
• Moderate to severe anaemia, which appears insidiously
• Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also be seen
• Regarded as a myelodysplastic disorder in the FAB classification and thus considered preleukaemic

II) Secondary acquired:

May appear secondary to

• Drugs, chemicals and toxins: Isoniazid, Cycloserine, Chloramphenicol, Cyclophosphamide, Alcohol, Lead, etc.,
• Haematological disorders: myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, acute leukaemia, myeloma, lymphoma and hemolytic anaemia.
• Miscellaneous: Carcinoma, myxoedema, rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.

Laboratory findings:

• Peripheral smear: Hypochromic, microcytic (sometimes normocytic) anaemia
• Absolute values: MCV, MCH and MCHC are reduced except in acquired type, where MCV is raised.
• Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with macronormoblastic erythropoiesis. Marrow iron stores are raised. Pathognomonic ring sideroblasts are present.
• Serum ferritin: Raised
• Serum iron: Raised
• TIBC: Normal
• Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Normal

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency?

1. Decrease in reduced glutathione
2. Decreased NADPH
3. Decreased lipid peroxidation
4. Decreased RBC membrane damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 & 2 are correct.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH.

G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzyme function reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, thereby increasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis.

• G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate.
• This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione.
• This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such as H2O2, thereby protecting against oxidant injury.
• Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage.
• When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these Heinz bodies.
• The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’.

Clinical features:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving the G6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A 10-year-old boy presented with fatigue. Investigations revealed: Hemoglobin, 9 g/dL; MCV, 60 fL; MCH, 20 pg; and serum ferritin, 185 μg/L. The TLC was elevated and showed predominant lymphocytes and neutrophils. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?

Normal values:

• Serum Ferritin: 50-150 μg/L
• Mean cell volume (MCV)-  80-100 fL
• Mean cell Hb (MCH)- 27–31 pg

TLC- Total leukocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anemia of chronic disorder

The given clinical scenario and the investigation findings are suggestive of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is anemia of chronic disorder.

Anemia of chronic disorders more commonly presents as normochromic normocytic anemia that later develops into microcytic hypochromic anemia rarely. It is caused due to production of erythrocytes.

Anemia of chronic disease is anemia resulting due to chronic diseases which produce systemic inflammation. During chronic inflammation, inflammatory mediators like interleukin - 6 (IL-6) stimulate the production of hepcidin from the liver. Hepcidin is an acute phase reactant that inhibits ferroportin on macrophages and also decreases transport of iron from stores to developing RBC precursors. This results in decreased proliferation of erythroid progenitors due to impaired iron utilization.

Other options:

Option B: Thalassemia also presents as iron deficiency anemia but it does not have elevated luekocytosis.

Option C: Iron deficiency anemia also presents as microcytic hypochromic anemia. But since there is deficient iron, the serum ferritin level will also be low. This patient has normal serum ferritin and hence does not have iron deficiency anemia.

Note:

MCV/RBC count (Mentzer index) can also be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio.

Option D: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation in β-globin that creates sickle hemoglobin (HbS). It does not present as microcytic hypochromic anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with swelling in the upper diaphyseal part of the tibia. X-ray of the swelling showed a periosteal reaction. A histopathological image of the biopsy is given below. Immunohistochemistry was positive for synaptophysin and mic 2. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing sarcoma

The given clinical scenario along with the image showing small round blue cells and immunohistochemistry (IHC) positive for synaptophysin and mic-2 point to a likely diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma.

Ewing sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patients affected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance.

It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus and flat bones of the pelvis. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocation between the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11.

Patients present with painful enlarging mass, fever, and anemia. The affected area is usually tender, swollen, and warm. Laboratory findings may show an elevated WBC count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

A histopathological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows sheets of uniform, round cells arranged in Homer-Wright rosettes. These cells are of neuroectodermal origin and have minimal cytoplasm and abundant glycogen. When they are arranged around a central fibrillary core in the form of clusters, the appearance is termed Homer-Wright rosettes. Immunohistochemistry is usually positive for synaptophysin and mic-2.

Given below is the histopathological appearance of Ewing sarcoma.

As tumor cells are rich in glycogen, they stain positive for periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain however, they stain negatively for reticulin.

The image given below shows PAS staining done in Ewing's sarcoma:

Radiological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows a destructive lesion in the diaphysis of long bones. Deposition of periosteal reaction in layers gives an onion-peel appearance (shown below).

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone. The histological features of osteosarcoma include pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant mitoses. The diagnosis is definitive with the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone arranged in a typically fine, lacelike pattern.

Given below is the histopathological image of osteosarcoma:

X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunray appearance as shown below.

Option C: Neuroblastoma is a tumor of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. It is derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood. On histopathology small round blue cells are seen. These cells are concentrically arranged around a faintly eosinophilic fibrillary material (neuropil). This appearance is called Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (shown below).

Option D: Osteoclastoma is also known as a giant cell tumour. The tumor cells are primitive osteoblast precursors and express high levels of RANKL. Histologically, the tumors consist of osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. These cells are usually present against a backdrop of mononuclear stromal cells.

The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of giant cell tumour/osteoclastoma:

The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumour showing the typical soap bubble appearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 19-year-old girl presents with a midline neck swelling that moves on deglutition. USG revealed a 2 cm x 2 cm nodule on the left lobe of the thyroid, extending into the strap muscles. The histopathology image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Papillary CA thyroid

The clinical scenario and the image showing papillae lined by cells with overlapping nuclei and Orphan Annie eye nuclei indicate a diagnosis of papillary carcinoma of thyroid.

Papillary carcinoma of thyroid presents as a painless nodule or mass in the neck or cervical node in women of reproductive age. The risk factors include exposure to ionizing radiation and Hashimoto thyroiditis.

It usually presents as a cold nodule on a scan. Histopathological examination shows branching papillae and follicles with fibrovascular stalk. Nuclear changes include ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei, pseudo-inclusions, and nuclear grooves. Psammoma bodies are often present.

Diagnosis can be made based on these nuclear features, even in the absence of papillary architecture. The prognosis is excellent, with a 10-year survival rate in excess of 95%.

The image below shows Orphan Annie eye nuclei with central clearing and margination of chromatin:

Other options:

Option A: Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a neuroendocrine tumor that is derived from parafollicular C cells, that secrete calcitonin.

Most of these tumors occur sporadically. Some are associated with familial multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome: MEN 2A and MEN 2B. They frequently present as a neck mass that may be associated with cervical lymphadenopathy. With the enlargement of the nodule, patients may have dysphagia and dyspnea.

Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells which form nests, trabeculae, or follicles. Amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules are present in the stroma. Calcitonin in the tumor cells and stroma is easily demonstratable by immunohistochemistry.

Option B: Follicular carcinoma thyroid on histopathology may show uniform cells forming small follicles containing colloid (resembling normal thyroid gland) or sheets of cells without colloid.

Anaplastic carcinomas are poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas with varied morphology including giant cells or spindle-shaped cells or both. There is minimal follicular differentiation with intratumoral necrosis.

Option C: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood often noticed after an upper respiratory infection.

It represents the persistence of the track of the thyroid gland and can be found adjacent to the midline. It presents as smooth, fluctuant (cystic) swelling that is often transilluminant. Classically, the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion.

Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue. Investigations revealed the following: Hb, 5 gm %; MCH, 24; low MCV; leukocytes, 11,000/uL, and platelets, 5 lakhs. The peripheral smear is shown below. What is the diagnosis?

Normal values:

• Mean cell volume (MCV): 90 ± 8 fL
• Mean cell Hb (MCH): 30 ± 3 pg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron-deficiency anemia

The given scenario of a 35 year old woman, her iron profile and peripheral smear showing microcytic hypochromic anemia are suggestive of iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorbtion and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Diagnosis is mainly by laboratory studies. The typical findings are:

• Low hemoglobin and hematocrit
• Low serum iron and ferretin
• Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
• Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis)

IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations if iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia.

Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is defined by a high MCV

Option C: Thalassemia presents much earlier in infancy, with reduced MCV and a normal/increased RBC count

Option D: Essential thrombocytosis is characterized by isolated rise in platelet count (>450,000) along with normal hemoglobin, hematocrit and iron stores.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with complaints of fatigue and dyspnea for 2 weeks. On examination, pallor was seen and hemoglobin was found to be 6 gm/dL. What finding will be seen on peripheral smear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microcytic hypochromic cells

Microcytic hypochromic cells will be seen on the peripheral smear. An elderly female presenting with fatigue and dyspnea with severe anaemia is suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia(IDA). The peripheral smear of IDA shows microcytic hypochromic red blood cells.

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional disorder in the world. IDA results from dietary deficiency, impaired absorption, increased requirement and, chronic blood loss. The cause of iron deficiency anaemia in an older man or post-menopausal woman is always gastrointestinal cancer until proven otherwise.

Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, cheilosis (fissures at the corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails).

Peripheral smear in IDA shows:

• Microcytic hypochromic red blood cells with an enlarged zone of central one-third pallor.
• Poikilocytes: pencil-shaped RBCs and, target cells.

The image given below shows a microcytic hypochromic blood picture in a peripheral smear

IDA is treated by giving oral, parenteral and packed cell transfusions depending on the severity of anaemia.

For oral iron replacement therapy,

• Up to 200mg of elemental iron is given.
• According to the Anemia Mukt Bharat initiative, adult women need to take 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid tablets once a week.

For parenteral iron therapy, the amount of iron needed by an individual is calculated by the formula:

Body weight(kg) x 2.3 x (15 - patient's hemoglobin, g/dL) + 500 or 1000mg (for stores)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, erythematous rash, and bone pain. X-ray of the skull shows multiple lytic lesions. Skin biopsy shows prominent nuclear grooves with eosinophils as in the image below. Immunohistochemistry for S100, CD1a is also shown in the images below. What would be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The above clinical scenario along with the histopathological image showing Langerhans cells with folded nuclei (image A), CD1a (image B), and positive S100 (image C), is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).

LCH occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is the BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

• Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease) - mostly seen in infants
• Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) - The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad - mostly seen in younger children
• Pulmonary LCH - mostly seen in adults

Clinical features include pain and swelling in the affected area. When calvarium is affected, it results in otitis media and mastoiditis. Spinal involvement results in compression fractures and neurological involvement. Vertebral involvement results in a rapid flattening of the vertebral body (vertebra plana).

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows a histopathological image of Langerhans cells with folded nuclei.

The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy. The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.

The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.

Option A: Rosai-Dorfman syndrome is otherwise called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy. Rosai-Dorfman disease is not a histiocytic neoplasm. It is an idiopathic disease characterized by Painless lymphadenopathy, usually of cervical nodes. The disorder predominantly affects children, adolescents, and young adults. It may present with nonspecific symptoms and management mostly involves observation rather than specific treatment.

Option B: Kimura disease is s a chronic inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that most commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy.

Option D: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurring in early infancy and childhood. It presents as reddish-brown papular lesions, which evolve to become orange. The lesions are most frequently seen in the face, scalp, and upper torso. They may be single or multiple lesions. Single lesions are the most common. The characteristic multinucleated giant cell, Touton cell is observed in 85% of juvenile xanthogranulomas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of melena. On examination, there was eczema of the skin with multiple petechiae. His platelet count was low but RBC and WBC counts were within normal limits. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. WASP gene mutation

The given scenario of recurrent episodes of melena, eczema, and multiple petechiae along with low platelet counts is suggestive of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. The diagnostic investigation in this patient is WASP gene mutation testing.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome(WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder. It is caused by mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) that primarily affects the T lymphocytes.

Normally, WASp regulates the actin cytoskeleton and thus helps in cell adhesion, migration, and the formation of synapses between antigen-presenting and target cells. In WAS, there is a progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood resulting in defects in cellular immunity.

The clinical features of WAS are recurrent bacterial infections, eczema, and bleeding due to thrombocytopenia. Patients with WAS are prone to develop B-cell lymphomas and autoimmune disorders.

The image given below shows eczema seen in WAS

Diagnosis is based on intracellular immunofluorescence analysis of WAS protein (WASp) expression in blood cells. IgM levels in the serum are low, but levels of IgG are usually normal. Reduced-sized platelet is a typical feature of WAS.

The only curative treatment is an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobulin G (IgG) supplementation, and topical treatment for eczema can be tried. Gene therapy trials are also under research.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with multiple skin lesions over the inner thigh and genital areas. It initially started as macule and later developed to become nodules. Some nodules have central umbilication. The histology of the lesion is shown below. What would be found on biopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Henderson-Patterson bodies

The given clinical scenario and histological image are diagnostic of molluscum contagiosum lesions, which show intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, called Henderson–Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies.

Infection is usually spread by direct contact, particularly among children and young adults. Multiple lesions occur on the skin and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the trunk and anogenital areas. Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules. A curd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication.

Smearing this material onto a glass slide and Giemsa staining shows diagnostic molluscum bodies, which are ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusions that are found in the cells of the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum and are up to 35 μm in size.

Other options:

Option A: Multinucleate giant cells (called Tzanck cells) are seen in herpes simplex virus infections. They are formed when individual epidermal cells containing viral inclusions fuse to produce giant cells. These can be demonstrated by the diagnostic Tzanck test, which is based on the microscopic examination of the vesicle fluid.

Option B: Donovan bodies are seen in donovanosis, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are minute, encapsulated coccobacilli in macrophages, which can be demonstrated in Giemsa-stained smears of the exudate.

Option D: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as condylomata acuminata. Koilocytes are lining cells that have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A chronic smoker presents to the clinic with shortness of breath. A mass is noted at the lower lobe periphery of the lung. A diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma is made. The biopsy will be positive for:

1. Thyroid transcription factor-1
2. p40
3. Napsin A
4. Chromogranin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3

The biopsy of adenocarcinoma of the lung will be positive for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and napsin A.

Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. It is associated with tobacco smoking, but less so than other histologic subtypes. It is the most common subtype in non-smokers and is associated with the loss of function of EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET or RET genes.

The majority express TTF-1, which is a protein required for normal lung development. Napsin A is a new marker and is more sensitive and specific than TTF-1 in the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma.

Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns: acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid. The lesions are small and are usually located in the periphery.  At the periphery of the tumor there is often a lepidic pattern of spread, in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septa.

Clinical features usually have an insidious onset. The incidence is usually at age 50 or more. The major presenting complaints are cough, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.

Other options:

Option B: p40, along with p63 is a marker for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Option D: Chromogranin is a marker for small cell carcinoma of the lung.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A chronic smoker with a smoking history of 24 packs presents with breathlessness and chest pain. Further investigations revealed the presence of a lung tumor. On staining, cells are positive for chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small cell carcinoma

The clinical scenario of a lung tumor associated with chronic smoking and tumor cells staining positive for chromogranin indicates that the most likely diagnosis in this patient is small cell carcinoma of the lung.

Small cell carcinoma of the lung belongs to the neuroendocrine tumors and originates from neuroendocrine progenitor cells, Kulchitsky cells that line the bronchial epithelium. It is a highly malignant tumor with a high association with cigarette smoking. It usually arises from the major bronchi.

Histopathology of small cell lung carcinoma shows clusters of small cells which are round, oval, or spindle-shaped, and a prominent nuclear molding. These cells have scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern), and absent or inconspicuous nucleoli. The Azzopardi effect is described as basophilic staining of vascular walls due to coating by DNA from necrotic tumor cells.

Neuroendocrine markers seen in small cell lung carcinoma include:

• Chromogranin
• Synaptophysin
• CD56

Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung are Cushing syndrome due to ACTH production and hyponatremia due to inappropriate ADH secretion. Small cell lung cancer-associated SIADH is due to the ectopic release of antidiuretic hormone. It is associated with increased thirst and hyponatremia.

Other options:

Option A- Adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor with differentiation in glands or mucin production by the tumor cells. These tumors are commonly found in women and in non-smokers. These tumors are more peripherally located and are smaller. On histopathology, the tumor shows a lepidic pattern of spread with tumor cells crawling along the normal-appearing alveolar septa. The tumor cells are positive for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) and Napsin A.

Option B- Squamous cell carcinoma is found to be more common in men and has a strong association with smoking. They have precursor lesions like squamous dysplasia, squamous metaplasia, or in situ carcinomas. On histopathology, it is characterized by keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Keratinization occurs in the form of squamous pearls. It is positive for p40 and p63 markers. Hypercalcemia is the common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with this type.

Option C- Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated malignant epithelial carcinoma. On histopathology, the cells are large, with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli with a moderate amount of cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A male patient presented with hemoptysis. On examination, hilar mass was present. The histopathological image is shown below. Immunohistochemistry revealed that the cells were positive for p40. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squamous cell carcinoma

The given clinical history and the histopathological findings showing keratin pearls are suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated with smoking.

Squamous cell carcinoma predominantly arises in the central segmental or subsegmental bronchi. The tumor may grow into the bronchial lumen and produce an intraluminal mass. In certain cases, the bronchial obstruction may lead to atelectasis or infection. The tumor may penetrate the wall of the bronchus and infiltrate the peribronchial tissue into the carina or the mediastinum.

This tumor may be associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like hypercalcemia. The symptoms could include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, lethargy, polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration.

Squamous metaplasia and dysplasia often precede frank squamous cell carcinoma. Carcinoma in-situ persists for many years and this may often be recognized on cytologic smears or in BAL fluid or brushings.

Gross appearance: The tissue is grey-white, firm, with areas of necrosis and hemorrhages. Red or yellow-white mottling and softening may be seen. The necrotic foci may cavitate.

Histopathology: They have precursor lesions like squamous dysplasia, squamous metaplasia, or in situ carcinomas. On histopathology, it is characterized by keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Keratinization occurs in the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm. It is positive for p40 and p63 markers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A man presented with fever, night sweats, and weight loss for 2 months. On examination, non-tender, rubbery lymph nodes were palpable in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions on both sides. Peripheral smear showed the presence of bi-nucleated cells. Which markers will be seen in this condition?

1 - CD15
2 - CD30
3 - CD19
4 - CD3
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 2

The probable diagnosis from the given clinical scenario and the histopathological description is Hodgkin's lymphoma. The bi-nucleated cells are called the Reed-Sternberg cells which are CD 15+ and CD30+ (option D- 1 and 2).

Hodgkin's lymphoma arises in a single lymph node or chain of nodes and spreads first to anatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. It usually presents as painless lymphadenopathy. The distinctive feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma is the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells.

WHO classifies Hodgkin's lymphoma into 5 subtypes:

1. Nodular sclerosis: Frequent lacunar cells
2. Mixed cellularity
3. Lymphocyte-rich
4. Lymphocyte depletion
5. Nodular lymphocyte predominance

The first 4 subtypes are considered classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. The RS cells are CD 15+ and CD30+. The lymphocyte predominant type is considered non-classical Hodgkin's lymphoma with CD15-, CD30-, CD20+, and EB -.
